title: Robustness as a Transferable Skill: Cross-Task Adversarial Defense for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are vulnerable to adversarial visual perturbations, while defenses often require task-specific adversarial fine-tuning. We investigate whether robustness learned on source manipulation tasks can protect independently specialized target policies without target-side adversarial training. We first show that even a single source defense update improves robustness on held-out tasks, establishing cross-task defense reuse independently of multi-source aggregation. To combine source updates, we introduce Source-Norm Transferable Robustness Vector (SN-TRV), which retains the direction of their mean while calibrating its magnitude using source-update norms. The resulting update is applied to the target visual encoder without target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or additional inference modules. Evaluations across three VLA backbones, fixed and adaptive attacks, and different source defense recipes show improved robustness over naive averaging and identify limits in attack coverage. Physical PiPER trials increase average success under printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.

Physical PiPER trials increase average success under printed adversarial patches from 20.3 to 45.8 . Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies have recently enabled general-purpose robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and low-level control. Models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, Octo, and demonstrate the potential of scaling vision-language knowledge to robotic tasks~ zitkovich2023rt2, kim2025openvla,octo2024,black2025pi0 . However, the reliance on visual observations also exposes VLA policies to adversarial perturbations that can directly cause physical execution failures. Recent studies reveal that physically realizable adversarial patches can severely degrade VLA manipulation performance. EDPA introduces model-agnostic adversarial patches and shows that adversarial fine-tuning of the visual encoder can recover robustness against such attacks ~ xu2025edpa . Other works investigate stronger transferable attacks and robustness evaluation frameworks, including UPA-RFAS, AttackVLA, and physical variation benchmarks~ lu2026uparfas,li2025attackvla, liu2025evavla . Correspondingly, recent defenses improve robustness through adversarial fine-tuning, attention-aware optimization, lightweight adapters, or certified robustness techniques ~ zhang2026sarf,yin2026vlaguard,fu2026stablevla,lu2026certvla . Despite these advances, existing VLA defenses primarily acquire robustness by optimizing the policy to be protected. When a policy is independently specialized for a new manipulation task, adversarial fine-tuning may need to be repeated even if robust source policies are already available. This motivates the following question: Can adversarial robustness learned on one manipulation task be reused as a transferable capability to protect another independently specialized policy? We find that visual defense updates learned on source manipulation suites can substantially improve the adversarial robustness of independently specialized target policies. Importantly, this effect is observed even when transferring a single source update, establishing defense reuse independently of any multi-source aggregation method. Combining multiple source defenses, however, raises two questions: how to estimate a transferable defense direction and how to determine its update magnitude. Naive averaging provides a natural aggregate direction, but partially misaligned source updates can attenuate its magnitude. To address this issue, we propose Source-Norm Transferable Robustness Vector (SN-TRV). SN-TRV estimates a source-consensus defense direction and recomposes it with a reference magnitude derived from source defense updates. The resulting vector can be transferred to a held-out target policy without target adversarial examples, target-side gradient optimization, or additional inference-time modules. The contributions of this work are: We establish empirical evidence of cross-task adversarial defense reuse in VLA policies, showing that even a single source defense update can protect independently specialized, held-out target policies without target-task adversarial fine-tuning. We identify a multi-source defense composition challenge and introduce SN-TRV, a source-norm-calibrated transfer rule that improves robustness over naive averaging without target-side adversarial optimization or additional inference modules. We systematically characterize defense reuse across fixed and adaptive attacks, source defense recipes, VLA backbones, and physical manipulation, revealing its effectiveness, attack-coverage dependence, and practical limitations. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Policies and Robustness Evaluation Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies such as RT-2, OpenVLA, Octo, and have demonstrated strong transfer and generalization across robotic manipulation tasks ~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,octo2024,black2025pi0 . LIBERO provides a widely used benchmark for evaluating knowledge transfer and long-horizon manipulation~ liu2023libero . Recent work has further examined VLA robustness under environmental and adversarial variations. EVA-VLA and LIBERO-Plus evaluate robustness under realistic distribution shifts~ liu2025evavla,fei2026liberoplus , while multi-view studies reveal failure modes such as view collapse under adversarial training~ waseda2026viewcollapse . These works mainly evaluate the robustness of a given policy after training or adaptation; we instead ask whether learned robustness can be reused across independently specialized VLA policies. Adversarial Attacks and Defenses for VLA Policies Physical adversarial perturbations can directly alter closed-loop robot actions~ wang2025adversarialvla . EDPA introduces model-agnostic adversarial patches and adversarial fine-tuning for VLA policies~ xu2025edpa , while subsequent studies consider universal transfer, attention manipulation, and broader attack objectives ~ lu2026uparfas,fu2026vlahijack,li2025attackvla . Recent cross-task attacks such as UniTexture further suggest that VLA vulnerability can contain task-shared structure~ dai2026unitexture . Correspondingly, SARF, VLA-Guard, RobustVLA, StableVLA, RoVLA, and CertVLA improve robustness through adversarial fine-tuning, representation correction, lightweight adaptation, or certification ~ zhang2026sarf,yin2026vlaguard,guo2026robustvla, fu2026stablevla,luo2026rovla,lu2026certvla . However, these defenses primarily optimize the policy being protected, typically requiring target-specific robustness optimization. Our work instead investigates whether defense knowledge learned on source tasks can protect a held-out target policy without target-side adversarial fine-tuning. Robustness Transfer and Parameter-Space Reuse Adversarial robustness transfer has been studied in conventional vision, including robustness inheritance from pretrained models to downstream tasks yamada2022robustness,nern2023transfer . These studies mainly examine downstream adaptation, rather than transferring defense-induced updates between independently specialized robot policies. Task Arithmetic~ ilharco2023taskarithmetic and TIES-Merging~ yadav2023ties demonstrate the reuse and combination of fine-tuning updates. RETAIN~ yadav2025retain interpolates pretrained and task-fine-tuned VLA weights to preserve generalist capabilities and improve out-of-distribution task generalization, while VLA-Pro~ si2026vlapro transfers procedural knowledge through adapters. In contrast, we transfer source-learned adversarial defense updates to independently specialized target policies without target-side adversarial fine-tuning. MAGIC~ li2025magic studies magnitude deviation in model merging and introduces layer-wise calibration, including data-free Weight Space Calibration (WSC). Rather than claiming magnitude calibration as a general novelty, we investigate source-only global norm calibration for cross-task adversarial defense reuse, with a tested WSC configuration as a baseline. title: TMA: Sim-to-Real Forceful Humanoid Manipulation via Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation
comment: Project page: humanoid-tma.github.io
summary: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.
full_text: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world. INTRODUCTION Dexterous manipulation is essential for humanoids to physically operate in human environments~ billard2019trends, chen2026manipulationnet . Recent data-driven approaches have rapidly advanced humanoid loco-manipulation, enabling increasingly complex interactions with objects and articulated environments~ gu2026humanoid . However, these systems are predominantly designed in what we term a geometry-dominant manner: success is determined mainly by where contact is established and how the robot moves with respect to object geometry and kinematic constraints, without explicitly regulating the evolving physical state of contact~ hogan2022contact . Consider door opening by a humanoid equipped with a multi-fingered hand. A lever handle can often be actuated by establishing appropriate contact and exploiting its favorable geometry and moment arm~ xue2026opening, doorbot . A round doorknob, however, exposes an interaction-dominant regime, where success depends critically on how fingers establish contact, distribute normal forces, generate sufficient frictional torque, and avoid slip~ holladay . Such tasks require not only accurate motion, but continuous regulation and adaptation of the increasing resisting torque with the evolving contact state. Enabling humanoids to perform this class of dexterous manipulation remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate interaction-dominant manipulation through round-doorknob opening, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser . In this task, action outcomes depend critically on physical properties not directly observable from vision or proprioception, including contact friction and internal mechanism dynamics such as spring stiffness and latch resistance. Before their physical consequences unfold, a stable grasp and an imminent slip may induce nearly indistinguishable visual and proprioceptive observations, yet lead to drastically different outcomes under the same motion command. Therefore, this observability gap makes tactile sensing particularly valuable, as it directly measures the local contact response induced by the robot's actions~ li2020review . This calls for a tactile-driven policy that treats contact not only as an actuation interface, but also as an information source for regulating interaction. However, tactile feedback alone does not resolve interaction uncertainty. While a reactive tactile policy can respond to instantaneous contact, many task-relevant physical properties are only revealed through how contact evolves under the robot's actions. The same instantaneous contact force, for example, may correspond to different frictional margins or mechanism responses depending on the preceding interaction. Effective interaction-dominant manipulation therefore requires accumulating evidence through physical interaction, inferring the underlying interaction conditions, and adapting motor behavior accordingly. To this end, we introduce Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA), a framework for interaction-dominant humanoid manipulation under real-world contact uncertainty. While retaining a history-conditioned adaptation structure, TMA departs from the Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA)~ kumar2021rma paradigm by shifting adaptation from observations accumulated during execution to interaction-driven observations deliberately acquired through active contact. Rather than only inferring environmental properties from the consequences encountered during policy execution, TMA exploits physical interaction to elicit tactile responses that reveal task-relevant interaction conditions. Contact thus serves a dual role: it is both the interface through which the robot acts on the environment and the sensing mechanism through which otherwise unobserved physical properties become inferable. We instantiate this principle by 1) structuring policy learning around tactile-observable interactions, 2) parameterizing tactile signals through cone geometry to ground policy learning in contact mechanics, and 3) adapting motor behavior online from recent tactile interaction history. The policy and adaptation encoder are trained entirely in simulation using reinforcement learning and supervised latent regression, then transferred zero-shot to the real-world humanoid system. At the system level, we integrate TMA with a frozen general locomotion controller, enabling forceful round-doorknob manipulation while maintaining whole-body stability. We evaluate TMA on zero-shot sim-to-real round-doorknob opening using a Unitree G1 https://www.unitree.com/g1 humanoid equipped with BrainCo Revo2 https://www.brainco-hz.com/docs/revolimb-hand/en/ dexterous hands. Across four commercially available doorknob models, TMA substantially outperforms Rapid Motor Adaptation and reactive tactile policy baselines. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of this task by a humanoid using a multi-fingered dexterous hand. Our contributions are threefold: We study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark for interaction-dominant dexterous humanoid manipulation, requiring coordinated multi-finger force interaction and whole-body stability. We propose Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA), an adaptive policy framework that exploits active tactile interaction history for interaction regulation and enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. We develop an integrated whole-body humanoid system that combines dexterous tactile manipulation with a general locomotion controller and demonstrates robust real-world doorknob opening. RELATED WORK -based Humanoid Manipulation. Learning-based humanoid manipulation has advanced rapidly, enabling increasingly diverse and complex whole-body interaction skills~ gu2026humanoid . Humanoid teleoperation maps operator commands to robot motion~ he2024omniho,ze2025twist,ben2025homie,lu2025mobile , allowing humans to guide task execution and collect demonstrations for policy learning~ he2024omniho,fu2024humanplus . Imitation learning uses teleoperated or video demonstrations to acquire autonomous manipulation policies~ fu2024humanplus,li2024okami , and can be combined with RL-trained whole-body controllers to support coordinated execution~ he2024omniho,fu2024humanplus . In parallel, large-scale simulation enables reinforcement learning of task policies through trial-and-error, with sim-to-real transfer supporting object transport~ dao2024box, zhao2025resmimic , dexterous grasping~ lin2025simtoreal , long-horizon loco-manipulation~ he2026viral , and articulated-environment interaction~ xue2026opening . Force-adaptive approaches further coordinate upper-body tracking and lower-body stability to sustain manipulation under substantial end-effector loads~ zhang2025falcon . However, these advances still model physical interaction predominantly at the level of motion, end-effector forces, or whole-body response, leaving finger-level forceful interaction underexplored. Our research targets forceful multi-fingered humanoid manipulation, where task success depends on the contact states and forces distributed across individual fingers and their evolution during interaction. -to-Real Transfer of Tactile Policies. Tactile sensing has increasingly enabled sim-to-real manipulation by exposing contact information not directly observable from vision and proprioception alone~ qi2023general,yang2024anyrotate . Prior work has transferred tactile policies from simulation to real robots for door manipulation~ ding2021sim,lee2024dextouch , tactile servoing and bimanual manipulation~ church2022tactile,lin2023bi , dexterous in-hand manipulation~ yang2024anyrotate,yuan2024robot,yang2023tacgnn , and multi-finger manipulation with dense force feedback~ zhao2026closing . These approaches bridge the tactile sim-to-real gap through sensor modeling~ dang2026hydroshear , observation translation~ church2022tactile,freud2025simshear , latent alignment~ yang2026tactile , and robust policy learning with domain randomization~ ding2021sim,yang2024anyrotate . Complementarily, motor adaptation enables policies to infer latent representations of unobserved interaction conditions from recent history and adjust behavior online~ kumar2021rma,qi2023hora . More closely related to our setting, tactile feedback has also been incorporated into history-conditioned adaptation and robust policy learning for generalizable in-hand manipulation, complementing proprioception~ yin2025learning,yang2024anyrotate and vision~ qi2023general . However, tactile policies based on discretized contact cues~ qi2023general,yin2025learning or scalar force magnitudes~ yang2024anyrotate capture only a partial view of the underlying force state. Our research preserves a force-aware contact state encoding both magnitude and direction, and adapts motor behavior online from its temporal evolution across multi-fingered interactions. PRELIMINARIES PROBLEM STATEMENT sec:problem We consider round-doorknob opening by a floating-base humanoid equipped with multi-fingered dexterous hands. Starting from a standing pose in front of a closed door, the robot must reach the knob, establish a frictional grasp, rotate the knob sufficiently to release the latch, and move the door panel to an open configuration without losing balance. The task therefore couples arm motion, multi-finger contact, doorknob-mechanism actuation, and whole-body stability. title: Refinement vs. Replanning: Inference Compute Allocation in Robot Policies
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Post-Training Adaptation of Robot Foundation Models
summary: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.

Introduction We can adapt a robot policy after training without changing its weights. At deployment, a frozen chunked policy has two coupled compute decisions: how much work each policy call spends generating an action chunk, and how often to call the policy again from a fresh observation. We call the first decision refinement and the second replanning frequency. Each policy call predicts actions. The environment executes the first , then the policy receives a new observation and runs again. Thus, sets the policy-call frequency: one call every executed actions. For SmolVLA, sets the number of denoising steps within each call. These choices couple computation and feedback. Additional refinement can alter the predicted actions. A longer execution prefix amortizes a policy call, but it delays feedback and exposes later actions from an older prediction to the environment. Holding predicted chunk length fixed, we ask one allocation question: under an explicit compute ceiling, how much computation should each SmolVLA policy call spend on denoising refinement, and how often should the policy run again from a fresh observation? We select the combination that maximizes closed-loop task success. Here, ``best'' means the highest empirical success rate among configurations that satisfy the stated compute ceiling. Counted arithmetic determines feasibility; we report nominal compute rates and realized attempt costs separately. We also report measured host latency, but it does not determine feasibility. We do not combine success and cost into one score or measure memory use. We study one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint smolvla and fix predicted chunk length at . Our contribution is a controlled study of the allocation between denoising work per policy call and policy-call frequency, together with its effect on task success and complete attempt cost. We do not claim that the selected allocation transfers to other checkpoints. SmolVLA also provides an asynchronous inference mode that overlaps action generation with action execution. We do not use that mode. In our synchronous evaluation, the policy finishes generating all actions before the environment executes the first ; the policy then receives a new observation and replans. Fixing this order lets us compare refinement and replanning without the additional effects of concurrent execution, observation staleness, or buffering. The results provide a controlled baseline for a later asynchronous study, but they do not identify the best asynchronous schedule or its performance. We do not measure asynchronous throughput or physical-robot latency. We test 12 configurations in 480 discovery attempts, then seven settings in 1,120 held-out attempts on eight tasks excluded from selection. We chose the refinement comparisons before the held-out evaluation. We added the execution-prefix comparisons after inspecting those results, so they motivate future tests rather than support a confirmed claim. The contributions are: [leftmargin=*,nosep] a compute-accounting formulation that connects SmolVLA's denoising work per policy call and its policy-call frequency at fixed chunk length; a controlled discovery and held-out evaluation that measures task success together with nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost; and evidence that most counted per-call arithmetic is independent of denoising, that fewer denoising steps improve held-out success in the primary comparison, and that success under less frequent replanning remains unresolved. Related Work Post-training allocation under a compute budget. Compute-optimal scaling studies ask how a fixed training budget should be divided between model size and data chinchilla ; related embodied work studies scaling in agent pretraining and world models pearcescaling . Including deployment demand can change the preferred allocation beyondchinchilla . These studies establish the need to state the budget and counting boundary. We instead adapt the inference configuration of one frozen policy and evaluate each allocation of deployment-time inference compute by closed-loop task success. Computation used to generate an action. Diffusion Policy generates action sequences through iterative conditional denoising diffusionpolicy . RoboMonkey spends additional inference compute on action candidates and verification robomonkey . This is one form of refinement: both proposal and verification cost belong to the policy call. SmolVLA provides the flow-matching policy used in our case study and also studies asynchronous inference smolvla . VLA-Perf examines how model architecture, hardware, placement, networking, and asynchronous execution affect VLA inference performance vlaperf . These works show that arithmetic and elapsed time depend on both the model and its execution system. Our case study holds the checkpoint, hardware, and synchronous execution path fixed so that the effects of refinement and execution prefix can be compared within one system. Choosing when to replan. ACT predicts action chunks to reduce the effective decision horizon act ; chunked action spaces have also been studied for reinforcement learning qchunking . Adaptive Action Chunking uses action entropy to choose how much of a predicted chunk to execute adaptivechunking . DVAC uses variation observed during denoising to adapt the execution prefix dvac . ElegantVLA schedules vision--language recomputation, reuse, and action generation during execution elegantvla . These methods change the schedule within an episode. We map fixed refinement and prefix settings first, separate selection from held-out evaluation, and report both nominal compute rate and realized attempt cost. This design evaluates axes available to an adaptive method; it does not compare a fixed deployment configuration with an online, within-episode schedule. SmolVLA Study Design and Configuration Selection sec:method This section applies the allocation procedure to adapt the inference configuration of one frozen checkpoint. Discovery maps the candidate settings and selects the comparisons; the held-out evaluation then tests those comparisons on tasks excluded from selection. Discovery and held-out evaluation We evaluate a public SmolVLA checkpoint on LIBERO libero , with \[ h \ 1,2,5\ , d \ 2,5,10,20\ . \] The predicted chunk length is fixed at , and the model's native deployment uses . We keep fixed the checkpoint, observations, preprocessing, action normalization, control period, and task-specific episode horizons. The discovery study evaluates these 12 settings on four Spatial tasks. Each task has five initial states and two rollout seeds, giving 40 paired task--state--seed identities. Every identity receives all twelve settings in randomized order, for 480 attempts. Two discovery tasks overlap pre-study pilot work; the other two were chosen before their study outcomes were observed. This partial exposure is why discovery supports selection rather than final evaluation. After discovery, we freeze three denoising comparisons, one at each compute ceiling. Their selected settings and comparators, plus native deployment, produce seven distinct settings. The held-out evaluation applies all seven to eight Goal and Object tasks excluded from selection. Each task has ten initial states and two rollout seeds, giving 160 attempts per setting and 1,120 in total. Prior exposure to these tasks during unrelated development is not assessed. No equivalence margin was prespecified, so similar observed success cannot establish equivalent quality. title: Certify, Then Select: Viability-Aware Runtime Steering of Frozen Diffusion Policies
comment: Under review
summary: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Project page: https://clmoro.github.io/cast.

Diffusion policies, safety filters, learned viability, conformal prediction Introduction sec:intro Diffusion policies learn dexterous manipulation from demonstrations~ chi2023diffusion . Once deployed, a policy meets constraints its demonstrations never contained: a person reaches across the table, a shelf is mounted above the workspace, the commanded effort must stay within a budget. Retraining for each is impractical. We want to enforce a constraint that arrives at run time, a request, on a policy that stays frozen. The classical tool is a safety filter: take the action the policy proposes and edit it as little as needed for a certificate, such as a control barrier function, to hold~ ames2017cbfqp,wabersich2021predictive,hsu2023safetyfilter . Variants for diffusion policies apply the same edit inside the denoising loop~ xiao2023safediffuser,romer2025dpcc . An edit answers the question ``is this action safe?''. It does not ask whether the task can still be completed. A small edit leaves the policy as good or as bad as it was. A large one, as under an effort budget or when a zone blocks the policy's route, leaves the robot where the policy has no data, and it stalls ( a). Neither helps the task: in our experiments no method that keeps the policy and has no critic reliably beats the plain output filter in joint task-and-request success ( ). A diffusion policy offers a resource that a deterministic controller lacks: for one observation it can propose many different, equally plausible actions. (Certified Action Selection at Test time, Algorithm~ alg:cast ) uses this resource twice. It draws a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certifies each against the request, and executes the certified chunk that a value ensemble ranks highest. Only if no sample is certified does it fall back to the filter. The certificate provides safety, the critic provides task success, and whenever a certified sample exists the executed action is one the policy itself produced. But certification looks one step ahead, and a generative controller can have safe actions available today but lack safe behaviours tomorrow. Runtime constraint steering should preserve the learned policy's future control authority, not merely certify its next action: -V prefers chunks after which certified samples remain likely ( b). title: RoboCoEvo: Expanding Robot Capabilities through Agent-Policy Co-Evolution
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables
summary: Integrating MLLM-based agents with robotic foundation models has attracted increasing attention as a means of enhancing robotic capabilities. However, the improvement of such integrated systems remains largely decoupled across their agent and model components, with advances in one component not necessarily benefiting the other, substantially limiting the capabilities of the combined system. As both MLLMs and robotic foundation models become increasingly capable, fully realizing their combined potential calls for co-evolution, an iterative process in which improvements in agents and robotic foundation models reinforce one another. We propose RoboCoEvo, a failure-guided co-evolution framework that couples the refinement of the agent's explicit and reusable executable knowledge with parameter learning in robotic foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models. Through a code-as-policy formulation, the agent develops and refines executable failure-detection and recovery programs, generating targeted corrective experience. Post-training consolidates the resulting corrective behaviors into the robotic model's end-to-end policy, improving autonomous task execution. Changes in the updated policy's failure distribution, in turn, guide subsequent revisions to the agent's programs. Experiments on BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin demonstrate sustained improvements in autonomous VLA task performance across successive co-evolution rounds.
full_text: Equal contribution. Correspondence to: yingxue.zhang@huawei.com. Work done during an internship at Huawei Noah's Ark Lab. Integrating MLLM-based agents with robotic foundation models has attracted increasing attention as a means of enhancing robotic capabilities. However, the improvement of such integrated systems remains largely decoupled across their agent and model components, with advances in one component not necessarily benefiting the other, substantially limiting the capabilities of the combined system. As both MLLMs and robotic foundation models become increasingly capable, fully realizing their combined potential calls for co-evolution, an iterative process in which improvements in agents and robotic foundation models reinforce one another. We propose , a failure-guided co-evolution framework that couples the refinement of the agent's explicit and reusable executable knowledge with parameter learning in robotic foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models. Through a code-as-policy formulation, the agent develops and refines executable failure-detection and recovery programs, generating targeted corrective experience. Post-training consolidates the resulting corrective behaviors into the robotic model's end-to-end policy, improving autonomous task execution. Changes in the updated policy's failure distribution, in turn, guide subsequent revisions to the agent's programs. Experiments on BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin demonstrate sustained improvements in autonomous VLA task performance across successive co-evolution rounds. Introduction sec:introduction Recent work has shown that MLLM-based agentic harnesses can enhance the capabilities of robotic foundation models~ roboharness,zhang2026harness . In these works, robotic foundation models provide visuomotor skills acquired from large-scale demonstrations~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,black2025pi05 , while agents support their policy execution through failure diagnosis, recovery, and coordination~ liu2023reflect,lin2025failsafe . This complementary division of roles enables the combined system to address limitations of the robotic foundation models. However, the improvement processes of the agent and the robotic foundation model in the combined system typically remain separate or only loosely coupled~ zhang2026robocop,yu2026coda , with advances in one component not necessarily benefiting the other. Without learning from corrective experience, the policy may remain dependent on agent assistance in similar situations. Meanwhile, an agent whose knowledge is not refined as the policy is updated may continue to target weaknesses that no longer constrain performance. Sustained improvement therefore requires a co-evolution mechanism that connects policy learning with the adaptation of agent assistance. For corrective interventions to yield lasting policy improvements, the policy must incorporate the demonstrated behaviors into its own capabilities. Agent interventions provide training experience at states where execution fails, including states induced by accumulated errors and underrepresented in the training distribution~ ross2011dagger . Interactive imitation learning obtains such corrections from human supervisors~ kelly2019hgdagger,liu2022sirius , while recent approaches automate recovery and generate corrective data for policy training~ zhang2026lrs,liao2026vlamotor,lang2026embodirsi . Training on this experience allows the policy to internalize behaviors previously supplied by the agent. As these failures are resolved, however, the policy's need for assistance changes, and further improvement requires corrective experience tailored to its remaining limitations. On the other hand, acquiring this experience requires the agent to adapt alongside the policy. It must reassess the updated policy's failures, determine where intervention is still needed, and revise its recovery strategies accordingly. Automated failure analysis can support this reassessment~ duan2024aha,yu2026retrace , while a coding agent can use execution feedback to refine the corresponding detectors and recovery programs. These revisions improve the agent's assistance and provide relevant corrections for the next policy update. However, applying conventional code-as-policy approaches without accounting for task-specific failure characteristics may compromise the accuracy of failure diagnosis and the efficiency of recovery, thereby limiting subsequent policy improvement. The two directions of improvement therefore form a continuous feedback loop: the robotic foundation model learns from the agent's interventions, and its remaining failures guide what the agent must diagnose and resolve next. We present (Figure~ fig:teaser ), a co-evolution framework that couples Policy-Guided Agent Evolution with Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion. The agent evolves through revisions to executable failure-detection and recovery programs. Guided by policy rollouts and execution feedback, it identifies recurring failure modes, develops and evaluates recovery strategies, and generates corrective demonstrations across varied task configurations using a code-as-policy formulation~ liang2022code . The robotic foundation model then incorporates these corrective behaviors into its end-to-end policy through post-training. Subsequent evaluation of the updated model identifies residual capability gaps and directs the next round of program refinement. This iterative exchange improves the agent's diagnosis and recovery strategies while expanding the policy's capacity for independent execution. We instantiate and evaluate with vision-language-action (VLA) models on BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin. Experiments demonstrate sustained improvement across successive cycles, with higher autonomous task success and stronger generalization to unseen configurations. In summary, our contributions are: Failure-Mode-Centric Agent--Policy Co-Evolution: We introduce RoboCoEvo, a failure-guided co-evolution framework that couples the refinement of executable agent knowledge with learning-based policy post-training. Through a recursive feedback loop, the general agent generates corrective experience to improve the policy, while the evolving policy reveals new capability gaps that guide further agent adaptation. Policy-Guided Agent Evolution: We develop a failure-mode-centric approach that organizes recurring policy failures into reusable executable detectors and recovery programs. As the policy evolves, the agent continuously refines programs for persistent failure modes and develops new ones for emerging failures, enabling its corrective skills to evolve alongside the policy. Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion: We introduce failure-conditioned augmentation to scale the corrective experience generated by reusable recovery programs. By learning from these targeted demonstrations, the policy progressively internalizes agent-generated recovery behaviors and expands its capabilities. Significant Policy Improvement and Data Efficiency: Experiments across BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboTwin, and RoboCasa demonstrate consistent policy improvements over successive co-evolution iterations. Extensive analyses further highlight the effectiveness of reusable failure-mode programs and targeted data augmentation in improving task performance and data-acquisition efficiency. 0= - 0<7 Related Work sec:related Agent-assisted robotic execution. LLM- and MLLM-based agents have been widely employed to enhance robotic execution without modifying the parameters of the underlying policies. Such agents have been applied to the detection and explanation of execution failures~ liu2023reflect,duan2024aha,yu2026retrace,zhou2025codeasmonitor and to intervention for failure recovery~ lin2025failsafe,wang2026roboduo , while hierarchical frameworks rely on them to orchestrate low-level policies and skills~ shi2025hirobot,team2025geminirobotics15,roboharness,zhang2026harness . As execution failures are difficult to anticipate, several systems further refine the agent's knowledge based on execution feedback, for instance by revising orchestration code~ roboharness , by accumulating executable skills~ wang2023voyager,wen2026roborsi , or by updating failure checks and recovery routines for failures grouped according to their underlying causes~ ding2026zetta,sun2026reskill . In these systems, however, the acquired improvements reside in the agent or its programs, whereas any learned policy responsible for low-level control retains fixed parameters. The capabilities of such a policy therefore remain unchanged, and the agent or its programs must compensate for its recurring failures at execution time. Learning from corrective experience. Policies trained through imitation are prone to compounding errors that lead them to states underrepresented in their demonstrations~ ross2011dagger . Interactive imitation learning mitigates this distribution shift by training on corrections collected at the states visited by the policy~ ross2011dagger,kelly2019hgdagger,liu2022sirius,hu2025rac , and RECAP incorporates such corrections into multi-round training with a learned value function~ amin2025recap . Because these corrections are typically provided by human supervisors, whose effort scales with the number of failures, recent methods have sought to generate corrective data automatically. IntervenGen and FLARE extend a small number of human recovery demonstrations to new scene configurations and to new or perturbed failure states~ hoque2024intervengen,zhao2026flare , CARE uses a motion-planning oracle to annotate failure states sampled from a distribution fitted to failed rollouts~ xiao2026care , and other approaches derive corrections from fixed language-model prompts, pretrained experts, privileged continuations, or residual reinforcement-learning specialists~ bernat2026magmagen,li2024scvla,snegirev2026kintsugi,xiao2025pld . These studies demonstrate that training on failure-targeted corrections can improve the policy itself. Nevertheless, approaches that extend human demonstrations still rely on a supervisor to demonstrate each new recovery skill, while automatic generators are constructed once and are not refined from the failures they correct. Coupled improvement of agents and policies. The works most closely related to ours couple an agent with policy training. LRS, VLAMotor, and EmbodiRSI use an MLLM agent or a motion planner to generate corrections from the failure states of a policy, on which the policy is subsequently fine-tuned~ zhang2026lrs,liao2026vlamotor,lang2026embodirsi . In these frameworks, however, each failure is corrected in isolation, so that the knowledge acquired in correcting one failure is neither retained nor refined for similar or subsequently emerging failures. Other frameworks improve the policy over multiple rounds but differ in how its corrective behaviors are acquired. Recova learns recovery behaviors with a separate recovery policy rather than with the task policy~ liu2026recova , and RoboClaw retrains its policies on their own rollouts and on human interventions under a fixed VLM controller~ li2026roboclaw . Robo-COP co-evolves the textual memory of an orchestrator with a policy but trains this policy exclusively on successful segments of its own executions, which restricts the learnable behaviors to those that its policy or scripted tools already partially exhibit~ zhang2026robocop . CoDA co-evolves a data engine with a policy by adapting its scene-generation and reward-shaping programs to the learning progress of this policy~ yu2026coda , and ENPIRE enables an agent to revise training recipes~ xiao2026enpire . In both cases, the corrective behavior is still obtained through the policy's own exploration or from demonstrations that do not originate at its failure states. title: Bring Back Language to Actions: Restoring VLM capabilities in VLA Models via Parameter Merging
comment: Accept at EACL 2027 (Main)
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector — the difference between VLA and VLM weights — and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines. Introduction The ability to reason about complex environments and to plan sequences of actions has long been a central challenge in artificial intelligence. Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have made significant strides in this direction, combining reasoning, visual perception, and scene understanding into unified models capable of high-level instruction following, task decomposition, and environment description wei2023chainofthoughtpromptingelicitsreasoning,yao2023reactsynergizingreasoningacting,radford2021learningtransferablevisualmodels,liu2023visualinstructiontuning,dai2026languagemovementprimitivesgrounding,aissi2026prismperceptionreasoninginterleaved — capabilities that make them compelling building blocks for autonomous robotic agents. However, these models remain confined to perception and reasoning, and cannot directly produce the low-level motor commands required for physical interaction. Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) bridge this gap by fine-tuning pre-trained VLMs on robot demonstration data embodimentcollaboration2025openxembodimentroboticlearning,walke2023bridgedata , enabling them to predict actions directly from visual observations and language instructions brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel . However, this fine-tuning comes at a significant cost: the action objective progressively overwrites the weight-space directions encoding visual-language understanding hancock2025actionslanguagefinetuningvlms , yielding a specialised model that excels at low-level control but can no longer reliably perform the high-level semantic reasoning needed for robust, generalist robotic agents. This tension between action specialisation and semantic preservation is a fundamental obstacle to building robotic systems that are both capable of language modelling and fine-grained motor control (see Figure~ fig:introfig ). Existing approaches to mitigating this degradation typically require architectural modifications or costly co-training on mixed datasets Zawalski24-ecot,hancock2025actionslanguagefinetuningvlms , making them difficult to apply post-hoc to already fine-tuned VLAs. Model merging offers a compelling alternative BECAME,yadav2025robust : by combining the parameters of a VLM and a VLA, one can in principle recover a model that retains both action prediction and vision-language capabilities. However, naive uniform blending treats all parameters equally and fails to account for the heterogeneous roles played by different weight matrices across the two models, yielding suboptimal trade-offs between semantic and action performance. In this work, we investigate how to merge a VLM and a VLA such that the resulting model retains the action capabilities acquired during fine-tuning while recovering the vision-language understanding of the original VLM. To this end, we extract the task vector by subtracting the VLM weights from those of the VLA and decompose it using Singular Value Decomposition to expose the individual components of this adaptation. For each such direction, we learn a scalar coefficient that controls how much of the VLA adaptation is retained in the merged model, jointly preserving action prediction performance and the original vision-language capabilities of the VLM. We demonstrate that this approach consistently outperforms uniform blending and established merging baselines across both vision-language benchmarks and robotic manipulation tasks, on two distinct VLA architectures. Our contributions are as follows: A post-hoc, lightweight merging method that decomposes the VLM--VLA task vector via SVD and learns per-component coefficients to jointly recover language understanding and preserve action capabilities, requiring only the optimisation of a small set of scalar merging parameters while keeping both source models fully frozen. An ablation study justifying fine-grained merging, showing per-component coefficients are necessary where global or per-layer scalars fail. A structural analysis of the fine-tuning directions at multiple scales of the SVD decomposition, identifying which components of the adaptation must be preserved to reconcile vision-language understanding and action prediction in the merged model. Together, these contributions offer a practical and substantially cheaper path toward robotic agents that combine reliable low-level control with the high-level semantic reasoning of their underlying VLM. Related Work Vision Language Action Models Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models extend Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by fine‑tuning them on large‑scale robot demonstration data embodimentcollaboration2025openxembodimentroboticlearning , enabling them to act as generalist policies that directly generate low‑level actions brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer,octomodelteam2024octoopensourcegeneralistrobot,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel . Actions are produced either autoregressively kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel,pertsch2025fastefficientactiontokenization or via continuous decoding such as flow matching black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . However, this fine-tuning causes them to largely lose their original vision–language capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Some works sidestep this issue by keeping the VLM frozen and training only a lightweight action module shukor2025smolvlavisionlanguageactionmodelaffordable,wen2025tinyvlafastdataefficientvisionlanguageaction , but this limits the model's ability to fully adapt its representations for embodied control. Others reintroduce text tasks during training either by training VLAs to generate both actions and text simultaneously Zawalski24-ecot,intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld or by aligning action representations with the language objective hancock2025actionslanguagefinetuningvlms . Both approaches require large-scale co-training to recover knowledge already present in the initial VLM. In contrast, our approach operates post-hoc on an already fine-tuned VLA, requiring no additional training of either source model. Model Merging Model merging has emerged as a cost-effective alternative to full retraining, enabling the combination of specialised models into a single capable model without additional data or compute. Model Soup~ wortsman2022modelsoupsaveragingweights averages the weights of models fine-tuned from the same checkpoint. SLERP jang2024sphericallinearinterpolationtextanchoring interpolates along the spherical geodesic rather than linearly, better preserving parameter norms. TIES~ yadav2023tiesmergingresolvinginterferencemerging resolves sign conflicts across multiple task vectors before averaging, requiring at least two independently fine-tuned models and thus not directly applicable to our setting. DARE~ yu2024languagemodelssupermario randomly drops a fraction of task vector parameters before rescaling the remainder. Fisher Merging~ matena2022mergingmodelsfisherweightedaveraging weights each parameter by its diagonal Fisher information, but requires computing and storing a matrix as large as the full model, making it costly at billion-parameter scale. AdaMerging~ yang2024adamergingadaptivemodelmerging learns task-wise or layer-wise merging weights but does not decompose the task vector into finer-grained components. All these methods operate with fixed or coarse-grained coefficients and none have been applied to reconciling a VLM with its VLA derivative. Closer to our work, decomposing task vectors via SVD has already been proposed to reduce interference between models trained on different tasks Gargiulo_2025_CVPR . title: Wireless Edge-Assisted Adaptive Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models in Physical AI
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, submitted to IEEE ICC
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable embodied artificial intelligence (AI) by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Emerging use cases in physical AI are expected to drive the need for efficient inference and communication, as the computational demands of the VLA models pose challenges for real-time control with limited onboard resources. Test-time scaling through latent reasoning allows these models to refine hidden representations without generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, but introduces a trade-off between task success, inference latency, and energy consumption. In this paper, we address the efficient collaborative inference under a realistic communication scenario. We propose a wireless edge-assisted framework for adaptive latent reasoning (WEALR) that augments onboard computation with edge computing. A decision-making agent jointly selects the execution location and latent-reasoning convergence threshold. We formulate this joint adaptation as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). A Lagrangian-constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) approach, namely trust region policy optimization Lagrangian (TRPO-Lag), learns to balance task performance and resource consumption under varying wireless conditions and task requirements. We evaluate the framework using LIBERO manipulation tasks, profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced wireless channels. Experimental results demonstrate that TRPO-Lag achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success rate compared to benchmark CDRL methods.

Test-time scaling through latent reasoning allows these models to refine hidden representations without generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, but introduces a trade-off between task success, inference latency, and energy consumption. In this paper, we address the efficient collaborative inference under a realistic communication scenario. We propose a wireless edge-assisted framework for adaptive latent reasoning (WEALR) that augments onboard computation with edge computing. A decision-making agent jointly selects the execution location and latent-reasoning convergence threshold. We formulate this joint adaptation as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Constrained Deep Reinforcement Learning (CDRL), Latent Reasoning, Physical AI, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models INTRODUCTION Physical artificial intelligence (AI) brings perception, reasoning and action into embodied systems that interact with the physical world wang2026phyairealtimephysicalai . Vision-language-action (VLA) models, such as OpenVLA openvla , support this capability by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Advances in these models create opportunities for generalizable physical AI, but their computational demands challenge deployment on resource-constrained robots. Task performance must therefore be balanced against onboard computation, energy consumption, and latency requirements jiang2026fastirunvla,zhou2026characterizing . In particular, timely robotic control requires communication and inference to jointly satisfy a latency service-level objective (SLO). We refer to robots capable of visual perception, instruction understanding, planning, reasoning, and action execution as physical AI devices (PADs) in this paper. Edge computing augments limited onboard computation by enabling PADs to offload inference to nearby edge servers, but its benefits depend on wireless propagation conditions acm_survey_ai_reasoning . This deployment perspective aligns with the vision of using radio access network (RAN) infrastructure to support AI applications at the network edge, such as mobile switching offices (MSO) 11141658 . However, faster edge computation comes at the cost of wireless transmission delay. In indoor environments such as homes and warehouses, blockage and multipath propagation create heterogeneous line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. Changes in PAD position affect achievable uplink (UL) rates and can offset the computational advantage of edge execution. Effective offloading must therefore account for wireless conditions alongside computation and control-latency requirements. Evaluating this tradeoff requires environment-specific channel models that capture blockage, multipath propagation, and spatial variations in link quality, which ray tracing can provide alkhateeb2019deepmimo, farzanullah2025wirelessmultimodalfoundationmodel . Reliable physical interaction requires VLA models to interpret diverse visual observations and language instructions and generate appropriate actions across tasks of varying difficulty. Supporting these capabilities motivates increasing model capacity through parameter scaling or allocating additional computation during inference. Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enable parameter scaling while limiting computation per input by activating only a subset of model parameters temiz2026wisdomwirelesssparsedecision . However, their memory and computational requirements can still challenge deployment on resource-constrained PADs. Test-time scaling offers a complementary approach that adjusts computational effort within a fixed model, making it particularly attractive for wireless edge deployment, where available resources and latency requirements limit inference costs acm_survey_ai_reasoning . Unlike explicit reasoning methods such as chain-of-thought (CoT), which generate intermediate text through sequential decoding, latent reasoning refines hidden representations without producing intermediate text tokens, potentially reducing the decoding overhead and latency associated with textual reasoning. The recurrent-depth architecture in~ geiping2025scaling enables large language models (LLMs), which serve as backbones of VLAs, to vary computational depth through shared parameters, offering adjustable inference effort within a fixed model footprint. For robotic inference, recurrent-depth VLA (RD-VLA) applies a related principle through a weight-tied recurrent action head and a convergence-based stopping criterion to adapt the number of reasoning iterations across observations tur2026rdvla . For example, grasping a small object may require more reasoning than moving through an unobstructed region. A single convergence threshold can therefore yield different reasoning depths across stages of a task and different tasks. Additional reasoning may improve action quality but also increases inference latency and resource consumption, motivating adaptive control of reasoning effort. These considerations motivate jointly selecting VLA execution location and reasoning effort under wireless, energy, and computation constraints. Related studies address complementary aspects of collaborative inference. The device-cloud framework in~ devicecloudmultiturnllm uses resource-constrained reinforcement learning (RL) to select LLM inference locations and multimodal inputs. Also, the EcoVLA approach proposed in ecovla selects energy-efficient VLA co-inference schemes under real-time constraints, adapting to network fluctuations and edge workload variations. The authors of~ liu2026mores propose MORES, a reasoning-as-a-service framework that distributes recurrent hidden-state updates between devices and servers, jointly adapting reasoning computation and latent-feature pruning under heterogeneous wireless conditions. While conversational LLM services typically prioritize response quality, VLAs must deliver actions within deadlines imposed by ongoing physical control jiang2026fastirunvla . Meeting these deadlines requires balancing task success against communication delay and resource consumption. Cumulative budgets couple decisions across requests, and shared edge resources couple decisions across PADs, motivating a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) formulation. Constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) addresses such problems by separating performance objectives from explicit operating limits~ ray2019benchmarking . This motivates the use of CDRL methods, including Lagrangian variants of proximal policy optimization (PPO) and trust region policy optimization (TRPO), as well as constrained policy optimization (CPO), for resource management in wireless networks. In particular, PPO-Lag has been adopted for joint unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) altitude control and Internet of Things (IoT) channel access~ 9177252 . In this paper, we propose Wireless Edge-Assisted Adaptive Latent Reasoning (WEALR), a framework that jointly adapts VLA execution location and reasoning effort. For each robotic task request, an agent selects local or edge execution and a reasoning convergence threshold. This threshold governs termination of the latent reasoning loop while allowing the realized reasoning depth to vary across observations within the task. We use TRPO-Lag, which learns the policy and constraint multipliers, connecting adaptive latent reasoning with wireless offloading and cumulative resource management. The key contributions are as follows: We develop WEALR to jointly select VLA execution location and reasoning threshold according to task requirements, wireless conditions, and available resources. We formulate a CMDP with per-PAD energy, shared edge-reasoning, and SLO constraints, and apply TRPO-Lag to optimize robotic task success. We evaluate task success, feasibility, and policy behavior using LIBERO manipulation tasks liu2023libero , profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced channels under varying wireless conditions and resource budgets. Both PADs and the server host pretrained VLA models with preloaded checkpoints; cold-start latency is neglected ecovla . Each episode comprises requests, with request originating from PAD and belonging to task suite . The controller selects an execution location and reasoning threshold for each request, fixed throughout the task. Requests are served sequentially, with only one active UL transmission at a time~ liu2026mores . We use synchronous VLA inference: each cycle begins after the previous action chunk is executed, avoiding potentially stale observations in asynchronous execution~ jiang2026fastirunvla . System Model Latent Reasoning for VLAs subsubsec:latenreasoning The VLA processes visual observations and language instructions to generate action chunks, each comprising a sequence of actions (e.g., five). During each inference cycle, recurrent updates refine the hidden representations until the predicted action chunk stabilizes, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:WEALR_framework (b) and (c). Thus, a single threshold governs each task, while the realized depth varies across observations. Unlike fixed-depth reasoning~ liu2026mores , a task-level threshold adapts depth across observations, potentially reducing recurrent updates while maintaining task success ~ tur2026rdvla . An offline dataset profiles task success, inference latency, energy, and recurrent-update counts across task suites and candidate thresholds, as summarized in Fig.~ fig:offlinedatasetcharacteristics . Increasing the convergence threshold reduces the mean recurrent iterations per inference across all suites, but generally lowers task success, with the largest degradation observed in LIBERO-10, which involves long-horizon tasks liu2023libero . These tradeoffs motivate adaptive threshold selection and provide the profiles used by the resource-management environment. title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 20 tables. Project page: https://guobapei.github.io/SuperGlance/ ; code: https://github.com/GuobaPei/SuperGlance
summary: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.

title: Distilling Safety Filters for Filter-free Multi-agent RL
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures and 6 tables
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can teach robot teams to navigate shared spaces, but trial and error causes collisions that real robots cannot afford. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters prevent these collisions by correcting unsafe actions, yet in a team the filter becomes a centralized optimization whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. We propose an approach that builds the filter's safety into the RL policy and examine how such a system behaves during filter-free deployment. However, the filter that keeps training safe also hides what the policy must learn: it masks the cost of unsafe actions, which actor-critic methods then overvalue, and it keeps near-collision states out of the training data. Our approach therefore learns only from executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning and distills the filter into the policy at synthetic near-collision states. We prove that filter distillation loss bounds the policy's constraint violation and hence how far agents can cross their safety margin, so errors never accumulate. When distillation states cover deployed states, the loss also bounds the collision probability at every step. Without a filter and acting only on local observations, our policies have no collisions in 1,800 test episodes with multiple agents. A policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to teams of twenty at constant per-agent computation and stays collision-free with up to eight agents. We test our policies on Crazyflie quadrotors with up to five flying at the same time.
full_text: Reinforcement learning (RL) can teach robot teams to navigate shared spaces, but trial and error causes collisions that real robots cannot afford. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters prevent these collisions by correcting unsafe actions, yet in a team the filter becomes a centralized optimization whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. We propose an approach that builds the filter's safety into the RL policy and examine how such a system behaves during filter-free deployment. However, the filter that keeps training safe also hides what the policy must learn: it masks the cost of unsafe actions, which actor-critic methods then overvalue, and it keeps near-collision states out of the training data. Our approach therefore learns only from executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning and distills the filter into the policy at synthetic near-collision states. We prove that filter distillation loss bounds the policy's constraint violation and hence how far agents can cross their safety margin, so errors never accumulate. When distillation states cover deployed states, the loss also bounds the collision probability at every step.
