We test our policies on Crazyflie quadrotors with up to five flying at the same time. Videos of the hardware experiments and code are available at . Introduction sec:intro Robots increasingly work in teams that share space, where each robot must reach its goal while avoiding collisions with other robots and obstacles. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach to learning such behaviours, but its trial-and-error nature causes collisions during training that can damage hardware, so real-world multi-agent RL requires safe exploration from the start. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters ames2017, ames2019 address this challenge: at each step, the filter minimally modifies the actions proposed by the policy to satisfy the collision-avoidance constraints, so only safe actions are executed during training fisac2018general . In multi-agent systems, however, pairwise constraints couple the team into a centralized quadratic program (QP) whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. Solving it requires every agent's state and proposed action; for agents, the joint QP takes \,ms, a third of the control period, against \,ms per agent for our policy (Sec.~ sec:scaling ). This motivates our objective: use a centralized safety filter to guarantee collision-free exploration during training, but learn a decentralized policy that no longer requires the filter at deployment. Simply removing the filter after training, however, leads to a fundamental distribution mismatch: the policy is trained under filtered action-to-transition mapping but deployed under an unfiltered one. CBF-RL yang2025 adds barrier-based reward shaping so that single-agent policies, trained with the filter, run without it at deployment. Because the filter maps many raw actions to the same safe action markgraf2025 , actor-critic methods such as soft actor-critic (SAC) can overvalue unsafe raw actions: SAC trained with the filter in the loop collides in of episodes when deployed without it (Sec.~ sec:ablations ). This observation motivates RL methods that learn only from actions in the data: we extract the policy from the executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning (IQL) kostrikov2022 (Sec.~ sec:learn-safe ). IQL alone is insufficient, however: because the filter prevents collisions, the replay buffer lacks the near-collision states that the unfiltered policy may reach. To cover them, off-support safety-filter distillation (OSFD; Sec.~ sec:osfd ) trains the policy on the actions of the training filter, queried at synthetic near-collision states, without environment interaction. Following centralized training with decentralized execution, only training uses the joint state, and the deployed policy is an attention-based actor on local observations whose parameters do not depend on the team size (Sec.~ sec:po ). We prove theoretically that this training controls safety once the filter is removed (Sec.~ sec:theory ). The distillation loss bounds a closed-form CBF residual that measures how much the unfiltered policy violates the filter's constraints, a bounded residual lowers the barrier by a bounded amount uniformly in time, so violations never accumulate, and, when the distillation states cover the deployed states, the loss bounds the collision probability at every step. The training loss thus certifies the safety of the filter-free policy, and every bound held on the trained policies we audited. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) Filter-free multi-agent RL: we propose a novel framework that trains collision-free with a centralized CBF filter and deploys a decentralized policy without it, by combining IQL-based policy extraction with OSFD. (2) Safety guarantees: bounds that tie the distillation loss to the safety of the unfiltered policy under single- and double-integrator dynamics (Sec.~ sec:theory ). (3) Scalable filter-free collision avoidance: our local-sensing policies have no collision in episodes on the training scenes, where CBF-RL collides in up to , a policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to twenty at a constant \,ms per agent (Sec.~ sec:exp ), and our policies fly up to five Crazyflie quadrotors without a filter (Sec.~ sec:hardware ). Related Work sec:related-work Safe RL with safety filters. Constrained RL achiam2017 bounds expected cumulative costs but not state-wise safety during training. Safety filters enforce constraints at every step through shielding alshiekh2018 , safety layers dalal2018 , Hamilton-Jacobi reachability fisac2018general, bansal2017 , also learned by RL fisac2019 , CBFs cheng2019, bejarano2024 or control barrier-value functions that unify the two choi2021cbvf . Learned filters handle model uncertainty choi2020 and black-box dynamics lavanakul2024 , but generally remain in loop at execution. CBF-RL yang2025 trains with a CBF filter and shapes reward so the policy runs without it. We instead address coupled multi-agent constraints and decentralized policies under partial observability. We close the train-deploy mismatch by in-support policy extraction and supervision beyond data rather than reward shaping. Multi-agent collision avoidance and safety constraints. Learning-based collision avoidance has been explored for ground and aerial swarms chen2017cadrl, long2018, batra2021, huang2024 . Decentralized barrier certificates wang2017 , shields elsayed2021, melcer2022 and CBF filters within multi-agent RL cai2021 avoid a central solve by splitting the constraints among agents, but remain in the loop at deployment, and neural approaches learn decentralized CBFs together with their controllers qin2021, zhang2023gcbf, zhang2025gcbf+ . In centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) lowe2017, yu2022mappo , critics use joint information during training, while each deployed policy acts on its own observation. We follow CTDE and additionally use a centralized filter for safe exploration and as a teacher for a filter-free decentralized policy. Data-driven RL, imitation learning and partial observability. Offline RL counters value overestimation at actions absent from the data levine2020 by constraining the policy to the behavior policy fujimoto2019, kumar2019bear, wu2019brac, nair2020, fujimoto2021td3bc , by penalizing out-of-distribution values kumar2020 or by learning values in-sample kostrikov2022, xu2023ivr, garg2023xql , also with multiple agents yang2021icq, pan2022omar . In-sample learning suits filtered transitions, where unsafe raw actions share safe outcomes, but leaves states missing from the buffer unsupervised. DAgger ross2011 queries an expert on the learner's own roll-outs; OSFD instead queries the training filter at synthetic near-collision states, without environment interaction. As in learning with privileged information chen2020lbc, lee2020 , we use the global state only during training and our local-observation attention actor builds on zhang2025gcbf+ . Our Approach sec:approach We now present our approach for learning decentralized collision-avoidance policies using a centralized safety filter during training (Fig.~ fig:method ). The actor is trained with two losses: an RL loss on the executed safe actions (Sec.~ sec:learn-safe ) and a distillation loss at synthetic near-collision states (Sec.~ sec:osfd ). Problem Formulation sec:formulation We consider disc-shaped agents of radius navigating toward individual goals in an environment with circular obstacles. Each agent follows either single-integrator (SI) or double-integrator (DI) dynamics, discretized with time step : Here, , and are position, velocity and control, with and, for DI agents, . title: Self-Calibrating Vision-Agent-Action: Deploying Pick-and-Place to New Robot Cells without Demonstrations or Fine-Tuning
comment: 7 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; supplementary video in ancillary files
summary: In simulation, Vision-Agent-Action (VAA) performs pick-and-place in robot cells with gripper or base-frame changes without robot demonstrations or fine-tuning. It uses pre-trained vision-language and language models for interpretation, measures the command map and camera geometry from its own motion and fingertips, estimates lens distortion, and plans grasps from measured object depth. A controlled study of eight public LIBERO-fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs) varies robot hardware, camera geometry, appearance, and base frame. Gripper and frame changes dominate their losses in the tested fractional design. Across 18 cells with these changes, frozen VAA achieves 230/360 successes (64%), the refined VAA 268/360 (74%), and the strongest released VLA on this subset 76/360 (21%). Paired ablations support the self-calibration bundle, lens estimation under compounded changes, and the measured-depth pipeline. On a two-step LIBERO-Goal chain with object state carried between instructions, VAA completes 54/60 chains in changed cells, while four evaluated VLAs complete none.

Robot manipulation, self-calibration, vision-language-action models, language-conditioned manipulation. Introduction Moving a manipulation system to another robot cell changes more than its images. A different gripper changes fingertip geometry and object contact. A rotated command frame changes the direction in which an action moves the tool center point (TCP). Camera pose, lens, lighting, support surfaces, and objects may also change. Collecting demonstrations and fine-tuning a policy for each cell adds deployment work. Public vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tuned on LIBERO can perform tasks in their training setup. Transfer to a new cell also requires their commands to produce the intended physical motion under changed hardware and coordinate frames. Fig.~ fig:teaser illustrates this deployment problem. We first examine where released VLAs lose success in a controlled cell design. Gripper and base-frame changes dominate their losses in the tested fraction. Both changes alter the relation between commands and fingertip or object motion. This diagnosis motivates measuring the new cell's geometry before manipulation. Vision-Agent-Action (VAA) performs this measurement and executes pick-and-place without robot demonstrations or fine-tuning. It combines pre-trained VLM/LLM components with self-calibration. Before the task, the robot observes its own motion and fingertips to establish a cell model. During the task, language models identify the relevant objects, while geometric modules determine where to grasp and where the TCP must move. Fig.~ fig:overview separates these stages. The study contributes: A controlled diagnosis identifying gripper and command-frame changes as dominant VLA transfer factors in the tested design. A self-calibrating pipeline combining command and camera measurement, lens estimation, and measured-depth grasp planning. Paired ablations and two-step manipulation testing the roles of cell measurement and calibration reuse. Related Work VLAs learn instruction-conditioned actions from demonstrations and combine visual, linguistic, and motor representations across tasks and embodiments~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05,smolvla,xvla,groot,vlajepa . Robustness evaluations examine their sensitivity to visual, physical, and task changes, including dependence on demonstrated trajectories~ liberoplus,liberopro,colosseum,intact . Camera- and embodiment-transfer methods address parts of this deployment problem through viewpoint adaptation or cross-embodiment representations~ anycamvla,camvla,mirage,shadow . Our study focuses on gripper and command-frame changes and tests explicit measurement of the new cell as a deployment procedure. Foundation-model agents use language, vision, code, and geometric tools to coordinate manipulation~ cap,voxposer,rekep,okrobot,capx,openrua,waa,rax . VAA similarly separates semantic interpretation from geometric execution, grounding object choices in measured scene geometry. RoboArchitect~ roboarchitect uses a coding model to evolve a harness around a frozen VLA over optimization episodes and is supplied with the pixel-to-base projection and action specification. VAA measures the command map, camera geometry, and lens of each new cell with the same code in every cell; its per-cell adaptation uses no task-success signal and no code modification. Hand--eye calibration, autonomous camera calibration, and visual self-modeling estimate relationships among robot motion, observed geometry, and coordinate frames~ tsai,easyhec,kalib,arccalib,selfmodel . VAA uses its fingertips as observed features and additionally measures command-channel motion and gripper behavior. Its evaluation connects these measurements to pick-and-place transfer under a parallel-jaw model. Controlled Study: Where Do VLAs Break? sec:study Tasks, Factors, and Baselines All experiments are in simulation. We use LIBERO-spatial~ libero , with 10 tasks and 2 initial states per task, giving 20 episodes per cell. Every method receives the same episodes. The controlled study contains changed design cells. The factors are arm (A: Panda to UR5e), gripper (B: Panda to Hand-E), camera pose (C: moved 10\,cm and rotated ), lens (D: ), light (E: dim warm illumination), table (F: blue cloth), objects (G: red bowl and blue plate), and base frame (H: rotation). Single-factor cells include additional levels: RB5 and Doosan arms; PGC, 2FG7, and Schunk grippers; a high camera; and a frame rotation. Combined changes follow a resolution-IV fraction: The fraction contains 15 changed cells and a nominal reference. Changed-cell totals exclude the nominal reference. In a resolution-IV fraction, main effects are not aliased with two-factor interactions, but their interpretation assumes negligible higher-order interactions; two-factor interactions remain aliased with one another. Five additional changed development cells provide whole-cell stress tests. The baselines are X-VLA, 0.5, 0, GR00T N1.7, OpenVLA, SmolVLA, 0, and VLA-JEPA~ xvla,pi05,pi0,groot,openvla,smolvla,tau0,vlajepa . We evaluate each released system with its own model, training, action interface, and authors' inference stack. VAA uses a third-person RGB-D camera and proprioception; the VLAs receive RGB images without measured depth. The RGB-only VAA ablation examines this sensor difference. Evaluation Protocol Each baseline uses one seed per evaluation run. Reference runs of the same setup yield 14/20 and 19/20 successes for OpenVLA, and 16/20 and 12/20 for SmolVLA. Frozen VAA was fixed before the design-cell evaluations. Execution refinements in VAA were selected using the training setup and development cells, with frozen design outcomes available. Both versions are reported on the gripper/frame subset selected from the factor diagnosis. For the chain evaluation, VAA was not developed on LIBERO-Goal, and the chain comprises the two most reliable pick-and-place steps in its shared scene. Factor Diagnosis sec:diagnosis Fig.~ fig:effects identifies gripper and base-frame changes as the dominant VLA losses in this fraction, and Fig.~ fig:vlacells shows one rollout per cell for the same task and initial state. The remaining evaluation focuses on cells that change the gripper or rotate the base frame. In cells that change neither the gripper nor the frame, several released VLAs retain high aggregate success, with performance varying by model. Both dominant factors change the relation between a command and the resulting motion of the fingers or object. Measuring that relation through controlled motion provides the cell-specific information used by VAA. Vision-Agent-Action sec:method Self-Calibration of the Cell Model VAA measures command effects, jaw behavior, and camera geometry before task execution (Figs.~ fig:overview and~ fig:pipeline ). These measurements replace assumptions inherited from the training setup. Command map and jaw behavior The robot commands small motions through the available action channels and measures the resulting TCP displacement: where is an action-channel command and is its measured local motion map. In the figures, command channels 0--2 are assigned to base / / directions through . The controller uses this map to interpret desired TCP displacements in the current cell. VAA also measures open and closed fingertip widths and the settling time after a gripper command. The usable opening constrains grasp selection, while settling time determines when to observe the commanded jaw state. The cell model uses parallel-jaw closure. Camera and lens geometry The robot observes its fingertips at multiple poses and associates these observations with its motion and proprioception to estimate camera intrinsics (focal length and principal point) and pose relative to the robot base . The resulting geometry maps base-frame coordinates to image pixels. VAA estimates radial distortion using table flatness as a constraint. Geometric errors from a changed lens can compound with camera and hardware changes even when the object remains recognizable. VAA also uses workspace exploration views, a table-height touch check, and real-time re-reading. Section~ sec:ablations evaluates these procedures separately. Grounding and Depth-Based Grasp Planning RGB-D observations provide object proposals. A pre-trained VLM (Qwen3.8, 27B) labels the proposals, and a pre-trained text LLM (Qwen3, 30B instruct) interprets the instruction to select a target and destination; both run locally without fine-tuning. A geometric resolver and size checks connect those semantic choices to measured scene entities. The grasp planner uses the target's own three-dimensional points to choose where the fingers should approach and close. The measured jaw opening constrains feasible grasp geometry, and the cell model connects the selected grasp to a TCP goal. Execution and Verification A closed-loop servo executes motion through the calibrated command map. Verification checks whether placement succeeded. After an unsuccessful attempt, VAA diagnoses the observed outcome and can retry. After initial calibration, a short drift check determines whether to reuse the cell model or recalibrate, separating cell preparation from execution of each instruction. The following ablations examine which measurements support the geometric pipeline under these types of changes. The full system succeeds in 50/60 episodes. title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.

A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160\,ms after subtracting network transmission time. Introduction sec:intro Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow an instruction through an unseen environment using first-person observations. Recent policies fine-tune video-based large language models to emit low-level actions as tokens~ zhang2025uninavid,wei2025streamvln , improving performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE~ anderson2018vlr,ku2020rxr,krantz2020vlrce . In autoregressive decoding, each predicted action becomes part of the input for the next prediction. The robot waits for these successive model calls before it can execute the plan. That delay recurs each time the robot uses a new observation to plan its next actions. Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN predict up to four actions per decision. Uni-NaVid executes at most two~ zhang2025uninavid , while StreamVLN executes the full prediction~ wei2025streamvln . In both policies, the execution limit is set in advance, regardless of how strongly the policy favors a particular plan given the current observations. This motivates using the policy's predictions to decide how much of a plan to execute before observing again. The small navigation action space lets us enumerate all prefixes needed to score short plans. We introduce VLN-Flash (Figure~ fig:overview ), a training-free decoder that packs these prefixes into a tree and scores them together in one forward pass through the navigation policy. Tree attention lets branches share the observed context while keeping each candidate's own action history. Matching the visible history and position indices to autoregressive decoding preserves the corresponding conditional distributions in exact arithmetic. The original language-model head reads out the action distribution for every branch. Scoring the whole tree lets the robot choose how many actions to execute at each decision. Execution length determines when new observations can influence the policy. Longer blocks reduce the number of decisions along a route, while shorter blocks allow earlier replanning with fresh visual feedback. Since the tree already scores all depths, selecting a shorter execution prefix requires no additional prediction pass. VLN-Flash uses these readouts for joint-probability plan selection and margin-based adaptive execution. Joint probabilities rank candidate action sequences using the policy's conditional predictions. To determine the execution length, we scan the score margin between the fixed stepwise-greedy branch and its strongest alternative from shallow to deep. The scan stops when the greedy branch's lead falls below a threshold, or when that branch ends. At the selected depth, the agent executes the highest-scoring branch and then observes again. The same tree scores thus determine both which plan to execute and how long to follow it. We measure decoding on identical inputs and ablate plan selection and adaptive execution. On Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN, VLN-Flash accelerates action decoding by nearly over native autoregressive decoding and improves success rate (SR) and success weighted by path length (SPL) on both R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with SR gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, the same StreamVLN policy completes 52 of 60 instructions with VLN-Flash versus 49 with autoregressive decoding. Our main contributions are as follows. One-pass action-tree decoding. VLN-Flash scores all short-horizon action prefixes in a single forward pass without retraining, preserving autoregressive conditional distributions in exact arithmetic. Shared scores for planning and execution. Joint probabilities rank candidate plans, and score margins determine how many actions to execute before observing again. Faster decoding and better navigation. VLN-Flash decodes actions nearly faster, improves SR and SPL on both benchmarks, and reduces action waiting time on a Unitree GO2. Related Work sec:related vision-and-language navigation. Early VLN benchmarks let agents select reachable viewpoints on predefined navigation graphs~ anderson2018vlr,ku2020rxr . VLN-CE replaces graph transitions with low-level actions in continuous 3D environments~ krantz2020vlrce . In this setting, NaVid predicts the next action from egocentric video~ zhang2024navid , while Uni-NaVid predicts a short action sequence~ zhang2025uninavid . Other policies use different action representations. NaVILA issues mid-level language commands for a locomotion controller~ cheng2025navila , and OmniNav predicts continuous waypoints~ xue2026omninav . JanusVLN stores visual semantics and spatial geometry in separate compact memories~ zeng2026janusvln . StreamVLN combines SlowFast context modeling with cross-decision KV reuse~ wei2025streamvln , and Efficient-VLN processes new frames incrementally using cache reuse and contiguous rotary positions~ zheng2025efficientvln . MemVLN combines pyramidal visual memory with a learned vocabulary of single-token mid-level actions~ liu2026memvln . LiveVLN reduces robot waiting by overlapping observation processing with action execution~ wang2026livevln . We focus on speeding up plan generation once the observation history is available. decoding for language and actions. Speculative decoding verifies proposals from a smaller model~ leviathan2023fast . Draft Verify drafts by skipping layers~ zhang2024draftverify , while Prompt Lookup retrieves candidate continuations from the input~ saxena2023prompt . Jacobi decoding updates token guesses by fixed-point iteration~ santilli2023parallel ; Lookahead uses these updates to build and verify candidate continuations~ fu2024lookahead . SpecInfer and Medusa verify branches with tree attention~ miao2024specinfer,cai2024medusa , and EAGLE-2 uses draft confidence to build the tree~ li2024eagle2 . Parallel decoding has also been studied for robot actions. PD-VLA reformulates autoregressive action decoding as a nonlinear system solved by parallel fixed-point iterations~ song2025pdvla . Spec-VLA adapts draft-and-verify decoding to action tokens with a relaxed acceptance criterion~ wang2025specvla . OFT combines parallel decoding, action chunking, and continuous-action regression in a fine-tuning recipe~ kim2025oft , while Discrete Diffusion VLA generates discrete action chunks through iterative refinement~ liang2026ddvla . For short navigation plans, the small action set lets us enumerate valid prefixes directly and score the complete tree in one pass. We use the resulting joint scores to select a plan and decide when to observe again. action execution. Adaptive chunk execution determines how many predicted actions to apply before incorporating new observations. AAC estimates action entropy from sampled chunks to select the execution length at inference time~ liang2026aac . Attention-based methods derive execution horizons from the policy's internal structure. AutoHorizon uses action self-attention~ wang2026autohorizon , while cross-attention dynamics provide a truncation signal when action predictions lose grounding in the current observation~ xu2026stop . Other approaches use the predicted motion or its consequences. PACE identifies low-speed transitions in the predicted chunk as replanning boundaries~ nie2026pace ; CA C uses a world model to compare the imagined consequences of candidate chunks and commits while those futures agree~ li2026ca3c . In reinforcement learning, ACH learns action values for multiple chunk lengths and selects the horizon according to the current state~ shin2026ach . We derive execution depth from the joint-score margin between navigation branches, reusing the scores produced by parallel action decoding. Method sec:method Given the policy input , VLN-Flash computes the conditional action distributions needed to score all valid plans of up to actions in one masked forward pass. These distributions support joint-probability plan selection (Section~ sec:selection ) and adaptive execution (Section~ sec:commit ). Figure~ fig:overview shows how the tree is packed, masked, and read out. Preliminaries sec:prelim At decision step , the instruction and egocentric video history form a policy input of length after visual encoding and tokenization. The fixed prompt and response header are included in , so its final position predicts the first action. We obtain the action distribution by applying softmax to the language-model logits for the four actions A plan is a predicted action sequence, with maximum length here. The agent executes a selected prefix before acquiring a new observation and replanning. The native autoregressive decoder needs forward passes to generate action tokens and the output terminator. The first pass processes and predicts the first action; the remaining passes produce the other actions and the terminator. All candidate plans at a decision condition on the same observed history. Their action prefixes describe possible continuations of that history. Once a branch is selected, the agent executes its actions and supplies the newly acquired observation to the next decision. Thus the planning horizon bounds what the decoder scores, while the execution rule determines when the policy observes again. title: MARS: Dynamic Routing of Reinforcement-Learned Atomic Skills for Multi-Stage Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr`itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.

The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Embodied Intelligence; Vision-Language-Action Models; Reinforcement Learning; Atomic Skills; Multi-Stage Robotic Manipulation Introduction sec:intro Robotic manipulation tasks, such as multi-object pick-and-place, object transfer, and laboratory sample handling, typically involve a sequence of operations, including grasping, transportation, alignment, placement, and insertion. These stages impose different requirements on the underlying control policy. General-purpose policies are often sufficient for relatively simple operations, such as object transportation and robot resetting, whereas alignment and insertion require higher control precision and execution stability. Consequently, relying on a single control policy throughout an entire manipulation task may make it difficult to simultaneously achieve general-purpose manipulation capabilities and precise control during critical stages. Combining pretrained generalist policies with skill-specific control policies optimized for particular manipulation requirements provides a promising approach to improving multi-stage robotic manipulation. However, different policies have distinct operating conditions and applicable ranges. Selecting an appropriate policy according to the robot state and task progress, while ensuring smooth transitions between policies, remains an important challenge in multi-policy coordination~ huang2026chembot,pang2026scivla . In recent years, generalist robotic policies, including RT-1, RT-2, Octo, OpenVLA, , , and SmolVLA, have demonstrated promising multi-task manipulation capabilities through large-scale robot data pretraining and joint modeling of visual, language and action information~ brohan2022rt1,brohan2023rt2,ghosh2024octo,openx2024oxe,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,shukor2025smolvla . Nevertheless, the performance of these generalist policies varies across manipulation stages, particularly in tasks involving precise alignment and contact-constrained operations, where action accuracy and execution stability remain challenging~ luo2025hilserl,xu2026rlt . To further improve robotic manipulation performance, recent studies have investigated reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training methods for VLA policies. One line of research improves manipulation performance by optimizing the action generation process or updating selected model parameters, as demonstrated by VLA-RL, SimpleVLA-RL, iRe-VLA, and ~ lu2025vlarl,li2025simplevlarl,guo2025irevla,intelligence2025recap . Another line of research aims to preserve the core capabilities of pretrained models while enhancing task-specific control through lightweight control modules, residual policies, or independently trained RL policies. Representative methods include RL Token (RLT), PARTS, Object-Centric Residual RL, and VLaRL~ xu2026rlt,su2026pretraining,kim2026object,saito2026vlarl . These studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in improving robotic manipulation from different perspectives and have provided a foundation for integrating pretrained generalist policies with specialized control strategies. Although reinforcement learning can improve the control performance of VLA models in specific manipulation tasks, optimizing a single policy for an entire multi-stage task remains challenging. When only a binary terminal reward indicating full-task success or failure is available, the policy receives no reward feedback for intermediate actions that contribute positively to task progress. This makes it difficult to accurately estimate the contribution of actions at different stages to the final task outcome, thereby complicating state-action value estimation and policy optimization. One possible solution is to decompose critical stages with clearly defined manipulation objectives into independent atomic skills and optimize each skill separately through reinforcement learning. By assigning local objectives and reward signals to individual atomic skills, specialized policies can be trained to address specific control requirements while reducing their dependence on full-task rewards. However, independently trained atomic skills only improve control performance within their respective stages. Determining when to activate each skill and how to coordinate transitions between specialized policies and the generalist VLA remains a key challenge for multi-policy coordination. Several studies have explored skill organization and dynamic routing mechanisms from different perspectives. AtomicVLA organizes manipulation capabilities through atomic skill modeling and an expert-based architecture, SMoDP introduces semantically structured policy specialization for compositional robotic manipulation, and SWAP enables dynamic selection among multiple VLA policies through policy value estimation~ zhang2026atomicvla,deng2026smodp,das2026swap . These approaches offer different solutions for atomic skill modeling, policy specialization, and dynamic selection. Nevertheless, for a system consisting of a frozen generalist VLA and multiple independently trained RL-based atomic skill policies, determining which policy is most appropriate at different stages of task execution remains a key challenge. Since individual policies have different control objectives and operating ranges, atomic skill selection should not rely solely on predefined manipulation stages but should also account for state changes throughout the sequential execution process. Meanwhile, descriptions of candidate policies provide policy-specific semantic information that can help the router learn correspondences between candidate skills and temporal state contexts. Motivated by these considerations, we formulate dynamic policy routing from two complementary perspectives: temporal state modeling and candidate policy matching. Specifically, temporal encoding is used to extract contextual information from sequential robot states, while skill descriptions are transformed into conditioned semantic queries that interact with temporal state features. This enables the router to construct policy-specific matching representations and provides a basis for dynamically selecting between the generalist VLA and reinforcement-learned atomic skill experts. To address these challenges, we propose MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills in multi-stage robotic manipulation. MARS decouples local skill optimization from high-level policy selection, enabling coordinated control between a generalist VLA and multiple specialized atomic skill policies. For atomic skill optimization, we first construct a shared RL Token adapter based on intermediate features extracted from the frozen VLA backbone. The adapter produces compact state representations that can be reused across different skill policies. Each atomic skill policy then takes the shared state representation and reference action chunks of the frozen VLA as inputs and is independently optimized through reinforcement learning for a specific local manipulation objective. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs a Mamba-base recurrent encoder~ gu2023mamba to capture temporal information from robot states and maintains a fixed-length historical feature window to preserve recent state changes. Meanwhile, the skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, which are further refined through self-attention to capture inter-skill relationships. Cross-attention is then applied to extract skill-relevant information from historical state features, providing contextual representations for subsequent policy selection. The skill-conditioned features are then used to predict routing probabilities for the generalist VLA and each atomic skill policy. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We propose MARS, a multi-policy coordination framework that integrates a frozen generalist VLA with independently optimized reinforcement learning-based atomic skill policies using shared RL Token representations and VLA reference actions. We develop a dynamic policy router that combines Mamba-based temporal modeling and skill-conditioned attention to select appropriate control policies based on temporal state information and candidate skill semantics. We evaluate MARS through simulation and real-world robotic experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness in atomic skill execution, dynamic policy routing, and full-task manipulation performance. To leverage the complementary strengths of generalist and specialized policies, we propose MARS, a multi-policy coordination framework that decouples local atomic skill optimization from high-level policy selection. In this framework, a frozen generalist VLA handles basic manipulation and provides reference actions for atomic skill learning, while multiple atomic skill policies undergo independent reinforcement learning optimization for specific manipulation objectives. A high-level dynamic router then selects appropriate control policies based on robot state information and candidate skill semantics, as illustrated in . title: ARC-VLN: Adaptive Recursive Computing-based Visual-Language Navigation
summary: Efficient aerial visual-language navigation (VLN) requires reducing model storage and inference costs while maintaining instruction-conditioned action prediction. We present ARC-VLN, a token-type-aware recursive computation framework built on a language backbone with shared parameters. ARC-VLN retains full-depth computation for text and action tokens while adaptively selecting exit depths for visual tokens. Representations of early-exiting visual tokens are retained, and active-token compaction shortens the sequences processed by subsequent recursive blocks. To mitigate routing collapse to a single exit depth, we design a dedicated learning strategy that encourages the model to distribute visual tokens across multiple exit depths.On OpenFly's Test-Seen and Test-Unseen subsets, ARC-VLN achieves the lowest navigation error and the highest success rate and success weighted by path length among all compared methods. Meanwhile, it reduces the average number of decision steps per trajectory, total floating-point operations, mean model inference time per trajectory, and average GPU memory usage during inference, indicating its great potential as a VLN backbone for lightweight applications.

Xiangyu Dong is with the College of Information Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang 110819, China (e-mail: dxy1999ai@163.com ). Yang Lu is with the School of Artificial Intelligence, Henan University, Zhengzhou 450046, China (e-mail: lykyc@henu.edu.cn ). Xiaoguang Ma is with the School of Artificial Intelligence, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300350, China (e-mail: coltlight@163.com ). Efficient aerial visual-language navigation (VLN) requires reducing model storage and inference costs while maintaining instruction-conditioned action prediction. We present ARC-VLN, a token-type-aware recursive computation framework built on a language backbone with shared parameters. ARC-VLN retains full-depth computation for text and action tokens while adaptively selecting exit depths for visual tokens. Representations of early-exiting visual tokens are retained, and active-token compaction shortens the sequences processed by subsequent recursive blocks. To mitigate routing collapse to a single exit depth, we design a dedicated learning strategy that encourages the model to distribute visual tokens across multiple exit depths. On OpenFly’s Test-Seen and Test-Unseen subsets, ARC-VLN achieves the lowest navigation error and the highest success rate and success weighted by path length among all compared methods. Meanwhile, it reduces the average number of decision steps per trajectory, total floating-point operations, mean model inference time per trajectory, and average GPU memory usage during inference, indicating its great potential as a VLN backbone for lightweight applications. Efficient inference, recursive parameter sharing, token-type-aware routing, visual-language navigation. Introduction Visual-language navigation (VLN) combines language understanding and visual perception to guide embodied agents according to natural language instructions~ zhang2025flexvln,tan2025sourcefree . In recent years, VLN studies such as CityNav~ lee2025citynav , OpenUAV~ wang2025openuav and OpenFly~ gao2026openfly have tightly integrated vision-language-action (VLA) models with perception and path-planning modules for aerial VLN. This integration enables natural language instruction parsing, semantic understanding of unfamiliar environments and autonomous navigation without prior maps, substantially improving aerial navigation in complex environments. To further improve VLN performance, studies such as FlightGPT~ cai2025flightgpt and FreeFly-Thinking~ zhou2026freeflythinking have introduced chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. By decomposing navigation tasks and modeling spatial relationships through multi-step logical reasoning, these methods strengthen long-horizon planning and autonomous decision-making in complex environments. As large-scale generative VLA models are adopted for aerial VLN, parameter counts and the computational cost of inference increasingly constrain practical deployment. On the one hand, navigation architectures built around large language models (LLMs) contain large numbers of unique parameters, imposing substantial model storage requirements. On the other hand, tokens in multimodal sequences serve distinct task roles, so uniformly processing all tokens through the full model depth may incur redundant computation. To address these challenges, we present ARC-VLN, an efficient aerial VLN framework based on adaptive recursive computing. The framework reuses weights across recursive stages of the LLM backbone to reduce the number of unique parameters. Building on this shared backbone, we introduce token-type-aware routing that allocates computational resources according to the roles of text, visual and action tokens in navigation. Our main contributions are as follows: (1) We propose a token-type-aware adaptive recursive computation framework for aerial VLN, which retains full recursive depth for text and action tokens while adaptively assigning exit depths to visual tokens. The sequences processed by subsequent recursive blocks are shortened through active-token compaction, reducing computation within the shared backbone. (2) We incorporate cross-entropy regularization against a uniform target into the auxiliary routing loss alongside load-balancing loss and z-loss, providing a non-zero corrective gradient to the corresponding logit even as the routing probability of an exit depth approaches zero. This regularization mitigates routing collapse to a single exit depth and promotes visual-token assignments across multiple exit depths. (3) On the evaluated OpenFly Test-Seen and Test-Unseen subsets, ARC-VLN uses approximately 2.7B unique language-backbone parameters and achieves the lowest navigation error and the highest success rate and success weighted by path length among the compared methods, together with greater computational efficiency. Related Work Visual-Language Navigation VLN connects language instructions with visual observations to guide navigation. Early work, such as the R2R benchmark introduced by Anderson et al.~ anderson2018vln , first integrated vision–language models with embodied navigation, accelerating the development of VLN models. Subsequent studies, such as REVERIE~ qi2020reverie and SOON~ zhu2021soon , further expanded the range of semantic granularity in instructions and increased target diversity. However, the topological assumptions of discrete indoor navigation graphs fundamentally limit the transferability of these approaches to unconstrained real-world environments. Aerial VLN benchmarks extend this setting towards outdoor scenes and more realistic flight. AerialVLN~ liu2023aerialvln establishes language-guided trajectory planning in continuous three-dimensional space, while OpenUAV~ wang2025openuav expands task coverage through aerial object search with varying levels of navigation assistance. CityNav~ lee2025citynav and OpenFly~ gao2026openfly further broaden semantic and environmental coverage through geography-aware instructions and greater scene diversity, respectively. To further improve understanding of complex scenes and long-horizon reasoning in VLN models, CoT-based methods~ lin2026evolvenav , including FlightGPT~ cai2025flightgpt and FreeFly-Thinking~ zhou2026freeflythinking , connect environmental perception with action generation through explicit intermediate reasoning. These advances have improved VLN performance and expanded its reasoning capability. However, reliance on large models introduces substantial storage demands and inference costs, posing challenges for real-time aerial VLN on resource-constrained platforms. Large Model Compression and Efficient Inference Parameter sharing reduces model storage by reusing weights across computational depth. Cross-layer sharing methods, exemplified by ALBERT~ lan2020albert and MobileLLM~ liu2024mobilellm , tie weights across layers or adjacent blocks to reduce unique parameters. Among recursive language models, Relaxed Recursive Transformers~ bae2025relaxed combine cross-layer parameter sharing with layer-wise low-rank adaptation to reduce parameter count while mitigating performance degradation. MoR~ bae2025mor combines parameter sharing with adaptive recursion for text tokens, improving both parameter and computational efficiency in language modeling. Dynamic computation reduces inference costs by allocating computational resources according to input requirements. Sequence-level early-exit methods, such as DeeBERT~ xin2020deebert and FastBERT~ liu2020fastbert , terminate inference based on prediction confidence but cannot independently assign processing depths to tokens within the same input. Token-level routing methods, including Mixture of Depths (MoD)~ raposo2024mod and p-MoD~ zhang2025pmod , provide finer-grained control by selecting which tokens participate in each layer’s computation. In addition, Mixture of Experts (MoE) controls computation through sparse expert activation. Across language models~ jiang2024mixtral,dai2024deepseekmoe and multimodal models~ lin2026moellava , this approach expands model capacity while activating only a subset of experts for each token. These methods improve computational efficiency through selective execution, but do not inherently reduce parameter storage, highlighting the need to address both costs in resource-constrained aerial VLN. To address storage and computational constraints in aerial VLN, we combine recursive parameter sharing with token-type-aware routing, retaining full recursive depth for instruction and action tokens while adaptively assigning computational depths to visual tokens. ARC-VLN framework Fig.~ fig:1 shows ARC-VLN, which tokenizes and embeds instructions into text representations. A visual encoder maps multiframe observations into the LLM hidden space. The input sequence comprises text tokens, visual tokens and an action prefix, in that order. Under causal attention, visual tokens can thus attend to preceding instructions. After an initial unshared Transformer layer, the sequence enters recursive blocks that reuse intermediate-layer weights. Before recursion, a router assigns visual tokens exit depths, while text and action tokens retain the full depth. Active-token compaction excludes exited visual tokens from subsequent blocks, shortening their input sequences. After recursive processing, all token representations are assembled and passed through a final unshared Transformer layer. The language model head then produces a probability distribution over action tokens, which is decoded into the navigation action for the current time step. The unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) executes the action and acquires new visual observations for the next navigation decision. The intermediate layers form recursive blocks, each containing layers with distinct parameter sets. For , corresponding layers across blocks share the same nn.Parameter objects through hard parameter tying. Each shared parameter set is initialized by averaging the corresponding pretrained weights. Parameter sharing reduces unique parameters while preserving the maximum effective computational depth. For the 32-layer LLaMA-2-7B model, setting retains the first and last layers as unshared layers. The 30 intermediate layers are reorganized into a block of 10 layers with distinct parameter sets, executed three times. This preserves an effective computational depth of 32 layers while reducing the number of unique decoder layers to 12. The number of unique parameters in the LLM backbone consequently decreases from approximately 6.7B to approximately 2.7B. title: Semantics First, Pixels Later: Mission-Driven Event Streams for Drone Video over Bandwidth-Starved Links
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures; includes the supplementary material as an appendix; a demonstration video is attached as an ancillary file
summary: A surveillance drone on a bandwidth-starved link cannot send the video its operator would need, yet the operator's questions are often not about pixels: did three people converge, when, and where? We study what should cross a link of 1 Mbps down to 1 kbps instead, and in what order. BPS, a behavior-primitive stream, sends semantics first and pixels later: it runs a detector and a tracker onboard and sends short records (25 bytes on average) of multi-frame events selected by a mission card of 16-125 bytes, ahead of positions and pictures. We measure it by what a ground-side language model answers from it, under a preregistered protocol with a held-out set, against H.265 read by the vision fine-tune of the same model, H.265 on which the ground runs our own perception, a stream of quantized tracks, and onboard captions. On the development set (84% of questions about convergence, mostly one location) the event stream answers 74.3% of questions at 0.13 kbps. A reader that receives nothing answers 57.4%, and the video reader 59.6% at 100 kbps and 64.7% on the source frames. When the ground instead runs our perception on the video, video matches the stream at 100 kbps, about 800 times the stream's rate, and falls behind at 64 kbps and below. A track stream matches it at 96 times the bytes and loses 0.03 at 17 times. On held-out data the result is weaker: with events taken from annotated tracks, an oracle, the stream beats H.265 at 100 kbps (+0.13), but with onboard perception it does not (+0.01 [-0.04, +0.06]) and is no better than receiving nothing. Sent alone through emulated links the event records answer 0.739 at 1 Mbps and still 0.724 at 0.3 kbps; an every-frame track stream holds down to 1 kbps and video with ground-side perception down to about 100 kbps. On a Jetson Orin Nano the unchanged pipeline runs at 4.5 fps and misses most events.

Introduction sec:intro Small unmanned aircraft carry cameras whose output the ground often cannot receive: tactical radios, satellite back-haul and contested spectrum deliver from about a megabit per second down to a few kilobits. A codec with low-latency settings can still push a small picture through ten kilobits per second in time ( ), but a small picture is not an answer. The operator often asks about behavior over time: whether a vehicle stopped and stayed, whether people converged on one spot, when a quiet area came alive. This paper asks what should be sent instead of video when the answer, not the picture, is what the ground needs. Our answer, (behavior-primitive stream), moves the perception onboard and sends its conclusions. A detector and a tracker run on the aircraft, a streaming engine turns tracks into multi-frame behavior primitives, and a mission card tells it which primitives, classes and regions matter. A scheduler sends event records of a few tens of bytes ahead of everything else, so the stream degrades gracefully: a narrowing link costs the ground its pictures first, then positions, and the events last. An event is opened as soon as the engine can decide it and closed when it ends, so the ground learns of a convergence about two seconds after it starts. Sending conclusions instead of evidence is not new: edge analytics systems filter frames by relevance~ canel2019scaling,wang2018bandwidth , cooperative perception sends object lists~ thandavarayan2020generation , semantic communication transmits task features~ guo2025videoqasc,shao2024task , and caption or event-log representations let a language model answer video questions~ zhang2024simple,dixit2026semantic . What is missing is a measurement: how much does a symbolic event stream lose or gain against the video it replaces, against simpler things a drone could send, and on emulated links from 1\,Mbps to 1\,kbps? We contribute that measurement as much as a method: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] A transmission code for aerial behavior. Track-level primitives sent as open and closed records of 14--53 bytes, compact mission cards, and a byte-counted packet format with a strict-priority scheduler and 256-byte fragmentation ( ). Seven primitives are defined and six run onboard; our data tests one of them, convergence, at scale. A preregistered protocol with matched readers and strong baselines. Questions are answered by a text-only language model reading the stream and by the vision fine-tune of the same base model reading H.265 video. Because that video reader turns out to use little of the bitrate, we add baselines that isolate the code from the reader: the video reader on source frames, video on which the ground runs our own perception, and a stream of quantized tracks. Hypotheses were preregistered, and a held-out set with its mission cards stayed sealed until the pipeline was frozen ( ). Findings, positive and negative. On development data the event stream at 0.13\,kbps answers more questions than the video reader does at any rate, though about three quarters of its margin over H.265 at 100\,kbps comes from questions where nothing happened. When the ground runs our perception on the video, video needs about 100\,kbps to support the same answers, and a track stream needs 96 times the stream's bytes (17 times at a loss of 0.03). On the held-out set, tested in two rounds, the stream built from annotated tracks beats H.265 at 100\,kbps, but the stream from onboard perception does not, and it is no better than a reader that receives nothing. Through links from 1\,Mbps down to 0.3\,kbps the event records lose 0.015 of accuracy, an every-frame track stream holds to 1\,kbps, and the event records tolerate 20 packet loss. On a Jetson Orin Nano the unchanged pipeline runs at 4.5\,fps; at the frame rate it can keep up with, event recall falls from 0.69 to 0.28 ( ). title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
summary: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over $π_{0.5}$) at 92.7 ms latency.

title: TopSDF: Topological Signed Distance Field for High-Quality Triangle Mesh Extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated its effectiveness for photorealistic novel view synthesis. However, extracting clean, watertight, explicit surface meshes from 3DGS remains a critical challenge. Previous methods approximate geometry via discrete Marching Tetrahedra, where each grid vertex is assigned a single scalar signed distance value. At complex geometric boundaries and thin structures, this suboptimal parameterization forces severe compromises across shared vertices, causing gradient collisions and geometric frustration. Furthermore, existing optimization objectives neglect element shape conditioning, producing degenerate triangles. We introduce TopSDF, a framework that models the signed distance state as a multivariate Gaussian random field. By learning latent topological covariances across tetrahedral vertices, our formulation expands local degrees of freedom for SDF estimates, allowing the candidate mesh vertices to be placed flexibly along the bipolar edges in the tetrahedra as driven by such topological correlation. Concurrently, we directly integrate variational meshing energies into the joint optimization, coupled with an energy-driven Gaussian densification strategy to improve triangle mesh quality. Our experiments across Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and ScanNet++ show that TopSDF achieves state-of-the-art mesh-based novel view rendering (+0.86 dB PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360) and triangle-mesh quality (from 0.37 to 0.49 aspect ratio).

The bottom row displays the corresponding extracted surface normal maps, illustrating reconstructed geometric structures, sharp boundary silhouettes, and topological surface continuity. fig:teaser Introduction Reconstructing highly detailed 3D models from multi-view photographs is a long-standing challenge. State-of-the-art methods are based on radiance fields and novel view synthesis (NVS) using NeRF~ nerf (Neural Radiance Field) and 3D Gaussian Splatting~ 3dgs (3DGS). Primitive-based radiance fields like 3DGS~ 3dgs capture intricate micro-details and render in real-time, but their discrete point-based representation implies the lack of a straightforward pathway for extracting an accurate and high-quality triangle mesh. These methods optimize a radiance field representation by minimizing photometric losses between rendered images and their corresponding ground truth views. To obtain surface geometry, it is necessary to apply mesh extraction as a post-processing or concurrent step~ milo , which predicts surface location and orientation for mesh conversion from the learned radiance fields. Recent methods extract meshes by first approximating signed distance fields (SDFs) using depth and normal rendering~ gw, radegs, gggs and then obtain triangle meshes using a marching tetrahedra algorithm. Hybrid models~ milo, gof, sof, 2dgs, come, gggs additionally use mesh-to-Gaussians alignment losses and appearance or geometry regularization terms. However, a fundamental limitation of these methods is their reliance on naive tetrahedral grids and signed distance values at discrete grid vertices, which comes at the expense of flexibility for placing the mesh vertices during marching tetrahedra procedure. Each grid vertex only stores a single distance value~ gw, come, milo , leading to compromised approximation of the within a one-ring neighborhood, and hence degradations in complex geometry regions, thin structures, or fine details. Acknowledging these topological relationships allows us to determine how the underlying surface is influenced by surrounding local grid vertices, from which the placement of the surface mesh vertices could be flexibly enhanced. To learn these correlations, we propose to model the SDF in a tetrahedra as a Gaussian random field, where we can the topological correlation using covariance matrices. We construct topological energy as the negative log-likelihood of the SDF state. To derive this closed-form solution, we leverage Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space~ treves2006topological (RKHS) to derive an equivalent form of the log-likelihood, and then use the Representer Theorem~ represent_theory to obtain the minimizer. This formulation allows us to estimate SDF updates at an arbitrary 3D point, which has the form of a weighted linear combination of feature correlations among grid vertices' SDF. We integrate this closed-form SDF estimates to the training of 3DGS, allowing the joint learning of 3D Gaussian attributes and tetrahedra SDFs for novel view synthesis and triangle mesh extraction. We demonstrate that the closed-form solution leads to more accurate reconstruction, state-of-the-art mesh-based novel view synthesis, and improves the convergence rate of the joint optimization of 3D Gaussians and mesh extraction. Concurrently, another vital yet systematically neglected factor in 3DGS mesh extraction is triangle mesh quality. Existing pipelines yield irregular, sliver-filled surface triangulations that require expensive, lossy post-processing, leading to poor quality of mesh-based novel view synthesis. We propose to leverage variational meshing energies~ variational_tetrahedral_meshing, odt for regularising tetrahedral element shapes and dihedral angles, resulting in more regular triangle meshes during the joint optimization. Additionally, we use such energies to guide the densification during 3DGS training. We perform energy integration at each 3D Gaussian from the corresponding tetrahedra to identify Gaussians that produce elongated triangles and subsequently split these Gaussians, therefore effectively dicing elongated triangles toward more equilateral ones. In summary, our core contributions are: We conduct extensive experiments and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on mesh-based novel view synthesis (NVS), surface reconstruction, and triangle mesh quality on multiple datasets under diverse settings, along with comprehensive ablation and empirical studies validating our theoretical findings. Related Work Novel View Synthesis. While Neural Radiance Fields~ nerf (NeRF) pioneered neural rendering using MLP-parameterized ray-marching---later improved in antialiasing~ mipnerf360, mipnerf and speed~ instantngp, tensorf, plenoxels ---3D Gaussian Splatting~ 3dgs, ren2025fastgs fundamentally revolutionized novel view synthesis by replacing volumetric integration with rasterized Gaussian primitives for real-time performance. Although concurrent extensions progressively optimize 3DGS for scale~ 3dgsmarkov, taming3dgs and image fidelity~ mip-splatting , these visual-synthesis techniques systematically neglect the challenge of recovering clean, explicit triangle surface meshes. Triangle-based approaches~ trianglesplating, meshsplatting, demtrianglesplatting enhance rendering quality using an unconstrained triangle soup rather than an explicit manifold mesh. Isosurface Extraction. Isosurfacing methods have a long history that has been built on different domains, including Delaunay Triangulation~ delaunay1934sphere, vism, tetweave , particle simulation~ witkinsurvey , and active contours~ cohensurvey . Reconstruction algorithms based on Marching algorithms have a limitation of sub-optimality, where the reconstruction is highly localized in space, with suboptimal assumptions about the input samples. In this research, we address this sub-optimality problem by relying on the topological feature assigned at each grid vertex, where the candidate vertices are placed more flexibly, enabling the capture of complex surface geometry where needed, without over-resolving ordinary smooth regions. In the past, some marching methods allowed placing multiple bipolar vertices along a single bipolar edge~ yamazaki_nomanifold, wywill_polygonalization . However, these approaches do not produce manifold triangle meshes and rely heavily on deterministic algorithms, lacking differentiability. Recently, Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra~ smt follows this spirit that allows the surface mesh to intersect multiple times along a single edge of a tetrahedron, which not only resolves the complex geometry structure, but also reduces the number of tetrahedra needed for constructing the volume grid. However, the applicability of Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra (SMT) is limited in 3DGS since there is no explicit surface mesh for multiple sampling along tetrahedral edges. Furthermore, to match the results of 3DGS and the extracted mesh, the mesh needs to be differentially rasterized as well, while SMT relies on discrete marching, restricting the differentiability. Another branch of research focuses on adaptive grid refinement, which helps resolve the fine features~ pis, mdc, flexicubes ; however, these approaches are difficult to avoid the cracks transitioning between levels of hierarchy (i.e. relying on octree grid), and break the fixed, regular layout needed for high-performance parallel implementation. For example, FlexiCubes proposed a differentiable method that relies on Dual Marching Cubes~ dmc , producing a non-manifold, self-intersecting triangle mesh. Conversely, our method extracts a manifold mesh from 3DGS, resolving the fine details. Surface Extractions from 3D Gaussians. While implicit SDF-based approaches~ li2023neuralangelo, neus, volsdf produce highly consistent geometries, they require prohibitively long optimization periods. Alternatively, mesh baking techniques~ bog, bakedsdf rely on a two-stage extraction process that accelerates rendering but compromises true geometric accuracy. Lastly, discrete mesh optimization~ Munkberg_2022_CVPR, flexicubes, tetweave performs well on single objects but lacks the scalability needed for complex environments. Leveraging 3DGS efficiency, recent surface-extraction methods take two main routes. Hybrid approaches co-optimize Gaussians with implicit fields~ neus, gaussianudf, 3dgsr, gsdf, 3dgs-sdf-infer , but MLP bottlenecks restrict their scalability. Alternatively, direct regularization methods modify the primitives or constraints: 2DGS~ 2dgs adopts lower-dimensional primitives; TopoSurfel~ toposurfel initializes Gaussians with Planar-based Gaussian Splatting~ pgsr (PGSR), then conducts post-training with Gaussian surfels; RaDe-GS~ radegs , PGSR~ pgsr , Quadratic Gaussian Splatting~ quad3dgs , and VCR-GauS~ vcr-gaus enforce multi-view and rendering consistency; while SuGaR~ sugar , GOF~ gof , and SOF~ sof introduce custom extraction pipelines. title: Towards Probabilistically Safe Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Deployment on Humanoid and Aerial Robots
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to acquire complex skills, but standard RL formulations do not guarantee that learned policies satisfy safety constraints, which limits their use in safety-critical settings. Existing safe RL methods with provable guarantees typically support only restricted classes of constraints and require unbiased estimators of the objective and constraint functions, which prevents their direct integration with state-of-the-art algorithms such as proximal policy optimization (PPO). In this paper, we extend the recently introduced robust safe gradient flow-based reinforcement learning (RSGF-RL) framework to overcome these limitations. Our formulation accommodates a general class of trajectory-level safety constraints, including chance constraints such as collision avoidance with a prescribed probability, and our analysis allows for biased value and gradient estimators. We show that, with high probability, the constraint violation throughout training is bounded by the estimator bias plus a term that vanishes as the number of rollouts grows, and decays to this level if the initial policy is unsafe. We also establish the convergence properties of the iterates to approximate KKT points of the original safe RL problem. Finally, we show that RSGF-RL implemented with PPO-style estimates enables zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body control policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone.

Safe reinforcement learning, model-free reinforcement learning, humanoid robots. Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful tool for enabling robots to acquire a wide range of complex skills~ JH-JL-AD-DB-VT-VK-MH:19,OA-MA-BB:20,EK-LB-AL-MM-VK-DS:23 . However, standard RL algorithms primarily optimize task performance, without guaranteeing that the learned policies satisfy safety constraints, either during training or after deployment. This lack of formal safety guarantees remains a major obstacle to the adoption of RL in safety-critical applications. Motivated by this challenge, a growing body of work on safe RL seeks to optimize policy performance subject to prescribed safety specifications~ LB-MG-AWH-ZY-SZ-JP-APS:22,JG-FF:15,SG-LY-YD-GC-FW-JW-AK:24 . A common approach formulates safe RL as a constrained policy optimization problem, where the constraint requires the expected cumulative value of a safety-related cost to remain below a prescribed threshold~ JA-DH-AT-PA:17,YC-MG-LJ-MP:17,SP-LC-MCF-AR:19 . Several algorithms have been proposed to solve such problems, including primal-dual methods~ SP-MCF-LFOC-AR:23,DD-KZ-TB-MJ:20 , constrained policy optimization (CPO)~ JA-DH-AT-PA:17 , projection-based constrained policy optimization (PCPO)~ TY-JR-KN-PJR:20 , and state augmentation~ AS-AIC-TJ-ZW-DHM-JW-HA:22 . Despite their empirical success, these methods generally do not guarantee constraint satisfaction throughout the learning process, and their convergence guarantees rely on restrictive assumptions. An alternative approach enforces safety at the level of individual control actions, typically by combining an unconstrained RL policy with a safety filter based on control barrier functions (CBFs)~ FPB-LB-APS:25,MA-RB-RE-BK-SN-UT:18,RC-GO-RMM-JWB:19,LY-BW-MdS-ADA:25,KH-HH-JFF:24 . While such methods can provide guarantees on the safety of the resulting closed-loop system, they do not directly address the problem of optimizing a policy subject to safety constraints. In this paper, we adopt the constrained policy optimization perspective, building on the recently introduced robust safe gradient flow-based reinforcement learning (RSGF-RL) framework~ PM-AM-JC:25-l4dc,PM-AM-JC:25-arxiv . RSGF-RL provides convergence guarantees to critical points of the constrained RL problem while maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout the learning process with high probability. However, several limitations restrict its integration with state-of-the-art RL algorithms and modern robotic systems: Limited class of safety constraints. The existing framework considers constraints that require that the expected value of cumulative safety costs remains below a given threshold. However, many safety specifications arising in robotics are naturally expressed as probabilistic constraints, such as requiring that the probability of colliding with an obstacle during an episode remains below a prescribed threshold, which are not equivalent to the expected cumulative cost formulations. Restrictive assumptions. The theoretical guarantees of RSGF-RL as provided in~ PM-AM-JC:25-l4dc,PM-AM-JC:25-arxiv require unbiased estimators of the objective and constraint functions and their gradients. In contrast, modern RL algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)~ JS-FW-PD-AR-OK:17 , Soft Actor-Critic (SAC)~ TH-AZ-PA-SL:18 , and DreamerV3~ DH-JP-JB-TL:25 employ estimation procedures that can introduce bias. This limits the integration of RSGF-RL with state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Additionally, the conditions under which~ PM-AM-JC:25-arxiv establishes convergence of RSGF-RL (such as the requirement that the estimated RSGF-RL update law converges to the true one with probability one) are quite restrictive. Lack of hardware validation. Previous evaluations of RSGF-RL have been limited to relatively simple simulation environments, leaving open whether its theoretical guarantees can be combined with the computational demands and practical challenges of RL policies for real robotic systems. In this paper, we develop an extension of RSGF-RL that addresses these shortcomings, and show that the resulting algorithm can be used to train RL policies for a variety of different tasks, with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. Our contributions are as follows. First, we extend RSGF-RL to a general class of trajectory-level constraints, which includes cumulative cost and probabilistic constraints. Similarly to the Policy Gradient Theorem~ RSS-AGB:18 , we show that gradient estimates for this class of constraints follow from the classical likelihood-ratio method in~ PWG:90 ; Second, we show that, with high probability, the constraint violation of the RSGF-RL iterates is bounded by the estimator bias plus a sampling-error term that vanishes as the number of rollouts used for value and gradient estimation grows. If the initial policy is safe, this bound holds throughout training; if it is unsafe, the violation decays to this level. We also show that, almost surely, the RSGF-RL iterates have a limit point that is an approximate KKT point of the constrained RL problem, with the approximation level again given by the estimator bias plus a term that vanishes as . Third, we show that RSGF-RL implemented with (biased) PPO gradient estimates enables zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body motor skills on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone. Some assumptions of our theoretical results are not met in the practical implementation of RSGF-RL used in these experiments.
