title: Real-Time Air Pollution Monitoring and Tracking via Adaptive Density-Driven Multi-UAV Coordination
summary: Accurate and timely air pollution monitoring and tracking are critical for protecting public health and supporting effective environmental management. This paper presents an adaptive Density-Driven Control (D$^2$C) framework for coordinating multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to track and map dynamically evolving pollutant distributions. The proposed framework extends the D$^2$C strategy to guide UAV trajectories based on predictive pollutant propagation and dynamically updated reference densities. A sensor-driven surrogate plume update mechanism is employed, in which reference samples are propagated using locally sensed concentration gradients and wind estimates through gradient attraction, wind advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion, enabling UAVs to maintain an accurate spatio-temporal representation of the pollution field. The framework utilizes a coordinated structure where individual UAVs share their local measurements with a central coordinator to maintain a unified set of reference samples, facilitating systematic target allocation and trajectory planning. Simulation results under both mild and strong wind conditions demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of Sinkhorn distance. Specifically, in scenarios where the plume drifts beyond a fixed monitoring domain under high-velocity, time-varying wind fields, the tested baseline methods fail to maintain tracking, whereas the proposed D$^2$C framework successfully adapts to the evolving distribution. These findings highlight D$^2$C as an efficient and resilient solution for atmospheric monitoring in dynamic environments.
full_text: Real-Time Air Pollution Monitoring and Tracking via Adaptive Density-Driven Multi-UAV Coordination Julian~Martinez, Ruchika~Singh, Mohammad~Afrazi, and~Kooktae~Lee Accurate and timely air pollution monitoring and tracking are critical for protecting public health and supporting effective environmental management. This paper presents an adaptive Density-Driven Control (D C) framework for coordinating multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to track and map dynamically evolving pollutant distributions. The proposed framework extends the D C strategy to guide UAV trajectories based on predictive pollutant propagation and dynamically updated reference densities. A sensor-driven surrogate plume update mechanism is employed, in which reference samples are propagated using locally sensed concentration gradients and wind estimates through gradient attraction, wind advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion, enabling UAVs to maintain an accurate spatio-temporal representation of the pollution field. The framework utilizes a coordinated structure where individual UAVs share their local measurements with a central coordinator to maintain a unified set of reference samples, facilitating systematic target allocation and trajectory planning. Simulation results under both mild and strong wind conditions demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of Sinkhorn distance. Specifically, in scenarios where the plume drifts beyond a fixed monitoring domain under high-velocity, time-varying wind fields, the tested baseline methods fail to maintain tracking, whereas the proposed D C framework successfully adapts to the evolving distribution. These findings highlight D C as an efficient and resilient solution for atmospheric monitoring in dynamic environments. Introduction sec:introduction Air pollution poses significant threats to human health and the environment manisalidis2020environmental . The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that it causes approximately seven million premature deaths annually manisalidis2020environmental . Major pollutants include particulate matter (PM), nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulfur dioxide (SO ), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and carbon dioxide (CO ). These substances are associated with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases, as well as acid rain, photochemical smog, and climate change. Ground-based stations are commonly used to assess air quality in urban and industrial areas. Although ground-based stations provide continuous local measurements, their fixed deployment restricts the area that can be observed saini2025robot, carotenuto2023low . The problem becomes more pronounced as wind, temperature inversions, and atmospheric turbulence alter the direction and rate of pollutant dispersion sorek2020strategies . As a result, the movement of pollution plumes may not be adequately captured by measurements from stationary networks. Satellite remote sensing offers a means of extending atmospheric observations beyond the locations covered by ground stations. Instruments such as MODIS and Sentinel provide measurements across extensive geographical regions holloway2021satellite, kaplan2020space . However, their spatial resolution and observation intervals restrict the detection of localized and rapidly changing pollution events. In addition, cloud cover and atmospheric interference can lead to gaps in the collected data stratoulias2024recent, holloway2021satellite . Thus, satellite observations provide broad coverage but remain limited in their ability to follow plume evolution at short time intervals. UAVs equipped with environmental sensors can obtain pollutant measurements at locations that are not covered by fixed monitoring stations kabir2021wildlife, kokate2023review, jaron2024assessment, liang2024integrated, facinelli2019cooperative, sharma2025unmanned . Deploying several UAVs over the same region makes it possible to examine the pollution field from different locations. In this context, pollution monitoring refers to estimating the spatial distribution of pollutant concentrations, whereas pollution tracking concerns the temporal changes in plume position and distribution. Both functions are important when investigating pollution phenomena that vary across space and time. A major issue, however, lies in the way measurement routes are assigned. Many existing coordination schemes prescribe the flight paths in advance, commonly using lawnmower or grid-based patterns galceran2013survey, gaalfalk2021sensitive . Once assigned, these paths provide little flexibility for responding to variations in pollutant levels or plume movement. UAVs may therefore spend measurement time in regions that no longer reflect the areas of interest. Allowing flight paths to change with the observed data is consequently an important consideration in multi-UAV coordination kabir2021wildlife . To address these challenges, this paper extends the Density-Driven Control (D C) framework kabir2021wildlife, lee2022density, afrazi2025density, afrazi2025enhanced to enable adaptive multi-UAV coordination for real-time air pollution monitoring and tracking. Although the Density-Driven Optimal Control (D OC) further improved the performance of D C by considering the optimality, they are mostly limited to the linear time-invariant (LTI) dynamics seo2025tcst, seo2025density, lee2025connectivity, lee2026tac, lee2026automatica,lee2026ai . Thus, D OC may not be directly applicable to air pollution monitoring missions, where the mobile platforms such as UAVs have nonlinear dynamics. The proposed approach leverages Optimal Transport (OT) theory villani2009optimal to dynamically guide UAVs toward regions having higher pollutant densities, effectively coupling predictive propagation with data-driven adaptation. The framework maintains a dynamically evolving reference density by updating reference samples with local concentration gradients and wind measurements. This enables UAV trajectories to adapt seamlessly to changes in the pollutant distribution. To achieve this in practice, each UAV uses onboard gas and particulate sensors to obtain localized, point-wise pollutant measurements rohi2020autonomous,al2023bayesian , together with local wind information. Each UAV collects local wind and concentration-gradient measurements and sends them to a central coordinator. The coordinator uses these inputs to update a common reference distribution. Its evolution is governed by four components: gradient attraction, wind advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion. The updated density distribution determines the targets for a separate motion-control stage, which generates trajectories while accounting for UAV dynamics. We evaluate the proposed centralized method against two alternatives: a prediction-only propagation model and a distributed ergodic coverage approach using Gaussian-process field estimation mantovani2026distributed . The latter coordinates multiple agents by matching the time-averaged spatial distribution of their trajectories to a time-varying target distribution. Comparing against these baselines allows us to isolate and evaluate the distinct performance benefits of our measurement-informed reference updates and centralized coordination over open-loop predictions and distributed ergodic alternatives. The main contributions of this work are threefold: 1) A centralized density-driven coordination framework for multi-UAV pollution monitoring and tracking, in which a common time-varying reference distribution is used to coordinate individual UAV targets and allocate coverage weights across the monitored region. This formulation enables multiple UAVs to distribute their sensing activities according to the spatial characteristics of the pollution field; 2) A measurement-informed reference update mechanism that incorporates locally sensed concentration gradients and wind measurements into the evolution of the shared reference distribution. By accounting for gradient attraction, wind-driven advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion, the proposed mechanism adjusts the reference samples according to changes in plume distribution and provides updated targets for UAV motion control; 3) A numerical evaluation of the integrated sensing, reference-update, and trajectory-control framework under spatially varying wind conditions. The proposed centralized approach is compared with a prediction-only propagation model and a distributed ergodic coverage method based on Gaussian-process field estimation, allowing the effects of measurement-based adaptation and centralized coordination on pollution monitoring and tracking performance to be examined. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the D C formulation and the centralized monitoring problem. Section III describes the pollutant propagation model, Section IV develops UAV sensing and reference-sample propagation, and Section V presents the integrated multi-UAV algorithm. For air quality monitoring, this distribution can be designed to assign greater sampling priority to areas with elevated pollution levels. Its construction may incorporate satellite observations, meteorological forecasts, industrial emission records, and ground-based measurements. While satellite data provide information on regional pollutant dispersion, emission inventories offer insight into their possible origins. Considering both sources in the reference density allows the identification of relevant regions and the allocation of UAV sampling accordingly. The use of UAVs also changes how environmental measurements are collected compared with conventional fixed ground monitoring systems yang2017real, bakirci2024enhancing . Rather than relying exclusively on measurements from predetermined locations, mobile platforms can obtain observations at different positions as pollution conditions evolve. Incorporating updated environmental information into D C allows the spatial allocation of sensing activity to change accordingly. title: Cache or Denoise Less? Residual Reuse in a Flow-Matching World Action Model
comment: Honorable Mention at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI (EEAI). Code and data available at https://github.com/gabhinav001/cache-or-denoise-less
summary: Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step. Cross-cycle caches such as C$^3$ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear. We compare the two in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter world action model, on LIBERO-Goal. Two uncached steps keep the success of ten: on all 500 initial states they are non-inferior within two percentage points, for one checkpoint and noise seed. Under PyTorch's default compile mode, they also cut a replanning call on an RTX A6000 from 202 to 92 ms. This leaves little room for caching. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11--14% of a call by our cost model. Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM's current time shift, C$^3$ache's eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. Resampling the noise on every call cost caches covering 60% or more of the path 14--40 points. These results argue for fewer-step baselines and for testing reuse under the deployed sampler and noise settings. We release our evaluation harness, logs and a checklist.

Introduction Diffusion and flow-matching policies~ diffusionpolicy2023,pi0,pi05 and world action models~ fastwam2026,dreamzero2026 produce each action chunk by integrating a learned flow from noise, one network evaluation per step. Distillation~ consistencypolicy2024,onestepdp2024,flashwam2026 and coarser schedules~ sbintuitions2026 cut the number of steps. Caches reuse computation within a denoising trajectory~ deepcache2024,wimbauer2024cache,teacache2025,magcache2025,taylorseer2025,bac2026,efficientvla2025 , across chunks~ falcon2025,streamingdp2024,xcache2026 or across control cycles~ vlacache2025,c3ache2026 . ~ c3ache2026 is a cross-cycle cache for Fast-WAM. A refresh call runs all ten steps and stores the residual that the action transformer adds at each of the first seven or eight. Until the next refresh, every call adds the stored residuals instead of recomputing those steps and runs only the rest in full. title: Drone Navigation for Fast, Safe Emergency Response
comment: Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
summary: In 2025, there was a total of 358 weather-related disasters worldwide affecting millions of people. For unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to autonomously aid these people, they need to be able to navigate around complex obstacles and reach their destinations to deliver supplies or quickly locate survivors in disaster-stricken areas. Our research addresses this need by providing a method to compute minimum-time trajectories in real time while providing guarantees of obstacle avoidance along the trajectory. Previous approaches treat the problem of computing time-optimal trajectories without considering obstacle avoidance. Our work not only includes obstacle avoidance constraints, but also improves overall mission time for navigation. We define mission time as the sum of planning time and traversal time. In time-sensitive emergencies, rapid trajectory planning is essential to ensure the prompt delivery of critical medical aid. As such, we consider the combined planning and traversal time as the key metric for how quickly the vehicle can reach a survivor. We show a sample mission in Fig. 1 where the quadrotor navigates through multiple canyon-like obstacles to deliver aid; during most of this trajectory, it is applying the near-maximum thrust.

For unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to autonomously aid these people, they need to be able to navigate around complex obstacles and reach their destinations to deliver supplies or quickly locate survivors in disaster-stricken areas. Our research addresses this need by providing a method to compute minimum-time trajectories in real time while providing guarantees of obstacle avoidance along the trajectory. Our work not only includes obstacle avoidance constraints, but also improves overall mission time for navigation. We define mission time as the sum of planning time and traversal time. In time-sensitive emergencies, rapid trajectory planning is essential to ensure the prompt delivery of critical medical aid. As such, we consider the combined planning and traversal time as the key metric for how quickly the vehicle can reach a survivor. We show a sample mission in Fig. fig:intro where the quadrotor navigates through multiple canyon-like obstacles to deliver aid; during most of this trajectory, it is applying the near-maximum thrust. Introduction Aerial robots have seen success in search and rescue~ Michael_JFR and the delivery of vital medical supplies. These tasks need to be accomplished as quickly as possible while safely navigating obstacles in complex environments. Our research focuses on generating time-optimal trajectories in real time while also respecting safety constraints and accounting for drag. A key challenge is that time-optimal trajectory planning methods can require multiple seconds [5], [6] of computation each planning instance. Long trajectory-computation times can substantially delay mission completion, even when the resulting flight path is fast. For this reason, practical performance must account for both traversal time and planning time. Other works have addressed this problem by using a simplified model such as a point-mass model (PMM). For example, recent work teissing2024real uses separate acceleration limits for each axis to compute minimum-time trajectories in real time. However, constraining acceleration independently along each axis does not fully utilize the vehicle’s collective thrust capability and can therefore produce suboptimal trajectories. This simplification can produce unnecessarily conservative and therefore slower trajectories. Our work seeks to bridge the gap between accurate methods with long computation times and fast methods that rely on simplifying approximations. We propose a time-optimal trajectory formulation that accounts for drag, actuator thrust limits, and obstacle avoidance while retaining the computational speed needed for real-time planning. Building on the framework proposed by Mao et al.~ mao2026time , this work uses Bernstein polynomials to formulate our time-optimal trajectory, model drag dynamics, and formulate the thrust constraint. Using Bernstein polynomial basis functions allows the problem to be solved more quickly, but polynomial representations are often considered poorly suited for time-optimal trajectories. This is because, in a straight line, the time-optimal trajectory exhibits bang-bang behavior, whose discontinuous switching cannot be represented exactly by a finite-order polynomial. Our method addresses this issue by representing the trajectory as a sequence of polynomial splines and optimizng the endpoints over the coefficients. This representation allows our method, as shown in Fig.~ fig:intro to approximate bang-bang trajectories while incorporating drag and multi-axis collective-thrust constraints. In this paper, we provide the following key contributions: We provide a time-optimal trajectory-generation method that considers both collective-thrust and obstacle-avoidance constraints using Bernstein polynomials. We propose a method to modify a polynomial trajectory representation to incorporate drag dynamics directly into the optimization. This method is applicable to both Bernstein and regular polynomials. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior mission time compared with other state-of-the-art-methods teissing2024real, foehn2021time when both planning time and traversal time are considered. Related Works sec:related-works Existing works on UAV path-planning and computing trajectories can be divided into two main families of approaches. The first approach is to utilize sampling methods such as Probablistic Road Maps~ kavraki1996probabilistic , Randomly-Exploring Random Trees~ lavalle2001randomized and its variations ~ webb2013kinodynamic . These methods typically sample the search space given an initial and final state, which is progressively explored until a solution is reached. While effective for small maps, they quickly become computationally expensive as the search space dimension grows. Moreover, the trajectories computed are not necessarily minimum-time. The second approach is optimization based, such as in ~ mellinger2011minimum and ~ hargraves1987direct , where polynomials are utilized to represent continuous time trajectories. This is made possible by the fact that quadrotor dynamics can be formulated as differentially flat systems, thus a trajectory in x, y, z and yaw dimensions can be sampled from these polynomials. However, these approaches neither take obstacle avoidance nor time optimization into account, and can result in the computation of suboptimal or potentially dangerous trajectories. There have also been many proposed solutions to the problem of computing time-optimal trajectories. Li et al~ lai2006time proposes a solution that is time-optimal in discretized, but not continuous, time space. Pontryagin's Minimum Principle (PMP) requires that a truly time optimal trajectory should have bang-bang characteristics in velocity, acceleration and/or thrust ~ ritz2011quadrocopter . Following this, Foehn et al ~ foehn2021time proposed an approach that has served as a baseline for time-optimal trajectory generation, through the concept of complementary progress constraints (CPC). However, a well-known drawback of this method is the long computation time, in minutes or hours, thus relegating it to be an offline method. A real-time approach was proposed by Teissing et al.~ teissing2024real , where velocity esimates are initialized and optimized at the waypoint positions. While time-optimal, these approaches neglect the consideration of collision avoidance. Multiple methods have been proposed to solve for the minimum time trajectory given a set of obstacles. Penicka et al.~ penicka2022minimum proposed an approach to generate safe and optimal trajectories by time using a sampling-based strategy to select the best set of velocity states. However, the computational complexity increases quadratically as the number of samples per waypoint increases, hence necessitating the inclusion of a receding horizon of waypoints by Romero et al.~ romero2022time for real-time replanning. Spedicato et al.~ spedicato2017minimum proposed a framework for computing minimum-time trajectories through a fixed-horizon spatial formulation, rather than directly optimizing the time variable. However, this reformulation is done using the Frenet-Serret frame, which introduces several complexities, such as nonlinearities and singularites. Furthermore, the use of Euler angles to represent orientation could potentially result in suboptimal solutions. Finally, Mao et al.~ mao2026time , whose work our approach is built on, shows that Bernstein polynomial based trajectories are competitive with popular baseline methods like MINCO ~ zhou2022swarm ~ wang2022geometrically in terms of compute time, while also guaranteeing that safety constraints are respected. However, the previous approach directly constrained velocity and acceleration along each dimension. This constraint formulation was shown to be suboptimal for generating minimum-time trajectories by ~ meyer2023top and ~ teissing2024real . Instead, we constrain the thrust norm represented by a 3D sphere, allowing us to utilize the maximum collective thrust of the drone and generate trajectories that are faster than those computed from constraining acceleration and velocity per axis. title: DiffWAM: Learning World Action Model from Consecutive Visual Difference
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as an important paradigm in robot learning, jointly predicting future scene states and robot actions from current observations and instructions. However, future states entangle task-related changes with large amounts of task-irrelevant content, such as static backgrounds, which weakens the model's ability to capture changes relevant to task execution. To address this, we propose Difference World Action Model (DiffWAM), a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances world representations by jointly learning future-state prediction and consecutive visual difference prediction. We define consecutive visual differences as differences between the latent representations of consecutive observations, providing an explicit learning signal for temporal variation. The framework comprises a World Expert for future frame prediction, an Action Expert for action generation, and a Diff Expert for predicting these latent differences along the trajectory. A structured unidirectional attention mask conditions the Diff, World, and Action Experts solely on the current-frame representation while blocking attention between experts. This design allows both the World and Diff Experts to be removed during inference, introducing no additional inference overhead. DiffWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and substantially improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks. Specifically, it attains average success rates of 98.8%, 92.65%, and 88.3%, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline (i.e., FastWAM) by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points, respectively.

However, future states entangle task-related changes with large amounts of task-irrelevant content, such as static backgrounds, which weakens the model's ability to capture changes relevant to task execution. To address this, we propose Difference World Action Model ( ), a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances world representations by jointly learning future-state prediction and consecutive visual difference prediction. We define consecutive visual differences as differences between the latent representations of consecutive observations, providing an explicit learning signal for temporal variation. The framework comprises a World Expert for future frame prediction, an Action Expert for action generation, and a Diff Expert for predicting these latent differences along the trajectory. A structured unidirectional attention mask conditions the Diff, World, and Action Experts solely on the current-frame representation while blocking attention between experts. This design allows both the World and Diff Experts to be removed during inference, introducing no additional inference overhead. achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and substantially improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks. Specifically, it attains average success rates of 98.8 , 92.65 , and 88.3 , outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline (i.e., FastWAM) by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points, respectively. Introduction Learning task-related representations is crucial for robotic manipulation, as a robot must understand scene content and changes relevant to task execution. Two main paradigms have emerged to this end. Vision Language Action models (VLAs)~ bib:vlasurvey1,bib:vlasurvey2 map observations and instructions directly to actions, which is simple and efficient but lacks explicit modeling of scene evolution during task execution~ bib:rt1,bib:rt2,bib:openvla,bib:openvla-oft,bib:pi0,bib:pi05,bib:groot-n1 . In contrast, World Action Models (WAMs)~ bib:wamsurvey1,bib:wamsurvey2 , building on the predictive world modeling paradigm~ bib:dreamerv3 , learn by predicting future scene states alongside robot actions, thereby acquiring a predictive understanding of task-related scene dynamics~ bib:motus,bib:lingbot-va,bib:fastwam,flowwam . Despite recent progress in WAMs~ bib:uwm,bib:dreamzero,bib:oawam,bib:lawam,bib:dswam , a key question remains: is future-state prediction alone sufficient to learn world representations that capture task-related changes? As illustrated in Figure~ fig:head , much of the scene content persists across consecutive observations, while task execution involves changes such as robot motion and object interactions. The full-state prediction objective supervises these changes together with persistent content, without providing a separate learning signal for temporal variation. Thus, the representation of task-related changes relies on what the model learns implicitly from predicting complete future states. This observation suggests a principle of visual foresight: a WAM should model not only what the future scene will look like, but also how it changes over time. Future-state prediction captures scene structure, object appearance, and spatial relationships, while consecutive visual difference prediction provides a separate target for temporal variation. We define a consecutive visual difference as the difference between the latent representations of two consecutive observations. Predicting this quantity, also referred to as diff prediction, provides explicit supervision for temporal variation without requiring additional motion annotations. By jointly modeling future states and their consecutive visual differences, a WAM can develop a more comprehensive world representation that integrates scene understanding with task-related dynamics for action generation. In this paper, we propose , a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that jointly learns future-state prediction, visual difference prediction, and action generation. A shared Observation Encoder encodes the current visual observation into world representations, which are used by a World Expert to predict future states, a Diff Expert to predict differences between consecutive frame latents, and an Action Expert to generate actions. A structured unidirectional attention mask allows each expert to attend to the current-observation representations while blocking attention between experts. This architecture integrates state and visual difference modeling into the world representations used for action generation, while keeping the prediction pathways separate. At inference, both the World and Diff Experts are removed, retaining only the Observation Encoder and Action Expert without additional inference overhead. Across LIBERO~ bib:libero , RoboTwin 2.0~ bib:robotwin2 , and real-world manipulation tasks, achieves average success rates of 98.8 , 92.65 , and 88.3 , respectively, outperforming FastWAM~ bib:fastwam by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce joint future-state and visual difference modeling in WAMs, enabling world representations to capture both scene content and task-related dynamics for action generation. We propose , a Mixture-of-Experts framework with a shared Observation Encoder and dedicated World, Diff, and Action Experts. A structured unidirectional attention mask separates the expert pathways, allowing the World and Diff Experts to be removed at inference without additional overhead. We validate on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness across simulated and physical settings. reduces the optimization steps required to reach 95 average success on LIBERO by 28.1 . Ablation studies validate the benefits of joint state and visual difference modeling. Related Work Existing embodied policy models can be broadly grouped into three paradigms according to their model outputs and supervision: VLA, WAM with Future Prediction, and WAM with Structured Signal Prediction. We detail these three paradigms below. VLA Vision-Language-Action models directly generate actions from visual observations and language instructions, learning representations for action generation without an explicit future-state prediction objective. This paradigm formulates the problem as learning a conditional action policy: where denotes the current observation, the language instruction, and the action sequence over a horizon of steps. Such policies typically couple a VLM backbone with an action expert, directly decoding actions from observation and instruction~ bib:vlasurvey3,bib:vlasurvey4 . Representative works following this paradigm include RT-2~ bib:rt2 , OpenVLA~ bib:openvla , ~ bib:pi0 , Octo~ bib:octo , Diffusion Policy~ bib:diffusion-policy , RDT-1B~ bib:rdt-1b , and Xiaomi-Robotics-0~ bib:xiaomi-robotics-0 . These methods directly map observations to actions, and VLM-based approaches can benefit from pretrained semantic representations. However, learning directly from demonstrations may also capture spurious correlations, potentially contributing to compounding errors and reduced generalization~ bib:vlasurvey5 . WAM with Future Prediction WAMs with future prediction jointly model future visual states and actions, extending action generation with an explicit representation of scene evolution. Conditioned on the current observation and language instruction, they model the joint distribution: where denotes the predicted future frames and the corresponding action sequence. Rather than modeling environmental dynamics implicitly, these methods explicitly predict future frames to ground action generation~ bib:wamsurvey3,bib:wamsurvey4 . Representative works following this paradigm include Motus~ bib:motus , LingBot-VA~ bib:lingbot-va , Fast-WAM~ bib:fastwam , GigaWorld-Policy~ bib:gigaworld-policy , IRASim~ bib:irasim , VideoVLA~ bib:videovla , Video Prediction Policy~ bib:video-prediction-policy , and WorldVLA~ bib:worldvla . Future visual prediction connects scene evolution with action generation~ bib:dust,bib:flare . Nevertheless, accurately predicting temporally coherent future frames in high-dimensional pixel or latent space remains challenging. For methods that condition action decoding directly on predicted future states, prediction errors may propagate into action generation~ bib:dreamvla . Moreover, predicting complete future states does not explicitly distinguish persistent scene content from inter-frame visual differences, leaving temporal variation to be learned implicitly within the state prediction objective. This can make it difficult to emphasize task-related changes over visually salient but task-irrelevant details~ bib:cot-vla . WAM with Structured Signal Prediction Beyond future-state prediction, some WAMs incorporate structured prediction targets, such as depth, semantic segmentation, optical flow, or pretrained visual features, to model additional aspects of the scene. Formally, such methods introduce a structured representation and model where denotes the predicted future frames, the corresponding actions, and an auxiliary structured signal, such as a depth map, semantic segmentation, optical flow~ flowwam,bib:flowdreamer , or a pretrained feature field (e.g., DINOv3 features~ bib:dinov3 ). These targets capture geometric, semantic, or motion-related information, depending on the chosen signal. By supplementing future-state prediction with such structure, these methods introduce additional inductive biases into visual modeling. Representative works include X-WAM~ bib:x-wam , AIM~ bib:aim , AGRA~ bib:agra , DeFI~ bib:defi , and MoLA~ bib:mola . These approaches specify particular geometric, semantic, or motion-related quantities as prediction targets. Their modeling emphasis therefore depends on the chosen signal, and targets obtained from external estimators may contain estimation errors. In contrast, directly models differences between consecutive frame latents alongside future states, integrating state and visual difference prediction within a WAM. These paradigms provide different ways to connect visual modeling with action generation. Our work extends future-predictive WAMs by explicitly modeling both future states and inter-frame latent differences, aiming to capture scene content and task-related dynamics within a shared world representation. Method Problem Formulation As illustrated in Figure~ fig:principle , jointly models future states, inter-frame visual differences, and actions conditioned on the current observation and a language instruction . Let denote the VAE latent representation of observation , the number of future visual states, and the action chunk length. The joint modeling objective is expressed in latent space as: where denotes the future visual latents, the action chunk, and the consecutive visual differences represented in latent space (labeled Future Diff in Figure~ fig:principle ), defined as We use visual difference prediction for this auxiliary task and diff prediction as its shorthand; the Diff Expert predicts the latent differences . Future-state prediction captures scene content, while visual difference prediction explicitly supervises inter-frame variation. Jointly learning these complementary prediction tasks shapes the current-observation representation used for action generation. The joint objective does not require the Action Expert to consume predicted future states or latent differences; each expert is conditioned on the current-observation representation and language instruction. Latent differences describe visual variation and may also include nuisance changes, rather than exclusively encoding changes caused by robot actions. Model Architecture Overv

title: Lao Siji: Adapting openpilot to Closed-Loop End-to-End Driving in Neural Reconstruction
comment: 9 pages
summary: We present Lao Siji, an end-to-end driving policy that ranks third in the 2026 NVIDIA AlpaSim E2E Driving Challenge, ahead of most entries built on foundation models. Instead of training from scratch on a general-purpose vision backbone, we adapt openpilot, an open-source L2 production model. We freeze its vision encoder and fine-tune the policy layers with an ego-state adapter and a route memory. On closed-loop rollouts in neural-reconstructed scenes, we supervise the policy with a privileged map teacher for lateral self-correction and a body-extent loss for road and obstacle clearance, while distilling the base model's remaining outputs to retain car following. Ablations show that self-correction samples carry the gain, while the clearance loss substitutes for them where no teacher exists. Longitudinal safety instead rests on the base model's lead-vehicle estimate behind a rule-based speed layer. Longer training, imitating human logs, and human-log speed targets yield either no measurable gain or adverse effects. Without further training, Lao Siji also places among the leaders on HUGSIM and Odyssey. The final training takes only one GPU-hour and shifts the weights by 3.9% from the shipped model. Code will be released after review.
full_text: Lao Siji Lao Siji ( ): Chinese slang for ``an experienced driver''. : Adapting openpilot to Closed-Loop End-to-End Driving in Neural Reconstruction Chengzhi Gao, Yongzhi Liu, Jinchang Xu, Weichao Zhuang , Guodong Yin School of Mechanical Engineering, Southeast University, Nanjing, China \\ Gaochengzhi1999@gmail.com, wezhuang@seu.edu.cn \\ Corresponding author We present Lao Siji, an end-to-end driving policy that ranks third in the 2026 NVIDIA AlpaSim E2E Driving Challenge, ahead of most entries built on foundation models. We freeze its vision encoder and fine-tune the policy layers with an ego-state adapter and a route memory. On closed-loop rollouts in neural-reconstructed scenes, we supervise the policy with a privileged map teacher for lateral self-correction and a body-extent loss for road and obstacle clearance, while distilling the base model's remaining outputs to retain car following. Ablations show that self-correction samples carry the gain, while the clearance loss substitutes for them where no teacher exists. Longitudinal safety instead rests on the base model's lead-vehicle estimate behind a rule-based speed layer. Longer training, imitating human logs, and human-log speed targets yield either no measurable gain or adverse effects. Without further training, Lao Siji also places among the leaders on HUGSIM and Odyssey. The final training takes only one GPU-hour and shifts the weights by 3.9 from the shipped model. Code will be released after review. End-to-end autonomous driving, post-training, imitation learning, neural reconstruction. Introduction sec:intro Since UniAD~ uniad established the paradigm of jointly optimizing perception, prediction, and planning in an end-to-end framework, the field has expanded along several major directions, including trajectory-scoring planners~ hydramdp,drivor , vision-language-action models~ autovla,alpamayo_r1 , and world-model-based planners~ epona,wa_jepa . Across these lines, most recent approaches pair a general-purpose vision backbone with a driving head and train over weeks on multi-GPU clusters~ epona,vavam , imposing a steep compute barrier for resource-constrained groups. Alongside this compute cost, research has centered on model architecture while leaving data curation and post-training far less explored~ codevilla2019,hiddenbiases_data,lead . Although complex designs have pushed scores on open-loop benchmarks such as NAVSIM~ navsim near human performance~ drivor , these scores reflect closed-loop driving capability only weakly (Table~ tab:main ). Photorealistic closed-loop simulators built on neural scene reconstruction, such as HUGSIM~ hugsim , AlpaSim~ alpasim , and Odyssey~ odyssey , help close this gap. We study closed-loop post-training in the 2026 NVIDIA AlpaSim End-to-End Driving Challenge~ alpasim_challenge . Our solution builds on openpilot~ openpilot , an open-source L2 driver-assistance model with a front-camera encoder pre-trained on large-scale real-world driving data. The model keeps its lane and follows a lead vehicle but cannot turn at intersections; before closed-loop training, lateral failures outnumber front collisions by 2.5 to 3.8 times (Table~ tab:cause ). The closed-loop supervision therefore targets the lateral path only. The vision encoder is frozen, and 5\, of the parameters are trained on rollouts in neural-reconstructed scenes. Following dataset aggregation (DAgger)~ dagger , a privileged map teacher corrects the lateral path on the states the policy reaches, and a body-extent loss enforces road and obstacle clearance where the teacher gives no target. Speed remains with the lead-vehicle estimate of the shipped model behind a rule-based layer. Ablations attribute the gain to the lateral self-correction samples; without them, the policy falls back close to the level of offline post-training. The clearance loss improves a policy trained without a teacher but adds no measurable gain once teacher targets are present. Longer training and human-log targets yield no resolved gain. The resulting policy, Lao Siji, ranks third in the challenge, ahead of most entries built on foundation models, with a final training stage of about one GPU-hour on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000D. Without further training, it is among the leading methods on HUGSIM~ hugsim and Odyssey~ odyssey and raises the NAVSIM~ navsim EPDMS of the shipped model from 80.5 to 88.7. Our contributions are as follows: We present a compute-efficient post-training recipe that adapts a production L2 model into a competitive end-to-end driving policy with strong cross-benchmark transfer, without training a vision stack from scratch (Sec.~ sec:method ). We conduct a systematic ablation across closed-loop states, supervisory signals, and the serving layer, isolating each component's strengths, redundancies, and boundaries between learned planning and inherited control (Sec.~ sec:main and~ sec:ablation ). We document negative results across data selection, rollout scaling, and training duration to inform post-training design under compute constraints (Sec.~ sec:nothelp ). Related Work sec:related Most post-training methods for end-to-end driving operate on logged states: Hydra-MDP~ hydramdp and DrivoR~ drivor distill rule-based trajectory scores into the planner, and AutoVLA~ autovla and Alpamayo-R1~ alpamayo_r1 use trajectory scores as rewards for reinforcement fine-tuning. Training on the states reached by the policy itself follows two paradigms. Online reinforcement learning runs on privileged state inputs (GigaFlow~ gigaflow , CaRL~ carl ) or on camera input in reconstructed scenes (RAD~ rad , AlpaGym~ alpagym ) and requires large rollout budgets. Dataset aggregation (DAgger)~ dagger and privileged distillation~ lbc,roach let an expert teacher label the states visited by the student. Three recent methods are closest to ours. RoaD~ road guides the rollouts of the policy toward the logged human trajectory, OPTED~ opted labels the states of a frozen-backbone student with a reinforcement-learning teacher in AlpaSim, and DriveZero~ drivezero distills such a teacher into a camera policy on logged frames, but none of them had released runnable code and weights at the time of submission. All three supervise a complete trajectory, speed included, and report the pipeline as a whole; we supervise the lateral path, give no deceleration target, and ablate the components of the recipe one at a time. Method sec:method Lao Siji extends a shipped driving model with navigation inputs and post-trains it in reconstructed scenes by dataset aggregation (DAgger)~ dagger (Fig.~ fig:system ). The longitudinal control of the shipped model is in production use on the road, and lateral failures are the main source of zero-score scenes before closed-loop training (Table~ tab:cause ). We therefore supervise only the lateral path and the clearance of the vehicle on the states the policy reaches (Sec.~ sec:priv ) and retain the skills of the shipped model with dedicated samples (Sec.~ sec:mix ). Base Model and Adapter sec:frozen sec:route We build upon openpilot Cinque~ openpilot , a production L2 driving model (Fig.~ fig:system (a)). It consists of a frozen vision encoder (352.9M parameters), a post-trained temporal transformer with a plan head (16.2M), and auxiliary frozen output heads (12.5M, including lead-vehicle estimation for adaptive cruise control). Since the base model accepts no route, we introduce an adapter that injects the ego state (velocity, acceleration, past four poses, and turn command) and navigation route into the vision tokens. The input is eight frame pairs 0.2\,s apart, and the encoder emits 32 tokens of width 512 per pair. The adapter comprises two transformer-decoder branches of identical design: 32 learned queries attend to branch input tokens via a two-layer decoder, and a linear projection yields a bias that is added to these tokens one to one. The ego branch (2.5M parameters, width 256) processes four tokens embedded from the ego state via an MLP. The route branch (0.6M parameters, width 128) processes an ego token and up to 40 route waypoints, each embedded with learned positional encodings. Both linear output layers are zero-initialized, ensuring post-training begins strictly from the base model's original distribution. Waypoints are drawn from a parameter-free route memory that accumulates incoming messages (each covering about 42 to 80\,m ahead), tracks ego displacement, and provides points from 6\,m behind to 72\,m ahead of the car (Fig.~ fig:system (b)); route inputs are dropped for 25\, of training samples for robustness. The policy outputs an 8-pose 4\,s plan and a lead-vehicle estimate, which the serving layer (Sec.~ sec:serving ) converts into a tracking reference. Closed-Loop Rollouts and Supervision sec:rollouts sec:priv Iterative rollouts. In each round, the policy is trained from the shipped weights on all samples accumulated so far and rolled out once across the training scenes; only states before the first infraction, as the scorer of the benchmark defines it (Sec.~ sec:setup ), are kept (in nuPlan scenes, states within 4\,m of the logged path). Earlier policies supply states, and only the final policy is served. The initial policy is trained on human logs alone (Sec.~ sec:mix ). The released recipe runs five sequential rounds: the first in 1 , 031 scenes of the AlpaSim nuPlan track, followed by four rounds in 719 PAI-AV scenes~ pai_av disjoint from evaluation scenes. The states of a round are supervised in one of two modes (Fig.~ fig:body ): with a self-correction target, or with no target and a clearance loss alone. Self-correction targets. Self-correction samples receive a trajectory target from a privileged map teacher (Fig.~ fig:body (a)). Its reference is the route centerline shifted by the lateral offset of the human driver (smoothed over 10\,m, at most 0.5\,m). From the state of the policy, a Frenet quintic closes the lateral and heading errors over the shortest horizon in \,s whose lateral acceleration stays within 4\,m/s . A state receives no target if no horizon meets this bound, if it is more than 5\,m or 60 off the reference or slower than 2\,m/s, or if the path passes an obstacle closer than the human did or comes within 1\,m + 0.84\,s speed of a lead vehicle where the served plan does not. Along the path, the target keeps the arc lengths of the served plan and moves them only forward: where the policy lags with nothing to yield to, it restores the speed of the human or of same-direction traffic, since the plan of the shipped model decays toward a stop in closed loop (Table~ tab:main ) and the benchmark penalizes slow driving. No target slows the policy down; decoupling the lateral path from the speed has precedents~ tfpp,simlingo and suits log-replay evaluation. Body-extent clearance. Target-free samples receive no trajectory target and are supervised only by penalties on the plan (Fig.~ fig:body (b)). Along the 4\,s plan, the vehicle footprint must keep 0.3\,m from road edges and from simulator-derived agent boxes in its path; in the nuPlan round, it is also penalized for entering oncoming lanes and lanes off the route. These penalties backpropagate solely through the normal component of each planned pose: they can steer or bend the trajectory away from obstacles, but cannot shorten it, so the policy cannot reduce the loss by decelerating. Self-correction samples carry the same clearance penalties but no lane penalties: their teacher keeps the human's lateral placement, which occasionally crosses a lane line, and penalizing lanes as well would leave the policy too rigid. The released recipe designates whole rounds as either target-free (nuPlan and third PAI-AV round, 41k samples total) or self-correction (remaining three PAI-AV rounds, 273k samples total). title: AerialOcc: Unified 3D Aerial Perception without Task-Specific Head
summary: Aerial perception systems are increasingly expected to support diverse tasks, yet existing solutions remain fundamentally tied to task-specific outputs. Detection, segmentation, and other perception objectives are usually learned either by separate models or by sharing a backbone with multiple task heads, leaving the model itself unaware of the common structure underlying these tasks. We are interested in asking: can a single perception representation support different levels of understanding without being designed for any specific task? We notice that occupancy is a promising task-agnostic representation for drone perception. By modeling the spatial existence and semantics of the environment, it naturally bridges different perception granularities, from coarse scene understanding to fine-grained object localization. Therefore, we introduce AerialOcc, a unified occupancy-based perception model that enables multiple drone perception tasks from a single inference process, without maintaining task-specific prediction heads. To facilitate this direction, we construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class occupancy dataset for aerial environments. Extensive experiments show that AerialOcc achieves competitive performance across diverse perception tasks while preserving a unified architecture. Our findings demonstrate that occupancy can serve as a universal perception interface, offering a new perspective toward flexible and scalable visual intelligence for autonomous drones from a common 3D scene representation. Models and data are publicly available at https://github.com/guxiang2002/AerialOcc

Introduction sec:intro Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) play a vital role in applications such as autonomous navigation, infrastructure inspection, and environmental monitoring. To effectively handle such complex environments, UAV systems require comprehensive 3D scene understanding~ gross2026occufly,ye2024uav3d , spanning semantic scene completion, 3D semantic segmentation, and 3D object detection. As these tasks involve distinct output interfaces, they are typically handled individually by specialized models or unified through dedicated task-specific heads. To effectively manage this heterogeneity, we aim to develop a unified aerial perception model that accommodates diverse tasks and enables knowledge sharing through a common scene representation. Current attempts to unify aerial perception tasks mainly fall into two paradigms, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:Motivation . Task-separated methods~ milioto2019rangenet++,yin2021center train independent models for different objectives, resulting in duplicated feature learning and isolated task representations. Task-centric methods share an encoder~ ye2023lidarmultinet,chen2025m3net but still rely on dedicated prediction heads tied to predefined outputs. Supporting a new task therefore commonly requires an additional head and task-specific supervision, limiting knowledge sharing and scalability across perception tasks. These limitations motivate us to design a flexible aerial perception architecture that supports multiple tasks and output granularities. Semantic occupancy has been widely studied in autonomous driving~ huang2023tri,li2023voxformer,yu2024context,wang2025uniocc and recently extended to aerial scenes~ lin2025mcop,gao2026skyshield,gross2026occufly . However, existing methods primarily focus on occupancy prediction as an individual task, rather than exploiting it as a shared representation for multiple perception objectives. Our proposed model operates at the voxel level, the basic unit of a 3D scene perception. By assigning each voxel a spatial state and semantic category, the same representation can produce complete scene geometry, semantic regions, and object instances. This makes semantic occupancy a natural common interface for different 3D perception tasks. Building on this insight, we present AerialOcc, a unified aerial perception model built upon a novel architectural paradigm centered on semantic scene completion. Our model leverages the dense voxel-level outputs inherent in semantic occupancy, converting them into the formats required by other vision-centric tasks. AerialOcc supports scene-, region-, and instance-level perception within a unified architecture, without the need to design a separate task-specific head for each task. To equip AerialOcc with dense geometric and semantic understanding, voxel-wise supervision is required. However, existing UAV datasets mainly provide 2D boxes~ jiang2021anti,rizzoli2023syndrone,khose2024skyscenes,yao2025uemm , pixel-wise labels~ azimi2019skyscapes,cai2025vdd,fonder2019mid,kolbeinsson2024ddos,marcu2023self,rizzoli2023syndrone,khose2024skyscenes , depth maps~ fonder2019mid,kolbeinsson2024ddos,marcu2023self,khose2024skyscenes , or 3D boxes~ ye2024uav3d,dhaouadi2025highlydata,lin2022capturing . Although aerial occupancy datasets have emerged, existing resources remain limited in semantic coverage and annotation diversity for training unified 3D perception models. We therefore construct AerialOcc-20K in CARLA~ dosovitskiy2017carla , providing dense geometric and semantic annotations across diverse aerial environments, with the benefits of accurate labeling and reproducible data generation offered by simulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of AerialOcc across the three perception tasks. On AerialOcc-20K, AerialOcc achieves 69.02 IoU and 29.93 mIoU for semantic scene completion, substantially outperforming the compared occupancy baseline. It also surpasses task-specific methods in 3D semantic segmentation and 3D object detection. Furthermore, its strong performance on OccuFly and competitive results on UAV3D demonstrate the transferability of the learned occupancy representation to real-world aerial environments. The contributions of this paper to aerial perception are summarized as follows: We propose AerialOcc, an occupancy-centric aerial perception model that derives semantic scene completion, 3D semantic segmentation, and 3D object detection from a shared occupancy representation without retaining learned task-specific prediction heads. To support the training and evaluation of AerialOcc, we construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class aerial occupancy dataset with dense voxel-wise semantic annotations across diverse altitudes and viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across multiple perception tasks and validate the transferability of the learned occupancy representation to real-world aerial environments. Related Work sec:related 3D Spatial Perception and Occupancy 3D perception has evolved from object-centric localization toward scene-centric representation. 3D detection methods~ lang2019pointpillars,yin2021center,liu2022petr,wang2022detr3d localize object instances, while semantic segmentation methods such as PointNet~ qi2017pointnet , PointNet++~ qi2017pointnet++ , and Cylinder3D~ zhu2021cylindrical assign labels to points or voxels. BEV-based methods~ philion2020lift,li2023bevdepth,li2024bevformer,liang2022bevfusion aggregate multi-view observations into a unified plane, but often compress vertical geometry. In contrast, semantic scene completion~ cao2022monoscene infers voxelized geometry and semantics from partial observations, while visibility-aware occupancy prediction explicitly distinguishes occupied, free, and unobserved regions. Based on this scene-centric formulation, recent occupancy methods improve multi-view fusion~ wei2023surroundocc,wang2024panoocc and 3D spatial modeling~ zhang2023occformer,ma2024cotr for road scenes. However, existing methods largely assume stable ground-vehicle viewpoints, whereas UAV occupancy under varying altitude, orientation, and vertical scene structure remains underexplored. UAV Datasets and Benchmarks Early UAV benchmarks primarily focused on 2D visual perception, including object detection and tracking~ du2018unmanned,liu2025boost,yao2024domain , semantic segmentation~ lyu2020uavid , and cross-modal vehicle detection~ sun2022drone . Later datasets introduced geometric supervision: WildUAV~ florea2021wilduav provides depth and camera poses for depth estimation, while UAV3D~ ye2024uav3d introduces 3D bounding boxes for object-level detection and tracking. Despite increasingly diverse annotation formats, these datasets primarily provide depth, surface, or object-level supervision and lack voxel-level supervision that distinguishes occupied, free, and unobserved regions, limiting their use for scene-level occupancy learning and evaluation. Recent aerial occupancy benchmarks have begun to address this gap. OccuFly~ gross2026occufly derives real-world aerial semantic occupancy annotations through 3D reconstruction for semantic scene completion, whereas SkyShield~ gao2026skyshield provides simulated occupancy supervision for low-altitude forward-view perception. Despite this progress, scene-centric occupancy remains less extensively benchmarked for UAVs than for ground vehicles, particularly across varied aerial environments. AerialOcc-20K Dataset sec:dataset Dataset Pipeline sec:dataset-pipeline The overall pipeline of AerialOcc-20K is illustrated in Fig.~ fig:AerialOcc-20K , consisting of simulation data collection, reference-sensor alignment, and occupancy annotation generation. Simulation Data Collection. AerialOcc-20K comprises 20 simulated scenes across four CARLA towns with diverse spatial layouts. Town03, Town05, and Town10HD provide varied urban road networks and building structures, while Town07 introduces complementary rural environments. Additional scenes are collected in Town10HD to enhance the coverage of complex urban geometry and semantic structures. During data collection, CARLA operates in synchronous mode at \(10\, \), with RGB images and semantic LiDAR measurements matched using a unified frame identifier. We collect 1,000 frames per scene, yielding 20K samples in total. As shown in Fig.~ fig:scene_composition , the dataset is split into 16 training and 4 validation scenes, with a distinct collection trajectory for each scene. Each frame records an RGB image, 3D point coordinates, semantic and instance labels, dynamic object velocities, sensor poses, and timestamps. Reference-Sensor Alignment. title: PlanDiv: Test-Time Scaling with Latent Plans for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures
summary: Test-time scaling improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies by drawing several action candidates and executing the best one. We find that its returns diminish quickly when the candidates are resampled from one decoder: they differ by noise rather than by plan, and for each of three resampling sources, going from four to eight candidates adds only 0.06-0.07 to the average number of completed tasks on CALVIN. We introduce PlanDiv, an action head that makes the candidates differ by plan: a lightweight planner proposes K latent plan hypotheses, a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan from a single backbone pass, and the policy executes the chunk that its own likelihood ranks highest. The plans are learned from demonstrations alone, without plan labels or rewards. With the backbone, data and training recipe held fixed, eight plan-conditioned candidates raise five-task chain success on CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D from 56.9% to 69.9%, while eight candidates from autoregressive, plan-free or same-plan resampling reach at most 64.9%. The same-plan baseline is PlanDiv's own checkpoint with the plan held fixed, so this gap comes from the plans, not from drawing more samples. On LIBERO-Long, four plans remove 40% of single-candidate failures, against at most 21% for matched resampling. On a real Franka arm the gain appears where a task admits more than one solution: PlanDiv is on par with a single-output OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline on a one-solution task and succeeds in 51 of 54 trials against 40 of 54 on two tasks with two solutions.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models map observations and an instruction to robot actions with a single pretrained backbone~ rt1,rt2,openvla , and the optimized fine-tuning (OFT) recipe made them fast through parallel decoding and action chunking~ oft . Test-time scaling has recently begun to improve these policies without retraining them: instead of executing the policy's single output, the robot draws several action candidates and executes the best one. RoboMonkey samples actions and ranks them with a learned verifier~ robomonkey , RoVer adds a process reward model~ rover , MG-Select removes the verifier and ranks samples by their divergence from a condition-masked reference~ mgselect , and CoVer widens the pool by rephrasing the instruction~ cover . These methods differ in how candidates are scored, but they share where the candidates come from: one decoder, queried repeatedly through temperature sampling, action perturbation or a rephrased instruction. We measure what this source buys under one training recipe (Sec.~ sec:diagnosis ), turning what prior work has observed~ mgselect into a controlled comparison. Resampling an autoregressive head, a plan-free masked-diffusion head, or a plan-conditioned head held to one fixed plan gives nearly the same curve: most of the gain arrives with the first four candidates, and the next four add only 0.06--0.07 completed tasks on CALVIN (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). The candidates themselves show why. Candidates resampled under one plan differ in 18 of their tokens, and even an oracle selector over eight of them succeeds in only 86 of sub-task start states, against 76 for a single candidate. If the policy commits to a wrong approach direction or sub-goal order, its samples tend to inherit that commitment, and no scorer can select a behavior that the candidate set does not contain. We introduce (for plan diversity; Fig.~ fig:overview ), an action head that makes the candidates differ by plan instead of by noise: it decodes one candidate per plan and lets the policy choose among them instead of averaging the plans. A lightweight planner turns learned seeds into latent plan hypotheses with a prior over them; a shared masked-diffusion executor, inherited from recent discrete-diffusion action decoders~ ddvla,udvla,mmadavla , decodes one action chunk per plan from a single backbone pass; and the policy executes the chunk it scores highest. Planner and executor are trained jointly from demonstrations alone by latent responsibility assignment, an objective in the style of soft expectation-maximization (EM) that credits each demonstration chunk to the hypotheses that explain it best, rather than to all of them equally or to a single winner. The OpenVLA backbone, tokenizer and action-token interface are unchanged, and one checkpoint serves any candidate budget . With the backbone, data, training recipe and selector matched, eight plan-conditioned candidates raise CALVIN five-task chain success from 56.9 to 69.9 , against 63.9--64.9 for the resampling sources. Same-plan resampling shares the checkpoint, the first candidate and each candidate's random numbers with , so the gap between them isolates the effect of the plans. Eight plan-conditioned candidates remove 30 of single-candidate failures on CALVIN and four remove 40 on LIBERO-Long, against 17--21 for matched resampling and 5--18 that prior test-time scaling reports on other base policies~ rover,robomonkey,mgselect . Four plans are already worth eight samples: they complete more tasks than eight resampled candidates from any of the three sources, and they cover more start states (88.8 against 86.1 for eight same-plan samples). Changing only the plan under fixed decoder noise alters the task outcome more than twice as often as changing only the noise. In simulation, eight candidates take 288\,ms, about a third of the time an autoregressive policy needs for one. Our contributions are: A controlled measurement. With the backbone, data, training recipe and selector matched, resampling one decoder has quickly diminishing returns: three resampling sources gain only 0.06--0.07 completed tasks from four to eight candidates, and even an oracle selector over eight same-plan resamples succeeds in only 86 of sub-task start states. . An action head that decodes plan-conditioned candidates, one per latent plan hypothesis, from one backbone pass; the plans are learned from demonstrations alone by latent responsibility assignment, with no plan labels or rewards. Evidence. At matched candidate count outperforms all three resampling sources on CALVIN and LIBERO-Long, including same-plan resampling from the same checkpoint; a fixed-noise intervention shows that the plan alone changes task outcomes, and without soft responsibilities or repulsion between plans the gain falls to that of plain resampling. On a real Franka arm, on tasks with more than one solution, removes 11 of the 14 failures of an OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline. Related Work sec:related -language-action models. VLAs fine-tune a pretrained vision-language model to output robot actions~ rt2,openvla . Recent models mostly change what the backbone produces before or alongside the action: spatial representations~ spatialvla , visual traces~ tracevla , visual chains of thought~ cotvla , future observations~ seer,worldvla,unifiedvla , or task-centric latent actions learned from video~ univla . Others make the policy smaller~ nora,vlaadapter , replace token decoding with flow matching or diffusion~ pizero,flower,diffusionvla , compress the action sequence~ fast , or keep improving a trained policy through interactive post-training~ riptvla . Each of them produces one action or action chunk per decision. keeps the backbone and changes only the action head and the candidates it produces at test time. action decoders. We build on the OpenVLA family: a pretrained vision-language backbone with a discrete action-token interface~ openvla,rt2 , adapted with parallel decoding and action chunking~ oft,pdvla . Our executor belongs to the recent line of masked-diffusion action decoders, which decode a chunk by iterative unmasking rather than left-to-right generation~ ddvla,udvla,mmadavla , following D3PM, MaskGIT and MDLM~ d3pm,maskgit,mdlm . We keep the decoder standard so that the comparison isolates the plan it is conditioned on. Non-autoregressive translation met the same multimodality problem in parallel decoding: it conditions the decoder on latent fertilities obtained from an external aligner and, at test time, decodes several of them and rescores the outputs with an autoregressive teacher~ nat . Our plans are learned without supervision and ranked by the executor's own likelihood. -time scaling for VLAs. Most prior work improves how candidates are selected. RoboMonkey draws samples by temperature or Gaussian perturbation and ranks them with a 7B verifier~ robomonkey ; RoVer adds a process reward model with direction-guided expansion~ rover ; MG-Select removes the verifier and ranks by the KL divergence to a condition-masked reference~ mgselect ; ELASTIC learns how to split compute between denoising steps and parallel samples~ elastic . V-GPS re-ranks the actions of a generalist policy with a value function learned by offline reinforcement learning~ vgps , and Bidirectional Decoding selects among sampled action chunks by their coherence with past decisions~ bid . CoVer changes the input instead, rephrasing the instruction and scoring instruction--action pairs with a contrastive verifier~ cover . changes the source of the candidates: its hypotheses are learned from demonstrations alone, and each one is decoded into its own candidate, so that the policy chooses among alternatives rather than averaging them. It is orthogonal in design to the selection-side methods, whose scores operate on whatever candidates they are given. hypotheses and latent plans. Expressive policy classes capture multimodal demonstrations within one conditional distribution, through discretized action modes~ bet,vqbet , a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) latent~ act or diffusion~ diffusionpolicy ; drawing several samples from it is the resampling we analyze in Sec.~ sec:diagnosis . Play-LMP and HULC learn a latent plan space from play data and condition a local policy on one sampled plan~ playlmp,hulc ; hierarchical and skill-based methods use temporally extended abstractions in the same spirit~ hiro,hac,spirl,latentskillspace . Choice Policies predicts candidate action sequences in one forward pass together with a learned score, trained winner-takes-all in the multiple-choice-learning tradition to model multimodal behavior with fast inference~ choicepolicy,mcl2012,smcl ; relaxed and evolving variants soften the winner-takes-all assignment~ rwta,ewta . Latent responsibility assignment is a soft, prior-weighted counterpart of that objective, an EM-style step induced by the masked reconstruction loss~ em , and our hypotheses share one executor rather than owning heads; sharpening our assignment toward winner-takes-all reduces the gain from extra candidates to that of resampling (Sec.~ sec:structure ). MoDE routes among expert denoisers by noise level~ mode , whereas our hypotheses are alternatives for the same decision; unlike CVAE policies~ cvae,act , we amortize no posterior and the planner proposes candidates explicitly. DLow maps one random variable through learned transforms into diverse latent codes of a pretrained generator~ dlow ; our hypotheses are trained jointly with the executor and carry a prior that ranks them at test time. In language modeling, Mode-Conditioning allocates samples evenly across modes obtained from labels or gradient clustering~ modc , PlanSearch searches over natural-language plans because sampled programs repeat one another's mistakes~ plansearch , Large Language Monkeys separates coverage from selection~ monkeys , and SoftCoT++ diversifies a latent thought through several learned initial tokens~ softcotpp . These settings count a problem as solved if any sample is correct; a robot must commit to one candidate before its outcome is known, so computes its plans from the current context, learns them jointly with the executor, and ranks them with a learned prior.
