title: Prompt Re-Specification and Target-Mask Availability in Mask-Conditioned Visual Reinforcement Learning for Moving-Platform Landing
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 12 tables
summary: Visual reinforcement learning (RL) policies that land a drone on a moving platform can fail when the landing pad looks different from the one used in training. Using binary target masks as the visual input removes most pixel-level appearance information while preserving the spatial representation of the target, and lets a text prompt specify the target. In simulation, we test whether a frozen (fixed-weight) mask-based DrQ-v2 policy can handle a new pad when only the prompt of its fine-tuned SAM 3 detector changes. A banana-themed pad lowered landing success from 75.6% to 12.0%, and SAM 3 rarely detected it under the original prompt. A revised prompt, chosen after testing several candidates, restored success to 68.4% with no weight updates. In a separate experiment with a policy trained on ground-truth masks, filling in masks that were missing while the pad was visible helped landing far more than the tested mask-centroid and area corrections. Tracking the pad over time supplied masks more often and also kept producing them after the pad was confirmed absent from the rendered image, but it did not establish a reliable improvement in landing success. Whether a usable mask reaches the policy at all thus appears to be an important limiting factor for this approach.
full_text: Prompt Re-Specification and Target-Mask Availability in Mask-Conditioned Visual Reinforcement Learning for Moving-Platform Landing Ho Tim Tsui\, , Jongyun Kim\, Visual reinforcement learning (RL) policies that land a drone on a moving platform can fail when the landing pad looks different from the one used in training. Using binary target masks as the visual input removes most pixel-level appearance information while preserving the spatial representation of the target, and lets a text prompt specify the target. In simulation, we test whether a frozen (fixed-weight) mask-based DrQ-v2 policy can handle a new pad when only the prompt of its fine-tuned SAM~3 detector changes. A banana-themed pad lowered landing success from 75.6 to 12.0 , and SAM~3 rarely detected it under the original prompt. A revised prompt, chosen after testing several candidates, restored success to 68.4 with no weight updates. In a separate experiment with a policy trained on ground-truth masks, filling in masks that were missing while the pad was visible helped landing far more than the tested mask-centroid and area corrections. Tracking the pad over time supplied masks more often and also kept producing them after the pad was confirmed absent from the rendered image, but it did not establish a reliable improvement in landing success. Whether a usable mask reaches the policy at all thus appears to be an important limiting factor for this approach. Introduction sec:intro Autonomous landing on moving platforms is an important capability for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in mobile recharging, logistics, inspection, and maritime operations~ goldschmid2024 . Cameras offer lightweight sensing without requiring communication with the platform or external positioning infrastructure~ falanga2017,ladosz2024 , and reinforcement learning (RL) can learn tracking, alignment, and descent together in one closed-loop policy. Ladosz et al.~ ladosz2024 trained such a policy with DrQ-v2~ yarats2022drqv2 . It maps camera images and onboard velocity and attitude to velocity commands, without access to the position or velocity of the platform. A policy that learns from unsegmented camera images can become tied to the appearance of the landing pad it saw during training~ polvara2020,ladosz2024 . If the pad is repainted or replaced, the policy may need new data and retraining. Promptable segmentation models~ kirillov2023sam,carion2026sam3 offer another route. A perception model finds the target from a text prompt and passes it to the controller as a binary mask. Most of the appearance of the pad then never reaches the policy, and a changed pad can be described by a new prompt. This alone does not make landing robust to appearance, because the perception model still has to detect the new pad. When direct detection fails, the perception frontend falls back on temporal propagation, as in video segmentation models with memory~ ravi2025sam2 , and this propagation can also fail or carry outdated target information into later frames~ ding2025sam2long . In closed loop, the frames that the policy sees also depend on its own earlier actions, and frame-level segmentation accuracy need not predict downstream performance~ philion2020 . This paper asks whether a frozen mask-conditioned RL landing policy can adapt to a new landing-pad appearance when only the segmentation prompt is changed, without updating any network weight, and what limits this adaptation. Throughout the paper, ``frozen'' means that the weights of a network are not updated after its training, so a frozen network has the same weights in every condition in which it is evaluated. We study the question in simulation with a DrQ-v2 actor that observes masks from a SAM~3 detector fine-tuned for the task. When a banana-themed pad replaced the training pad, direct detections and landing success collapsed under the original prompt. A revised prompt brought back most of the detections and most of the landing success. A substitution diagnostic with a separately trained ground-truth-mask policy points to the property involved. With raw SAM-derived masks, this policy almost never landed. Filling in only the masks that were missing while the target was visible restored landing, whereas correcting the centroid and area of the masks that were produced did not. The perception frontend already uses temporal tracking to supply masks through detection gaps. Reinitialising the tracker at each direct detection made the target available more often, but it also produced more nonempty masks after renderer-confirmed target absence, and the resulting difference in landing success was not established. The central contribution of this work is an empirical account of prompt-conditioned segmentation as the observation interface of a frozen RL landing policy when the target appearance changes. It identifies target-mask availability as a key limitation for control. Three connected investigations support it. A matched appearance and prompt evaluation (Section~ sec:appearance ) shows that revising the prompt recovered most of the landing performance lost under the tested appearance change. A frozen-policy substitution diagnostic (Section~ sec:diagnosis ) shows that, among the interventions tested, restoring missing masks mattered far more for landing than correcting mask geometry. A comparison of temporal memory management (Section~ sec:temporal ) shows that greater target continuity comes with more nonempty output after renderer-confirmed target absence and does not automatically improve landing. The results concern one substantially different pad appearance, a prompt revised by the authors, and one trained actor, all in simulation. Related Work sec:related Moving-Platform Landing Classical systems treat moving-platform landing as modular estimation and control. Image-based visual servoing uses image-space target features and optical flow~ herisse2012,serra2016 , and feed-forward variants add an estimate of the platform velocity~ cho2022 . Falanga et al.~ falanga2017 predict the platform motion with an extended Kalman filter while detections are unavailable, and Paris et al.~ paris2020 plan trajectories whose final velocity matches the estimated platform motion. These systems bridge visual gaps with an explicit state estimate, but they rely on an engineered marker and a structured pipeline. Learning-based methods replace part or all of this pipeline. They use extracted relative state~ rodriguezramos2019 , sub-task decomposition~ goldschmid2024 , or image-based policies transferred with domain randomisation~ polvara2020,ladosz2024 . The end-to-end policy of Ladosz et al.~ ladosz2024 assumes that the pad design was seen during training, and its environment and learner are the closest to ours. Other recent methods handle partial observability inside the policy, with a long short-term memory network over landing-specific keypoints~ shin2026 or recurrent RL over noisy and missing state measurements~ aikins2024 . We keep the actor feed-forward and deal with appearance and missing observations in the perception interface. Perception Representations for Learned Control The representation passed from perception to a learned controller decides which errors the controller has to tolerate. A driving policy shielded from raw perceptual input by a modular perception layer transferred from simulation to a real vehicle~ mueller2018 , and agents given intermediate vision representations learned faster and generalised better than agents learning from pixels alone~ zhou2019 . In visual RL, images masked with Segment Anything improved generalisation to unseen visual conditions~ wang2023samg . Segment Anything~ kirillov2023sam segments objects from visual prompts, and SAM~3~ carion2026sam3 extends promptable segmentation to concepts given as text, so a text prompt can describe a new target without retraining the controller. In our setting the appearance change concerns the landing target itself, and the adaptation is made through the text prompt. Bounding boxes and keypoints are more compact alternatives to masks; we do not compare interface types. Because perception metrics need not reflect downstream performance~ philion2020 , we evaluate the interface by closed-loop landing. Temporal Memory in Video Segmentation Video object segmentation carries information across frames. SAM~2~ ravi2025sam2 conditions each frame on a streaming memory of earlier predictions, XMem~ cheng2022xmem organises memory into sensory, working, and long-term stores, and DAM4SAM~ videnovic2025dam4sam adds distractor-aware memory selection to SAM~2.1. Memory can also spread mistakes: SAM2Long~ ding2025sam2long shows that the greedy memory selection of SAM~2 lets a wrong or missed mask affect later frames. These methods are evaluated by segmentation accuracy on recorded video. We instead measure how memory management changes the observations that a closed-loop controller receives, and how landing outcomes differ. Task and System sec:system Landing Task sec:task A quadrotor lands on a non-communicating moving platform using only onboard visual and ego-state observations. The simulation environment is built on gym-pybullet-drones~ panerati2021 . It is adapted from the moving-platform landing environment of Ladosz et al.~ ladosz2024 and shares its nominal start height, horizontal reset range, and maximum platform speed. The vehicle is the Crazyflie~2.X model of the simulator with a rigid, downward-facing camera, and a proportional--integral--derivative (PID) controller tracks its velocity commands. The landing target is a m ~ ~ m pad bearing a fixed greyscale circular landing-marker texture, which is not randomised during training. Each episode starts with the UAV at a height of m and a horizontal offset from the platform drawn uniformly from ~ along each axis. The platform moves along a straight line at a speed drawn uniformly from ~ m\,s^ -1 and a heading drawn uniformly from . The physics simulation runs at Hz , the PID controller at Hz , and the actor at Hz . Fresh camera images are segmented at Hz , so the actor acts on each mask for two consecutive decisions. An episode ends at the first contact or after s . A landing succeeds when the UAV touches down with its horizontal collision footprint, of radius m , inside the pad. Both horizontal offsets from the pad centre, measured in the pad frame, must therefore be at most m , and no limit is placed on touchdown velocity. Any other contact is a crash, and an episode still airborne at s is a timeout. Table~ tab:task_setup summarises the parameters. Perception Frontend sec:frontend The perception frontend turns each fresh camera image into the mask and perception metadata that the actor observes. It uses three frozen models. The direct detector is a SAM~3 image segmenter~ carion2026sam3 that was fine-tuned for this project with the text query ``landing pad'' and then frozen (Appendix~ app:provenance describes what is known about this fine-tuning). At inference it receives the same prompt and uses confidence and mask thresholds of 0.5 at an internal resolution of 1008 pixels. DAM4SAM~ videnovic2025dam4sam , a tracker built on SAM~2.1 Hiera-Tiny~ ravi2025sam2 , propagates the target when direct detection fails, with its native object-presence processing enabled. A CLIP ViT-B/32 image encoder~ radford2021clip supplies similarity metadata. A direct SAM~3 mask always takes precedence. title: RescueVLM: Model-Agnostic Vision-Language Framework for Rescue Drone Imagery
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures
summary: A single unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) mission over an incident site produces hundreds of images, far more than a rescue commander can review under time pressure, and human screening of destruction imagery carries a documented psychological cost. The two obvious remedies both fail in search and rescue (SAR) practice: cloud vision-language model (VLM) services are excluded because the imagery must not leave the incident network under GDPR and German civil-protection (BOS) rules, and fine-tuned specialist detectors age quickly while retraining and re-certifying them exceeds most SAR organizations resources. We present RescueVLM, an open-source, training-free and model-agnostic triage tool built on SketchVLM: a general-purpose open-weight VLM runs fully on-premise and is swapped for a newer model through a simple dropdown selection, so triage quality grows with the underlying models because all task knowledge lives in prompts and an output contract rather than in trained weights. One natural-language query over a mission folder returns a ranked shortlist with per-image justifications, editable SVG overlay annotations, and a GPS map of the hits. In a qualitative evaluation on German fire-brigade field data from three real deployments and a live fire exercise, a single query condenses an entire survey mission into a handful of annotated frames that a commander can review at a glance.

One natural-language query over a mission folder returns a ranked shortlist with per-image justifications, editable SVG overlay annotations, and a GPS map of the hits. In a qualitative evaluation on German fire-brigade field data from three real deployments and a live fire exercise, a single query condenses an entire survey mission into a handful of annotated frames that a commander can review at a glance. search and rescue, vision-language models, UAV imagery, model-agnostic, disaster response Introduction sec:intro Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have become a primary sensor for situational awareness in disaster response~ surmann2021indoor,fernandes2018harvey . Mapping and survey flights produce a plain folder of hundreds of georeferenced JPEGs per mission; at Hurricane Harvey, 112 flights generated roughly 150~GB of imagery and video across the deployment~ fernandes2018harvey . In our own deployment during the July 2021 Erftstadt/Blessem flood, the bottleneck was never capturing imagery but getting current, condensed information to the commanders who had to act on it~ surmann2022erftstadt,surmann2024lessons . This is the problem RescueVLM addresses: turning a folder of survey images into a short, explained, map-anchored shortlist a commander can act on in minutes (Fig.~ fig:flood ). Three constraints make this problem specific to SAR, and together they rule out the obvious off-the-shelf solutions. The first is privacy. SAR imagery is personal data of the most sensitive kind: victims, injured or deceased persons, private interiors exposed by structural collapse, license plates. Under the GDPR and German BOS practice, uploading such imagery to a foreign cloud API during a live operation is de facto excluded; local, on-premise inference is a requirement, not an optimization. Yet most recent VLM-for-UAV systems assume exactly the cloud frontier model that such deployments cannot use (Sec.~ sec:related ). The second constraint is that fine-tuned specialists do not survive in practice. A task-specific detector or grounding model~ wang2026locateanything is exemplary the day it ships and superseded the day a better fine-tune appears, and for a SAR organization each replacement means new training data, training, validation, and, for operational BOS use, acceptance testing. Incident imagery is moreover rare, privacy-restricted, and heterogeneous (the datasets in this paper span vegetation, structural, industrial, and flood incidents) , and our own earlier fine-tuned SAR detector~ surmann2023uavs shows precisely this treadmill . The durable artifact in this domain is the framework around the model, not the model. The third constraint is the psychological cost of human review. Today, teams of humans screen post-disaster imagery frame by frame, and this exposure is documented to cause harm, from operator stress when viewing victim imagery at the World Trade Center~ murphy2014disaster to PTSD symptoms among military drone operators~ chappelle2014drone ; a NOAA cartographer among the first to screen post-Katrina aerial imagery recalls sitting at her desk in tears~ noaa2019aerial . A pre-triage that surfaces only the handful of images that matter reduces the volume of content that operators would need to review~ hughes2025seeing . RescueVLM answers all three constraints at once. We rebuild SketchVLM~ collins2026sketchvlm , a training-free, model-agnostic framework in which a VLM explains its answers by emitting editable SVG overlays on the input image, for on-site SAR use: whole mission folders are queried in bulk against a local Ollama~ ollama2026software backend, with ~ googledeepmind2026gemma4 on a single workstation GPU, no cloud dependency, and no fine-tuned weights. Because the model is reached through a standard API, a better open-weight VLM is a drop-in replacement and the tool inherits the improvement the same day. We make three contributions. RescueVLM, an open-source adaptation of SketchVLM for fully local, training-free triage of SAR UAV imagery, into which any vision-capable open-weight model drops as a replaceable engine. A bulk folder mode that ranks images per natural-language query with per-image justifications, normalized SVG annotations, an explicit cross-image deduplication instruction for 70--80\, meander overlap, and ranked hits geo-anchored on a map via EXIF-GPS. A qualitative use-case evaluation on German fire-brigade field data (vegetation fire, structural fire, hazardous-substance reconnaissance, and flood) on responder-grade single-GPU hardware. Related Work sec:related A fast-growing line of work applies vision-language models to aerial disaster imagery. UAV-VLRR~ yaqoot2025uavvlrr and UAV-VLA~ sautenkov2025uavvla use GPT-class cloud models for scene interpretation and text-to-mission planning; DisasTeller~ chen2026disasteller is a multi-LVLM agent framework for post-disaster damage assessment and reporting, and RAPID~ yang2026rapid is, like us, a training-free damage-assessment pipeline. Seeing the Storm~ hughes2025seeing uses multimodal LLMs to filter overwhelming disaster media so managers view only relevant items, a direct precedent for our exposure-reduction thesis. RescueVLM differs from all of these on three axes at once: it runs fully on-premise (cloud systems cannot be deployed on GDPR-restricted incident imagery), it treats the model as a swappable engine behind an output contract, and it targets bulk set-level triage-ranking with cross-image deduplication rather than per-image captioning or classification. A second line fine-tunes specialist grounding and detection models. Open-set detectors from Grounding DINO~ liu2024groundingdino to the current LocateAnything-3B~ wang2026locateanything produce sharp boxes on the categories they were trained for, but their value lives in the weights, which is exactly what the next fine-tune replaces; none of them rank a set, justify a decision in text, or deduplicate events across a meander flight. We treat such models as replaceable engines a framework can call, not as the system. On the human-factors side, and beyond the evidence of screening harm cited in Sec.~ sec:intro , RescueVLM inverts the screening workflow so that far fewer people see far fewer disturbing frames while the human remains the decision maker, a design informed by the appropriate-reliance literature~ lee2004trust . Finally, that a local open-weight VLM can be ``good enough'' is increasingly supported~ deitke2025molmo , and on-premise deployment for GDPR-sensitive data has direct precedent in clinical text~ wiest2024privacy . Two reliability caveats shape our design: off-the-shelf VLMs hallucinate objects~ li2023pope , and forcing structured (JSON) output can degrade reasoning~ tam2024speakfreely , which is why triage ordering, not diagnosis, is the tool's contract. System Description sec:system RescueVLM inherits the core paradigm of SketchVLM~ collins2026sketchvlm : a training-free VLM tool that explains its answer by emitting a non-destructive, editable overlay on the input image. We rebuild it for privacy-preserving, on-site triage of survey imagery. The tool is a web application that analyzes folders of mission images. In this mode, the responder points the tool at a folder of mission JPEGs and asks one natural-language question across the whole image set. The interface supports a quick mode that randomly samples up to 50 images from a given folder and a full-dataset mode that processes larger collections sequentially in batches of up to 50 images. The 50-image limit per batch is imposed by GPU VRAM constraints. Before submission, each image is resized in the browser to a maximum longest side of 1024\,px and re-encoded as JPEG. Images are preceded by labels of the form , with GPS coordinates included when available. Image indices remain consistent across batches and the interface. Each batch is analysed independently, producing a short summary and a list of relevant images with consistent image numbers, brief explanations, and visual annotations. Once all batches have been processed, the same model receives the original question and the collected findings, including filenames and available GPS coordinates, in a final text-only request. It is instructed to identify repeated observations of the same event, compare their severity, and produce a combined answer and an overall image ranking. This step uses the batch findings without viewing the images again. The selected images retain their annotations from the batch analyses. If the final synthesis fails, the individual batch results are displayed together; failed batches are explicitly reported. Follow-up questions use the collected text findings and conversation history without resending the images. A single thin server route proxies the browser to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and streams the reply back as server-sent events. The provider is selected by the model tag: tags prefixed are routed to a local Ollama~ ollama2026software server, so imagery never leaves the incident network; routes to remote providers exist in the code but stay disabled during operations. The interface queries the local Ollama tag list and offers every installed vision model in a dropdown, with no change to code, data, or weights. In our deployment configuration the engine is ~ googledeepmind2026gemma4 on a single high-end GPU, validated on a 32\,GB RTX 5090. All task knowledge reaches the model as text, on two levels. title: Ultra-CAN: A Lightweight Blind ISAC Receiver for Chaos-Based Telemetry and Local-Seed Ranging in the Internet of Drones
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to IEEE Internet of Things Journal
summary: The Internet of Drones (IoD) needs secure telemetry and proximity sensing within the SWaP-C constraints. We show that a single blind neural receiver driven by one chaos-based waveform performs both functions without a separate radar transceiver. In telemetry mode it decodes a peer's burst blindly; in radar mode it regenerates the per-burst chaotic reference locally and ranges the echoes of its own transmission. Ultra-CAN pairs a shared $64$-dimensional representation with two ultra-light backbones, an attention-pooled Conv1D network and a multi-head QKV network ($27.6$k--$44.2$k parameters), feeding communication and sensing heads. Both ship as int8 TensorFlow Lite Micro firmware; the Conv1D receiver decides a burst in $16.9$ ms on a $240$ MHz microcontroller with $24.2$ KiB of activations, a measured energy of $2.2$-$3.4$ mJ per burst, and float-equivalent decisions, sustaining up to $59$ bit/s of telemetry or a $7.4$ Hz range track. The two variants rank first and second among learned demodulators in four aerial swarm scenarios, with a pooled BER down to $4.6 \times 10^{-4}$ on the single-echo link ($2.4 \times 10^{-3}$ with three echoes). Its sensing head identifies true obstacles in $66.8\%$ of peer-laden bursts (vs $42\%$ matched filtering, $44\%$ OFDM-ISAC, $48\%$ peak-picker ceiling). A peer-exclusion gate cuts peer reports from $4.4\%$ to $0.02\%$ of answered bursts, answering $23.5\%$ of total bursts ($75\%$ on the exact tap) with $0.70$ m/s velocity tracking. In-domain refitting recovers telemetry BER by up to three orders of magnitude under 3GPP channels, jamming-aware training restores the link, and frequency agility adds a $6$--$9$ dB margin against partial-band jamming.

We show that a single blind neural receiver driven by one chaos-based waveform performs both functions without a separate radar transceiver. Internet of Drones (IoD), Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC), Edge AI, Chaos-Based Communications, Chaos Shift Keying, Multi-Task Learning, Physical-Layer Security, Frequency Hopping. Introduction sec:intro eural receivers have already outperformed classical demodulators on chaos-based aerial links ultra_can_letter ; the proliferation of Internet of Drones (IoD) and Flying Ad-hoc Networks (FANETs) now drives a paradigm shift in tactical and mission-critical Internet of Things (IoT) applications, ranging from search and rescue to autonomous surveillance bekmezci2013_fanet, mozaffari2019_uav_comms, shakhatreh2019_uav_survey . In these scenarios, micro-UAVs must maintain secure, anti-jamming communications while simultaneously sensing their environment to keep swarm formations and avoid collisions. The stringent Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWaP-C) constraints of such platforms make the integration of separate communication and radar subsystems impractical. Traditional approaches treat communication and radar sensing as independent functions, each requiring dedicated hardware and signal-processing chains. The emerging paradigm of Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) unifies these functionalities on a single platform and a shared waveform liu2022_isac, magbool2025_isac_survey . UAV-specific designs now span THz transceivers zhang2025_thz_uav_isac , STAR-RIS links eghbali2025_star_ris_uav , and energy-aware integrated sensing, computation, and communication liu2025_uav_iscc_aoi . In this context, chaotic signals generated by Logistic or Bernoulli maps are attractive for aerial ISAC: their noise-like spectrum and Dirac-like autocorrelation provide physical-layer security --- as long as the map parameters and per-symbol seeds are not disclosed --- and jam resistance for telemetry, while the sharp correlation peak supports delay-based ranging kaddoum2016 . Conventional chaos-based receivers are sensitive to multipath and Doppler escribano2016, cai2025 , and their coherent counterparts require the transmitter's per-symbol chaotic state pecora1990 , which is not available in the non-cooperative setting considered here. Recent DCSK variants add permutation and multilevel code indexing wang2025_dcsk_iot, li2025_dcsk_tcas , but they target the waveform and modulation order rather than a shared sensing read-out. Deep Learning (DL) demodulators such as LSTM-OFDM-DCSK zhang2020 , TDNN-LSTM zhang2022 , and MC-DLCSK mobini2025 improve over correlators, but their recurrent or fully-connected stages cost more memory than a flight controller comfortably offers. In our previous work ultra_can_letter we introduced Ultra-CAN, an ultra-lightweight neural decoder that outperforms heavier DL demodulators on Chaos Shift Keying (CSK) signals under AWGN and Rayleigh fading. While that baseline was strictly limited to single-task bit classification in simulation, this manuscript proposes a fundamentally novel Multi-Task ISAC architecture. Specifically, our new proposed model introduces the capability to perform local-seed ranging, alongside a novel peer-exclusion gate for swarm safety, and validates the complete dual-mode system on physical edge hardware (ESP32-S3) with measured SWaP-C constraints and jamming resilience, none of which were present in ultra_can_letter . This paper evolves Ultra-CAN into a Multi-Task Learning (MTL) Edge AI receiver for IoD ISAC. The contribution goes beyond decoding accuracy: one waveform family carries telemetry and sensing echoes, and one receiver extracts both from a shared representation, with one forward pass per burst in each mode. The noise-like, aperiodic waveform keeps that receiver hard to intercept and hard to jam. The receiver decodes the telemetry bit in telemetry mode and identifies the delay of the obstacle echo in radar mode, while remaining robust to the Doppler shifts induced by high mobility. Two equally lightweight backbone variants are studied: the attention-pooled Conv1D decoder of our Letter and a multi-head QKV attention variant. Both share the same communication and sensing heads, and both are benchmarked against the LSTM-OFDM-DCSK and MC-DLCSK neural receivers and a blind statistical receiver on the same chaotic aerial link, under the same operating region, and under the same jamming attacks. The telemetry link is non-cooperative: no waveform state is disclosed over the air. The contributions of this paper are as follows. A dual-mode ISAC receiver: telemetry mode decodes a peer's chaotic burst blindly, while radar mode uses the node's own chaotic burst as the sensing reference, regenerated from the local seed, so that one waveform family carries telemetry and range with no separate radar transceiver and no state exchange over the air. Two ultra-light backbones that share one -dimensional representation, an attention-pooled Conv1D network and a multi-head QKV attention network, with and float32 parameters respectively. A geometry-supervised sensing head that fuses the shared neural representation with a local-seed delay-profile descriptor to classify the true obstacle lag instead of the strongest multipath tap, reaching obstacle-ID rate in peer-laden swarms against the empirical peak-picker ceiling ( ) and 5G-NR OFDM-ISAC baselines ( ). A per-burst peer-exclusion gate that trades the answered fraction for safety and keeps peer reports at or below on the answered bursts, together with a velocity estimate obtained from a short track of successive range estimates rather than from a single burst. A measured microcontroller deployment of both receivers as int8 TensorFlow Lite Micro firmware: the Conv1D variant decides a burst in ~ms in a ~KiB arena, preserves both the float BER (two symbols in ) and the float sensing decisions, and turns the measured latency into a closed-form rate budget: up to ~bit/s of telemetry, or a ~Hz range track, in the two time-multiplexed modes of a ~MHz microcontroller, against ~kbit/s for an accelerator-class node. A reproducible evaluation framework spanning four aerial swarm scenarios, 3GPP TDL channels, four jamming archetypes, frequency agility, and low-probability-of-intercept analysis, with open-source artifacts released for all figures and tables. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related reviews the waveform families and the learned receivers. Section~ sec:system_model defines the IoD ISAC model, the swarm geometry and the channel variants. Section~ sec:architecture presents the receiver. Section~ sec:evaluation reports the experimental results, Section~ sec:discussion discusses the design envelope, and Section~ sec:conclusion concludes. Related Work sec:related Waveforms for Aerial ISAC Three waveform families dominate the ISAC literature, and they differ in what they can carry, not in range resolution: at equal bandwidth the resolution is fixed by . FMCW. Frequency-modulated continuous wave radars estimate the range from the beat frequency patole2017_automotive_radar . The transceiver is simple, cheap and an excellent ranger, but a chirp carries no telemetry: multiplexing data onto it requires modulating the sweep slope or interleaving sensing and data packets, at a cost in efficiency. This waveform is also the most exposed of the three, because its time-frequency signature is trivially detectable and cheap to replicate, and co-located FMCW radars blind each other when several drones share the same airspace. OFDM. Multicarrier ISAC is today the dominant academic approach: the pilot symbols already needed for channel estimation are reused to estimate the delay of the returns sturm2011_ofdm_radar, zhang2021_jcs, liu2022_isac . Its spectral efficiency is high, but the waveform pays a high peak-to-average power ratio and therefore heavier, more power-hungry amplifiers han2005_papr --- a direct SWaP-C penalty on a micro-UAV --- and it offers no physical-layer protection against a receiver that can afford to listen. PRN/DSSS. Pseudo-random codes --- the Gold families used by GNSS being the canonical example --- spread a binary sequence over the band and are the classical answer to both ranging and jam resistance gold1967, scholtz1982 . They are easier to generate digitally than the floating-point iteration of a chaotic map, but they are periodic: the resulting range profile carries sidelobes (ghost targets) that an aperiodic waveform does not exhibit, and the number of mutually orthogonal codes usable in the same airspace is finite, so a dense and dynamic swarm must arbitrate code assignment. Chaotic waveforms. Chaos is structurally stronger in physical-layer security and jam resistance --- a noise-like aperiodic waveform neither advertises its presence nor offers a stationary structure to exploit~--- and in swarm scalability, because each drone can seed an independent, statistically near-orthogonal waveform without a code-assignment protocol kaddoum2016 . The price is exactly where this paper intervenes: without the transmitter's chaotic state the demodulation is non-cooperative, and classical correlators fail once the aerial channel adds Doppler and multipath escribano2016, cai2025 . Learned Chaos Receivers The learned receivers closest to this work are the recurrent demodulators of zhang2020, zhang2022, mobini2025 . They recover part of the gap left by correlation detectors, at a cost in parameters and latency that matters on a micro-UAV, and they remain single-task. Multi-task learning has been used to share representations between radio tasks caruana1997, ruder2017 , and the route from such networks to a microcontroller is pruning, int8 quantization and hardware-aware kernels han2015, hubara2017, deng2020_model_compression . What is missing is a receiver that (i) decodes blindly, (ii) ranges from a radar burst with a locally regenerated reference, and (iii) supports both modes inside a footprint compatible with a flight controller. Ultra-CAN is designed around these three constraints. title: Right Goal, Wrong Body: Re-grounding Frozen VLAs under Actuation Shift
comment: Accepted at the SPAIS Workshop at CoRL 2026
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are capable of producing desired robotic behaviors in ideal settings. However, they often fail when the robot's actuation changes at deployment. For example, remounting, mechanical wear, or command latency changes can lead to failed tasks and unsafe behaviors. To address the inevitable actuation shift, we propose ReGround, an inference-time method that keeps the VLA frozen and re-grounds its intended motion. ReGround learns the deployed robot's dynamics from task-agnostic motor babbling, and then tracks the policy's intended motion while staying close to the policy's own plan. ReGround activates only upon detecting a shift, and needs no rewards, demonstrations, or retraining. We show via two VLAs, eight LIBERO tasks, and five shift settings that ReGround can restore near-oracle success, such as raising $π_{0.5}$'s success from 0.16 to 0.90 under 400 ms latency, while remaining safer than a linear-calibration baseline. Project website and open-source code: https://umersiddique94.github.io/ReGround/.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are capable of producing desired robotic behaviors in ideal settings. However, they often fail when the robot's actuation changes at deployment. For example, remounting, mechanical wear, or command latency changes can lead to failed tasks and unsafe behaviors. To address the inevitable actuation shift, we propose ReGround, an inference-time method that keeps the VLA frozen and re-grounds its intended motion. ReGround learns the deployed robot's dynamics from task-agnostic motor babbling, and then tracks the policy's intended motion while staying close to the policy's own plan. ReGround activates only upon detecting a shift, and needs no rewards, demonstrations, or retraining. We show via two VLAs, eight LIBERO tasks, and five shift settings that ReGround can restore near-oracle success, such as raising 's success from 0.16 to 0.90 under 400\,ms latency, while remaining safer than a linear-calibration baseline. Project website and open-source code: umersiddique94.github.io/ReGround . Introduction sec:intro Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance across diverse robotic manipulation tasks by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and vision-language representations to map observations and language instructions directly to actions~ brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,oxe2024,octo2024,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,shukor2025smolvla . However, a VLA is typically trained assuming a particular relationship between its action commands and the robot's resulting motion. Changes in the action coordinate frame, controller gains, or command latency can alter this relationship, causing the same action predicted by the VLA to produce a different physical motion. We refer to this mismatch as actuation shift, where the task and observations remain unchanged, but the mapping from the VLA's action commands to the robot's physical motion has changed. A natural solution is to retrain or fine-tune the policy on the deployed robot, but this requires additional task demonstrations, computation, and access to model weights~ julian2020never,tobin2017domain,peng2018sim,zhao2020sim . This motivates our central question: At deployment, how can a frozen VLA remain effective and safe when the robot's actuation has changed? Actuation shift is not only a performance issue but also a safety concern~ liu2024safety . A VLA may still be able to identify the correct task and target object while producing actions that lead to unintended robot motion, resulting in overshoot, unintended contact, object displacement, or other unsafe behavior. Existing work on VLA robustness has primarily studied changes in visual observations~ fei2025liberoplus , while adaptation to changes in robot actuation generally relies on additional fault data, demonstrations, or policy updates~ jo2026uncovering . Training-time approaches, such as rapid motor adaptation and meta-learning, improve robustness by exposing policies to variations during training or adapting them after deployment~ kumar2021rma,nagabandi2019learning . More recently, test-time methods have also shown that frozen policies can be steered without parameter updates by using reward, value, or verifier signals to guide action selection~ nakamoto2024steering,kwok2025robomonkey,dai2025rover . Closest to our work is the inverse-dynamics transfer, which maps intended motion to actions under changed execution dynamics~ christiano2016transfer . However, these methods were not designed for frozen VLAs that output action chunks, nor do they address actuation shift. We address this gap with ReGround, an inference-time method for adapting frozen VLAs under actuation shift. Our key insight is that actuation shift changes how the robot executes the VLA's actions, while the frozen VLA still knows what motion is needed to complete the task. ReGround therefore recovers the motion intended by the VLA under the training-body dynamics and computes new actions that reproduce this motion on the deployed robot. To achieve this, a model of the training body rolls out the VLA's action chunk to obtain a reference trajectory. A deployed-body model learned from task-agnostic motor babbling is then used to determine how the robot should act to follow this trajectory under the changed dynamics. A trust region then keeps the corrected actions close to the VLA's original plan, while a residual monitor activates ReGround only when an actuation shift is detected. On across eight LIBERO tasks and five shift settings, ReGround restores 0.90--0.98 success, including 0.16 to 0.90 at 400\,ms latency. For both VLAs, ReGround reduces unsafe episodes relative to linear calibration. Preliminaries sec:prelim Language Action Models. A VLA is typically trained via imitation learning on diverse robot demonstration datasets , by maximizing that maps observation and an instruction to a chunk of actions, of which the first are executed before re-querying~ black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla . Each is a 6-D EEF delta for an operational-space controller plus a gripper command. We define robot state as the robot EEF pose in 6-D rotation form, gripper state, joint positions, and velocities (25-dimensional in total), which evolves under dynamics ~ Puterman94,sutton1998reinforcement and since contains only the robot, every model we learn is task-agnostic. To denote the robot training and deployed bodies, we use and , respectively. -time alignment and policy shaping. title: DexFormer 2.0: Towards a Cross-Embodiment Foundation Policy for Dexterous Grasping
summary: Dexterous grasping policies are usually trained for one arm paired with one hand. Every new pairing then needs its own policy, and the number of policies grows with every arm and hand added. We ask whether a single policy can control many arm-hand combinations and transfer to pairings and hands it has never seen. This is hard because robots differ in the number, layout, and dynamics of their joints, so their observations and actions share no common interface. We present DexFormer 2.0, a single reinforcement learning policy for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping. It maps every robot to a canonical joint interface with validity masks, encodes each joint's morphology with attention biased by the kinematic tree, and uses a Transformer-XL memory to infer embodiment-dependent dynamics from recent interaction. Trained on 18 combinations of four arms and six hands, it reaches 89% stable success on seen combinations and 51% on six held-out arm-hand pairs, outperforming GRU and DexFormer 1.0 baselines. Without fine-tuning, it also grasps with four new hand types and, through retargeting, with parallel grippers. Ablations show that memory, the kinematic-tree bias, and broader pairing coverage each matter for transfer. On a physical Flexiv arm, distilled students transfer zero-shot from simulation with two hands, including a held-out pair. Project website: https://davidlxu.github.io/dexformer2-web/.

Introduction sec:introduction Dexterous grasping policies are commonly developed for a fixed robotic embodiment: one arm, one hand, and one carefully matched action space. This specialization makes policy development expensive as hardware diversifies. Replacing either the arm or the hand changes the kinematic chain, reachable workspace, joint limits, control response, and contact geometry; replacing both compounds these changes. A straightforward solution is to train a separate policy for every arm--hand pairing, but the number of policies grows with the Cartesian product of available arms and hands, preventing knowledge sharing across related embodiments. Learning one policy across heterogeneous arm--hand systems is challenging for three reasons. First, different hands expose different numbers and arrangements of active joints, so their observations and actions do not naturally share a fixed interface. Second, the same action value has a different physical meaning under different joint axes, limits, link placements, and kinematic depths. Third, morphology alone is insufficient: closed-loop grasping also depends on contacts and embodiment-specific dynamics that must be inferred over time. We present DexFormer 2.0, a morphology-aware recurrent policy for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping ( ). We represent every robot through a canonical set of 29 joint slots---seven arm joints and up to 22 hand joints---together with validity masks. Each joint receives a 16-dimensional morphology descriptor encoding its axis, attachment position, joint and velocity limits, semantic role, and kinematic depth. Our MorphNode encoder adds an attention residual biased by the robot's kinematic tree and joint roles, and a Transformer-XL maintains a 16-step temporal context over the fused features. A shared actor head then produces a masked Gaussian policy over the canonical action space, using the same network across all arm--hand pairings. We study a single policy over four robot arms and six dexterous hands, forming 24 arm--hand combinations. We randomly select 18 combinations for training and reserve the remaining six for testing. Evaluation on both training and uses the same ten object identities, isolating embodiment generalization from object-identity generalization. The policy reaches 89.01 stable success on the seen combinations and 51.18 on the , and it keeps 48.85 on when the objects are ten unseen YCB objects~ calli2015ycb . Without fine-tuning, it also grasps with four hand types that never appear in training, and its actions can be retargeted to four parallel grippers. Our contributions are: We introduce a joint cross-embodiment training paradigm: one policy is trained on many arm--hand embodiments together, through canonical joint slots and validity masks. The policy, without fine-tuning, transfers to and to hand types absent from training, and even to parallel grippers. We develop a topology-aware recurrent policy architecture that combines per-joint physical descriptors, a gated spatial-attention residual, Transformer-XL memory, and a shared actor head. The architecture conditions control on morphology without using a dedicated policy or output head for each embodiment. We show that temporal memory, kinematic-tree bias, and pairing coverage each matter for transfer: removing memory or the tree bias roughly halves success on , and training on 18 instead of 12 combinations raises it from 5.65 to 51.18 at a matched interaction budget. Related Work sec:related-work Dexterous grasping and sim-to-real transfer. Reinforcement learning has enabled contact-rich dexterous control. Andrychowicz et al.~ andrychowicz2020learning showed that domain randomization~ tobin2017domain can transfer simulated in-hand manipulation policies to a physical hand, and later work extended this route to faster reorientation and rotation~ handa2023dextreme,qi2022inhand . For grasping, UniDexGrasp~ xu2023unidexgrasp and UniDexGrasp++~ wan2023unidexgrasp learn object-general policies through goal conditioning, geometry-aware curricula, and iterative generalist--specialist learning, while UniGraspTransformer~ wang2025unigrasptransformer distills object-specific experts into a shared Transformer policy. DexNDM~ liu2026dexndm addresses the reality gap in in-hand rotation using joint-wise learned dynamics. These studies target object generalization and deployment for one embodiment; we share a grasping policy when both the arm and hand vary. Generalist policies across embodiments. Morphology-agnostic control has a long line of work in simulated locomotion. Graph and modular policies share parameters across limbs through message passing~ wang2018nervenet,huang2020smp , and Transformer policies replace message passing with attention over joint tokens, optionally conditioned on morphology~ kurin2021amorpheus,gupta2022metamorph . For manipulation, large imitation-learning models pool demonstrations from many robots~ openx2024,octo2024,doshi2024crossformer , but they mostly cover parallel-jaw grippers. One Policy to Run Them All~ bohlinger2025onepolicy introduces the Unified Robot Morphology Architecture (URMA), using morphology-aware encoding and decoding to share a locomotion policy across diverse legged robots, later scaled through embodiment randomization~ bohlinger2025extreme . RMA~ kumar2021rma adapts a locomotion policy to changing dynamics from history. Dexterous grasping additionally requires coordinated arm motion and multi-finger contact control. Cross-embodiment dexterous control. CrossDex~ yuan2025crossdex learns a shared grasping policy using human-hand eigengrasp actions and hand-specific retargeting. GET-Zero~ patel2025getzero incorporates kinematic graph structure into a Transformer for transfer across hand designs in object rotation. DexFormer~ zhang2026dexformer instead conditions on observation history to infer morphology and dynamics implicitly. DexGrasp-Zero~ wu2026dexgraspzero uses a morphology-aligned graph representation and physical-property injection for cross-hand grasping. We seek one stochastic policy that controls all embodiments in . The observation contains the robot joint state, object pose and target position, fingertip states and contact forces, and a 64-point object point cloud. Joint-Level Morphology Representation sec:morphology-representation For each canonical joint , we construct a descriptor . It contains the joint axis expressed in its parent-link frame (3 dimensions), joint attachment position (3), the center and half-range of its position limits (2), velocity limit (1), a semantic one-hot role for arm or finger identity (6), and normalized kinematic depth (1). Unlike a categorical robot identifier, the descriptor exposes local physical structure that can be shared with . Each joint combines its descriptor with six state features: position, velocity, previous action, and a three-dimensional joint location. This forms a 22-dimensional feature , accompanied by the validity mask. The mount pose, i.e., the relative wrist-to-palm pose, contributes seven additional values. Kinematic ancestry is derived from the robot model and used to compute joint-to-joint tree distances. MorphNode Spatial Encoder sec:morphnode MorphNode combines a body MLP path with a topology-aware MorphAttention residual. In the body path, masked joint features and validity bits are flattened separately for the arm and hand and encoded by an arm encoder, a hand encoder, and a mount encoder for the mount pose. Each output is adapted to 128 dimensions, and a fusion MLP produces the body feature . The arm, hand, and mount encoders are MLPs with layer widths 128--96, 64--96, and 64--64, and the fusion MLP has two 128-unit layers. The MorphAttention residual projects the 29 joint features to 128-dimensional tokens and appends five context tokens: object state, goal state, contacts, remaining task observations, and mount pose. Two spatial attention layers, each with four heads, update these 34 tokens. title: NF-VLA: A Normalizing-Flow Baseline for Vision-Language-Action Learning
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026 G2A Workshop
summary: Autoregressive normalizing flows (NFs) provide a tractable density for learning and sampling continuous robot actions. We show that a single maximum-likelihood objective can train vision--language--action (VLA) policies competitive with leading methods on manipulation benchmarks. We present NF-VLA, which combines conditional autoregressive normalizing flows with score-based action refinement. Its deep--shallow architecture concentrates visual, language, and proprioceptive prefix conditioning in a high-capacity deep block, while unconditioned shallow blocks provide a shared invertible action transformation. The vision--language backbone and flow are jointly trained by exact maximum likelihood on Gaussian-smoothed action chunks. The same learned density supplies a single score-based correction at inference, refining generated actions to account for training-time smoothing without a separately trained denoiser. Trained on LIBERO from a pretrained vision--language backbone without robot pretraining, NF-VLA achieves 98.35\% success across the four standard suites and 72.6\% on LIBERO-Plus using the same checkpoint without further fine-tuning. Ablations show that deep-only prefix conditioning and score-based refinement both improve closed-loop success. Together, these results establish carefully structured autoregressive flows as a competitive approach to VLA control, with one learned density supporting policy training, action generation, and refinement.

Together, these results establish carefully structured autoregressive flows as a competitive approach to VLA control, with one learned density supporting policy training, action generation, and refinement. Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect pretrained visual and linguistic representations to robot control, allowing policies to generate actions from images and language instructions~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla . A central design choice is the action model: it determines how observations condition the action distribution and how that distribution produces executable commands. Existing approaches include discrete action prediction, continuous regression, diffusion, and flow matching~ kim2024openvla,kim2025oft,chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2024pi0 . Normalizing flows (NFs) offer a formulation in which an invertible transformation defines both a continuous density and a sampling procedure. Their tractable change-of-variables likelihood allows direct maximum-likelihood training~ dinh2016density,papamakarios2017maf . TARFlow~ zhai2025tarflow and the STARFlow family~ gu2025starflow,gu2025starflowv,shen2026starflow2 demonstrate the potential of Transformer autoregressive flows for visual and multimodal generation, with STARFlow introducing a deep--shallow architecture for scaling latent image generation. These developments motivate a study of conditioning and sampling in autoregressive-flow VLA policies: where and how to inject multimodal context, and whether the learned density's score can improve actions after sampling. Recent work establishes normalizing flows as capable robot policies. NinA~ tarasov2025nina introduces coupling-based action decoders for VLAs, emphasizing efficient generation, while RoMAN-Flow~ romanflow develops autoregressive-flow policies for offline reinforcement learning and one-step policy distillation. Building on this progress, we focus on the manipulation performance obtainable from likelihood-based imitation learning itself. The central design question is how to organize multimodal conditioning and sample refinement within a single continuous-density model. We present NF-VLA, a VLA policy that combines conditional autoregressive flows with score-based action refinement. Building on the deep--shallow architecture of STARFlow~ gu2025starflow , we concentrate visual, language, and proprioceptive conditioning in a high-capacity deep block, while shallow blocks provide a shared invertible transformation between action coordinates and intermediate latents. The vision--language backbone and action model are trained jointly with a single exact maximum-likelihood objective on Gaussian-smoothed actions. At inference, the same learned density supports flow inversion and a single Tweedie denoising correction computed from its own score~ efron2011tweedie,zhai2025tarflow . Learning, sampling, and refinement therefore share one density model, without a separately trained denoiser or an additional training objective. Starting from a pretrained vision--language backbone, NF-VLA is trained jointly on the full LIBERO dataset without robot pretraining or reinforcement-learning post-training. It achieves 98.35 success across the four standard LIBERO suites~ liu2023libero , including 97.8 on LIBERO-Long. The same checkpoint achieves 72.6 on LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus without further fine-tuning, demonstrating strong aggregate performance under benchmark perturbations. These results place NF-VLA competitively alongside leading VLA policies in the benchmark comparisons. Ablations support the two design choices: concentrating prefix conditioning in the deep block improves average LIBERO success by 1.20 percentage points over all-block prefix conditioning, and a single score-based refinement step improves success by 1.90 percentage points using the same trained checkpoint. Our contributions are threefold: We present NF-VLA, an autoregressive-flow VLA baseline trained end to end with a single likelihood objective and using the learned density for both sampling and score-based action correction. We evaluate conditioning placement and mechanism, finding that deep-only prefix conditioning achieves higher average success than all-block conditioning in our tested configurations. We additionally quantify the control benefit of self-score correction and report the inference costs of the evaluated designs. We evaluate the resulting policy on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, reporting strong standard-task performance alongside a perturbation-dependent robustness profile. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models sec:related_vla Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision--language representations to language-conditioned robot control. RT-2~ brohan2023rt2 represents robot actions as text tokens, allowing vision--language models to learn control alongside web-based vision--language tasks. OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla develops an open-source VLA with discretized action prediction and demonstrates adaptation to new manipulation tasks. Subsequent work explores alternatives to token-by-token action decoding: OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft combines parallel decoding and action chunking with continuous-action regression, showing that action representation and training objectives are consequential design choices. Generative action models provide another approach to continuous control. Diffusion Policy~ chi2023diffusionpolicy models action sequences through conditional denoising diffusion and executes them with receding-horizon control. Within VLAs, ~ black2024pi0 couples a pretrained vision--language model with a flow-matching action expert, while SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla develops a compact architecture with a flow-matching decoder. Normalizing Flows sec:related_flows NFs model continuous densities through invertible transformations with tractable Jacobian determinants. Real NVP~ dinh2016density uses affine coupling layers, while inverse autoregressive flow~ kingma2016improved and masked autoregressive flow~ papamakarios2017maf exploit autoregressive structure to obtain triangular Jacobians. More recently, TARFlow~ zhai2025tarflow combines affine autoregressive transformations with Transformers for image generation, and the STARFlow family~ gu2025starflow,gu2025starflowv,shen2026starflow2 develops latent-space flows with deep--shallow architectures for visual and multimodal generation. Flow matching~ lipman2022flowmatching is also connected to NFs: it trains continuous-time flows by regressing vector fields along probability paths. Recently in robotics, Ghugare and Eysenbach~ nfcontrol investigate their use in behavior cloning and reinforcement learning. Within VLAs, NinA~ tarasov2025nina replaces FLOWER's action decoder with Real NVP-style coupling flows~ dinh2016density , evaluating MLP and Transformer conditioners and emphasizing inference efficiency. RoMAN-Flow~ romanflow uses autoregressive flows with context supplied to every flow block, followed by advantage-weighted offline policy optimization and one-step distillation. SERNF~ sernf combines normalizing-flow policies with action-chunked critics for off-policy fine-tuning on real robots. Our focus is the performance of the likelihood-trained VLA policy itself: we concentrate direct conditioning in the deep flow block and reuse its action density for inference-time refinement, retaining a single maximum-likelihood training objective. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries Normalizing Flows sec:normalizing_flows An NF represents a continuous probability distribution through an invertible transformation with a tractable Jacobian determinant~ dinh2016density,papamakarios2017maf,zhai2025tarflow . For a variable and conditioning information , let map data to a latent variable with standard Gaussian density . The change-of-variables formula gives The Jacobian is taken with respect to while holding fixed; the conditioning encoder need not be invertible. For a composition of invertible blocks, , define and . The log-Jacobian determinants add across blocks, yielding the negative log-likelihood Maximum-likelihood training minimizes its expectation over the training distribution. Generation reverses the transformation: sample and compute . Autoregressive Flows sec:autoregressive_flows Autoregressive flows make the Jacobian determinant tractable by restricting each coordinate's transformation parameters to depend only on preceding coordinates~ kingma2016improved,papamakarios2017maf . For an ordered input , let and denote the shift and scale. An affine autoregressive block and its inverse take the form The Jacobian is triangular with diagonal entries , giving A causally masked network can compute all coefficients in parallel for an observed input, whereas inversion recovers coordinates sequentially from the generated prefix. For vector-valued tokens, the affine transformation acts elementwise, with each token's coefficients conditioned on preceding tokens. Transformer autoregressive flow (TARFlow)~ zhai2025tarflow parameterizes these coefficients with causal Transformers and stacks blocks with alternating autoregressive orderings. STARFlow~ gu2025starflow builds on this formulation with a deep--shallow architecture: in the generative direction, a deep block maps Gaussian noise to intermediate latents, which subsequent shallow blocks transform into model outputs. Conditioning can be supplied as a prefix to the deep block while the shallow blocks remain unconditioned. We adopt STARFlow as NF-VLA's autoregressive flow backbone and adapt this architecture to observation-conditioned continuous action chunks. title: Stochastic Self-Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in robotics through imitation learning, yet fine-tuning them with on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is limited. In group-based RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), every rollout step requires multi-step ODE integration, and the sampler's limited stochasticity leads to rollout groups with low variance. We propose VLA-SSD, which addresses both high inference latency and limited stochasticity. In particular, our method self-distills a pretrained flow-matching action head into a stochastic one-step policy by conditioning a single-jump generator on a Brownian path. We derive a conditional action density via our stochastic one-step policy, enabling efficient post-training via likelihood-ratio RL algorithms. We show that distilling VLA-SSD from the $π_0$ VLA reduces the action head's forward-pass time by a factor of 7.7, at the cost of a 5.5% relative decrease in the success rate on the LIBERO benchmark. However, by leveraging the increased sample diversity of VLA-SSD during group generation, post-training a $π_{0.5}$ VLA using GRPO yields a 20.6% relative improvement.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision--language--action (VLA) models have achieved significant advances by leveraging knowledge from pre-trained vision--language models in robotics~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla . However, state-of-the-art VLAs have yet to achieve comparable generalization to other foundation models due to their reliance on imitation learning from expert demonstrations for adaptation to embodiments and environments~ black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,kim2025openvlaoft,nvidia2025groot,shukor2025smolvla . Frontier flow-based VLAs generate continuous action chunks with a flow-matching action head~ black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05 . Yet, enabling them to improve via on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is still limited by the inference time of multi-step ODE integration and a lack of stochasticity. To improve efficiency, one-step flow-based policies have been introduced for continuous control~ zhan2026mean,ziakas2026fmq , replacing multi-step ODE integration with a single transport step learned via self-distillation~ song2023consistency,boffi2024flowmaps,geng2025meanflow,boffi2025selfdistillation . However, in RL methods using multi-sample advantage estimation, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), the baseline is derived directly from a group of trajectories given the current state. Because flow-matching rely entirely on the initial random noise draw for stochasticity, they restrict the action diversity within the sampled group, resulting in a degraded training signal~ shao2024deepseekmath . To enable exploration, existing approaches increase sample diversity by introducing an external noise network or reverting to multi-step samplers that inject noise at each integration step~ pirl2025,reinflow2025,flowmapgrpo2026 . title: ReRead: Wrong Predictions, Useful Representations - Correcting Frozen Robot Policies by Re-reading Their Own Representations
summary: When a pretrained robot policy fails on challenging tasks, common remedies include retraining the backbone, adding an external visual encoder, or introducing a memory module. We argue that wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations: a policy can retain the required information yet fail to read it out as the correct action. To test this view, we propose ReRead: with the backbone frozen, a corrector re-reads the current and two previous caches to predict an action residual. The corrector sees no images, is trained solely on offline demonstrations from all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and adds only 4.17% latency. Ablations and interventions show that the correction relies on the backbone's own representations: none of four external visual encoders adds further gain, and swapping in past caches from other trajectories sharply increases action error. On the 11 hardest RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, ReRead improves the success rates of LingBot-VLA, $π_{0.5}$, and Fast-WAM by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points, respectively. In paired evaluation on all 50 tasks, it raises Fast-WAM's average success rate from 90.73% to 92.66%. On a Flexiv dual-arm robot, it raises success on a phase-ambiguous task from 0% to 36%.
full_text: \@title [t] c \@author Overview of ReRead. fig:reread_teaser When a pretrained robot policy fails on challenging tasks, common remedies include retraining the backbone, adding an external visual encoder, or introducing a memory module. We argue that wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations: a policy can retain the required information yet fail to read it out as the correct action. To test this view, we propose ReRead: with the backbone frozen, a corrector re-reads the current and two previous caches to predict an action residual. The corrector sees no images, is trained solely on offline demonstrations from all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and adds only 4.17 latency. Ablations and interventions show that the correction relies on the backbone's own representations: none of four external visual encoders adds further gain, and swapping in past caches from other trajectories sharply increases action error. On the 11 hardest RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, ReRead improves the success rates of LingBot-VLA, , and Fast-WAM by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points, respectively. In paired evaluation on all 50 tasks, it raises Fast-WAM's average success rate from 90.73 to 92.66 . On a Flexiv dual-arm robot, it raises success on a phase-ambiguous task from 0 to 36 . Introduction sec:intro When a pretrained robot policy fails on challenging tasks, common remedies include retraining the backbone, adding an external visual encoder, or introducing a memory module~ octo2024,memoryvla2026,hamlet2026 . These remedies share an implicit assumption: if the predicted actions are wrong, the policy's representations must lack task-relevant information. But failure has another possible cause: the policy already has the information it needs, yet fails to read it out as the correct action. Similar findings in image recognition show that retraining only the classifier can improve accuracy while keeping the learned representations fixed~ kang2020decoupling,kirichenko2023dfr . Robot tasks have a further property: the current frame is often insufficient to determine the action, because the action also depends on the current task phase. The information needed to distinguish phases is not in the current frame, but it may already reside in the internal representations of the policy's previous decisions, which are discarded once the actions are output. We therefore argue that wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations. The attention keys and values (K/V) cached by the backbone, the robot state, and temporal information form an internal memory, and we call its task-relevant information the representation. (In Figs.~ fig:reread_teaser and~ fig:newm_overview , ``R'' stands for ``Representations''.) The process that maps the internal memory to an action is the readout, and the action finally returned is the prediction. A backbone error may arise because the required information was never in the caches, or because it is in the caches but is not read out as the correct action. In the latter case, it is the readout that needs to be improved, and the backbone need not be retrained. This corresponds to the classical decomposition under squared loss: the prediction error equals the representation error plus the readout gap. To test this view, we propose ReRead (Fig.~ fig:reread_teaser ): with the backbone frozen, a new corrector re-reads the representations cached by the backbone. The backbone generates candidate actions as usual, and ReRead stores the native visual and action K/V from each of its decisions. Using the candidate action as the query, the corrector reads the caches of the current and the two previous decisions and outputs an action residual, which is added back to the candidate action. The corrector sees no images, does not retrain the backbone, and does not re-encode the history. It is trained solely on offline demonstrations with an action MSE loss and adds 11.66 ms of latency per decision (4.17 ). We train ReRead on offline demonstrations from all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0~ robotwin2_2026 . Fast-WAM~ fastwam2026 has a reported average success rate of 91.83 on these tasks, but its failures are concentrated in a few tasks: the 11 tasks with the lowest published success rates (Hard11) account for about 66.5 of the failures. We use Hard11 as an evaluation subset to analyze cases in which the policy retains the required information but predicts the wrong action, and evaluate the overall effect of re-reading on all 50 tasks. The experiments are organized around four questions. First, when the backbone errs, is the required information still in the caches? Re-reading the current cache alone reduces the native candidate's open-loop MSE by 61.45 . With ReRead, the success rates of LingBot-VLA, , and Fast-WAM on Hard11 improve by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points, respectively. In our paired evaluation on all 50 tasks, Fast-WAM's average success rate rises from 90.73 to 92.66 . Second, can prediction and representation be evaluated separately? Intervention experiments show that the corrected action is determined mainly by the caches: increasing the error of the candidate action 2-fold increases the error of the corrected action by only 12.08 , whereas replacing the past caches with those from other trajectories of the same task increases it 12.37-fold. Third, do backbone failures stem from insufficient perception? None of the four external visual encoders outperforms ReRead, whereas replacing the past caches markedly changes the corrected action. These results do not support the perception-bottleneck explanation. Fourth, when the current frame cannot distinguish phases, where is the required information? On a phase-ambiguous task, ReRead raises the success rate from 2 to 50 in simulation and from 0 to 36 on a real Flexiv dual-arm robot. Swapping in caches from the opposite phase moves the corrected action toward the other phase, indicating that the required information lies in the caches of previous decisions. Our contributions are as follows: We propose a new perspective: wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations. We decompose the prediction error into the representation error and the readout gap, and estimate the part that re-reading can eliminate. To test this perspective, we propose ReRead, which freezes the backbone and trains a corrector solely on offline demonstrations to re-read the backbone's cached representations and correct the actions. Our training and inference code and model weights are publicly available at . Interventions and ablations show that the correction relies on the backbone's own caches. Phase information also remains in the caches of previous decisions. Prediction and representation can therefore be evaluated separately. Related Work sec:background Gap between Representations and Outputs. Good internal representations do not imply good outputs. In image recognition, the representation and the classifier can be adjusted separately for long-tailed recognition~ kang2020decoupling , and the representations of models that rely on spurious correlations still contain robust features~ kirichenko2023dfr . In language models, truth signals that do not depend on the surface form of the answer can be read out from internal activations~ burns2023ccs , and simply intervening on attention-head activations improves answer truthfulness~ li2023iti . Probing studies examine both how much information can be read out from representations~ pimentel2020probing and how much these readouts depend on the capacity of the probe itself~ hewitt2019control . Unlike these works, we focus on the continuous actions of frozen robot policies, where the information is also spread across the past few decisions, and we directly quantify how much error re-reading can eliminate. Temporal Memory in Robot Policies. History helps policies distinguish visually similar task phases. Octo processes recent observations~ octo2024 . MemoryVLA and HAMLET represent, retrieve, or compress history to condition action generation~ memoryvla2026,hamlet2026 . GeoMem-VLA stores geometric and observation representations in temporal memory and retrieves them to guide action generation~ geomemvla2026 . HyVLA-0.5 compresses visual history through temporal-spatial attention before passing the resulting representations to the VLM~ hyvla2026 . These methods use history to condition action generation. If the error lies in the readout, adding historical context does not necessarily help. In contrast, ReRead leaves the backbone's inputs and candidate generation unchanged and, once the candidate action is produced, uses a corrector to read the current and past caches. Residual Correction for Frozen Policies. Residual policies add a small adjustment on top of existing actions while preserving the backbone's original capabilities. Residual Policy Learning and FISH use reinforcement learning to optimize a residual on top of the backbone~ silver2018rpl,fish2023 . Policy Decorator freezes a large imitation policy and learns a small residual through online interaction~ yuan2025policydecorator . Dejavu freezes a VLA, retrieves information from an experience database, and learns action corrections from interaction rewards~ dejavu2026 . Within a framework of multi-round human corrections, I3L also evaluates a supervised residual correction scheme~ i3l2026 . These methods all rely on online interaction, rewards, or additional human-correction data. ReRead uses only existing offline demonstrations and reads the backbone's caches from the current episode to test whether they retain the information needed for correct actions. Separating Prediction from Representation sec:theory Whether an action prediction is wrong and whether the caches contain useful information are two different questions. We distinguish them by decomposing the prediction error into the representation error and the readout gap. Problem Formulation sec:preliminaries At the -th decision, the frozen backbone receives images , the robot state , and the instruction , denoted , and generates a candidate action chunk from sampling noise where is the chunk length and is the action dimension. The native K/V, state, and temporal information produced by this decision together form a cache. ReRead combines the current and past caches into a memory and learns a residual correction supervised by the expert action , while the backbone parameters remain frozen. Two Sources of Prediction Error sec:correction_theory In what follows, we fix the backbone and the evaluation distribution and omit the subscript . We denote the corrector's input by and its output residual by . The mean squared error after adding a residual is , where is the error of executing the candidate directly. Under squared loss, the best prediction from is the conditional mean . By the projection property of the conditional mean~ hastie2009esl , we have The first term is the representation error: the minimum prediction error given the candidate action and the caches. Hence, even when the prediction error is large, the representation error can still be small; the optimal residual exactly eliminates the entire readout gap. The optimal readout is not directly available, but its prediction error can be bounded above with a trained corrector. When , Here, is the fraction of the error actually reduced by the corrector.
