title: AsymEEF: Bimanual Manipulation with Asymmetric End Effectors
summary: Teleoperated demonstrations are costly to collect and rarely reusable across end-effectors with different kinematics and action spaces. This burden grows in bimanual manipulation, where each end-effector pair may require new data. We present AsymEEF, a framework for executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation and unified bimanual policy learning. Given a small source dataset, AsymEEF transfers demonstrations to heterogeneous combinations of two-, three-, and five-fingered end-effectors without additional teleoperation. Kinematic teacher anchors provide geometric supervision, while sparse real-world X-Calib anchors correct discrepancies in grasp execution. A shared encoder maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space, and a morphology-conditioned decoder reconstructs target commands. Generated trajectories undergo replay filtering for task-level executability. The representation also supports a unified bimanual visuomotor policy trained across multiple pairs. Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines, achieves a mean replay-valid expansion gain of 16.6 times in simulation, and is evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots. Project website: https://asymeef.vercel.app/.
full_text: Method sec:method Problem Formulation and Overview sec:method_overview We consider bimanual systems composed of two identical arms equipped with an ordered end-effector pair . Given a small set of successful demonstrations collected with a source pair , our goal is to generate executable demonstrations for a target pair without teleoperating each target combination. We assume that the target EEFs can perform the required interactions, although differences in their actuation spaces and kinematic structures prevent direct reuse of joint trajectories. We represent an EEF state as , where is the world-frame pose of its functional wrist frame and contains its normalized independent actuator values. AsymEEF separates cross-EEF state alignment from trajectory-level validation. Kinematic teacher anchors and a few real-world calibration anchors supervise a shared encoder--decoder. This interface converts source trajectories to target EEF pairs, while full-task replay determines which trajectories are retained. The resulting demonstrations support both pair-specific policy training and unified learning across pairs. Cross-EEF Anchoring sec:cross_eef_anchoring Geometry-Guided Teacher Anchoring For each EEF, we annotate functional contact points on URDF links. Differentiable forward kinematics maps to their positions . We express these points in the functional wrist frame, adopt consistent left/right conventions, and normalize lengths by an EEF-specific characteristic scale. The points are divided into two opposing groups with weighted centers and . We define the grasp center, opening width, and signed opposition direction as For multifingered hands, the approach direction is the signed normal of a plane defined by three fingertips in a fixed semantic order. For two-fingered grippers, it points from the EEF base toward the grasp center. Thumb-tip positions, thumb-pad normals, and named finger-chain keypoints provide additional descriptors where available. Together, these quantities form a functional geometry descriptor without requiring identical joint layouts. For each directed pair , we use scrambled Sobol sampling on a morphology-aware grasp manifold and reject source states with invalid functional frames. Given an admissible , a kinematic teacher optimizes the target actuator state and a target-to-source functional-frame transform : Here, aligns grasp centers and signed gap and approach directions, while applies the contact constraints appropriate to pair type : effective aperture and active contacts, thumb--opposed-contact relations, or multifinger-chain geometry. When used, the wrist penalty discourages pose changes during in-hand refinement, favoring compensation through target actuators; some pair types instead fix selected pose degrees of freedom. We solve from multiple target initializations and retain the best distinct candidates passing geometric, directional, and physical-gap gates. Defining to map target-frame coordinates into the source functional frame gives for a world-frame source pose . The procedure requires registered kinematics, actuator limits, and functional-point annotations, but no task demonstrations or physical-robot measurements. X-Calib Real-World Calibration Anchoring Kinematic similarity does not capture assembly offsets, actuator coupling, or contact compliance. X-Calib therefore adds real grasp keyframes for the available physical EEFs. Each calibration intent specifies an object, a discrete workspace location, and a grasp orientation. Stable arm and hand configurations are recorded through manual teaching. Keyframes sharing form weak correspondences. Each anchor is represented as , where contains valid target states and preserves alternative configurations for the same grasp intent. Functional wrist poses are recovered through full-robot forward kinematics; arm joints are used only for pose recovery and are excluded from the EEF latent. Teacher anchors provide broad spatial coverage, while X-Calib captures hardware-specific deviations, as shown in Figure~ fig:teacher_anchor . Shared EEF-State Interface sec:shared_eef_interface Encoder--Decoder Architecture The shared interface maps variable-dimensional EEF states to a fixed-dimensional latent and decodes them according to the target morphology: where and describe URDF-derived actuator morphology and kinematic adjacency. EEF identity only selects these structural descriptors; it does not select separate network parameters. The Shared EEF-State Encoder constructs one token per independent actuator. Each token combines its current value, local FK position relative to the functional wrist, and static features describing joint type, axis, mounting transform, range, and mimic relationships. A topology-biased Transformer~ vaswani2017attention processes these tokens together with a learned state token. Kinematic adjacency biases attention toward neighboring joints while retaining global interactions between fingers. Wrist translation and a continuous six-dimensional rotation representation~ zhou2019continuity are embedded separately and fused with the state-token output to produce a 24-dimensional latent. The decoder conditions target-morphology actuator queries and a wrist query on this latent. Shared actuator and pose heads then recover the target actuator state and functional wrist pose. Our implementation uses 128-dimensional tokens, three Transformer layers, four attention heads, and supports up to 12 independent actuators. The latent jointly represents wrist pose and internal hand configuration without manually assigned semantic blocks. Figure~ fig:architecture summarizes the architecture and its connection to the latent bimanual policy. Joint Training Objective We jointly train one encoder and one decoder on both anchor sources: For brevity, and denote conditioning on . Let combine actuator-state error, wrist-translation error, and rotational geodesic error. Self- and cross-reconstruction are defined as The set loss applies soft selection among valid target states according to their combined actuator and wrist errors, rather than constructing an averaged target configuration. Teacher anchors correspond to singleton target sets. Requiring complete latent equality would suppress configurations that a dexterous hand can express but a gripper cannot. We therefore align only a training-time projection : The expectation is taken over corresponding anchor states. The regularization term maintains latent variance, reduces redundancy, preserves sensitivity to changes in internal hand configuration, and limits local amplification in cross-EEF mappings. Subsequent generation and policy learning use the full 24-dimensional latent rather than the alignment projection. Demonstration Generation and Validation sec:generation_validation Cross-Pair Transfer and Replay We map each EEF state on the shared source timeline as follows: where indexes trajectory steps. Decoded wrist poses are converted to arm commands through constrained inverse kinematics, while decoded actuator states control the target EEFs. The complete task is then replayed through simulation physics or on the target physical robot. Locally aligned states do not guarantee successful interactions over an entire trajectory. We therefore retain a candidate only if it satisfies kinematic feasibility, joint continuity, collision constraints, valid contact sequences, and task success. Intended object contacts are permitted; unintended collisions are rejected. We neither overwrite object states during replay nor apply external forces to rescue failures. Accepted executions provide observations and control sequences for the target pair. Thus, anchor consistency guides transfer, but task execution determines whether a generated trajectory becomes a usable demonstration. Figure~ fig:misalign compares the transferred target states with the source functional grasp frame and alternative alignment strategies. For tasks where objects impose tight grasp-orientation constraints beyond simple pick-and-place, both alternatives can fail when mounting-induced wrist-frame offsets are not adequately accounted for. We discuss these failure modes in Sec.~ sec:experiments . Progressive Spatial Expansion To increase simulation coverage, we divide successful seeds into approach, grasp, and manipulation segments and remap wrist trajectories to randomized object configurations. Expansion starts with small perturbations around the seeds and gradually covers larger object translations, robot-base perturbations, and workspace boundaries. Arm trajectories are recomputed with IK, while EEF states are retained or transferred through the shared interface. Every candidate undergoes the same replay validation, and successful trajectories can seed subsequent rounds. This procedure concentrates generation on regions that continue to produce valid demonstrations, rather than sampling a broad configuration space indiscriminately. Unified Latent Bimanual Visuomotor Policy sec:unified_policy We freeze the encoder and decoder and encode all demonstrations offline. For the seven-joint arms in our system, the proprioceptive state is Actions use the same layout, but contain future arm-joint targets and latent encodings of desired EEF states rather than current measurements. Native and generated demonstrations from different pairs can therefore be mixed without morphology-specific policy heads. We evaluate ACT~ zhao2023learning and ~ black2025pi05 as representative backbones for the unified latent bimanual visuomotor policy. Both receive visual observations and the shared proprioceptive state and predict action chunks through the same interface. Each retains its original training objective: ACT is trained for action-chunk prediction, while uses its native flow-matching objective. This separates the cross-EEF representation from the choice of imitation learner. At inference, the frozen encoder maps wrist poses and EEF feedback to latent observations. Arm actions are realized in either joint- or task-space mode. In the former, when arm qpos is included in the training action representation, the policy directly predicts arm-joint targets, while the target-conditioned decoder recovers EEF actuator commands. In the latter, decoded wrist targets are converted online to arm commands through IK. The modes are mutually exclusive, avoiding redundant arm commands while retaining fixed-dimensional observations and actions across EEF pairs. This design also provides a natural extension to cross-embodiment transfer across arm morphologies. Unless otherwise noted, all subsequent policy evaluations use the joint-space mode.

title: JEPTERA: A Platform Agnostic JEPA-Assisted Model Predictive Planner for Urban UAV Navigation
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to conference
summary: Urban navigation for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) requires planning that accounts for environmental geometry, vehicle dynamics, and moving obstacles. This paper presents JEPTERA, a navigation architecture that integrates a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), Model Predictive Control (MPC), PID control, and a safety layer. JEPA predicts the UAV's motion response to candidate commands for MPC action selection, while the safety layer checks trajectories against occupied space and predicted obstacle motion. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations separate the planning core from simulator interfaces. An ablation study evaluated six configurations across three gym scenarios, totaling 180 runs. The complete architecture achieved the highest aggregate success rate, completing 28 of 30 runs. Additional tests completed one route across three city maps without collisions. Separate integration tests demonstrated operation in Gazebo/ROS 2, MuJoCo, and CARLA without modifying the core planning logic. These results support the feasibility of the integrated architecture for simulated urban UAV navigation and its portability across simulator interfaces.

Additional tests completed one route across three city maps without collisions. Separate integration tests demonstrated operation in Gazebo/ROS 2, MuJoCo, and CARLA without modifying the core planning logic. These results support the feasibility of the integrated architecture for simulated urban UAV navigation and its portability across simulator interfaces. UAV navigation, joint-embedding predictive architecture, model predictive control, collision avoidance, cross-simulator portability Introduction Autonomous UAVs require reliable navigation in dynamic urban environments. Buildings that constrain the airspace, along with moving obstacles, necessitate online planning based on continuously updated observations zhou2021egoplanner,tordesillas2022faster . Such conditions demand a planning system capable of accounting for environmental geometry, the UAV's motion constraints, and the predicted movement of obstacles, in order to determine safe maneuvers while still achieving the desired objectives hewing2020learningmpc . Model predictive control (MPC) selects actions by optimizing predicted motion under system objectives and constraints falanga2018pampc,hewing2020learningmpc . The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) provides a framework for prediction in representation space lecun2022path , subsequently explored through I-JEPA for images and V-JEPA 2 for action-conditioned robot planning assran2023ijepa,assran2025vjepa2 . These developments highlight the potential of representation space prediction for UAV navigation among static and dynamic obstacles. Although MPC–PID with a safety layer provides reliable navigation, its performance may degrade in complex dynamic environments where anticipating obstacle motion is essential hewing2020learningmpc . This limitation motivates integrating JEPA-based motion prediction with MPC to improve navigation reliability under challenging conditions. This paper proposes JEPTERA, a platform-agnostic UAV navigation architecture integrating JEPA-based motion prediction, MPC, PID control, and safety layer. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations decouple the planning core from platform interfaces. Evaluation includes component ablations, navigation across three urban maps, and cross-simulator integration tests. To summarize, our main contributions are threefold. a planning architecture combining JEPA-based motion prediction with MPC, PID control, and a safety layer; a shared planning core integrated across simulators through adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations; and an evaluation comprising 180 ablation runs, navigation across three urban maps, and cross-simulator integration tests. Related Work UAV Trajectory Planning and Predictive Control UAV trajectory planning must balance environmental geometry, motion feasibility, and computational efficiency. The Dynamic Window Approach selects local velocities for collision avoidance, while minimum-snap optimization generates smooth quadrotor trajectories fox1997dwa,mellinger2011minsnap . Fast-Planner combines kinodynamic search with trajectory optimization for high-speed flight zhou2019fastplanner . EGO-Planner reduces planning overhead through ESDF-free gradient-based optimization zhou2021egoplanner , while FASTER navigates known and unknown environments with a backup trajectory in verified free space tordesillas2022faster . MPC selects actions using predicted dynamics over a planning horizon liu2017mpcplanning,jalalmaab2017feasibility . PAMPC incorporates perception requirements into quadrotor control falanga2018pampc , while K \"o hler et al. integrate segment-based shortest-path planning with MPC for mobile robots in cluttered environments kohler2025mpc . JEPTERA uses JEPA-based UAV motion predictions to evaluate candidate actions within MPC, with PID providing low-level control. Predictive World Models for Planning Learning-based world models are used to estimate future states or representations, serving as a foundation for decision-making. Within the autonomous intelligence framework proposed by LeCun, JEPA learns to make predictions in a latent space, rather than reconstructing every detail of the input lecun2022path . I-JEPA applies this principle to predict representations of specific target portions of an image based on available context assran2023ijepa . Furthermore, V-JEPA extends this predictive learning approach to video data, yielding representations that encompass information regarding both appearance and motion bardes2024vjepa . The use of predictive representations for action-taking is further developed through V-JEPA 2, which incorporates an action-conditioned world model for robot planning assran2025vjepa2 . Meanwhile, DreamerV3 demonstrates the use of a world model to learn behaviors via reinforcement learning hafner2025dreamerv3 . Both approaches highlight the role of predictive models in decision-making, yet they employ different mechanisms for learning and action selection. JEPTERA positions JEPA as a model for predicting a UAV’s motion response to candidate actions, while action selection is performed via MPC. Safety-Aware Planning and Platform Integration A safety layer can complement a primary controller by checking or modifying actions based on safety constraints delecki2025diffusion . Ames et al. formulated control based on Control Barrier Functions (CBF) using quadratic programming to integrate control objectives with safety requirements ames2017cbf . Zeng et al. incorporated discrete-time CBFs into MPC, ensuring that safety constraints are considered throughout the prediction horizon zeng2021mpccbf . Such approaches provide a foundation for incorporating safety as an explicit component of action selection. Another approach is the predictive safety filter, which evaluates proposed actions using predicted dynamics and modifies them, if necessary, to satisfy constraints wabersich2021safetyfilter . In JEPTERA, a safety check is implemented as an additional layer on top of the JEPA–MPC action selection process. The influence of this layer is evaluated through an ablation study to assess its impact on collisions, navigation success, and travel efficiency. Proposed Method Architecture Overview At each planning cycle, the system updates voxel occupancy and obstacle tracks from the latest LiDAR observations. Route guidance and an observed free-space corridor support continuous optimization of the control sequence and path geometry. The optimizer uses locally linearized JEPA motion-effect predictions and a nominal response model. Optimized and backup plans are subsequently re-evaluated and checked for admissibility. An execution guard checks the held command between planning updates, while a platform adapter converts the resulting velocity reference into the controller interface. State and Environment Representation The translational state of the UAV used in planning consists of its position and velocity , expressed in the world coordinate frame Position and velocity are expressed in meters and meters per second, respectively. Information regarding the UAV's attitude is also used by the execution guard. Observations from each platform are converted into a common coordinate convention and set of units before being used by the planner. Each component specifies the desired velocity along a world coordinate axis, measured in meters per second. These references are continuous values and are distinct from motor commands. The selected commands undergo execution checks and rate-of-change limiting before being converted for the low-level controller interface. Three dimensional occupancy mapping provides a representation of free, occupied, and unknown space to support robot navigation hornung2013octomap . The environment is represented by a voxel occupancy map and a set of obstacle tracks . The voxel map is constructed from LiDAR observations to distinguish between space that is observed to be occupied, observed to be free, or unknown. This representation is used to support route searching, corridor generation, and trajectory validation. Separately, LiDAR observations over time are used to associate objects and estimate their motion. title: Learning and Verifying Progress: Closed-Loop Agentic Planning with Progress-Enhanced Execution for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Long-horizon vision-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to track instruction progress and recover from local errors before they propagate across subtasks. However, executors trained on expert trajectories encounter policy-induced state shifts during deployment, and their stop signals do not reliably indicate subtask completion. We introduce Learning and Verifying Progress for VLN (LeaP-VLN), an agentic VLN system that couples progress-aware execution with independent progress verification through plan--execute--verify--recover cycles. LeaP-VLN leverages progress both explicitly, through a progress verifier that verifies subtask completion before the agent advances and triggers dual-phase recovery upon route deviation, and implicitly, by co-training the executor on progress reasoning and action prediction to enhance the executor's progress awareness and corrective control. To adapt the executor to this closed-loop interface, we propose a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum: behavior cloning on expert demonstrations, followed by joint training on demonstrations, expert action corrections, and progress-reasoning supervision. Policy-generated trajectories expose the executor to both intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts, aligning training with the deviations encountered during closed-loop execution. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation.

We introduce Learning and Verifying Progress for VLN (LeaP-VLN), an agentic VLN system that couples progress-aware execution with independent progress verification through plan--execute--verify--recover cycles. LeaP-VLN leverages progress both explicitly, through a progress verifier that verifies subtask completion before the agent advances and triggers dual-phase recovery upon route deviation, and implicitly, by co-training the executor on progress reasoning and action prediction to enhance the executor's progress awareness and corrective control. To adapt the executor to this closed-loop interface, we propose a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum: behavior cloning on expert demonstrations, followed by joint training on demonstrations, expert action corrections, and progress-reasoning supervision. Policy-generated trajectories expose the executor to both intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts, aligning training with the deviations encountered during closed-loop execution. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation. Introduction Vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow a natural-language route instruction in a previously unseen environment anderson2018r2r,krantz2020beyond,ku2020room . In long-horizon settings, instructions specify sequences of landmark transitions and spatial relations. The agent must therefore predict appropriate actions while inferring from evolving egocentric observations which parts of the instruction have been completed and what remains to be executed. Moreover, local execution errors or instruction misinterpretations can compound across successive subtasks, causing increasing drift from the intended route and making subsequent stages harder to complete. Reliable long-horizon VLN requires progress tracking, accurate subtask execution, and recovery from local failures. Existing VLN approaches differ in how they organize instruction interpretation and action execution, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig-teaser . End-to-end policies built on vision-language models (VLMs) map the complete route instruction, the visual history, and the current observation directly to actions zhang2024navid,zhang2024uni,zeng2025janusvln . Route understanding, progress tracking, and action prediction are integrated into a single policy, leaving instruction progress implicit and subtask transitions difficult to control explicitly. Hierarchical planner--executor systems separate high-level route reasoning from low-level control: a planner specifies target locations, waypoints, local instructions, or modular skills, and an executor carries out the corresponding navigation actions zhou2024navgpt,long2024instructnav,xin2026agentvln,zhang2026qwenrobotnavtechnicalreportscalable . This separation makes intermediate navigation goals explicit, but reliable execution still depends on the executor's ability to handle policy-induced deviations and the planner's ability to assess subtask outcomes. Two challenges arise at this interface. First, executors trained on expert demonstrations face policy-induced state shifts during closed-loop execution, including intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask boundary shifts. Second, unverified subtask transitions can propagate local failures into inaccurate route-progress estimates. Existing recovery strategies either replan from a potentially deviated state wang2026reflectvln,xin2026agentvln or backtrack without correcting instruction grounding shi2025smartway . Reliable execution therefore requires handling both intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts, verifying subtask outcomes, and coupling state recovery with instruction re-grounding. To address these gaps, we introduce LeaP-VLN, a closed-loop agentic VLN system that exploits subtask progress on both sides of the planner--executor interface (Fig.~ fig-teaser , bottom). On the planner side, progress is handled explicitly. A high-level multimodal agent decomposes the route instruction into local subtasks and orchestrates plan--execute--verify--recover cycles. An independent verifier assesses subtask completion and route alignment using the observed execution history. The agent advances only after completion is verified, and the corresponding terminal state is stored as a trusted recovery anchor. Upon route deviation, dual-phase recovery restores a trusted execution context and re-grounds the pending subtask for a refined retry. On the executor side, progress awareness is learned implicitly by co-training the executor on progress reasoning and action prediction. We propose a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum that first initializes the executor through behavior cloning on expert demonstrations, then co-trains it using these demonstrations and expert-corrected intra- and inter-subtask policy rollouts. Learning to reason about progress content improves action prediction while promoting progress--action consistency, aligning the executor's decisions with the internal subtask progress. Our contributions are summarized as follows. We introduce LeaP-VLN, a closed-loop agentic navigation system for long-horizon VLN that integrates progress-aware execution, progress verification, and dual-phase recovery to maintain route alignment and limit error propagation across subtasks. We develop a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum for training a low-level VLN executor. By co-training action prediction and progress reasoning on expert demonstrations and policy-generated trajectories, the curriculum trains the executor to handle intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts during closed-loop execution. We achieve state-of-the-art success rates on R2R-CE and RxR-CE among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets. Component ablations evaluate the contributions of agentic planning, progress-enhanced training, and test-time verification and recovery, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation. Related Work Long-Horizon Vision-Language Navigation Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to translate language instructions and visual observations into sequential navigation actions. The task has progressed from R2R's graph-based indoor navigation to more challenging settings, with VLN-CE introducing continuous control and RxR featuring longer routes and greater linguistic diversity anderson2018r2r,krantz2020beyond,ku2020room . Recent VLM-based policies directly map instructions and visual histories to actions across diverse tasks zhang2024navid,zhang2024uni,cheng2024navila,wei2025streamvln , while generalist models broaden task coverage zhang2025embodied,gong2026abotn1 and hierarchical memory enriches visual context zeng2025janusvln . However, these policies entangle route understanding, progress estimation, and action generation within a unified policy, leaving the currently active instruction stage implicit and allowing local execution errors to accumulate as navigation progresses, eventually leading to task failure. Hierarchical Planning and Execution in VLN Hierarchical embodied agents decompose long-horizon tasks into high-level planning and low-level control. NavGPT adopts this paradigm for VLN by combining explicit high-level reasoning with a separate navigation controller zhou2024navgpt . Subsequent methods extend this paradigm through local instruction dispatch, modular skill selection and waypoint prediction long2024instructnav,han2026seqwalker,wei2025ground,xin2026agentvln,zhang2026qwenrobotnavtechnicalreportscalable . Despite these advances, existing methods either accept executor termination without verification, risking premature subtask transitions, or replan from a potentially deviated state, allowing errors to propagate. Consequently, local execution errors can accumulate over long-horizon navigation and ultimately lead to task failure. Progress Monitoring and Error Recovery in VLN Progress estimation provides intermediate signals for tracking instruction completion, identifying navigation milestones, and determining when to terminate execution. Recent methods incorporate jointly trained semantic reasoning wang2026progressthink or self-reflection at critical progress states guo2026awarevln , enabling more interpretable assessments of what has been completed and what remains. However, progress assessment performed by the action policy itself allows overconfident execution errors to remain undetected. Beyond progress monitoring, navigation errors are addressed through policy-triggered backtracking shi2025smartway , training-time correction yu2026correctnav , or reflective replanning during inference wang2026reflectvln . However, existing test-time mechanisms either replan from an already deviated state or backtrack without revising the instruction that caused the failure, leaving repeated errors unresolved. Problem Formulation sec-problem We consider VLN in continuous environments (VLN-CE), where an agent receives a natural-language instruction at the beginning of an episode. At each step , the agent observes an egocentric RGB image and executes a low-level action ( forward, turns). The objective is to reach the destination specified by . We use to denote the active local instruction dispatched to the executor, which may be adjusted from based on verified execution progress. A low-level VLN executor predicts actions conditioned on the active sub-instruction , the visual history , and the current observation , The executor's STOP signal triggers high-level progress verification, which determines whether to advance to the next subtask, continue the current subtask, or initiate recovery. The following sections detail the subtask planning, executor training, verification, and recovery mechanisms. This memory maintains trusted execution context throughout navigation. The agent invokes the executor as a short-horizon navigation tool within a plan--execute--verify--recover loop. title: WA-JEPA: Goal-Aware Predictive Feedback Action Refinement for a World-Action Model
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, including supplementary material. Code available at https://github.com/Dovisya/WA-JEPA
summary: JEPA-based world models predict action consequences in latent space, but representative planning approaches rely on candidate-action search, requiring repeated evaluation of action sequences and incurring substantial online computational cost. Direct action generation avoids this search, yet how to leverage latent predictions to guide action generation given task goals remains a key challenge in translating learned physical dynamics into effective decisions. We introduce WA-JEPA, a world-action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal and predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states, then refines the proposal through two complementary feedback paths, using the task goal as a reference. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) uses differences between the latent representations of predicted scenes and the task goal to guide chunk-wise action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement. Jointly learned from offline demonstrations, this process iteratively updates the same plan before execution, making future predictions directly participate in action generation without candidate-action search. We evaluate short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. The results show that goal-aware predictive feedback supports competitive task performance while maintaining a compact model and low online computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Dovisya/WA-JEPA.

Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement. Jointly learned from offline demonstrations, this process iteratively updates the same plan before execution, making future predictions directly participate in action generation without candidate-action search. We evaluate short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. The results show that goal-aware predictive feedback supports competitive task performance while maintaining a compact model and low online computational cost. Code is available at . Introduction sec:intro Robot control requires generating actions from observations and task goals to bring the environment toward a desired state. World models learn action-conditioned dynamics to predict how actions change the environment, informing decisions before execution~ zhou2024dinowm,maes2026lewm . Research based on joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) models these changes in latent space without reconstructing future images~ assran2025vjepa2 . DINO-WM learns action-conditioned dynamics over pretrained visual features, whereas LeWM jointly learns a visual encoder and latent predictor~ zhou2024dinowm,maes2026lewm . These models allow predicted scenes and task goals to be compared in a common feature space, providing a basis for visual goal-directed control. Translating latent predictions into executable actions is central to control with these world models. Methods such as LeWM use candidate-action search: a planner repeatedly samples action sequences, predicts their consequences, and updates the sampling distribution according to the distance between predicted outcomes and the goal. This approach uses learned dynamics to select actions, but repeated candidate evaluation incurs substantial online computation. Imitation learning instead learns action generation from offline demonstrations and directly outputs control sequences without candidate search~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion,zhou2026patchpolicy . However, these policies do not explicitly use predicted action consequences when generating control sequences. World–action models jointly model future observations and actions, allowing predictive learning to support action generation~ wu2024gr1,ye2026dreamzero . Building on these advances, we investigate how predictions of action consequences can improve goal attainment while retaining the computational efficiency of direct action generation. We explore goal-aware predictive feedback as an approach to this problem: the model compares the predicted outcomes of its current action proposal with the task goal in JEPA latent space and uses this information to iteratively refine the same plan before execution, without candidate-action search. We introduce , a world--action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. Given observation history, proprioception, and the task goal, the model first generates an action proposal, and the world model predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) compares the predicted scene for each chunk with the task goal. It combines this discrepancy with the current action representation and predicted state to learn action-token corrections, translating goal discrepancies in visual representations into guidance for action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves predicted scene representations, providing context for subsequent action refinement beyond goal discrepancies. Together, the two paths combine goal-directed chunk-wise corrections with detailed future-scene context. Action and prediction supervision from offline demonstrations jointly train the model to cycle through action generation, future prediction, and feedback correction, repeatedly updating the same pending plan before execution. The process uses a fixed number of forward stages, making predictions part of deployment-time action optimization without candidate-action search. It thus grounds goal-directed action refinement in learned relationships between actions and changes in the physical environment. We evaluate at three levels: short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. Following LeWM's short-horizon protocol, we compare against world-model planners, imitation-learning methods, and offline reinforcement-learning methods. achieves strong goal-reaching performance, matching or improving LeWM's success rates while accelerating complete-plan generation by -- . For long-horizon tasks, we integrate into the Anchored Planning framework of Aim Short to Reach Far~ liu2026aimshort without retraining. High-level retrieval supplies intermediate visual goals, and predictive feedback generates the corresponding actions, improving cross-task mean success and reducing decision latency relative to AP (LeWM). For full-task execution, we adapt a standard imitation-learning policy head and evaluate on Push-T and LIBERO-Goal~ liu2023libero . Comparisons with recent imitation-learning, VLA, and WAM baselines show strong task performance and a favorable performance--computation trade-off. These results show that goal-aware predictive feedback effectively connects future prediction to action refinement across local goal reaching, hierarchical long-horizon control, and full-task execution. Related Work sec:related JEPA and visual representation learning. JEPAs learn predictive representations in latent space without reconstructing pixels. This paradigm provides a foundation for world models that anticipate how the environment evolves under a given action sequence. I-JEPA predicts latent image-region representations~ assran2023ijepa , V-JEPA extends this approach to video~ bardes2024vjepa , and V-JEPA~2 connects video pretraining with action-conditioned prediction and robotic planning~ assran2025vjepa2 . LeWM combines predictive learning with distributional regularization to learn visual encoders and action-conditioned latent dynamics from pixels~ maes2026lewm . Alternatively, DINOv2 provides transferable pretrained visual features~ oquab2023dinov2 , and DINO-WM learns action-conditioned prediction over their dense spatial structure, enabling visual goal reaching through candidate-action search~ zhou2024dinowm . uses frozen DINOv2 with learned scene pooling and task-conditioned fusion to represent observations, predicted scenes, and goals in a common feature space. We feed predictions and goal discrepancies back into action generation for refinement. Imitation learning models and vision--language--action. Imitation learning trains policies on demonstrations: ACT predicts action chunks~ zhao2023act , Diffusion Policy models action distributions through denoising~ chi2023diffusion , and VQ-BeT learns discrete action representations~ lee2024vqbet . Patch Policy connects dense pretrained visual features to lightweight action generators~ zhou2026patchpolicy . Many VLA models retain demonstration-based action learning while incorporating vision--language pretraining to connect visual observations and language instructions to control. OpenVLA-OFT combines parallel decoding, action chunking, and continuous action regression for efficient adaptation~ kim2025openvlaoft . VLA models also incorporate future prediction: DreamVLA forecasts dynamic, spatial, and semantic information to condition a diffusion action model~ zhang2025dreamvla . focuses on visual-goal-aware action refinement in latent space, explicitly using future predictions to guide task execution. World models and world--action models. =-1 World models support control through planning or policy learning. TD-MPC2 combines latent dynamics with value-based trajectory optimization~ hansen2023tdmpc2 , and Dreamer learns policies through latent imagination~ hafner2019dreamer . WAMs bring future prediction and action generation into a unified model. DreamZero jointly generates video and actions using a pretrained video diffusion backbone~ ye2026dreamzero . RynnVLA-002 jointly learns action-conditioned image prediction and observation-conditioned action generation~ cen2025rynnvla . Fast-WAM retains video co-training but skips future prediction at inference to reduce decision latency~ yuan2026fastwam . LaDi-WM conditions a diffusion policy on predicted future features to iteratively refine its action outputs~ huang2025ladiwm . These designs differ in how predictions support action learning and inference. uses visual-goal-aware predictive feedback during inference: explicit discrepancies between predicted scenes and visual goals guide chunk-wise residual updates, while unpooled future-scene context coordinates refinement across the plan. Both paths update the same proposal before execution. World--Action Modeling through Predictive Feedback sec:method Problem formulation and overview We study robot control learned from offline demonstrations, where observations and task goals condition actions for completing specified tasks. At decision time , the model receives the most recent images and corresponding proprioceptive states, , together with an image depicting the task goal. An action sequence consists of temporally ordered action chunks, each containing consecutive controls of dimension . As shown in Fig.~ fig:architecture , couples action generation with latent world prediction through goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal. The world model predicts scene features and proprioceptive states at each chunk boundary, and these predictions guide proposal refinement relative to the task goal. We use to index action chunks and to index internal refinement stages. Refinement updates the same pending plan without advancing environment time; new observations obtained after execution inform the next decision. We omit the batch dimension throughout. Representing the scene relative to the goal Predictive feedback requires future scenes and task goals to be compared in a common feature space. We use frozen DINOv2 to extract visual features from observation images, goal images, and future images used during training. The same fusion and pooling parameters are used for all images, so the world model's prediction targets and the goal encoding share a representation space. We embed standardized proprioceptive states as an additional token and fuse it with each frame's scene features. Temporal attention then integrates the observation history. title: ACiT: Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers
summary: Visuomotor policies condition action prediction on visual and proprioceptive observations. While historical proprioceptive sequences carry rich dynamic priors, current methods treat them as equal to high-dimensional vision, causing the proprioceptive signal to be overwhelmed. To identify what is lost in equal-conditioning fusion, we analyze proprioceptive data and find that strong inter-joint coupling is the key action-determining structure. This finding aligns with the neural sensorimotor loop, in which proprioception first forms a body-centered prior and vision is later calibrated via parietal remapping. Inspired by this, we propose ACiT, Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers, which reinforces historical joint-coupling as the primary condition with vision as a later calibration. This design is instantiated through three modules: Inverted State Encoding builds a proprioceptive prior via per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention. State-Visual Grounding lets joint tokens query visual evidence, making vision goal- and calibration-only. Inverted Action Chunking decodes per-joint trajectories independently. ACiT improves success rates on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, with the largest gains on those that require dynamics and coordination. The same conditioning design transferred to the VLA backbone pi_0-ACiT yields significant gains with better execution efficiency.
full_text: Visuomotor policies condition action prediction on visual and proprioceptive observations. While historical proprioceptive sequences carry rich dynamic priors, current methods treat them as equal to high-dimensional vision, causing the proprioceptive signal to be overwhelmed. To identify what is lost in equal-conditioning fusion, we analyze proprioceptive data and find that strong inter-joint coupling is the key action-determining structure. This finding aligns with the neural sensorimotor loop, in which proprioception first forms a body-centered prior and vision is later calibrated via parietal remapping. Inspired by this, we propose ACiT, Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers, which reinforces historical joint-coupling as the primary condition with vision as a later calibration. This design is instantiated through three modules: Inverted State Encoding builds a proprioceptive prior via per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention. State-Visual Grounding lets joint tokens query visual evidence, making vision goal- and calibration-only. Inverted Action Chunking decodes per-joint trajectories independently. ACiT improves success rates on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, with the largest gains on those that require dynamics and coordination. The same conditioning design transferred to the VLA backbone -ACiT yields significant gains with better execution efficiency. 5 1.0 3 Introduction Visuomotor policies predict actions from multi-view observations and proprioception. Early work conditioned on a single current state, where ACT maps the current joint state and images to an action chunk~ act . Diffusion Policy conditions on a short observation history instead~ dp . A single frame proved insufficient to resolve action ambiguity, while history carries dynamics and hidden-state information, so proprioceptive history was explicitly incorporated. Recent models such as A2A and Chronos explicitly model proprioceptive history~ a2a,chronos . Another line discretizes historical states or actions into tokens to better integrate with LLM backbones, at the cost of losing continuous coupling structure~ fast,vita,vqbet . Reconstruction-only tokenization can also erode control-relevant information~ salt . These works validate the value of using history from both continuous and discrete directions, and state history is becoming a consensus for action prediction. These advances have not converged at the conditioning interface. First, mainstream methods map historical proprioceptive states as an independent modality, either discretely or continuously, and place them alongside a pooled global visual vector as conditions for action generation. This naive fusion lets high-dimensional, low-SNR visual features entangle and dominate the conditioning, leading to degraded robustness or spurious shortcuts~ slotflow,imprint . Second, we analyze the state history and the action itself: the effective dimensionality of the action distribution is far below the number of joints, and joints are strongly coupled, as shown in Fig.~ fig:intro \((a)\). However, existing methods model temporal dependencies and pack all joints into one vector, so the inter-joint coupling, a structure critical to action, can only be implicit inside the token. Therefore, how to encode historical state information, how to fuse modalities, and how to feed the result into action decoding is an open problem. Inspired by neuroscience, the human chain from peripheral proprioception to body-centered action generation is as follows (Fig.~ fig:intro \((b)\)): muscle and joint receptors continuously encode joint angle, velocity, and tension and project through large-diameter myelinated afferents~ proske2012proprioceptors,windhorst2007muscle . The somatosensory cortex and posterior parietal cortex aggregate proprioceptive history into a body-state representation, forming a body-centered prior~ avillac2005reference,asada2018proprioception . The posterior parietal cortex then remaps visual goals from retinal coordinates into body-centered coordinates, with proprioceptive context modulating this remapping~ avillac2005reference,heed2015tactile . Finally, the parietal-motor pathway sends the calibrated body-centered representation to action generation~ wolpert1995internal,miall1996forward . The key computational asymmetry is that proprioception provides a continuous, low-latency body-state stream, whereas visual goals are remapped and integrated into the body-centered representation afterward. We map this sensorimotor loop to Bayesian cue integration: the fast, continuous proprioceptive stream forms a prior over the body state, visual goals provide goal evidence (a likelihood-like term), and calibrating the prior yields a posterior-like body-centered representation for action generation. Based on this, we propose ACiT on top of ACT, the smallest architecture that still carries the full interface (multi-view images, proprioception, and a chunked action decoder), so that the encoder and the head stay fixed while only the conditioning changes. It has three modules. First, Inverted State Encoding compresses each joint's entire history into a token and directly models inter-joint coupling with self-attention. Second, State-Visual Grounding treats vision as a per-joint goal-calibration signal and does not let it directly enter the encoder. Third, Inverted Action Chunking treats each joint as a token on the action side, and each joint independently generates its complete trajectory chunk. The decoder does not need to translate between ``visual coordinates'' and ``joint coordinates''. The historical proprioceptive sequence and action generation share a more consistent feature space. To separate the interface from the backbone, we port the same conditioning to a pretrained VLA and obtain -ACiT, which keeps 's architecture and changes only how the state enters it. Experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin~2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks show that ACiT and -ACiT improve success on most tasks, with improved robustness under visual perturbations, especially on tasks that depend on dynamics and joint coordination. Our contributions are as follows: We formulate the conditioning interface as Bayesian sensorimotor cue integration, with history as the prior and vision as the calibration evidence, and realize it as an explicit asymmetric fusion. We propose ACiT, which uses three inverted Transformer modules to explicitly build and preserve the inter-joint coupling dynamics in the state history instead of flattening them. We validate ACiT on LIBERO, RoboTwin~2.0, and real-world tasks, where it improves the average success rate by 5.7 to 10.8 points over the strongest baseline. -ACiT improves the average success rate by 26.9 points at 20.2 lower inference latency than . Related Work sec:related Early visuomotor policies condition on a single frame: ACT maps the current joint state and images to an action chunk~ act , and Diffusion Policy instead uses a short observation window~ dp . Later work makes the state history explicit in the conditioning input~ a2a,chronos . A parallel line discretizes states or actions so that autoregressive backbones can consume them~ vqbet,fast,omnisat,vita , at the cost of losing continuous structure, and reconstruction-only tokenization can erode control-relevant information~ salt . Under both interfaces proprioception enters as one flat vector or a one-dimensional token sequence, so the coupling among joints stays implicit. Pooling both modalities into one condition leaves nothing to stop the high-dimensional visual stream from dominating and introducing spurious shortcuts~ slotflow,imprint . One line responds by letting the robot state steer vision, through robot-centric pooling~ rcp or active visual attention~ avavla , yet the asymmetry is applied to perception rather than to the conditioning itself. Large VLA backbones inherit the same symmetric interface, concatenating one proprioceptive token with visual and language tokens~ pi0,pi05,groot . Topology-aware models inject the kinematic graph as a structural bias for cross-embodiment transfer~ getzero,human2locoman . ACiT shares that motivation but acts on the conditioning interface: it carries history per joint, keeps the resulting prior primary, and lets each joint retrieve its own visual calibration in a single generation pipeline. title: Transferable Neural CBFs via Generalized Closure
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC 2027)
summary: Classical control barrier functions (CBFs) provide safety constraints for controllers, but designing them by hand is difficult for underactuated vehicles and the resulting safe sets can be overly conservative. Neural CBFs can learn more informative barriers from data, yet a learned barrier is usually verified only for one fixed obstacle configuration. We study whether one neural barrier can be reused across environments by expressing the state relative to each obstacle. The key gap is that these relative coordinates may discard information needed to predict their own evolution. We give a generalized closure condition that represents this missing information as a residual and a lifting theorem that transfers a verified relative-coordinate barrier to every obstacle in a family. A rank test also identifies when symmetry alone cannot justify the transfer. We validate the conditions on a double integrator, a planar aircraft, and a 12-state quadrotor. Coordinates that fail the test lead to obstacle penetration or to a barrier condition that fails near hover, whereas body-frame coordinates close exactly for the quadrotor. The resulting barrier transfers to new maps without retraining and is effective in the reported deployment and fast-start experiments.

Classical control barrier functions (CBFs) provide safety constraints for controllers, but designing them by hand is difficult for underactuated vehicles and the resulting safe sets can be overly conservative. Neural CBFs can learn more informative barriers from data, yet a learned barrier is usually verified only for one fixed obstacle configuration. We study whether one neural barrier can be reused across environments by expressing the state relative to each obstacle. The key gap is that these relative coordinates may discard information needed to predict their own evolution. We give a generalized closure condition that represents this missing information as a residual and a lifting theorem that transfers a verified relative-coordinate barrier to every obstacle in a family. A rank test also identifies when symmetry alone cannot justify the transfer. We validate the conditions on a double integrator, a planar aircraft, and a 12-state quadrotor. Coordinates that fail the test lead to obstacle penetration or to a barrier condition that fails near hover, whereas body-frame coordinates close exactly for the quadrotor. The resulting barrier transfers to new maps without retraining and is effective in the reported deployment and fast-start experiments. INTRODUCTION Control barrier functions (CBFs) turn a safety specification into a constraint on the input that a quadratic program enforces online ames2017cbfqp , and the same program can filter the output of any nominal controller gurriet2018backup . The barrier itself must be constructed, and that is the bottleneck. For systems with bounded inputs in which the input reaches the obstacle constraint only after several integrations, high-order CBFs xiao2019hocbf give a systematic construction, but the designer chooses the function and its gains, and nothing guarantees that the resulting constraint can be met within the input bounds. On underactuated vehicles, whose ability to stop depends on attitude and rates as well as on distance and velocity, such a barrier is hard to make both valid and informative. Hamilton--Jacobi reachability computes the largest safe set, the viability kernel aubin1991viability , on a grid, at a cost exponential in the state dimension bansal2017hj , and learned value functions extend it to higher dimension for a fixed environment and without formal guarantees bansal2021deepreach . A third approach is to learn the barrier from its defining inequalities dawson2023survey . A learned function is a certificate only if those inequalities hold, and a growing line of work verifies learned barriers formally zhang2023exact,hu2024symbolic,vertovec2025scalable,tayal2024verified . In each of these works, the verified object is one barrier for one fixed environment, verified in full-state coordinates, so that any change of the environment requires retraining and reverification. Shared and compositional constructions remove the dependence on the environment. A shared network is evaluated on the local configuration of each agent qin2021decentralized,zhang2025gcbfplus , or one network is trained in coordinates relative to a single obstacle, evaluated once for each obstacle of a map, and combined by a smooth minimum derajic2026cncbf or, as here, by one constraint per obstacle. The object to verify then lives on the relative coordinates of one obstacle, whatever the number and placement of the obstacles. Such networks transfer across maps in practice, but none of these constructions is formally verified, so the transfer rests on conditions that are never checked for the learned function. Equivariance results evaluate the barrier at a transformed full state, so no information is lost wiltz2025equivariances , but coordinates chosen for learning often discard information on which the dynamics depend. This paper states when the per-obstacle construction is valid. For the barrier condition to transfer, the relative coordinates must determine their own time derivative, up to a residual whose range they determine, and then a barrier condition on that holds on a compact set of relative coordinates holds for every obstacle in every map. A rank test shows in advance when symmetry alone cannot guarantee this. Coordinates that fail it penetrate obstacles on a planar aircraft and fail the condition near hover on a 12-state quadrotor. Body-frame coordinates pass it, and the barrier learned in them is deployed on new maps without retraining. We check the hypotheses on sampled boxes and states, so the result is a statistical estimate of where they hold, not a proof over the whole domain, and the deployed controller adds discrete-time safeguards that the theory does not cover. The contributions are the following: -6pt Generalized closure and a lifting theorem: a per-obstacle barrier condition that holds on a compact set of relative coordinates holds for every obstacle in every map, and if one input meets all obstacle constraints the state stays safe until it leaves the lifted domain, with the missing information made explicit as a residual (Theorem~ thm:lift , Corollary~ cor:safety ). A rank condition, comparing the rank of the coordinates with , that is necessary for symmetry to guarantee closure and can be checked before training, and explicit residual sets for three systems (Proposition~ prop:count , Table~ tab:count ). Body-frame relative coordinates that close exactly for the full 12-state quadrotor, and a barrier learned in them, checked at sampled states, and deployed without retraining on maps not seen in training (Proposition~ prop:body , Section~ sec:results ). RELATED WORK sec:related Learned barriers and their verification Neural certificates are trained by penalizing violations of their defining inequalities at sampled states dawson2023survey , which alone does not make them certificates. Zhang et al.\ verify ReLU barriers exactly by exploiting the piecewise-linear structure of the network zhang2023exact . Hu et al.\ propagate symbolic bounds through the gradient of ReLU barriers and their Lie derivatives hu2024symbolic , and Vertovec et al.\ extend linear bound propagation to the gradient of smooth networks vertovec2025scalable , both in the family of certified bound-propagation (CROWN) relaxations zhang2018crown on which our verifier is also built. Tayal et al.\ train barriers for stochastic systems that are valid by construction through Lipschitz bounds on the network and its derivatives tayal2024verified , and give probabilistic guarantees for deterministic systems through conformal prediction tayal2025cpncbf . We check in relative coordinates instead, statistically and once for an obstacle family, and lift the result to every map by a theorem. Shared and compositional barriers Qin et al.\ learn decentralized barrier certificates whose network takes an agent's own state and the states of its neighbours within an observation radius, with the trained parameters reused for every agent qin2021decentralized . GCBF+ generalizes this with graph neural networks over neighbours and sensed obstacles zhang2025gcbfplus . Closest to the present work, CN-CBF learns one network relative to a single, possibly moving, obstacle from reachability data, evaluates it for every obstacle, and composes the results with a smooth minimum derajic2026cncbf . It writes the relative state of a unicycle in the robot frame, observing that the world-frame relative dynamics are not a function of the relative state. We make that observation a condition, give a test for it, and handle the case in which it fails. In these works the learned certificate is not verified, so transfer is observed in experiments, although GCBF+ proves that a function meeting its graph CBF conditions certifies safety for any number of agents. CN-CBF computes its training targets by reachability on a four-dimensional relative grid, which would be twelve-dimensional for the full quadrotor here. The minimum of barriers is a nonsmooth barrier whenever one input meets every active constraint glotfelter2017nonsmooth , and whether such an input exists within the input bounds is a separate question breeden2023compositions , which we assume rather than solve. Symmetry and reduction Control systems with symmetries reduce to their quotient grizzle1985symmetries . Wiltz and Dimarogonas show that when the dynamics are equivariant, a CBF computed for one constraint yields CBFs for its transformations, and that when the constraint is also symmetric a reachability-based CBF need only be computed on a subset wiltz2025equivariances . We address coordinates that do not determine the state up to symmetry, as coordinates chosen for learning often do not, make the missing information an explicit residual whose range the coordinates determine, and give a rank test that reveals the shortfall in advance. Backup sets Backup control barrier functions replace the viability kernel by the states from which a fixed backup policy keeps the system safe, an inner approximation that is checked online by forward simulation and enforced along the predicted trajectory inside the QP chen2021backup , and policy neural CBFs learn the barrier as the value of a fixed policy, without verification so2024pncbf . We use such rollouts in two roles, to label the training data and as a discrete-time safeguard in deployment. title: TacBridge: Learning Unified Tactile Representations through Cross-Sensor Correspondence
summary: Optical tactile sensors record tactile videos that capture local deformation and its temporal evolution during contact, supporting robot manipulation, force estimation, and tactile representation learning. Differences in imaging geometry, background appearance, illumination, resolution, and deformation response lead to sensor-dependent observations of the same contact across GelSight, DIGIT, GelSlim, TacTip, and other optical tactile sensors. This variability limits representation transfer and the joint use of multi-sensor data. We introduce TacBridge, a framework for learning unified representations from multi-sensor tactile videos through cross-sensor correspondence. Specifically, multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training learns spatiotemporal representations across sensors. We then train the same masked model jointly on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction, using paired source and target videos of matched contact events. Experiments on cross-sensor translation and downstream perception demonstrate the cross-sensor generalization and task transferability of the learned tactile representations.
full_text: Optical tactile sensors record tactile videos that capture local deformation and its temporal evolution during contact, supporting robot manipulation, force estimation, and tactile representation learning. Differences in imaging geometry, background appearance, illumination, resolution, and deformation response lead to sensor-dependent observations of the same contact across GelSight, DIGIT, GelSlim, TacTip, and other optical tactile sensors. This variability limits representation transfer and the joint use of multi-sensor data. We introduce TacBridge, a framework for learning unified representations from multi-sensor tactile videos through cross-sensor correspondence. Specifically, multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training learns spatiotemporal representations across sensors. We then train the same masked model jointly on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction, using paired source and target videos of matched contact events. Experiments on cross-sensor translation and downstream perception demonstrate the cross-sensor generalization and task transferability of the learned tactile representations. Introduction Optical tactile sensors use embedded cameras to record local elastomer deformation during contact, providing robots with fine-grained tactile feedback. They have been widely used for object-property recognition, slip detection, force estimation, and contact-rich manipulation yuan2017gelsight,lambeta2020digit,donlon2018gelslim . By capturing local contact details, this high-resolution tactile feedback complements external vision and conventional force sensing in tasks such as small-part localisation and insertion, grasp-outcome prediction, and cloth-texture recognition li2014localization,calandra2017feeling,yuan2018cloth . Different from a single tactile image, tactile videos further capture the temporal evolution of local deformation as contact is established, maintained, and released. The growing diversity of tactile sensors has fragmented tactile data into sensor-specific domains. Sensors such as GelSight, DIGIT, and GelSlim differ in their optical layouts, elastomer materials, and illumination, shaping how they capture contact. Even for the same object, contact location, and motion trajectory, their tactile videos can exhibit markedly different appearances and deformation patterns. This variability makes it difficult to combine data across sensors and learn transferable tactile representations. Recent sensor-invariant and multi-sensor representation learning has begun to reduce this fragmentation by embedding heterogeneous tactile observations into shared feature spaces guptasensor,fenganytouch,higuera2025sparsh,yang2024binding,zhao2024transferable,cao2023learn . However, learning from multiple sensors does not by itself reveal which differences arise from the sensing device and which reflect changes in the underlying physical interaction. We argue that event-level cross-sensor correspondence can provide a more direct constraint. When different sensors observe the same contact event, their recordings may differ substantially in appearance and temporal response while sharing the same underlying interaction. Such paired observations explicitly link sensor-specific views, helping the model separate device-induced variation from shared contact content. In this work, we use such event-level correspondence to learn tactile representations across different tactile sensors. Specifically, TacQuad provides synchronized real observations from DIGIT, GelSight Mini, and DuraGel fenganytouch , while ToucHD-Sim provides matched simulations of an interaction under nine optical sensor appearances feng2026anytouch2 . In both datasets, paired tactile videos capture the same underlying interaction under different sensor conditions. This pairing grounds cross-sensor learning in a shared physical interaction, rather than relying on unpaired distribution-level alignment. Building on these, we encode sensor identity as a switchable conditioning signal, allowing the same tactile interaction to be represented in different sensor domains. The spatiotemporal encoder is first pre-trained with masked autoencoding, then trained with event-level correspondence from TacQuad and ToucHD-Sim to separate sensor-specific variation from the underlying physical interaction. Finally, we evaluate the learned representation through controllable cross-sensor translation and downstream robotic tactile perception tasks. Our contributions are: We introduce a correspondence-based framework for learning unified tactile video representations from paired observations of matched contact events across heterogeneous optical tactile sensors. We develop a latent translator that maps source tactile features to their target-sensor counterparts, reusing the learned encoder and decoder for controllable cross-sensor tactile video translation. We demonstrate that the learned representation transfers effectively to downstream robotic tactile perception tasks and generalises to new tactile data, achieving strong performance with a frozen encoder and lightweight prediction heads. Related Work Tactile Representation Learning and Temporal Modelling Optical tactile sensors produce observations that depend on their sensing design. GelSight, DIGIT, and GelSlim differ in form factor and optical configuration yuan2017gelsight,lambeta2020digit,donlon2018gelslim , while devices such as DuraGel and Tac3D further expand the range of tactile measurements zhang2024duragel,zhang2022tac3d . Differences in illumination, elastomer properties, and mechanical construction affect the appearance and deformation patterns recorded during contact, motivating representation learning across heterogeneous sensors. Recent tactile representation learning seeks to make heterogeneous sensor data useful within a shared feature space. Multi-sensor training brings together observations from different devices, including both static images and dynamic sequences, to learn features that can be reused across sensing conditions fenganytouch,zhao2024transferable . Multimodal alignment provides a complementary approach by connecting touch with other modalities to reduce sensor-dependent discrepancies yang2024binding . Alongside these efforts, self-supervised learning enables tactile representations to be trained without labels for each downstream task higuera2025sparsh . Reconstruction-based objectives, in particular, encourage models to infer missing contact information from visible observations, providing a foundation for masked tactile representation learning cao2023learn . Tactile interactions evolve over time, and individual images do not fully describe how contact develops, moves, or is released. Learning from tactile videos therefore requires representations that capture both spatial contact patterns and changes across frames. Masked video modelling provides a relevant approach by learning to reconstruct missing content from the surrounding spatial and temporal context, as demonstrated by VideoMAE tong2022videomae . Our work extends this reconstruction-based approach to paired tactile videos from different sensors, using cross-sensor correspondence to supervise both target frames and their temporal differences. Cross-Sensor Tactile Translation Sensor-invariant representation learning addresses device variation by learning features that remain useful across tactile sensors guptasensor . Cross-sensor translation instead predicts how a given contact would be observed by a target sensor. Touch2Touch uses paired tactile observations to train a conditional latent diffusion model for this mapping, while T2D2 introduces depth as an intermediate representation to enable translation without cross-sensor paired data rodriguez2025crosssensor . Translation has also been explored across sensing principles. Grella et al. compare generative and regression-based approaches for mapping optical DIGIT images to capacitive CySkin outputs under corresponding physical stimuli grella2024translation . Cross-sensor relationships can also be incorporated into representation learning. UniForce combines paired reconstruction with force-equilibrium constraints to learn a shared latent force space for force estimation and manipulation chen2026uniforce . UniTac focuses on multimodal tactile understanding and generation, integrating touch with language to describe object properties, identify sensors, and align semantic outputs with tactile representations tu2026unitac . Our method incorporates paired cross-sensor supervision into masked tactile video representation learning, using visible source-video patches and a target-sensor condition to reconstruct target observations and their frame-to-frame differences. The learned representation supports both translation and downstream perception, without explicit force-equilibrium or language-semantic constraints. Tactile Simulation Tactile simulation supports controlled variation of objects, interactions, and sensing configurations. Taxim uses example-based optical simulation to approximate GelSight observations si2022taxim , TACTO provides fast and configurable visuo-tactile rendering wang2022tacto , and TacSL supports scalable GPU-based tactile simulation akinola2025tacsl . Tactile Gym~ lin2022tactilegym instead leverages rigid-body physics to simulate contact depth as tactile observation, supporting various tactile sensors and sim-to-real robotic tasks~ lin2023bitouch . These approaches extend the range of contact and sensor configurations that can be studied beyond physical data collection, although differences between simulated and real observations may remain. Simulation also enables cross-sensor correspondence learning by holding the underlying interaction fixed while varying sensor conditions. We use matched simulated pairs from ToucHD-Sim to complement real cross-sensor pairs from TacQuad fenganytouch, feng2026anytouch2 , extending paired reconstruction training to a broader range of sensor appearances. Methodology sec:method TacBridge learns a shared tactile representation through multi-sensor pre-training followed by event-paired cross-sensor learning. This representation enables controllable tactile video generation through a conditional latent flow model guided by source-video features and target-sensor information. We further evaluate its transferability to downstream tactile perception tasks and its adaptability to new tactile data using the same frozen encoder. Fig.~ fig:overview illustrates the framework. Multi-Sensor Tactile Pre-training We first pre-train a masked autoencoder he2022masked on tactile videos from multiple sensors. The encoder processes visible video patches, while separate reconstruction heads predict masked content and frame-to-frame differences within the same sensor domain. These objectives encourage the model to capture spatial contact patterns and their temporal evolution. The pre-trained encoder and reconstruction heads then initialise cross-sensor representation learning.
