title: ROSE: A Shared Cross-Embodiment Facial-Motion Latent Space for Humanoid Robot Expression
summary: Natural, coherent full-face dynamic expressions are central to making humanoid robots socially approachable, yet existing systems commonly realize only limited lip motion or scripted expressions. The limitation is both physical and algorithmic. A compact head leaves little room for densely packed, independently controllable actuation; meanwhile, learned systems often generate an avatar video, landmarks, or facial parameters and then infer actuator commands through visual retargeting. This render-and-invert path adds latency and artifacts, and it does not reliably transfer generated behavior to a physical robot. We present ROSE (RObot facial expression through Shared motion Embeddings), a framework that integrates biomimetic hardware, cross-embodiment motion representation learning, and multimodal motion generation. On the hardware side, we build a flexible tendon-sheath transmission structure that integrates 34 actuators into a 19.5 cm biomimetic head. By decoupling actuator placement from facial action points, it enables coordinated full-face expression within a compact volume. On the algorithmic side, ROSE-VAE learns an identity-independent shared facial-motion latent space from human, digital-human, and robot observations. ROSE-Flow directly maps text, audio, or their combination to trajectories in this motion space without using video as a generator input. ROSE-ACT then converts these trajectories into constrained actuator commands. Our system demonstrates how high-density biomimetic hardware and a shared executable facial-motion representation can jointly unify cross-embodiment learning, multimodal generation, and physical robot expression.

Introduction sec:intro Imagine a humanoid robot turning toward a visitor and answering a question about an exhibit. Its answer may be accurate and its voice natural, yet the interaction can still feel distant if its face remains largely still or moves out of sync with speech. In face-to-face communication, facial movements help people interpret not only what is said but also the speaker's intent and engagement. Coordinating facial expression with speech and context is therefore an important part of making a humanoid robot feel socially present and approachable.~ breazeal2003emotion,bennewitz2005towards,kuno2007museum . Reproducing expressive facial motion requires coordinated actuation within a compact head. Previous robotic faces have explored pneumatic and motor-driven mechanisms coupled with compliant skin~ kobayashi2003realization,oh2006design . These mechanisms provide the physical capacity for expression, but controlling them requires translating desired facial movements into actuator commands compatible with the robot’s mechanical constraints. Existing approaches often address facial-motion generation and robot execution in separate stages. In the generation stage, audio-driven face animation methods produce visual or parametric outputs, including 3D meshes~ cudeiro2019capture and portrait videos~ xu2024vasa . In the execution stage, these outputs are translated into robot actuator commands, for example through visual self-modelling or retargeting of generated facial motion~ hu2024human,hu2026lipmotions . These image- and parameter-based pipelines benefit from learned facial-motion priors, but connecting the two stages requires converting between representations. Image-based outputs must be analyzed to recover facial motion, while parametric outputs must be mapped to the target robot’s actuator configuration and motion limits. This motivates a shared facial-motion representation that connects human, digital-human, and robot observations with conditional motion generation and actuator control. We therefore propose (RObot facial expression through Shared motion Embeddings), illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser . ROSE connects motion encoding, text- and audio-conditioned generation, and robot execution through a shared facial-motion latent space. Generated motion is mapped to constrained actuator commands without intermediate image reconstruction. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] A shared facial-motion representation across embodiments. ROSE-VAE (variational autoencoder) factorizes identity and motion and learns a shared motion basis with orthogonality regularization across human, digital-human, and robot observations. Its motion coefficients provide a common representation for observation encoding, conditional generation, and actuator mapping. Text- and audio-conditioned motion generation. ROSE-Flow combines text conditioning with frame-local audio attention in a dual-stream Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT). A staged training strategy with model merging unifies audio-to-motion, text-to-motion, and joint text--audio-to-motion generation. Direct latent-to-actuator execution. learns to translate shared motion latents into actuator states from paired robot images and actuator states, enabling execution without intermediate image reconstruction. We demonstrate this capability on a compact face robot. A compact biomimetic face robot. We develop a face robot integrating 34 actuators through a flexible tendon-sheath transmission. By decoupling actuator placement from facial action points, the design supports coordinated full-face expression within a compact head. Related Work Biomimetic mechanical faces and expression control. Mechanical facial research has long been shaped by two coupled questions: how to place enough independently controllable degrees of freedom in a limited head volume, and how to realize target expressions as stable physical motion. Early platforms used linkages, pneumatics, and compliant skin to realize basic expression and social behavior~ brooks1998cog,kobayashi2003realization,hashimoto2006development,nakaoka2009creating,lin2016expressional,asheber2016humanoid,faraj2021facially . Subsequent work has explored learned facial mimicry, Bayesian optimization, and preference-guided expression generation to achieve more natural facial control~ chen2021smile,yang2022optimizing,tang2023automatic . More recent systems incorporate speech, human co-expression, and neural control into physical mechanical faces~ li2024driving,hu2024human,zhang2025morpheus . Hybrid actuation and visual self-modeling further reveal a trade-off between the precision of rigid mechanisms and the spatial efficiency of tendon transmission~ zhang2025morpheus . Our approach uses a shared facial-motion latent space to connect expression generation with actuator control, allowing generated motion to be mapped to actuator commands without intermediate image reconstruction. Speech- and text-driven facial-motion generation. Audio-driven talking-face animation has progressed from visemes and 3D geometric driving~ zhou2018visemenet,cudeiro2019capture to cross-modal disentanglement, Transformer models, and emotion-conditioned facial motion~ richard2021meshtalk,fan2022faceformer,ji2021audio,peng2023selftalk,peng2023emotalk , and later to single-image portrait animation and real-time video synthesis~ zhang2023sadtalker,liu2024anitalker,xu2024vasa,guo2024liveportrait,xie2024xportrait . These methods generally output images, meshes, landmarks, or expression blendshape coefficients and focus on visual appearance, identity preservation, and lip synchronization. Avatar-to-robot retargeting~ hu2026lipmotions demonstrates the value of large-scale human-face priors, but still depends on an avatar video and a downstream visual bridge. In our framework, we instead generate motion-latent trajectories in a shared facial-motion space, where audio provides high-temporal-resolution conditions for articulation, while text specifies global intent and expression style. Video is therefore not an input source at deployment. Disentangled motion representations and conditional flow generation. Identity--motion decomposition enables cross-identity animation and reenactment~ wang2022lia,xnemo2025 ; in robotics, visual self-modeling also shows that shared visual representations can be connected to embodiment~ chen2022fully . Diffusion and flow models move generation into continuous latent spaces~ peebles2023dit , while flow matching and rectified flows offer direct and efficient formulations for conditional trajectory generation~ lipman2023flow,liu2023rectifiedflow . ROSE combines identity--motion decomposition with conditional flow generation in a shared facial-motion latent space across humans, digital humans, and robots. Frame-local audio conditioning guides motion generation, and a learned actuator mapping connects the generated trajectories to physical execution. ROSE connects facial observation, conditional motion generation, and robot execution through a shared motion latent . ROSE-VAE encodes facial observations into this space, ROSE-Flow generates motion-latent trajectories conditioned on text and audio, and maps these trajectories to actuator commands. The deployment pipeline is where either input modality may be omitted. Generated motion is thus mapped to robot commands without intermediate image reconstruction. Robot Platform sec:hardware Our robot platform is designed to accommodate 34 actuators for facial expression and neck motion. It combines tendon-sheath transmission with local rigid mechanisms to support flexible actuator placement and constrained motion paths. Actuators are concentrated near the top and rear of the head, with tendons routed to the brows, eyelids, cheeks, and lips. Local linkages, pushrods, and shafts additionally drive the jaw, mouth corners, philtrum, and eyeballs, while the neck supports pitch, roll, and yaw. title: WiTac: Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Similar tactile contacts can call for different corrections depending on the configuration of the hand, object and target. Rather than supplying touch and wrist vision separately, fusing them before policy injection better grounds tactile features in visual context, yielding more accurate contact representations. We introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that learns such representations before action generation. Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of SharpaDex data, WiTac deeply fuses tactile signals with hand motion and wrist views into a comprehensive contact representation. Conditioning downstream VLA policies (GR00T N1.7 and $π_{0.5}$) on WiTac substantially improves task success over vision-only base policies across four contact-rich manipulation tasks (+28.8% and +15.0% on average), and further outperforms a wrist-free tactile encoder by 18.8% and 7.5%, respectively. Offline analyses further show that incorporating wrist vision yields more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task-contact discrimination, greater feature stability under tactile noise, and clearer action-direction readout from similar contacts.Project page: https://wrist-informed-tactile-representations.github.io/.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Contact-rich manipulation requires actions that respond jointly to local touch and surrounding task geometry. When inserting a battery into a slot, similar finger loading can accompany different battery--slot alignments and call for distinct corrective motions. Local tactile deformation alone leaves this spatial configuration ambiguous, whereas close-range wrist cameras observe the hand, grasped object, and nearby target geometry, providing the spatial reference needed to interpret contact during manipulation. Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies such as GR00T~ gr00tn1_2025 and ~ pi05_2025 already receive camera images in their vision-language streams, yet they lack pre-fusion with tactile signals to ground grasp- and contact-related states. Recent visuotactile designs incorporate touch into policies by supplying standalone tactile features alongside visual streams~ sparsh2024,simpletouch2026 , modulating visual features with tactile signals~ tacfilm2026 , or encoding discrete residuals from visually predicted touch~ restacvla2026 . However, separate tactile inputs leave local touch ungrounded in the surrounding visual geometry, while visual modulation and residual coding do not directly form continuous contact representations that preserve detailed touch within its wrist visual context. To address this limitation, we introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that fuses touch with wrist vision before policy injection to produce grounded visuotactile contact tokens ( ). Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of synchronized dexterous manipulation data from SharpaDex v1.0~ sharpadex_v1_2026 , WiTac summarizes each finger's tactile history with robot state and wrist-relative fingertip kinematics, then queries wrist patch features through cross-attention to form finger-level contact tokens. Pretraining jointly supervises contact-state and history reconstruction, masked wrist-feature recovery, and action-conditioned wrench-response prediction, encouraging the tokens to retain physical contact detail as they incorporate visual context. During policy learning, the frozen WiTac encoder conditions VLA policies through a lightweight gated cross-attention interface alongside their native visual, language and state inputs. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, WiTac consistently boosts closed-loop success on both GR00T N1.7 and over vision-only base policies (+28.8 and +15.0 on average) and its wrist-free variant (+18.8 and +7.5 ), while offline analyses confirm improved contact reconstruction, joint task--contact discrimination, noise stability, and action-direction readout. Our contributions are: We propose WiTac, a pretrained contact encoder that fuses tactile histories, hand kinematics, and wrist observations into finger-level contact tokens before action generation, through joint physical and visual supervision. We demonstrate the utility of frozen WiTac representations across two VLA backbones and four real-world contact-rich tasks, achieving higher success than vision-only policies and wrist-free tactile encoding on every task. Through representation analyses, we show that WiTac provides more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task--contact discrimination, lower feature drift under tactile noise, and more accurate action-direction readout than wrist-free encoding. Related Work sec:related Tactile and visuotactile representations. Pretrained tactile encoders provide reusable features for contact perception and manipulation. Sparsh~ sparsh2024 learns touch representations through self-supervised objectives on tactile images, while T3~ t3_2025 combines sensor-specific encoders with a shared Transformer across sensors and tasks. AnyTouch~ anytouch2025 unifies static tactile images and dynamic tactile videos across multiple visuo-tactile sensors through masked modeling and cross-sensor alignment, and Sparsh-X~ sparshx2025 extends representation learning to image, audio, motion, and pressure signals from a multisensory tactile sensor. Physical supervision offers another route: UniVTAC~ univtac2026 reconstructs tactile appearance and predicts deformation, marker locations, and relative object pose from simulated tactile observations. External vision and language can also shape tactile representations: early work uses self-supervision to learn compact visuotactile features for contact-rich policy learning~ lee2018visionsense , VITaL~ vital2024 aligns visual and tactile embeddings through temporal contrastive pretraining, OmniVTLA~ omnivtla2025 aligns touch with visual and linguistic concepts in a dual-encoder architecture, and VT-MUSE~ vtmuse2026 pretrains sequential visuotactile latents through cross-modal alignment and masked sensory reconstruction. Visuotactile policies for parallel-jaw grippers. Vision-language-action (VLA) models such as GR00T~ gr00tn1_2025 and ~ pi05_2025 provide generalist visual, language, and motor capabilities that recent gripper-based systems extend with touch through policy conditioning or predictive world modeling. For reactive control, RDP~ rdp2025 pairs a slow latent diffusion policy with high-frequency closed-loop tactile feedback. Within VLA policies, SimpleTouch~ simpletouch2026 passes tokens from a frozen pretrained tactile encoder to a tactile expert trained with action supervision and future-latent prediction, TacFiLM~ tacfilm2026 maps pretrained tactile features to feature-wise scale and shift parameters that modulate the visual encoder, and ResTacVLA~ restacvla2026 encodes the quantized residual between wrist-predicted and observed touch with uncertainty gating. To anticipate contact evolution, DreamTacVLA~ dreamtacvla2025 aligns multi-scale views with touch and refines draft actions using future tactile states predicted by a world model, while OmniVTA~ omnivta2026 couples a two-stream visuo-tactile world model and contact-aware fusion policy with a 60\,Hz reflexive controller. World-action models further unify dynamics prediction and control: VTAM~ vtam2026 treats optical tactile images as an additional view of a pretrained video backbone with a flow-derived force proxy, Dream-Tac~ dreamtac2026 jointly predicts future visual observations, tactile dynamics, and actions using a contact-aware attention bias, and FAWAM~ fawam2026 and ForceWAM~ forcewam2026 predict future wrenches alongside actions. Scaling tactile manipulation to dexterous hands. Moving from parallel-jaw grippers to multi-fingered dexterous hands introduces distributed contacts across fingers, higher-dimensional kinematics, and heavier visual self-occlusion. To bridge embodiments, FTP-1~ ftp1_2026 maps heterogeneous tactile signals into morphology-aware tokens processed by a shared tactile Transformer expert, and ME-Dex 1.0~ medex2026 aligns gripper and dexterous-hand tactile inputs onto a canonical hand template within a three-expert world-action model. For multi-fingered hands specifically, SaTA~ sata2025 anchors tactile features to wrist-frame fingertip poses, ViTacFormer~ vitacformer2025 fuses vision and touch via cross-attention with an autoregressive tactile-prediction head, and STAR~ star2026 jointly predicts masked wrist-image and tactile patches during pretraining before passing separate tactile tokens to a VLA policy. At the policy and world-model level, T-Rex~ trex2026 combines a temporal tactile VQ-VAE with a variable-rate Mixture-of-Transformers to exploit high-frequency tactile feedback, DeCAL~ decal2026 pairs contact-gated fusion with latent visuo-tactile co-imagination, and DexTacWAM~ dextacwam2026 compresses per-finger touch into a video diffusion world model to jointly predict visual and contact dynamics. Rather than training a generative video-tactile world model during policy learning or supplying deployment tactile tokens encoded without wrist views, WiTac pretrains a frozen wrist-informed contact encoder that fuses ten-finger tactile histories, kinematics, and wrist imagery before conditioning VLA policies through lightweight gated cross-attention. Wrist-Conditioned Contact Representation sec:method WiTac fuses fingertip touch, hand kinematics, and wrist views into finger-level contact tokens before action generation. We pretrain the encoder via self-supervision, then freeze it to condition a VLA policy through gated cross-attention. (a--c) overviews contact encoding, representation pretraining, and policy injection. Let denote the scalar deformation maps of all ten fingers at time , and their eight-frame history including the current frame. WiTac receives , current RGB images from both wrist cameras, and the robot state , while forward kinematics provides each finger's pose (3D position and orientation) in its respective wrist frame. title: Prepare Lighter and Faster for Open-Vocabulary Queries: A Query-Wise 3D Segmenter for Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027
summary: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding aims to localize and segment arbitrary objects beyond predefined categories. However, existing approaches based on Gaussian Splatting often rely on expensive preprocessing and lengthy training, limiting their applicability when fast and lightweight solutions are desired. We propose a lightweight, training-free framework for query-driven 3D instance segmentation on Gaussian Splatting. Instead of conventional mask-wise CLIP embeddings, we use dense pixel-level CLIP features to preserve fine-grained semantic information and enable flexible text-driven localization without relying on predefined instance proposals. Given a text query, we identify a high-quality target region in a carefully selected pivot view and propagate it across views using a video segmentor, providing consistent and comprehensive coverage of the target instance. We then lift the resulting 2D tracklets to 3D Gaussians through a novel visibility voting strategy, yielding accurate 3D segmentation masks with clean object boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups over existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of our framework for efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.
full_text: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding aims to localize and segment arbitrary objects beyond predefined categories. However, existing approaches based on Gaussian Splatting often rely on expensive preprocessing and lengthy training, limiting their applicability when fast and lightweight solutions are desired. We propose a lightweight, training-free framework for query-driven 3D instance segmentation on Gaussian Splatting. Instead of conventional mask-wise CLIP embeddings, we use dense pixel-level CLIP features to preserve fine-grained semantic information and enable flexible text-driven localization without relying on predefined instance proposals. Given a text query, we identify a high-quality target region in a carefully selected pivot view and propagate it across views using a video segmentor, providing consistent and comprehensive coverage of the target instance. We then lift the resulting 2D tracklets to 3D Gaussians through a novel visibility voting strategy, yielding accurate 3D segmentation masks with clean object boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups over existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of our framework for efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training. Introduction sec:intro Open-vocabulary 3D understanding enables recognition and segmentation of arbitrary objects beyond fixed taxonomies, supporting applications such as robotic perception, AR/VR, and embodied AI. Gaussian Splatting methods 2dgs, 3dgs have emerged as efficient approaches for representing high-quality 3D scenes while enabling real-time rendering. Recent advances in fast optimization and feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting yonosplat, anysplat, instantsplat, noposplat, fastgs enable the reconstruction of 3D scenes from multi-view images within seconds to minutes. The widespread adoption of 3D Gaussian representations has made sharing pretrained 3D Gaussian assets across teams a common practice. However, despite this progress, efficient open-vocabulary interaction via open-vocabulary 3D segmentation with pretrained 3D Gaussian scenes remains underexplored. Most existing solutions langsplat, legaussian, opengaussian, instancegaussian, langsplatv2, liang_supergseg_2024, saga, panogs, opensplat3d adopt training-based pipelines that integrate vision-language features from VFMs into Gaussian-based 3D scene representations as an additional training stage after the 3D Gaussian primitives are learned (see ). These methods distill language/instance features into Gaussian splats through multi-stage contrastive learning or feature fusion. In practice, they extract thousands of multi-granularity SAM masks and corresponding mask-level CLIP embeddings across all training views, followed by feature distillation or fusion over these masks and post-processing steps to refine instance-level representations. Although these approaches demonstrate open-vocabulary scene understanding, their preprocessing and training stages are computationally expensive and can take hours to process a scene, making them impractical for instant usage. Recent efforts ludvig have explored lifting-based alternatives that partially alleviate preprocessing and training bottlenecks by directly lifting vision foundation model (VFM) features into 3D Gaussian splats. While this approach significantly accelerates scene-level understanding, the lifting process itself still requires over 10 minutes per scene to fuse features across the entire scene, even when only specific objects or regions are of interest. This leads to redundant computation and memory overhead. Moreover, this method exhibits a relatively high query latency of over 1.3 seconds per query, and the resulting 3D masks often lack precise object boundaries, still requiring additional SAM-based refinement. Both paradigms redundantly encode full-scene information even when queries concern only a single instance, making them inefficient for interactive systems. In real-world applications where users demand iterative interaction with a specific set of objects of interest, each query must be processed efficiently to provide immediate feedback. Users often need to identify or interact with objects right after reconstruction, rather than waiting through hours of preprocessing or optimization. To characterize this latency, we introduce the concept of Time-to-First-Query (TTFQ) -- the elapsed time between loading a reconstructed vanilla 3D scene and enabling the first open-vocabulary query and segmentation results. A low TTFQ is critical for responsive, scalable, and user-centric 3D systems, where fast turnaround directly translates to better usability and deployment feasibility. Motivated by the need to minimize TTFQ for instant responsiveness, we propose a training-free query-wise framework for open-vocabulary 3D segmentation on Gaussian Splatting scenes. Designed with high flexibility architecture, the framework can seamlessly integrate different vision-language and video segmentation backbones without retraining, making it adaptable to evolving vision foundation models without structural modification. Given a reconstructed 3D scene represented by Gaussian primitives, we perform 3D instance segmentation from a text query without requiring any additional training. Particularly, our method directly localizes and propagates relevant 2D regions associated to the text query across camera views of the scene. These propagated masks are then lifted into 3D through a lightweight visibility voting mechanism, producing precise and complete 3D segmentation with clean boundaries under one second per query. This lightweight, training-free design circumvents the heavy preprocessing required by previous pipelines and enables interactive open-vocabulary 3D segmentation on resource-limited use cases. More importantly, we demonstrate that such query processing leads to state-of-the-art segmentation accuracy while preserving low query latency. Our contributions are: A novel query-wise approach for open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation in Gaussian Splatting scenes, shifting from heavy precomputing scene-level semantics to lightweight precomputing and focusing on on-demand query-driven segmentation. A dense pixel-level CLIP features that preserve fine-grained semantics beyond mask-level embeddings, enabling flexible localization of arbitrary object regions without predefined masks or feature distillation. A novel and robust multi-view 2D instance localization strategy that maps text queries to image regions via a convolutional flood-fill algorithm and propagates them across views for geometrically consistent, spatially complete 3D segmentation. A lightweight visibility voting mechanism that aggregates multi-view 2D instance regions to construct an occlusion-aware 3D instance mask, enabling real-time rendering while maintaining high-quality segmentation with minimal computational overhead. Related Work sec:relatedworks have greatly advanced open‑vocabulary recognition and dense perception. CLIP~ clip provides strong open-vocabulary understanding, while DINO~ dino improves dense visual representations and Grounding DINO~ groundingdino combines them for phrase-level grounding. Other works~ owlvit,fu2025llmdet extend VLMs to detection and reasoning. However, many such methods alter CLIP during pretraining, reducing compatibility with existing open‑vocabulary systems. ProxyCLIP~ proxyclip and DeCLIP~ wang2025declip instead improve dense prediction while preserving CLIP compatibility. For video object segmentation, SAM~ sam , SAM 2~ sam2 , and HQ‑SAM~ samhq provide strong baselines for robust segmentation and tracking. Efficiency‑focused variants~ edgetam, efficienttam, fastsam further accelerate SAM‑based tracking with lightweight designs. Leveraging advances in vision–language models and video segmentation, we build a framework that integrates efficient open‑vocabulary models with tracking‑based segmentors and 3D cues to achieve precise and temporally consistent 2D instance localization. was first explored using dense point clouds~ takmaz2023openmask3d,nguyen2023open3dis, nguyen_any3dis_2024, openscene, he_segpoint_2024, conceptgraph . These approaches typically operate on RGB-D data and have demonstrated strong open-vocabulary understanding capabilities. However, the growing adoption of radiance-field-based scene representations has motivated the development of methods that leverage multi-view RGB images to achieve richer visual appearance and more efficient scene reconstruction. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ nerf,mipnerf,mipnerf360,instantngp and Gaussian Splatting~ 3dgs,2dgs, yonosplat, anysplat, fastgs enable high‑quality 3D reconstruction from multi‑view RGB images. However, their radiance-field-based representations differ substantially from point clouds, introducing a distribution gap that motivates dedicated methods for open-vocabulary 3D understanding in these reconstruction frameworks. Early NeRF- and Gaussian-based approaches~ lerf,langsplat,legaussian,opengaussian,instancegaussian,kim_garfield_2024,bhalgat_n2f2_2024,opensplat3d,langsplatv2 formulate segmentation as a scene-level optimization problem, performing instance and language feature learning by aggregating information from thousands of 2D masks into 3D primitives, requiring hours of preprocessing and long training cycles. Efforts to reduce training cost include Dr. Splat~ drsplat , which proposes training-free feature registration but still incurs substantial preprocessing overhead. VALA~ vala introduces visibility-aware feature aggregation to accelerate optimization but still requires costly scene-level semantic preprocessing. LUDVIG~ ludvig extracts patch‑wise CLIP features and lifts them via global optimization, resulting in time‑to‑first‑query above 10 minutes and suboptimal masks due to the lack of clean supervision. Pixel-based methods lerf,langsplat, kim_garfield_2024, bhalgat_n2f2_2024, langsplatv2, legaussian operate in image space, where features become meaningful only after rasterization to a target view. Pixel-based methods must re-query instances for each viewpoint, whereas point-based methods query instances directly in 3D and render them efficiently via Gaussian rasterization. title: ReuseMem: One Memory, Multiple Goals in Robot Manipulation
summary: Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes.

Introduction sec:introduction Memory enables robots to act on information that is no longer visible. In everyday assistance, the same experience may become useful for several requests that arise only later. An earlier observation may identify an object, reveal its original location, or establish the order of events. The robot need not know which of these uses will matter when it observes the scene. This calls for one memory that supports multiple later goals as the environment changes. Consider a robot observing the contents and original positions of two cases before they are closed and relocated (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Bringing the case containing a USB drive to a tray requires remembering its contents; returning it requires its origin. The same experience supplies different facts for different actions. After the transfer, the case must be grasped from the tray, while its destination still comes from the recorded past. Memory-augmented policies have advanced historical retrieval and its use in control~ memoryvla,halo,imprint,mem4act,hamlet . Persistent experience systems also reuse past observations for later requests through retrieval and planning~ memer,memora,messymem,mem . Building on these advances, we ask how the same recorded experience can reliably support different later manipulations. Success on several tasks with separate histories does not directly answer this question. The relevant unit is a common experience, whose usefulness must persist across requests that need different evidence and produce different actions. Such reuse couples two challenges. The robot must select the past observations needed for each request, then use them with the current scene to generate an appropriate action. Remembering an object's identity or former position does not specify where to grasp it now. Earlier actions can change the scene while leaving the historical facts valid. Training must therefore connect evidence selection to action under these changing current conditions. ReuseMem addresses this problem with a goal-independent Writer, a learned Reader, and a lightweight action interface. The Writer retains visual features and separate temporal entries without an advance inventory of objects or relations. The Reader selects complementary observations for each request. Its supervision comes from comparing how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states for the same goal. Historical facts remain fixed while the required actions vary. The action interface then learns from the updated Reader's selections, combining remembered evidence with current observations through fusion and low-rank adaptation of a frozen pretrained policy. Practical reuse also requires controlling storage and response time. Recordings often contain many similar views, yet their order can distinguish events relevant to later requests. To limit storage, ReuseMem stores matching visual features once while retaining a separate temporal entry for each observation. To reduce response time, fixed memory projections are computed once per action-sampling call and reused as the action is refined, while the policy still reads the selected memory anew at every step. Four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios evaluate different goals from common recordings, both independently and in continuous execution. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. Ablations and memory interventions examine evidence selection and action use, while storage and response measurements assess the cost of reuse. Our contributions are: One memory, multiple manipulation goals. We introduce ReuseMem, a framework that records experience before later goals are known and reuses the same visual memory for different manipulations as the current scene changes. Action-guided memory learning. We train memory retrieval by comparing how different selections of past observations support expert-action prediction across current states for the same goal. A lightweight action interface learns to combine the selected evidence with current observations. Efficient memory reuse. We reduce memory storage and repeated computation while retaining the temporal structure of experience. Repeated visual features are shared across temporal entries, and fixed memory projections are reused within each action-sampling call. Related Work sec:related Memory for robot control. Memory augments generalist visuomotor policies~ diffusionpolicy,octo,openvla,pi0 through visual or event-based banks~ memoryvla,dnr,eventvla,sam2act , recurrent states or test-time adaptation~ membodied,rememvla,muvla,robottt . Moment tokens, past-action prediction and action-history denoising provide temporal training signals~ hamlet,ptp,actmemvla , while ECoMEM builds instruction-conditioned concept records~ ecomem . HALO guides retrieval with video question answering and sparse attention~ halo . Imprint pretrains multi-stream memory with reconstruction and progress estimation before policy adaptation; its recurrent variant updates memory independently of language~ imprint . Mem4Act combines semantic and perceptual supervision with memory-first training~ mem4act . ReuseMem learns preferences between explicit evidence selections from expert-action prediction across current scenes, then trains the action interface with the Reader's deployment selections. MemoryBench, RoboMME and RMBench assess historical dependence~ sam2act,robomme,rmbench ; our evaluation pairs different requests with the same recording. Experience for later requests. Persistent memory supports subsequent reasoning, planning and manipulation~ memer,memora,messymem,mem,pal . Scene graphs organize observed objects, locations and interactions~ conceptgraphs,roboexp,dynamem,scenegraphil . MemER reuses keyframes across successive requests through a high-level VLM that issues subgoals to a low-level policy, while MessyMem links interaction-updated scene graphs to visual records for VLM planning~ memer,messymem . MEMORA edits typed records, MEM combines video and text, and PAL stores semantic events and executable subtasks~ memora,mem,pal . These systems establish the value of experience beyond its original task. ReuseMem focuses on the learned path from retrieved visual evidence to current action generation, using a common recording to evaluate different manipulation purposes. Efficient memory and inference. Compression and caching address different costs. Token Merging reduces redundancy within visual transformers~ tome ; NativeMEM compresses historical frame views, and MemBodied maintains fixed-size recurrent state~ nativemem,membodied . MemoryVLA merges similar bank entries~ memoryvla , while SimpleMemVLA reuses native-video prefixes during inference~ simplememvla . ReuseMem separates shared appearance storage from temporal occurrences, preserving the order and identity of recorded entries. Its cache covers fixed memory projections within one action-sampling call, while new observations refresh the action input. Method sec:method ReuseMem records experience before its later goals are known, retrieves evidence for each request, and uses that evidence to act from the current scene (Figure~ fig:architecture ). The Writer and memory bank preserve visual and temporal information. The Reader and action interface learn how to use it. Problem setting. sec:problem A recording produces a common memory bank before its later goals are supplied. Every goal reads this same recorded history. Later observations form an execution history without overwriting it. Given a goal , retrieval selects past observations. An action policy combines them with the current observation and robot state. The base policy is frozen, while retrieval parameters and action-interface parameters are learned. Memory Bank sec:archive The Writer comprises frozen visual encoding, feature sharing, temporal-entry creation and learned causal key computation. Each observation yields appearance features . An appearance pool stores immutable prototypes that multiple temporal entries can reference, avoiding repeated storage of matching features. Each entry keeps its own frame index, observed metadata, validity, prototype reference , and retrieval key. The Writer finds the nearest prototype by pooled cosine similarity and shares it only when both a similarity threshold and a maximum per-token distance bound are satisfied. Otherwise it appends a new prototype. The token-level check preserves locally distinctive observations that a pooled similarity could miss. This appearance sharing avoids duplicate feature storage while preserving separate temporal entries. Prototypes are never averaged or overwritten. The original frame index and spatial grid supply the native positional term . The reconstructed observation and its causal retrieval key are Here contains observed metadata, and uses only current and preceding entries. The key encoder is learned with the Reader; visual encoding and the sharing rule are fixed. Neither future goals nor expert actions enter recording. Visual features preserve evidence for different later uses while matching the pretrained policy's visual interface. Appendix~ app:memory-interface gives the reconstruction, admission and representation details. Memory Retrieval sec:retrieval A request can depend on several moments: remembered contents identify a case, while its earlier position supplies a return destination. The Reader retrieves complementary observations from the common bank (Figure~ fig:reader ). The instruction is pooled into a query over causal keys. The Reader searches eight candidate anchors, chooses four references, and selects three supporting observations for each reference using the goal and temporal relation. Eight evenly spaced coverage observations supplement these references and supports. Stable deduplication and temporal filling yield 24 historical slots. Histories shorter than this budget use masked padding. A path records the discrete choices, and gives the selected indices. Its score sums the masked log probabilities of the nonnull learned choices: All goals use the same recorded history. Deployment takes the highest-scoring eligible choice at each decision. Appendix~ app:retrieval gives the scoring functions, and Algorithm~ alg:read specifies the selection procedure. title: WinDEX: Metric 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild for Dexterous Teleoperation and Policy Learning
summary: Human manipulation data are widely used to train robots for human-like dexterity. However, low-cost, large-scale collection in the wild remains challenging. Existing methods remain limited in geometrically grounded metric-scale reconstruction, real-world generalization and inference speed. We present WinDEX, integrating (1) geometric-temporal optimization for metric 3D hand annotation from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, combined with visual-inertial SLAM for world-frame reconstruction; (2) WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo, local detail and temporal context, with a data-model flywheel of model-assisted annotation and retraining; (3) distilled models for offline reconstruction and causal streaming, supporting reinforcement learning and teleoperation; and (4) low-cost CyberCap stereo-inertial capture, forming the WinDEX-Hand dataset with 1,000 hours of training annotations and held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D and independent optical motion-capture evaluation sets. Offline reconstruction runs at 43.61 FPS and causal streaming at 171 FPS. On held-out data, offline reconstruction achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 14.5 pixels in-the-wild reprojection error and, with visual-inertial odometry, 37.29 mm world-frame joint error. We achieve 7.6 and 3.6 times the task success rates of reinforcement learning policies trained with WiLoR and HaWoR motion references, respectively, and demonstrate real-time arm-hand teleoperation. Project website: https://fruitrabbit.github.io/WinDEX/.

Project website: . World-frame 3D hand pose estimation, egocentric stereo vision, learning from demonstration, teleoperation. Introduction sec:intro oboticists have long sought to guide dexterous robotic manipulation using human motion trajectories. Hand poses and trajectories guide teleoperation ref:handmap,ref:anyteleop,ref:televison,ref:dexcap and provide demonstrations, pose priors, and tracking references for reinforcement learning (RL) ref:dexmv,ref:dexvip,ref:maniptrans . Hand trajectories also provide action supervision for video-based policies and vision--language--action models ref:egomimic,ref:egovla,ref:beingh0 , condition world models that predict manipulation outcomes ref:dwm , and supply geometric information for grasp synthesis ref:graspreview,ref:manipnet . These applications share a need for reliable 3D hand motion in relation to the surrounding scene. We adopt metric 3D hand poses and their trajectories in a gravity-aligned world frame as our 3D hand representations, describing wrist motion and finger articulation independently of the moving camera (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Recovering this representation across everyday environments at scale is our central problem. Existing acquisition routes include optical motion capture, calibrated multi-camera rigs, sensor gloves and wearable trackers, and video recording. Optical systems and multi-camera datasets such as ARCTIC, DexYCB, HOT3D and AssemblyHands provide detailed reference measurements ref:arctic,ref:dexycb,ref:hot3d,ref:assemblyhands , but depend on instrumented environments. Gloves and exoskeletons support portable capture ref:dexcap,ref:dexumi while retaining hardware on the hands. Monocular RGB cameras permit egocentric or exocentric recording without hand instrumentation. More broadly, video collections such as Ego4D and Ego-Exo4D cover diverse first- and third-person activity ref:ego4d,ref:egoexo4d , but a single view leaves depth and absolute scale ambiguous, and external cameras limit recording to their fields of view. Wearable recording extends coverage ref:nymeria,ref:egodex . In particular, head-worn stereo can follow the wearer without placing equipment on the hands, while a calibrated baseline provides a geometric constraint on metric depth. Project Aria and Quest tracking systems demonstrate the potential of wearable multi-view sensing ref:aria,ref:megatrack,ref:umetrack . Scalable in-the-wild capture still requires reliable annotation under occlusion, peripheral visibility and simultaneous camera and hand motion. To recover metric hand trajectories from these recordings, both model architecture and training supervision must accommodate wearable capture. Monocular image and video estimators, including HaMeR, WiLoR, HaWoR and Dyn-HaMR ref:hamer,ref:wilor,ref:hawor,ref:dynhamr , use appearance and motion priors to resolve single-view ambiguity. POEM and its successor exploit calibrated multi-view geometry ref:poem,ref:poemv2 ; ViDiHand integrates localization and reconstruction without an external detector ref:vidihand . For compact fisheye stereo, an integrated architecture must additionally use the known baseline and viewing rays, preserve local finger detail, and distinguish hand motion from camera motion. On the data side, laboratory capture limits environmental coverage, and tracker-generated labels require independent accuracy evaluation ref:hot3d,ref:egodex . Dense, reliable 3D supervision across diverse natural recordings remains costly. These needs motivate joint localization and reconstruction with stereo and temporal context, coupled to a scalable pipeline for producing and checking training annotations. We present WinDEX, a system integrating wearable capture, geometric--temporal annotation, learned reconstruction and robot interfaces (Fig.~ fig:system ). Low-cost CyberCap collects fisheye stereo RGB and inertial data without hand instrumentation. To obtain metric supervision, geometric--temporal optimization fits hands to manually reviewed 2D keypoints, filters 3D labels by reprojection error, and uses SLAM camera trajectories to recover world-frame motion. To address depth ambiguity, preserve finger detail and account for camera motion, WinDEX-Net combines calibrated stereo, local crops and odometry-conditioned temporal features for end-to-end, fisheye-native localization and reconstruction. Predictions accelerate annotation, and retraining closes the data--model flywheel. WinDEX-Hand separates generated 3D training labels from evaluation references: human-annotated in-the-wild 2D references and independent optical 3D ground truth (Section~ sec:dataset ). To balance accuracy and response time, distillation yields offline WinDEX-Window and causal, real-time WinDEX-Stream. Hand2Policy uses pose-tracking rewards for reinforcement learning; Hand2Teleop coordinates arm--hand teleoperation using only CyberCap stereo and IMU for operator tracking. Against human-annotated in-the-wild 2D references and optical 3D ground truth from held-out recordings, WinDEX-Window achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy and temporal smoothness. Under matched training settings and budgets, Hand2Policy reaches 61 mean simulated grasp--lift--place success versus 8 for WiLoR and 17 for HaWoR, with policy transfer to physical robots. The main contributions of this work are as follows: To obtain metric 3D hand annotations from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, we combine geometric--temporal optimization with visual--inertial SLAM to recover hand articulation and metrically scaled trajectories in a consistent world frame. To accelerate reconstruction, we introduce WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo geometry, local hand detail and temporal context. Model-initialized optimization and retraining form a data--model flywheel that expands supervision. To support offline learning and live control, we distill WinDEX-Net into WinDEX-Window and WinDEX-Stream. Hand2Policy and Hand2Teleop further connect the models to reinforcement learning with policy transfer and real-time arm--hand teleoperation, respectively, with validation on physical hardware. To make collection accessible at scale, we use the low-cost CyberCap stereo--inertial device for everyday manipulation and construct WinDEX-Hand from the annotated recordings, with held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D references and independent optical motion-capture ground truth. Section~ sec:related reviews related work, and Section~ sec:overview formulates the system. Sections~ sec:capture and~ sec:flywheel describe metric annotation and model-assisted corpus construction. Section~ sec:deliver presents the deployment models and robot interfaces; Section~ sec:downstream reports experiments, followed by limitations in Section~ sec:limits . Related Work sec:related Human Hand Motion for Robot Control and Learning subsec:consumers Human hand motion supports teleoperation, policy learning, and action representations for vision--language--action (VLA) and world models. AnyTeleop ref:anyteleop converts visual hand estimates into robot commands through learning-free retargeting and collision-aware motion generation. DexCap ref:dexcap matches human and robot fingertips through inverse kinematics and learns point-cloud diffusion policies from wearable demonstrations. For policy learning, DexMV ref:dexmv reconstructs hand--object poses from paired RGB-D views in a configured recording volume, translates them into robot states and actions, and trains policies in corresponding simulated tasks. ManipTrans ref:maniptrans pretrains a generalist trajectory imitator and learns residual corrections for object interaction, assuming supplied hand--object trajectories. EgoVLA ref:egovla and Being-H0 ref:beingh0 use hand trajectories as action supervision for VLA pretraining from human videos. Dexterous World Models ref:dwm condition visual-dynamics prediction on hand motion. These uses depend on reliable motion representations. WinDEX addresses this shared need by recovering metric, world-frame hand motion from everyday scenes. Hand Motion Capture and Egocentric Datasets subsec:scale Hand-motion datasets differ in capture hardware, image modality and label reliability. DexCap combines electromagnetic gloves with SLAM cameras ref:dexcap ; DexUMI uses joint encoders in a robot-specific exoskeleton and ARKit wrist tracking ref:dexumi . Both retain hardware on the hands. Headset datasets also differ from our RGB stereo setting. UmeTrack uses four monochrome fisheye cameras and marker-based optical ground truth ref:umetrack . HOT3D records Aria and Quest 3 streams with optical ground truth in an instrumented laboratory; their stereo tracking streams are monochrome, with an additional RGB view on Aria ref:hot3d . EgoDex scales recording through Apple Vision Pro's ARKit tracker ref:egodex , whose predicted labels can degrade under occlusion and rapid motion. It supplies joint confidence but does not report independent motion-capture validation or a reprojection-error acceptance threshold. We evaluate on held-out WinDEX-Hand recordings, using independent optical ground truth for 3D accuracy and human-annotated 2D references for in-the-wild image consistency. Table~ tab:positioning compares the capture and supervision choices. Monocular image and video methods ref:hamer,ref:wilor,ref:hawor,ref:dynhamr recover detailed hand pose and shape using learned appearance and motion priors. Metric depth remains dependent on additional assumptions because a single view does not directly determine absolute scale. title: Vegetation Health Classification for Low-Data and Edge Hardware Deployment
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with cameras are popular, viable tools for vegetation and environmental health monitoring. However, existing image classification methods are incompatible with UAV implementation for independent practitioners in remote, resource-constrained environments due to large dataset requirements, GPU hardware, inflexible retraining, and low interpretability. This paper presents a lightweight, interpretable vegetation classification algorithm operating with as few as five reference images per class, without GPUs or heavy machine learning frameworks. It uses a 2D hue-saturation histogram feature representation and Earth Mover's Distance or Quadratic Form Distance, paired with a log-likelihood probability score, to classify images into three vegetation health categories. We evaluated six systems: three custom pipelines and three established models across low-data scenarios ($n = 5, 10, 25$) and a full-data regime of 2,172 drone images from 28 South American locations. Our custom pipelines achieve competitive Top-1 accuracy (81--85\%) under low-data constraints, maintaining sub-1ms inference times that enable real-time classification and subsequently tasks such as seeding and watering. The algorithms also support incremental retraining without full model reconstruction. We validate edge feasibility by deploying the QFD variant on an ESP32 microcontroller, achieving 82.8\% accuracy with 1.01\% heap memory utilization (45kb), demonstrating that effective vegetation classification is achievable on low-cost, low-power embedded hardware without cellular connectivity.
full_text: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with cameras are popular, viable tools for vegetation and environmental health monitoring. However, existing image classification methods are incompatible with UAV implementation for independent practitioners in remote, resource-constrained environments due to large dataset requirements, GPU hardware, inflexible retraining, and low interpretability. Our custom pipelines achieve competitive Top-1 accuracy (81–85 ) under low-data constraints, maintaining sub-1ms inference times that enable real-time classification and subsequently tasks such as seeding and watering. We validate edge feasibility by deploying the QFD variant on an ESP32 microcontroller, achieving 82.8 accuracy with 1.01 heap memory utilization ( 45kb), demonstrating that effective vegetation classification is achievable on low-cost, low-power embedded hardware without cellular connectivity. Introduction sec:intro Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with cameras and video recorders have emerged as a powerful tool for environmental monitoring due to their cost effectiveness and versatility. The role of drone imagery as a vegetation health assessment tool stretches across numerous domains and applications, such as wildfire risk monitoring, agriculture, and biodiversity conservation, especially when tools such as infrared imaging aren't available manfreda2018use, anderson2013lightweight, gonzalez2016unmanned, wang2026uav, ghali2022deep . Compared to the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), which is based on infrared imaging, pure color detection systems are less accurate in terms of measuring plant health since it actually measures physiological changes in chlorophyll density and plant stress, which are only visible in more severe stages in pure color. This makes NDVI a great choice for large scale environmental monitoring. However, in many practical scenarios independent practitioners or small organizations working on remote conservation efforts do not have access to infrared imaging, necessitating pure color classification rouse1974monitoring, pettorelli2005using . This is especially true for commercial drones, which are increasingly being equipped with onboard cameras and used for exactly this kind of monitoring work. These platforms are often operated in remote areas without cellular or network coverage, making it impractical or impossible to stream imagery back to a remote computer for processing. They also typically lack the dedicated GPU hardware found on higher-end research-funded platforms, and may rely on legacy microcontrollers or other low-power embedded hardware for onboard computation. In addition, many tasks done by drones reqiure real-time classification to make decisions under field conditions, such as reforestation seeding and watering stamatopoulos2024uav, ahansal2022towards . However, far fewer of these models simultaneously satisfy the computational and logistical constraints faced by resource-limited practitioners operating in remote field environments albanese2022low . To address the aforementioned practical issues with previous approaches, this paper presents a lightweight, interpretable vegetation classification algorithm designed to operate with as few as five reference images per class, without requiring GPU hardware, extensive model retraining, or heavy external machine learning frameworks. The algorithm is designed with the out-of-the-box practitioner in mind: rather than assuming access to hyper-optimized pipelines or high-performance infrastructure, it targets the hardware and workflows that independent field operators are most likely to actually have available. Because our algorithm runs its inference entirely on-device, it is well suited to deployment directly onboard commercial drones and low-power embedded hardware, including in areas where cellular or other network signals cannot reach, removing the need to transmit imagery back to a remote computer for processing and also increasing operational range. To validate this directly, we deploy and benchmark the algorithm on an ESP32 microcontroller as a representative example of the low-cost, low-power hardware a practitioner might have on hand that has been proven to possess capabilities for computer vision processing esp32datasheet, chang2025design . Related Work sec:relatedWork This section provides an overview of existing literature, highlighting capabilities of existing small classification models while also noting constraints in these methods. Aerial Vegetation Monitoring and Color Spaces The field of real-time automated vegetation classification has grown alongside both drone and machine learning technology. In particular, supervised approaches such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and CNNs have demonstrated great, deployable accuracy scores for identifying vegetation health shi2015support, shi2025evaluation, jintasuttisak2025accurate . Neural networks have also gained massive popularity recently. With the help of ImageNet, architectures such as Ultralytics' YOLOv8 are adaptable enough to fit into this domain, achieving extremely high accuracy with massive datasets jocher2023ultralytics . HSV was selected as the color representation method over RGB because prior research has consistently demonstrated that luminance functions as a confounding factor in RGB-based image classification song2023new, hernandez2016optimal . Furthermore, HSV facilitates more straightforward distance calculations through eliminating the need for normalization and enabling efficient value isolation. This methodological choice is well-established within the literature sural2002segmentation, yang2015greenness, wenbo2025identification, hassanein2018new, swain1991color . Deep Learning and Few-Shot Baselines in Data-Scarce Regimes Additionally, Few Shot Learning (FSL) methods have been proposed as a solution to low-data situations. By learning generalizable feature embeddings from related tasks or by employing metric-based similarity frameworks, FSL methods have been proven to be robust, accurately classifying vegetation scenes with as few as five labeled examples per class zhang2024convolutional, snell2017prototypical, uzhinskiy2021one . While these advancements represent significant steps forward, they present meaningful practical limitations that motivate the approach taken in this study. Massive data requirements: The performance of supervised deep learning and Support Vector Machines comes at the cost of a massive data requirement. They often require hundreds to thousands of annotated images to be robust, requiring many hours by experts to sort through and categorize them for training. High computational expenses during training time, resultant inflexible training cycles: SVMs and neural networks require a complete retraining cycle to be completed when even minor amounts of new data is added losing2018incremental . In field conditions where an operator might want to continuously add newly collected data to a model, this restraint is incredibly difficult to work around with. Black-box neural networks: Neural networks and FSL methods essentially act as black boxes lipton2018mythos . After training, the embeddings and internal representations of images are high-dimensional and unintuitive, and as a result essentially inaccessible to any independent practitioner trying to apply these technologies. Low interpretability in SVMs: SVMs seem like a solution to this problem at first; they are more transparent and offer a more intuitive and well-understood geometric representation of images, but in most cases that involve vegetation classification, feature extraction must be programmed specifically for this domain, and a complex kernel has to be applied. For the vast majority of users applying SVMs, they essentially become a black box after applying a kernel trick due to the program now introducing infinite dimension space and no directly interpretable feature weights tharwat2019parameter . Edge Deployment Constraints Although FSL methods largely solve the data issue, they almost always rely on deep feature extraction based off of frameworks such as ResNet and EfficientNet he2016deep, tan2019efficientnet . While highly effective and easy to deploy, they are computationally expensive both during training and on inference time, especially when deployed on devices without dedicated GPUs, older field laptops, the processors on commercial drones, and legacy microcontrollers. For real-time assessment and analysis, this computational overhead is a serious challenge and delays conservation efforts. Methodology sec:methodology This section outlines how we organized the comparative study to test our lightweight algorithm against traditional and deep learning / neural baselines. Dataset Sourcing The dataset consists of drone-captured vegetation imagery sorted into three classes: Dry, mixed, and dense. Dry vegetation consists of essentially no healthy vegetation and is usually either completely bare or dried out. Mixed vegetation images have some mixture of healthy green vegetation together with dried out vegetation or bare dirt. Dense vegetation images are dominated by green, lush vegetation. There are a total of 2172 images in the dataset. 783 of them are dense vegetation, 625 are dry, and 764 are mixed. The drone imagery is taken from 28 different locations within South America from OpenAerialMap openaerialmap . 21 of these locations were sorted for all three classes, and an additional 7 locations were sorted specifically to add to the dry class due to a severe dataset size mismatch in comparison to the mixed and dense classes. Out of the dry images, 330 come from the original 21 locations, and the additional 295 were supplemented from the additional locations. All 2172 images were manually classified by the first author to establish ground truth. Ambiguous, low-quality, or nondescript images were excluded. Feature Representation and Extraction All systems except for the Siamese Network, utilize the same standardized feature representation layer. This shared foundation isolates algorithm-level differences in performance and accuracy from variation based on feature extraction. The 2D histogram employed by four of the five systems evaluated comprises 15 hue columns and 8 saturation rows. Each hue column covers 24 degrees of the color wheel, while each saturation row covers 12.5 of the saturation spectrum. When constructing the histogram, pixels with values exceeding 240 or falling below 20 are excluded from consideration. These extreme values are perceptually ambiguous and usually just come from camera glare, deep shadows, or image processing artifacts. As a result, they contain very little real information about the hue composition of an image and are disregarded. Finally, each pixel is assigned to the corresponding histogram cell, and the resulting histogram is normalized to account for variations introduced by the value threshold and potential differences in image dimensions. This feature histogram is shared across all systems. Prior to inference, both EMD algorithms prune the histogram for values under 0.5 and renormalize the histogram in order to avoid slowing down the algorithm with more bins with tiny values that largely do not end up influ

title: ThinkWAM: Rethinking Latent Futures for Action Refinement
comment: 21 pages, including references and appendix. Project page: https://thinkwam-project.github.io/
summary: World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. An initial action chunk may be flawed. A future prediction that is not conditioned on the chunk may fail to reflect the changes that the proposed actions would induce in visual representations, limiting its usefulness for refinement before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, showing that the corrected future representations improve the final action.

The lower panel summarizes success rates and mean inference latency. fig:teaser \@startsection paragraph 4 @ 1.5ex plus 0.4ex minus 0.2ex -1em Introduction sec:intro Robot manipulation requires anticipating what an action will cause. A visually plausible reach can miss an object, an apparently stable grasp can slip, and a locally reasonable motion can leave a later placement incomplete. Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot control, and scalable robot transformers, web-supervised visual-language backbones, and generalist policies have broadened the range of tasks that a single policy can perform~ brohan2022rt1,brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer,octomodelteam2024octoopensourcegeneralistrobot,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel,pi05 . Diffusion and flow-matching action heads further support continuous, multimodal action chunks~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,lipman2023flowmatching,black2024pi0 . Yet the usual decision interface maps the current visual context directly to an action or action chunk, without an explicit representation of what it will cause. World-action models (WAMs) address this gap by coupling action generation with a predictive representation of the environment~ du2023learninguniversalpoliciestextguided,wu2023unleashinglargescalevideogenerative,cen2025worldvlaautoregressiveactionworld , and latent-space variants avoid reconstructing every future pixel~ hafner2019learninglatentdynamicsplanningpixels,assran2025vjepa2,lin2026jepawam,zhang2026vjepapolicy,huang2026foresight . These models use future prediction as training supervision, expose future-informed features to the action head, or use predicted consequences to guide action sampling~ an2026feedbackwm . Here, we study how a complete action proposal can update predicted futures and how those updates can guide action refinement before execution (Sec.~ sec:related-latent ). An initial action chunk may be flawed. If future prediction is independent of that chunk, a mistimed grasp and a well-timed grasp can receive the same predicted continuation, limiting its usefulness for refinement. We therefore seek feedback in both directions before execution: predicted futures guide the action, while the proposal updates those futures. We introduce , a latent WAM that implements this interaction through a proposal--rethink--refine loop (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). The policy predicts visual latents at multiple future horizons and uses language features and affordance-guided memory to propose a complete action chunk. The proposal then conditions learned residual corrections to the base future latents. A second pass through the same ActionDiT head consumes the corrected futures and generates the refined action chunk. Sensory--motor accounts motivate this loop: agents predict the sensory consequences of their own actions to guide behavior~ rao2024sensory . Two ideas from predictive coding motivate our representation choices. Predictive coding shapes representations through prediction-error minimization~ rao1999predictive . We use affordance supervision to shape the shared visual context toward where actions make contact, and write a weighted summary of this context into memory. Dynamic predictive coding motivates hierarchical prediction across temporal scales~ jiang2024dynamic . We therefore allocate more tokens and use finer aggregation for near-future targets than for distant ones. Our contributions are: We introduce , a proposal--rethink--refine architecture that corrects multi-horizon future latents using the policy's own proposal and injects the corrected latents into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the final action. We propose an affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, motivated by predictive coding. We demonstrate strong generalization on LIBERO-Plus, the randomized setting of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa24, and real-world manipulation tasks, with achieving competitive overall results while maintaining low inference latency. Related Work sec:related VLA policies and world action models. sec:related-vla Visuomotor and VLA policies map the current context directly to the next action~ brohan2022rt1,brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel or to an action chunk produced by chunked, diffusion, or flow-matching heads~ octomodelteam2024octoopensourcegeneralistrobot,pi05,zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanualmanipulation,chi2023diffusionpolicy,lipman2023flowmatching , without modeling what these actions will lead to. World action models (WAMs) make future states explicit alongside actions. Video-conditioned policies use predicted future frames to guide control~ du2023learninguniversalpoliciestextguided , whereas other models predict future frames and actions jointly, from a GPT-style causal Transformer that is pretrained on large-scale video for future-frame generation and then fine-tuned to output actions and future images together~ wu2023unleashinglargescalevideogenerative , to autoregressive action--image modeling~ cen2025worldvlaautoregressiveactionworld , coupled video--action diffusion~ zhu2025uwm,bi2025motus , and action encoding as latent frames of a pretrained video model~ kim2026cosmospolicy . Because generating future video is costly, FastWAM and ImageWAM ask whether test-time imagination or full video generation is necessary~ yuan2026fastwam,imagewam . Cycle WAM enforces video--action consistency with a training-time cycle-reconstruction objective~ cyclewam2026 , whereas lets the policy's own action proposal correct the predicted future at inference (Sec.~ sec:rethink ). Another line replaces raw appearance with physically grounded cues closer to what an action must change, such as point trajectories~ wen2023atm , dynamic-region, spatial, and semantic knowledge~ zhang2025dreamvla , affordance~ mo2021where2actpixelsactionsarticulated , and affordance and depth guidance for video and action features~ zhang2026devadecoupledvideoactionmodel . follows this direction by injecting an affordance-weighted residual into the memory that conditions both action passes. Latent world-action models. sec:related-latent Latent WAMs predict future states in a learned representation space rather than in pixels, commonly that of joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs)~ assran2023selfsupervisedlearningimagesjointembedding,bardes2024revisitingfeaturepredictionlearning,assran2025vjepa2 , which learn by predicting the representations of masked targets. They differ mainly in how future predictions inform action selection. One route uses future prediction as auxiliary supervision that shapes the policy's representations: JEPA-WAM learns a joint current--future target in a V-JEPA space and drops the transition head at deployment~ lin2026jepawam , and FRAPPE aligns future representations with multiple visual teachers during training and retains its future-prefix streams at inference~ zhao2026frappe . A second route supplies future-predictive features to the action expert at inference. V-JEPA Policy exposes the predictor's context-position keys and values (K/V) to its action expert~ zhang2026vjepapolicy ; ForeWAM reads hidden K/V at future positions~ huang2026foresight ; LiLa-WAM jointly produces action velocities and future-related representations in a shared stream~ lilawam2026 . LaWAM decodes a policy-predicted latent action into a future feature that conditions its action expert~ lawam2026 . Action review and refinement. Several methods use predictive feedback to review or revise action proposals during control. Staircase Policy re-predicts future latents at sub-chunk boundaries to update unexecuted actions~ staircase2026 . ThinkWAM instead predicts a proposal-conditioned residual on multi-horizon base future latents and injects the corrected latents into a second pass of the same action head (Sec.~ sec:rethink ); the path is trained jointly, with demonstration futures supervising the predicted latents and the refined-action loss shaping the corrected representation. Multi-horizon prediction. sec:related-horizon Predicting at several temporal distances trades off local precision against longer-range foresight. Prior work varies the horizon of predicted actions~ moh2025 or predicts future representations at multiple horizons~ ding2026hifor,nativeva2026 . title: Lazy-MOSAIC: Accelerating Skill-Centric Manipulation Planning with Learned Skill-Effect World Models
comment: Under review
summary: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io.
