A cheap learned skill-effect world model expands the optimistic graph (faded cyan); promising hypotheses (magnified cyan) are certified in physics simulation, with successful rollouts entering the certified graph (black) and forming the complete plan. The returned plans contain only certified skills. Right: Wrench retrieval in a semi-structured workshop. The robot must clear clutter, reposition the wrench, grasp it, and place it in the goal region (green). fig:optimistic_certified_graphs Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io . Introduction sec:introduction Consider a robot tasked with retrieving a wrench from behind clutter in an automotive workshop (Fig.~ fig:optimistic_certified_graphs ). This is an instance of the semi-structured settings we target in this work: the robot knows the workspace and the object types it may encounter, but which objects are present and where they rest varies from task to task. The wrench may lie beyond the gripper's reach, requiring the robot to push other objects aside and reposition the wrench before attempting a grasp. Solving such tasks with generic skills such as pushing, pulling, grasping, and transporting requires reasoning not only about which skills to compose but also about the world states they produce, since a skill that makes little immediate progress toward the goal may enable a later skill to succeed. A planner therefore needs a world model---any function that predicts the outcome of executing a parameterized skill from a given state---to compare alternative skill sequences, and such models differ in cost and fidelity. Recent skill-based planners use a physics simulator as their world model, relatively accurate but expensive to query mosaic, saleem2020selective . mosaic is a recently introduced planner of this kind. Rather than growing a search forward from the start state, it conducts a non-sequential search in which skills guide exploration toward regions of the state space where they are likely to succeed. Generator skills, grounded with specific parameters, propose behaviors in these regions, and connector skills link them by solving boundary value problems. This allows to discover non-obvious enabling steps, e.g., repositioning an object to allow a feasible grasp. However, every candidate generator and connector is simulated before entering the search graph, whether or not it contributes to the solution. Over 80 of 's planning time is spent forward-simulating skills to compute their outcome (Fig.~ fig:mosaic-time ). To address this computational challenge, we draw on ideas from lazy search bohlin2000lazyprm, dellin2016lazysp . Lazy search defers edge evaluation, treating each edge as a hypothesis until it must be resolved. It assumes, however, that the vertices will strictly either be valid or invalid, and that invalidating an edge leaves the rest of the graph unaffected. In , vertices and edges are both skills, and the outcome of a skill is known only after it is simulated, violating the assumption that lazy search makes. In this work, we introduce , which extends lazy search to graphs whose vertices, not only edges, are hypotheses. It interleaves two world models: a cheap learned skill-effect model, which predicts the outcome of a skill, and an expensive high-fidelity model, here the physics simulator. builds its graph from the cheap model's predictions, queries the expensive model for skills along a promising candidate solution path, and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs the graph locally, keeping the state actually produced and every unaffected hypothesis rather than discarding all of them. Only fully simulated grounded skills ever appear in the returned plan. This crucially preserves physics simulation-based validation, helping alleviate the risk of unexpected contact in safety-critical tasks. Our contributions are twofold: We introduce , which extends lazy search to skill-centric planning, where deferring a skill also defers the state it produces, so that vertices as well as edges are hypotheses and an invalidated prediction affects a subtree rather than a single edge. We show how a cheap learned world model can drive this search, deciding which skills are simulated and in what order, while certification guarantees that its accuracy affects only planning efficiency, never the validity of a returned plan with respect to the high-fidelity model. Related Work sec:related draws on three lines of work: skill-based long-horizon planning, lazy search and planning with models of different fidelity, and learned models of action feasibility and effects. Skill-based long-horizon planning. Task and motion planning (TAMP) garrett2021integrated interleaves symbolic search with motion planning, but relies on symbolic abstractions of the preconditions and effects of each skill that are either specified by hand crosby2016skiros or learned from data konidaris2018skills . Skill-chaining methods rooted in the options framework sutton1999options, konidaris2009skillchaining express preconditions and effects as initiation sets and termination conditions in the state space rather than as symbolic predicates, and grow chains incrementally from the start or goal state so that each skill terminates where the next can be initiated. Skills whose initiation sets lie far from the explored frontier are therefore hard to discover. Planning directly with a physics simulator as the transition model dates back to kinodynamic planners such as KPIECE sucan2009kpiece , which propagate the system through the simulator and mitigate its cost by steering where the search tree grows. mosaic introduced a different paradigm in which the skills themselves drive the search: generator skills propose configurations and trajectories wherever they are likely to succeed, connector skills join them into a solution, and a physics simulator supplies the effects, so that no symbolic abstractions or hand-specified preconditions are required. Its planning time, however, is dominated by the simulator, since every skill it considers is rolled out before it enters the graph. retains this structure and changes when, and how often, the simulator is invoked. Lazy search and models of different fidelity. When edge evaluation dominates the cost of search, lazy planners defer evaluating an edge until the search has evidence that it is worth the cost. The degree of deferral ranges from evaluating an edge as soon as its successor is expanded cohen2014lwastar to evaluating only edges on the current shortest path bohlin2000lazyprm, dellin2016lazysp , with intermediate schedules in between mandalika2019gls and known conditions under which laziness is beneficial haghtalab2018lazysp . PACHS yang2025pachs defers the expensive rollout of an edge, using a learned critic to decide which edges are worth evaluating. The edge to evaluate next can also be chosen from a learned or inferred prior on edge validity bhardwaj2019experience, hou2020posterior . Closest to our setting, saleem2020selective plan among movable objects with two models of different fidelity, reserving physics simulation for the actions that require it and using cheap analytic models for the rest. In all of these, it is assumed that the vertices and edges will only be valid or invalid, so an invalidated element leaves the rest of the graph unaffected. In our setting, deferring a skill also leaves the state it produces unknown, so the contents of vertices are hypothesized as well, and a differing hypothesis affects everything built on it. This calls for a repair mechanism that lazy search does not provide. Learned models of feasibility and effects. Learned models have been used to replace costly checks, as in the proxy collision checkers of Fastron das2017fastron , or, in TAMP, as predictors of the feasibility of a single skill wells2019feasibility, wang2021learning or of an abstract plan yang2023piginet that let the planner prune candidates before refining them. All of these estimate validity alone, since the state after the action is either known geometrically or not needed. In contact-rich manipulation the effect of a skill on the objects in the scene is precisely the unknown. Learned dynamics models address this, whether planned over directly chua2018pets, hafner2023dreamerv3 or made object-centric for manipulation driess2022compositional , and recent large-scale world models plan in the space of generated video du2023vlp . Closest to the model we learn, liang2022search search over transitions produced by learned per-skill effect models, and STAP agia2023stap chains skills through learned per-skill dynamics models, scoring a sequence by the product of learned skill value functions. In all of these, the output of the learned model is used without verification, as planning transitions or as the training signal for a policy. This can be hazardous in safety-critical tasks such as those in industrial, semi-structured environments, where it is safer to use the most accurate models available (i.e., physics simulation) to alleviate risk of unexpected collisions. instead treats the learned model as the cheap one of two world models: its predictions guide a deliberate, non-sequential search over skills and decide which of them are worth a query to the expensive model, the physics simulator, and every trajectory in the returned plan has been validated by the latter. Algorithmic Background sec:background In this section we briefly review the skill-centric planning problem and the components of mosaic on which builds. Let denote the world state space, the product of the robot configuration space and the configuration spaces of the movable objects. A binary condition indicates whether a state satisfies a property of interest, e.g., whether it is a goal state, and denotes the set of binary conditions. A trajectory is a mapping , and denotes the space of all trajectories. A parameterized skill consists of a policy (e.g., a learned network, an analytic controller, or a motion planner) and a parameter space ; executing with parameters produces a trajectory . distinguishes two types of skills (Fig.~ fig:gen_conn ). title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters
comment: Tech Report
summary: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Frontier vision-language models are beginning to show remarkable capabilities in physical control. Recent studies of GPT-6 Astra demonstrate that a general-purpose model can generate robot actions, perform manipulation, and improve its behavior through physical feedback~ galbot2026astra,astranomy2026,li2026physrsi . What makes these results particularly intriguing is that such capabilities are not acquired primarily from robot demonstrations. Instead, they appear to draw on the broad knowledge developed during large-scale pretraining, including visual perception, spatial understanding, reasoning, and code generation~ codeaspolicies2023,spatialvlm2024 . These observations suggest a compelling possibility: the knowledge needed for more capable robot policies may already exist within frontier VLMs. Yet most vision-language-action models still rely on relatively small VLM backbones, such as the 2B Cosmos-Reason2 in GR00T N1.7~ gr00tn17 . While effective, these models may not fully capture the rich knowledge emerging in frontier VLMs. This raises a fundamental question: can frontier-scale representations unlock greater potential in learned robot policies? To investigate this question, we introduce , which scales the VLM backbone of a learned robot policy to 552 billion parameters using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017~ deepseekai2026deepseekv41flash . Inspired by the action-expert architecture of GR00T~ gr00tn1 , we connect a VLM to a trainable diffusion transformer (DiT) that converts multimodal representations into continuous robot actions. Rather than relying on explicit reasoning at every control step, the policy learns to directly translate pretrained representations into actions. We systematically compare VLM backbones ranging from 2B to 552B parameters, holding the action architecture, initialization, robot demonstrations, and optimization budget fixed. This allows us to examine how much robot learning can benefit from stronger pretrained representations without introducing additional action-side supervision or pretrained robot-action experts. We argue that the value of a robot foundation model should be measured not only by its performance on familiar tasks, but by how efficiently it learns, how well it generalizes, and how precisely it acts. We therefore evaluate \ across LIBERO~ libero , LIBERO-PRO, RoboCasa~ robocasa , DexJoCo~ dexjoco , and real-world manipulation, focusing on three fundamental capabilities. First, sample efficiency: on LIBERO-Goal, \ achieves 87.8 success with only 10 demonstrations per task, surpassing a 2B backbone trained with 50 demonstrations (85.6 ). Second, generalization: under LIBERO-PRO perturbations, it achieves 45.1 average success, compared with at most 31.3 for the smaller backbones, indicating stronger transfer beyond the training distribution. Third, precise manipulation: on a real bimanual charger-insertion task, it succeeds in 9 out of 10 reference-layout trials, compared with 4 out of 10 for the 2B backbone. The improvement is concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment and insertion rather than reaching or grasping. Together, these results suggest that frontier representations are particularly valuable when robot data is scarce, the environment changes, or fine-grained coordination is required. Crucially, frontier-scale capacity does not necessarily imply prohibitive inference latency. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash uses a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture, activating only a fraction of its 552B parameters per token~ deepseekmoe2024,deepseekai2026deepseekv41flash . Moreover, \ extracts features from the causal encoder of the VLM without autoregressive reasoning or text generation. It achieves a median inference latency of 216\,ms per action chunk using four H200 GPUs ( ). This demonstrates that frontier VLM representations can support practical, subsecond robot control, although at a higher hardware cost than smaller backbones. On the real robot, lower latency does not translate into faster execution: although has the highest per-chunk latency of the three policies, it completes successful trials in a median of 114.4\,s, 13 less time than + Action Head (132.0\,s), because it aligns and inserts the plug 28 faster ( ). Our findings point toward a promising direction for VLA development. Frontier pretrained representations can substantially improve data efficiency, robustness, and contact-sensitive manipulation. Rather than treating frontier VLMs only as high-level reasoning agents, we show that they can serve as the representational foundation of fast, learned robot policies. We hope this work encourages a shift toward fully exploiting frontier-model pretraining as a central ingredient in building more capable and generalizable VLAs. Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*,nosep] We introduce , a VLA framework that connects a 552B frontier VLM to a trainable action DiT, enabling continuous robot control without autoregressive reasoning. We systematically investigate backbone scaling from 2B to 552B across simulation and real-world manipulation, demonstrating substantial gains in sample efficiency, generalization, and contact-sensitive control. We demonstrate practical subsecond inference with a sparse frontier VLM, showing that large pretrained representational capacity can be brought into learned robot policies at manageable latency. Related Work sec:related_work VLM as Policy. Language models select skills or write task plans~ saycan2022,innermonologue,progprompt . PaLM-E conditions planning on sensor observations~ palme . Other systems generate controller code, spatial value maps, or keypoint constraints for motion planning~ codeaspolicies2023,instruct2act,voxposer2023,rekep . Studies of Astra assess direct action generation, cooperation with learned policies, and improvement through feedback with fixed model weights~ galbot2026astra,astranomy2026,li2026physrsi . Vision-Language-Action Models. Early policies learn from diverse tasks or multimodal prompts~ gato,rt1,bcz,robocat,vima,languagetable . Cross-embodiment policies extend this approach across robots~ openx2023,octo2024,hpt,crossformer,xvla,univla . BridgeData V2 and DROID expand real robot data, MimicGen synthesizes demonstrations, and EgoDex provides egocentric hand trajectories~ bridgev2,droid,mimicgen,egodex . RT-2, OpenVLA, and FAST represent actions as tokens~ rt2,openvla,fast . Continuous action chunks can be predicted by regression, diffusion, or flow matching~ act,oft,dp,cogact,rdt,pi0,gr00tn1 . Recent VLAs study open-world transfer~ pi05,geminirobotics and cross-embodiment alignment~ qwenrobotmanip . Visual pretraining supplies transferable features~ r3m,mvp,vc1,theia , including DINOv2 and SigLIP features used in OpenVLA~ dinov2,siglip,openvla . RoboFlamingo adapts pretrained VLMs for imitation, GR00T N1.5 freezes them, and Knowledge Insulation separates action-expert gradients from VLM adaptation~ robotflamingo,gr00tn15,knowledgeinsulation . Compact models and efficient action interfaces reduce training or inference cost~ tinyvla,robomamba,smolvla,vlaadapter,efficientvla2026 . Controlled comparisons revisit backbone choice, feature readout, and policy design~ robovlms,vlm4vla,vlmrepr2026,starvla . Demonstration sweeps test how much robot data adaptation requires~ howmanydemos2026 . We compare backbones up to 552B with a fixed action DiT and demonstration budget. Spatial Reasoning for Robot Manipulation. Manipulation policies use language-conditioned spatial maps, multiview features, or point clouds~ cliport,peract,rvt,rvt2,dp3 . Spatial supervision ranges from points and 3D references to action traces~ spatialvlm2024,robopoint2024,roborefer2025,zhou2026robotracer,yu2026groundingpi,llarva . Intermediate language, trace prompts, and high-level trajectory predictions can guide action selection~ ecot,cotvla,rt_h,tracevla,hamster . World Action Models. Video can specify a task, supply visual subgoals, or provide synthetic demonstrations~ vid2robot,physicalintelligence2026pi07,dreamgen . UniPi recovers actions from generated video~ unipi2023 . Other approaches learn visual and action predictions together~ gr12023,gr2,vla3d,videovla,nvidia2026gr00t2,dreamzero,cosmospolicy,motus . DreamVLA forecasts perceptual features, DeFI separates forward and inverse dynamics, and ImageWAM uses image-editing features for control~ dreamvla2025,defi2026,imagewam2026 . Method sec:method Model Architecture sec:overview has two parts ( ): a frontier vision-language backbone that encodes the camera images and the language instruction, and an action head trained from scratch that turns these representations and the robot state into a chunk of continuous actions with flow matching. Evaluations of GPT-6 Astra show useful manipulation through feedback-guided interaction and cooperation with learned policies, but repeated reasoning and action review make each decision slow and costly~ galbot2026astra . does not reason in text: it reads the backbone once per action chunk and maps its representations directly to actions. The backbone supplies the knowledge of frontier-scale pretraining, and the action head learns continuous control from robot demonstrations. The language and visual backbones are frozen, while the feature adapter, state and action encoders, diffusion transformer, and action decoder are trainable. Vision-language backbone. sec:backbone We adopt DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017~ deepseekai2026deepseekv41flash as the vision-language backbone, a mixture-of-experts model with 552B parameters. A vision encoder converts camera images into visual tokens, and a language backbone, organized into a 20-layer causal encoder and a 20-layer decoder, processes them together with the instruction in the reference chat format of the model. We run the causal encoder and read the features supplied to the attention operation of the next layer: a sequence of visual and text tokens, each with dimensions. Computation stops at this interface, so the decoder never runs. We keep every token in order, with its modality label, so the action head can attend to image and non-image tokens separately. Action head. sec:action_head The action head follows the GR00T N1.7 architecture~ gr00tn17 and consists of a feature adapter, state and action encoders, a diffusion transformer (DiT), and an action decoder, all initialized randomly and trained on robot demonstrations. The feature adapter applies layer normalization and a two-layer linear projection that maps each backbone token from to a common width of 2048, followed by a four-layer self-attention transformer in which visual and language features interact under action supervision. Embodiment-specific multilayer perceptrons encode the robot state and the noisy actions, padded to a common layout; each future action becomes a token with a learned position embedding, and the action encoder also receives the flow time. The action DiT has 32 layers that alternate self-attention and cross-attention. Self-attention runs jointly over the state and noisy action tokens, and cross-attention reads the adapted backbone features; successive cross-attention layers attend to non-image and image tokens in turn, and token masks exclude padding. Adaptive layer normalization supplies the flow time to the transformer, and an embodiment-specific action decoder maps the output action tokens to a predicted velocity for the whole chunk. Across backbone comparisons, the action head keeps the same architecture and common random initialization; only the input width of the feature adapter follows the backbone. Training and Inference sec:training_inference Flow matching. We train the action head with flow matching~ lipman2023flowmatching . Given a demonstration chunk , we sample Gaussian noise and a flow time , and form the noisy chunk , which moves linearly from noise to the demonstration. The action head learns the velocity of this path, where denotes the adapted backbone features

title: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain. Code and data will be made publicly available.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce , a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain. Code and data will be made publicly available. Introduction build on top of the capabilities of , steering them from general purpose chat models to policy networks that can output low-level actions for the manipulation of robots or vehicles~ pmlr-v229-zitkovich23a, xu2024drivegpt4, hwang2025emma, li2026recogdrive, wang2025alpamayo . The main motivation for using them in autonomous driving is that they can inherit the reasoning and generalization capabilities of to better handle long-tail and scenarios, which modular pipelines struggle with~ hwang2025emma . Indeed, these models show promising results, with many of them~ li2026recogdrive, zhou2025autovla, Renz_2025_CVPR, Fu_2025_ICCV, tian2024drivevlm, wang2025omnidrive, hwang2025emma topping open- and closed-loop benchmarks such as NAVSIM~ NEURIPS2024_32768f7f , NAVSIMv2~ cao2025pseudosimulation , Bench2Drive~ NEURIPS2024_017761f9 , and nuScenes~ 9156412 . A newer line of work uses a different type of foundation model to build on top of, namely, video generation models. By fine-tuning these models to denoise action tokens along with video tokens they are turned into what has recently been termed ~ ye2026world . The main argument as to why might be more adequate for embodied AI applications is that they can take advantage of the dynamic representations of how the world evolves that they inherit from their backbone video generation model. Likewise, some of these models~ shi2026drivewam, Xia_2026_CVPR, fu20264d, liu2026universe, zhao2026simwam have demonstrated performance on multiple autonomous driving benchmarks. However, the vast majority of the samples that compose these benchmarks are nominal driving scenarios where unexpected events don't usually occur, so how these models react to safety-critical scenarios, and in particular to imminent hazards in their path, remains understudied. Evaluating this reliably places requirements both on the inputs the models see and on how their reactions are measured. On the input side, the scenes should ideally be real rather than simulated, and they should match the input configuration each model was trained on. On the measurement side, each safety-critical scene should be paired with an otherwise identical counterpart that lacks the hazardous object, so that the object's causal effect on the predicted trajectory can be isolated. For such a pair to be informative, the object must be placed where a reaction is actually required, i.e., on the ego vehicle's path, and it must appear consistently in every camera view and history frame whose field of view covers its location. In addition, the metrics should describe how a model reacts, not only whether it collides: aggregate collision rates cannot distinguish a model that ignores a hazard from one that reacts, but too weakly or too late. To our knowledge no benchmark meets all of these requirements at once. To address this gap, we introduce , a benchmark for evaluating how and react to objects inserted in their path ( ). Since many and are trained on NAVSIM~ NEURIPS2024_32768f7f or ~ nvidia2025paiav , we build on these two datasets, so that these models are evaluated on inputs matching their training configuration, with the same cameras, calibrations, history length, and frame rate. Into each sample, we separately insert a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, and a stationary car at a controlled position on the ego vehicle's path, rendering the object consistently across all camera views and history frames and modifying only the pixels of the object and its shadow. Each edited sample thus forms an exact counterfactual pair with its original, so any change in the predicted trajectory is caused by the inserted object. We evaluate four , namely Alpamayo~1.5~ nvidia2026alpamayo15 , Alpamayo~2~ nvidia2026alpamayo2 , AutoVLA~ zhou2025autovla , and ReCogDrive~ li2026recogdrive , and two , namely DriveWAM~ shi2026drivewam and SimWAM~ zhao2026simwam , and find that they react weakly to inserted objects and fail to avoid the collision in most cases. To understand why, we examine two potential factors: reasoning and the individual stages of the multi-stage training recipes that some of these models follow. For inserted pedestrians, the Alpamayo models recognize the hazard in their CoT but mostly fail to act on it. Finally, a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes teaches ReCogDrive to brake hard, generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes. Together, these findings suggest that the models often recognize hazards but lack the behaviors to act on them. Our contributions can be summarized as follows. We introduce , a benchmark of exact, pixel-level counterfactual pairs built on real NAVSIM and scenes, with metrics that capture whether and how models react to objects in their path. We evaluate four and two and show that they largely fail to handle such imminent hazards. We investigate how CoT reasoning and the individual training stages affect their reactions. We show that fine-tuning only ReCogDrive's action head on edited scenes teaches it to brake for hazards, including unseen objects and fully real scenes, at almost no cost to nominal driving. Related Work VLAs and WAMs for Autonomous Driving. fine-tune pretrained to predict robot actions in the language space~ pmlr-v229-zitkovich23a , an idea quickly adopted for predicting driving trajectories or low-level actions for autonomous driving~ xu2024drivegpt4, tian2024drivevlm, wang2025omnidrive, hwang2025emma . Later moved action prediction out of the language space, using special action tokens~ zhou2025autovla or a dedicated action head, ranging from MLPs~ Shao_2024_CVPR, Renz_2025_CVPR to generative models~ Fu_2025_ICCV, li2026recogdrive, wang2025alpamayo . have recently emerged as an alternative to , replacing the backbone with a pretrained video generation model~ ye2026world, PaiJ-RSS-26 . Driving either denoise action tokens conditioned on (partially) denoised video tokens~ shi2026drivewam, Xia_2026_CVPR , denoise both jointly~ fu20264d , or use future video prediction only as an auxiliary training objective, avoiding frame generation at inference~ liu2026universe, zhao2026simwam . Although many of these models achieve results on open- and closed-loop benchmarks, their ability to handle safety-critical scenarios remains understudied. Safety Evaluation of End-to-End Planners. Several benchmarks evaluate driving models in safety-critical scenarios. SafeBench~ xu2022safebench and Bench2Drive~ NEURIPS2024_017761f9 provide such scenarios in the CARLA simulator~ pmlr-v78-dosovitskiy17a , the latter as part of a broader multi-ability evaluation, while Fail2Drive~ gerstenecker2026fail2drive pairs CARLA routes containing distribution shifts, such as unseen obstacles, with in-distribution counterparts and reports consistent performance drops. However, since CARLA renders synthetic images, planners trained on real-world data, such as the and we study, cannot be evaluated there without a large sim-to-real gap. WOD-E2E~ Xu_2026_CVPR curates real long-tail driving scenes for open-loop evaluation, selected for rarity rather than for requiring an immediate reaction, and interPlan~ 10803052 augments nuPlan scenarios with long-tail events such as jaywalkers and accident sites, but only at the object level, so it cannot evaluate sensor-based planners. To keep sensor inputs realistic, another line of work builds safety-critical scenarios on top of real driving scenes using neural reconstruction or generative models. NeuroNCAP~ 10.1007/978-3-031-73404-5_10 builds a closed-loop safety testing framework on NeRF~ 10.1145/3503250, 10657387 reconstructions of nuScenes scenes, and HUGSIM~ 11314796 builds a closed-loop simulator on 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl:hal-04088161 reconstructions of nuScenes and other datasets, whose harder scenarios include aggressive vehicles. Challenger~ xu2025challenger and SMD~ pmlr-v306-zhou26aj instead generate multi-view nuScenes videos of safety-critical scenarios, while Geng et al.~ geng2025driving extend generative rendering to closed-loop evaluation with adversarial vehicles. Since many open-weight and , including all models we evaluate, are trained on NAVSIM or , evaluating these models on such benchmarks would confound their failures to react with sensor and domain shift. RealEngine~ jiang2025realengine and NavSafe~ bao2026navsafe reconstruct nuPlan scenes, matching the training domain of NAVSIM-based models, but imminent hazards requiring a prompt reaction are only a subset of their scenarios. Since all of these methods re-render or synthesize the entire camera image, none of them yields exact counterfactual pairs with the original sensor data, whereas modifies only the inserted object's pixels, isolating its causal effect on the predicted trajectory. Counterfactual Safety Evaluation. Closest to our work are two contemporaneous studies that edit real scenes to measure the causal effect of objects on predicted trajectories. Yang et al.~ yang2026beyond inpaint away pedestrians near the ego corridor in nuScenes and NAVSIM frames and find that end-to-end and planners rarely exhibit genuine avoidance. Luo et al.~ luo2026exceptiondrive insert hazards into nuScenes views via instruction-based image editing and show that planners frequently drive into them. Our work differs from these studies in four ways. First, places the object exactly on the ego vehicle's ground-truth future trajectory, so it always obstructs the path the vehicle actually drove. Second, it uses the camera calibration to render the object into every camera view and history frame, leaving all other pixels unchanged. Third, we evaluate every model on scenes that match its training distribution, so that performance drops caused by domain shift are not mistaken for failures in safety-critical scenes. Fourth, we also evaluate . sec:reactbench pairs real driving scenes with edited counterparts in which an object blocks the ego vehicle's path at close range, so that a prompt reaction, either braking or a safe nudge around the object, is needed to avoid a collision. Object Compositing subsec:object_compositing To keep the inserted object consistent across camera views and timesteps, control its 3D position precisely, and modify only the pixels of the object and its shadow, we render 3D assets with Blend

title: Aerial Person Detection under Edge Constraints: Held-Out Evaluation and Edge-Ground Verification
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, 8 tables. Code, truth registers and result files: https://github.com/numberz-ai/aerial-person-detector
summary: A search drone sees a missing person as a few pixels, carries a small computer, and shares a narrow radio link. We study person detection under those limits; the primary evaluations were declared before they ran, and later analyses are marked exploratory. In an exploratory comparison, holding out recording blocks inferred from thermal frame identifiers cut recall at a fixed false-alarm target from 32.7% to 12.3%. With nothing tuned on test blocks, a 46,000-parameter detector gated by a contrast cue finds 10.4% of people against 5.7% for the same network applied everywhere. A standard detector, YOLO11n, trained under the same folds finds 54.5% at a similar false-alarm rate for about eleven times the arithmetic, and on our 4K field footage at 117 m has a walking person among its top 16 detections in up to 92% of frames against 74% for our board. Run alone, YOLO11n's thresholds set at one location overshot their false-alarm target 1.7 to 3.4 times at new locations, and its best configuration at altitude cost 4 to 24 standard passes per frame. Re-scoring its 16 best crops (154 KB per frame) with an 842,000-parameter ground model, thresholds frozen on a validation location, raised recall from 44.9% to 53.7% against the same 16 crops with YOLO's own scores; in a post hoc paired analysis over 15 test locations the gain was +8.8 points [+2.4, +12.5]. Pooled false detections fell from 0.86 to 0.64 per frame, but that paired change was not distinguishable from zero. Coverage of a still person in earth tones was very low for both detectors in the clips we flew.
full_text: A search drone sees a missing person as a few pixels, carries a small computer, and shares a narrow radio link. We study person detection under those limits; the primary evaluations were declared before they ran, and later analyses are marked exploratory. In an exploratory comparison, holding out recording blocks inferred from thermal frame identifiers cut recall at a fixed false-alarm target from 32.7 to 12.3 . With nothing tuned on test blocks, a 46,000-parameter detector gated by a contrast cue finds 10.4 of people against 5.7 for the same network applied everywhere. A standard detector, YOLO11n, trained under the same folds finds 54.5 at a similar false-alarm rate for about eleven times the arithmetic, and on our 4K field footage at 117~m has a walking person among its top 16 detections in up to 92 of frames against 74 for our board. Run alone, YOLO11n's thresholds set at one location overshot their false-alarm target 1.7 to 3.4 times at new locations, and its best configuration at altitude cost 4 to 24 standard passes per frame. Re-scoring its 16 best crops (154~KB per frame) with an 842,000-parameter ground model, thresholds frozen on a validation location, raised recall from 44.9 to 53.7 against the same 16 crops with YOLO's own scores; in a post hoc paired analysis over 15 test locations the gain was +8.8 points [+2.4, +12.5]. Pooled false detections fell from 0.86 to 0.64 per frame, but that paired change was not distinguishable from zero. Coverage of a still person in earth tones was very low for both detectors in the clips we flew. Introduction When a hiker goes missing, a search team needs to cover ground faster than people on foot can. Small drones help, but each one sends live video to a pilot who watches one screen. Three limits decide what a small drone can do on its own. A person seen from 100~m or more covers a few pixels. The computer on board is small and draws from the flight battery. The radio carries a fraction of one video stream, and less when several drones share it. Three questions follow. How well does a detector that fits on a Pi-class board find people in recordings and places it was not tuned on, at a false-alarm rate an operator can live with? How does a standard detector do under the same conditions, and what does it cost? And when the board falls short, how much does sending a few small crops to a larger model on the ground recover, and at what cost in bytes? We answer them on public data and on our own footage. The primary evaluations were written down with their read-outs before they ran; analyses added later are labelled exploratory. The contributions fall under three themes. Generalization and evaluation integrity. We check two public aerial datasets for overlap between their published training and test splits, evaluate on folds that hold out inferred recording blocks (thermal) and whole locations (mountain search imagery), and measure how far thresholds set at one location drift at others. Accuracy and resource trade-offs. We compare a cue-gated 46,000-parameter detector with the same network applied everywhere, train a standard detector (YOLO11n~ yolo11 ) under the same folds, run both on 4K field footage at four heights, and report measured board power for our pipeline. Selective ground verification. We measure a ground model that re-scores the board's 16 best crops, behind our detector and behind YOLO11n, with frozen thresholds, a same-crops control and a shuffled-label control; we report its benefit, its transmission cost and what remains to be validated. This is a measurement study. It does not propose a new detector architecture, and the edge--ground split it measures is an established pattern (Section~ sec:related ). It does not validate an autonomous search system. For people hidden under forest canopy, airborne optical sectioning~ schedl2021 is the stronger approach and the one we plan to build on; our study covers fast, wide-area colour search, where it does not apply. Our own board detector is beaten by the standard one on accuracy; we report that plainly. What holds up is the ground verification step behind YOLO11n: over the same candidates it raised recall, with the paired change across locations clear of zero. Its effect on false detections was mixed across locations. The study builds on our earlier work on gated sensing on airborne video~ venkat2026sisr , which reported where such pipelines lose evidence. Related work sec:related People from the air. Bo i\'c- tuli\'c et al.\ introduced HERIDAL, aerial images from mountain search exercises, and showed that deep detectors find people in it~ heridal . Sambolek and Ivasic-Kos built SARD for the same purpose~ sard . Broyles et al.\ released WiSARD, paired visual and thermal images from wilderness search flights~ wisard . Suo et al.\ released HIT-UAV, a high-altitude thermal set~ hituav , and Makrigiorgis et al.\ a set of small people seen from a drone~ kios . Manzini and Murphy set out open problems for computer vision in wilderness search, drawn from an actual search~ manzini2023open , and Murphy and Manzini described how drone imagery should be collected for such work~ murphy2023improving . Yu et al.\ studied tiny people in wide images~ tinyperson . Hidden people and real searches. Three works bear directly on our findings (Table~ tab:related ). Bimber's group developed airborne optical sectioning (AOS), in which thermal images taken along a flight path are combined into a synthetic aperture that suppresses occluding foliage, and Schedl, Kurmi and Bimber applied it to search and rescue~ schedl2020 . Their autonomous drone ran the integration, a YOLOv4-tiny classifier and route adaptation on a Raspberry~Pi~4 with a neural compute stick, sent only classification results over the link, and found 38 of 42 hidden people in 17 field experiments with one false alert on predefined paths~ schedl2021 . It is, to our knowledge, the strongest result for people under forest canopy, and an earlier demonstration of on-board detection with a minimal link. Its demonstrated envelope differs from wide-area search: flights at about 35~m and 1~m/s along predefined paths, about 6~ha over eight flights, people who stay still while the aperture is integrated, a body warmer than its surroundings, and accurate camera poses for every image. How it performs at 100~m and above, in warm conditions, or over larger areas per flight was not part of that study. Manzini and Murphy applied a detector that scored 78.6 precision and 84.0 recall on HERIDAL, and an anomaly detector, to 18,759 frames from the search for Patricia Wu-Murad; neither produced a useful lead, and the detector missed members of the search team while labelling bushes, rocks and branches as people~ manzini2023open . They describe conditions benchmarks rarely contain: imagery collected during an operation, oblique flights below the treeline where canopy was dense, a wide variety of imagery, and no agreed measure of performance. They call for more realistic data, models that handle that variety, and agreement on metrics. Nathan et al.\ released colour imagery from a police search at about 300~m over forest, on which anomaly detectors reached precision below 3.5 and a supervised YOLOv12 model failed~ nathan2026anomaly . Our still-person result agrees with all three: colour detection rarely finds a still or partly hidden person, and benchmark scores do not carry to the field. What we add is a measurement of that gap under held-out locations and frozen thresholds, and of what ground verification buys at a known link cost. We do not test AOS. Cheap stages ahead of expensive models. Viola and Jones made the attentional cascade standard in detection~ violajones . Kang et al.\ placed cheap models ahead of an expensive detector to skip video frames on a server~ kang2017noscope . Event-triggered control trades how often a system acts against how well it performs~ heemels2012 . Splitting a network or a pipeline between a device and a server is studied as split computing or edge--cloud inference~ kang2017neurosurgeon,matsubara2022split ; our edge--ground split is an instance of it, and a second stage that re-scores a first stage's candidates is the classic cascade. Single-stage detectors of the YOLO family are the usual choice for small boards~ yolo11 ; we use one as the baseline. Evaluation. Kaufman et al.\ describe leakage between training and test data and how it inflates results~ kaufman2012leakage . Aerial frames taken seconds apart from one flight are near-duplicates, so a frame-level split lets the same scene appear on both sides. Evaluation on shared recordings and on unseen recordings answer different questions; both are legitimate, and we report the second because a search drone flies over ground it has not seen. Data and splits HIT-UAV (thermal). 2,898 long-wave infrared frames with 12,312 labelled people~ hituav . We infer recording blocks from the frame identifiers: they run in 39 contiguous blocks, each with one light condition and one altitude, and each block sweeps the camera angles. We treat each block as one recording session. The dataset does not label sessions; this grouping is inferred by us and not validated against flight logs, so held-out blocks are not established to be independent flights or unseen sites. The block list is in the released truth register. All 39 blocks have frames in both the published training and test splits. We use five folds of whole inferred blocks, balanced on labelled people. Within each training pool, one block in four (by a seeded hash) is held back for validation. HERIDAL (mountain search). We use the repackaging of HERIDAL by Pyrro (Zenodo record 5662351), which its release page describes as a modified version. In this release, 66 of the 103 published test images are byte-identical to training images, and the test-only location codes are aliases of training codes (GRO of GOR, MOB of BLA). We make no claim about other distributions of HERIDAL. After dropping duplicates and merging aliases we keep 1,582 frames, 3,091 people and 15 locations, in three folds of whole locations. One further training location per fold is held out for validation. The duplicate pairs, the alias map and the split manifest are in the released truth register. Our footage. Hunter Klobucar, an FAA Part~107 certificated remote pilot, flew a drone recording 3840-pixel-wide (4K) video at 29.97 frames per second, camera pointing down, over a trail and tree edge. On the first day a person walked the trail at 117.5, 89.2, 60.3 and 9.3~m (195 labelled samples). On the second, one person stayed still in four poses at 117, 90, 60 and 30~m, with and without a bright vest (276 samples). No model saw this site or camera in training. Truth for the walker comes from frame differencing re-centred on the body and checked by eye. Truth for the still person comes from one marked point per clip carried by image registration. Hits and false alarms. Every detector outputs scored points; for box detectors the point is the box centre. A point is a hit when it lies inside a labelled box grown by 1.5~px on each side. Matching is one to one and greedy by descending score. A second point on an already matched person counts as a duplicate, not a false alarm. A point inside no grown box and no ignore region is a false alarm. In the field, a hit is a point within 0.25~m on the ground of the labelled position. We report 95 intervals from a bootstrap over inferred blocks or locations, not frames. Learned arms have a shuffled-label control with the same architecture and data; for the ground model behind YOLO11n the control was trained for the same 12 epochs as the real model (an earlier 3-epoch control is also reported). Two terms. Candidate coverage is the share of people present among the top 16 detections or crops. Detection recall is the share the full system reports under the stated false-alarm rule. Field numbers in this paper are candidate coverage. M

title: Counting What Matters: Reducing Redundant Object Detections in Overlapping UAV Mapping Imagery for Disaster Response

However, the image overlap required for orthophoto generation causes every physical object to be detected multiple times across images, while dynamic objects may be omitted from or duplicated in the resulting orthomosaic. full_text: Counting What Matters: Reducing Redundant Object Detections in Overlapping UAV Mapping Imagery for Disaster Response Max Schulte Hartmut Surmann Julien Meine Westphalian University of Applied Sciences (WH) Gelsenkirchen, Germany max.schulte@w-hs.de, hartmut.surmann@w-hs.de, julien.meine@w-hs.de 1 UAV mapping flights enable rapid aerial reconnaissance of large-scale incident sites in civil protection. However, the image overlap required for orthophoto generation causes every physical object to be detected multiple times across images, while dynamic objects may be omitted from or duplicated in the resulting orthomosaic. Analysis based on the orthophoto alone is therefore structurally insufficient. We address this by detecting objects on the individual images and merging redundant detections across them. This task lies between multi-object tracking and re-identification, as mapping flights form temporally ordered but sparsely sampled sequences with object reappearances across flight strips. We fine-tune YOLO detectors on a new domain-specific nadir dataset from real civil protection operations, roughly doubling mAP50 over the previous system, and propose re-identification approaches based on 3D positions from sparse reconstruction, DINOv3 appearance embeddings, and their combination via constrained greedy clustering. On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, an association-only evaluation using ground-truth detections shows that the combined weighted multi-pass approach provides the best trade-off between association quality and count error. It is integrated into the open-source web application ARGUS and visualized as verifiable, correctable object groups for first responders. Introduction sec:introduction Rapid and reliable reconnaissance is the foundation of tactical decision-making in civil protection fwdv100 . UAVs with RGB or thermal cameras have become an established tool for this assessment and are increasingly deployed by fire brigades and civil protection units bbk2024 . Beyond live video, autonomous mapping flights, i.e., lawnmower patterns with a nadir-facing camera, provide systematic coverage. The overlapping images are typically fused into orthophotos that serve as up-to-date situation maps. Through regular participation in real deployments, field tests, and exercises with partner fire brigades, we identified a recurring operational need. Beyond the visual map, responders need a fast answer to seemingly simple questions such as how many people and vehicles are present in the mapped area, and where. Results must be available within minutes on local hardware, must not silently miss people, and must remain verifiable by the operator. Our starting point is ARGUS surmann2023 , an open-source web application that manages UAV mapping flights, generates fast orthophotos, and runs object detection on the captured images. Answering such counting and localization questions automatically is harder than it appears, for two structural reasons. First, detection on the final orthophoto alone is insufficient. Orthomosaic generation implicitly assumes a static scene, so moving objects such as people and vehicles may appear duplicated, incompletely rendered, or be omitted entirely brack2025 . Occlusion complicates this further, as some objects are visible only from specific viewing angles. Information lost during orthophoto generation cannot be recovered downstream, so objects must be detected on the individual mapping images. Second, per-image detection creates massive redundancy. The 60–80\, image overlap required for mapping causes every physical object to be observed in many images. On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, naively summing per-image detections overestimates the true number of physical objects by a factor of roughly 4 to 20 (depending on the dataset), with each object visible in nine images on average. A useful situational picture therefore requires merging these redundant detections so that each physical object appears on the map only once (Fig.~ fig:allToGruped ). This merging task occupies a middle ground between multi-object tracking (MOT) and re-identification (re-ID). The images of a mapping flight form a temporally ordered single-camera sequence, which superficially looks like a tracking problem. However, consecutive images are seconds apart, the viewpoint shifts by several meters between frames, and objects routinely leave the field of view and reappear much later in adjacent flight strips of the lawnmower pattern. Sequential tracking assumptions consequently break down. We show that an off-the-shelf tracker (DeepSORT) in fact fails almost completely on this data. Instead, we cast the task as a constrained clustering of detections into physical objects, combining spatial and visual cues under the constraint that detections from the same image must never be merged. This framing also motivates our evaluation protocol, which complements MOT association metrics with clustering-based measures and the application-relevant count error. We present a complete pipeline from detection to visualization and make the following contributions: A fine-tuning study of eleven YOLO-based detector variants, including dedicated small-object architectures, on a new domain-specific nadir dataset from real civil protection deployments and exercises, showing that a plain YOLO11x at 1280\,px input resolution outperforms the specialized architectures and roughly doubles mAP50 over the detectors previously used in ARGUS . Position-based, appearance-based, and combined re-identification approaches for merging redundant detections across overlapping mapping images, built on a same-image-constrained union-find clustering. Positions are obtained by backprojecting detections into a sparse 3D reconstruction, and appearance is encoded by DINOv3 embeddings without any identity-annotated training data. We further report a light evaluation of Depth Anything~3 as a learned alternative to classical reconstruction. An association-only evaluation on four identity-annotated real-world flights, using shared ground-truth detections to isolate association and ablate position, appearance, fusion, and multi-pass variants. Integration of the pipeline into the open-source ARGUS application, where merged objects are presented as verifiable and correctable groups rather than opaque final counts, together with the released fine-tuned detector. Related Work sec:related Small Object Detection in UAV Imagery Object detection in UAV imagery is closely tied to small object detection (SOD). From typical mapping altitudes, people and vehicles occupy only a small portion of the image, and repeated downsampling in convolutional backbones erodes their already sparse features nisa2025, ning2024 . Current research is dominated by YOLO modifications. A recurring pattern is an additional high-resolution P2 detection head that attaches an earlier backbone feature map to neck and head, preserving fine spatial detail wang2025sod, lu2025 . DRM-YOLO bi2026 combines a P2 head with a redesigned backbone, cross-scale feature fusion, and a dynamic detection head, and reports one of the strongest published results on the VisDrone2019 benchmark zhu2021 , and is one of the few in this area with a ready-to-use published model architecture. As a model-agnostic alternative, slicing-based inference such as SAHI akyon2022 processes overlapping image tiles separately at the cost of many additional inference calls per image. This was the strategy of the previous ARGUS pipeline. Most published SOD gains, however, are demonstrated on nano or small model variants at the default 640 px input resolution, and whether they transfer to large variants at high input resolutions, as required here, is rarely examined. Our detection study addresses exactly this setting. Merging Detections Across Images Multi-object tracking is the established approach for associating detections over an image sequence. Tracking-by-detection methods such as DeepSORT and BoT-SORT combine motion prediction with IoU- and appearance-based assignment ciaparrone2020, aharon2022 and have been applied directly to UAV videos fonod2025 . However, they presuppose densely sampled sequences with little inter-frame motion. Kostiv et al.~ kostiv2025 study the low-frame-rate limit for UAV footage and observe vanishing box overlap, frequent identity switches, and redundant track initializations, conditions that mapping flights exacerbate through multi-second capture intervals and the lawnmower pattern, under which objects reappear in non-consecutive images. A second line of work moves the association from image coordinates into a shared spatial frame. Kiefer et al.~ kiefer2023 geolocate detections via camera metadata and accumulate them in likelihood-based memory maps. Yang et al.~ yang2023 project detections onto an assumed ground plane and associate interrupted tracks by world-space distance. Both rely on accurate metadata and flat-scene approximations suited to open water or flat fields. HomView-MOT ji2026 instead estimates homographies between views and computes a physically more plausible IoU on a common plane, again presupposing planar scenes. Recent surveys see potential in full 3D environments for tracking li2025 , but existing UAV work operates almost exclusively on dense video with simplified scene models. Recent feed-forward reconstruction models predict geometry directly from images, but an aerial benchmark found classical COLMAP schoenberger2016 metrically superior and reported drift/duplicated structures at larger image counts wu2025 . Depth Anything~3 lin2025 is the most recent representative of this family. Its suitability for large nadir mapping flights had not been examined, which we address in Sec.~ sec:reid:position . Appearance-Based Re-Identification Classical person and vehicle re-ID learns discriminative embeddings from identity-annotated datasets he2021, sun2024 . Such annotations do not exist for nadir mapping imagery from civil protection contexts. Self-supervised foundation models offer a way out. DINOv2 features oquab2024 have been used without re-ID-specific fine-tuning to correct track identities lee2025 , to resolve ambiguous associations alongside spatial cues he2025dino , and, combined with depth and camera poses, to track object instances through 3D environments zhao2024 , with the caveat that generic embeddings do not always separate similar instances reliably huang2025 . DINOv3 simeoni2025 further improves dense feature quality, explicitly including high-resolution aerial imagery among its demonstrated use cases. To our knowledge, no prior work addresses cross-image re-identification of people and vehicles in overlapping still images from UAV mapping flights, where neither dense temporal sampling nor identity-annotated training data are available. We close this gap by combining reconstruction-based 3D positions with foundation-model embeddings under an explicit clustering formulation. Object Detection sec:detection The re-identification stage operates on per-image detections, so a robust detector with high recall is a prerequisite. Objects missed in individual images may fragment the later association, and in civil protection use, silently overlooked people are the most critical failure mode. As the detectors previously used in ARGUS proved insufficient (Sec.~ sec:eval ), we conducted a dedicated fine-tuning study. Datasets sec:detDatsets Training combines VisDrone2019 zhu2021 , the established UAV detection benchmark, with a new domain-specific dataset (Fig. fig:argusDatasetDetSamples ). Since VisDrone imagery differs from our target domain (predominantly oblique viewing angles, lower resolutions, and general urban scenes), we built the ARGUS dataset. It contains 423 high-resolution nadir images (typically above \,px) with over 7,200 bounding-box annotations for the classes human and vehicle, collected during real civil

title: Instructions Before Actions: Prospective and Retrospective Language Supervision for Driving Vision-Language-Action Data
summary: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers announced by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59%, but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision.
full_text: Instructions Before Actions: Prospective and Retrospective Language Supervision for Driving Vision--Language--Action Data Driving vision--language--action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers announced by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23--59 , but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision. Autonomous driving, vision--language--action, navigation instructions, prospective supervision, retrospective annotation, instruction-following. Introduction Driving vision--language--action (VLA) models combine visual understanding with trajectory planning, and several accept natural-language navigation instructions~ shao2024lmdrive,renz2025simlingo,alpamayo15,alpamayo2 . In principle, this enables a passenger to direct a vehicle instead of simply accepting a precomputed route. Yet an accurate trajectory prediction does not show that the model used the instruction. Driving benchmarks can be dominated by recent ego motion~ li2024ego,zhai2023rethinking , and recent work reports instruction insensitivity in driving and robot VLAs~ hu2026lcs,fei2025liberoplus,you2026language2drive . An important distinction lies in when training language was created. Most driving-language datasets attach instructions or descriptions retrospectively, after a trajectory has been observed~ roy2024doscenes,arai2024covla,qian2024nuscenes,sima2024drivelm . But in deployment, a passenger or navigation app provides the instruction prospectively, before the maneuver. This type of data may describe the same eventual turn, but they differ in temporal availability, natural lead time, and information available to the speaker. A retrospective annotator can see how the maneuver ends, but a prospective navigator cannot. This matters when a model must decide when an instruction applies, rather than merely identify which maneuver occurred. Prospective data need not require expensive manual annotation. Navigation apps continuously issue spoken directions before upcoming maneuvers. Recording those prompts alongside camera observations and GNSS trajectories produces naturally timed instruction--vision--action examples. Passengers also provide a complementary source, often saying ``right here'' or referring to nearby objects instead of road names or metric distances. These distinctions matter for applications beyond conventional turn-by-turn navigation as after arriving at a destination, a passenger might ask an autonomous vehicle to move to a particular curb or building entrance. Such requests require grounding language in the observed scene and planning a safe, permitted maneuver. We bring these perspectives together in one study. We compare navigation-app language, record prospective app and passenger instructions with Autonomous Driving Vision-Language-Action Triad Engine (ADVLAT-Engine), and test whether four driving VLAs trained on app recordings actually respond to passenger language. We also collected retrospective annotations from four people for the same driving videos, allowing us to compare instructions given before the maneuver with those written after observing it, while holding the recorded driving scene and trajectory fixed. Figure~ fig:taxonomy summarizes the supervision sources. The existing experiments establish trajectory and instruction-following results; we specify the retrospective-annotation comparisons as planned analyses rather than report results that have not yet been computed. Our contributions are: A source-and-timing taxonomy for driving language supervision. ADVLAT-Engine and a controlled study of three navigation apps, alongside matched app and passenger instructions. A benchmark of four driving VLAs using paired instruction removal and counterfactual tests at real intersections. A retrospective annotation corpus from four annotators, with a proposed evaluation framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision. Related Work sec:related Language-Driven Navigation and Conditional Driving Early language-based navigation systems connect verbal goals or landmarks to embodied action. LM-Nav~ shah2023lm uses language and visual observations to navigate toward landmarks, whereas conditional imitation learning~ codevilla2018conditional explicitly separates steering behavior by high-level maneuver commands. These examples show why the ability to choose among legal actions at the same intersection matters: predicting the most likely road-following trajectory is not sufficient for following a new route instruction. More recent language-conditioned driving systems include LMDrive~ shao2024lmdrive , SimLingo~ renz2025simlingo , Alpamayo~1.5 and 2~ alpamayo15,alpamayo2 , Qwen-Drive~ zhou2026qwendrive , and Impromptu~VLA~ chi2025impromptu . Their architectures and instruction interfaces differ, motivating matched instruction-removal and counterfactual evaluation rather than comparisons based only on displacement error. Driving-Language Datasets and Temporal Supervision Talk2Car~ deruyttere2019talk2car pairs nuScenes scenes~ caesar2020nuscenes with free-form commands. nuScenes-QA~ qian2024nuscenes , DriveLM~ sima2024drivelm , doScenes~ roy2024doscenes , and CoVLA~ arai2024covla offer complementary forms of driving-related language, with differences in whether text is an instruction, description, or answer to a question. Learning to Drive (L2D)~ huggingfaceblog constructs navigation-style language from previously logged routes. The important distinction for our study is not simply whether language accompanies a trajectory, but whether it was available before the maneuver or derived after observing it. Post-hoc language can be valuable supervision, but an annotator may know the executed turn and has no naturally observed instruction lead time. Prospective app and passenger recordings retain when a command was given, including windows well before a turn enters a short prediction horizon; that lead time is relevant for variable-horizon planning~ roy2026doplan . We do not claim that all prior driving-language datasets have the same annotation mechanism; the timing and intended semantics must be considered individually. Retrospective Annotation, Hindsight Relabeling, and Efficiency Automatic annotation for autonomous driving has often focused on geometric labels: OpenAnnotate2~ zhou2024openannotate2 , 3D-BAT~ zimmer20193d , and ActiveAnno3D~ ghita2024activeanno3d help reduce effort in labeling scene structure. Language creates a related but different problem. In robot learning, hindsight experience replay~ andrychowicz2017hindsight and instruction augmentation~ xiao2023robotic associate completed trajectories with goals or descriptions that they satisfy. These strategies expand training data by exploiting outcomes, and need not produce bad policies. Yet they can differ from a navigator's original request in specificity, temporal placement, and information available to the speaker. ADVLAT-Engine is complementary: it automates collecting already-spoken instructions rather than synthesizing hindsight labels. Our four-annotator corpus permits a same-video comparison of these mechanisms instead of assuming one source is universally better. Causal Confusion and Evaluating Instruction-Following Conditioned policies can exploit predictive shortcuts without learning the intended control variable. De Haan et al.~ dehaan2019causalconfusion study causal confusion in imitation learning and the value of targeted interventions while Codevilla et al.~ codevilla2019limitations analyze generalization issues in driving behavior cloning. Closed-loop imitation learning also suffers distribution shift because a policy changes the observations it later receives~ ross2011dagger . Recent driving-language evaluations compare removal or alteration of an instruction~ martinezsanchez2026natural,renz2025simlingo,hamid2026icrdrive,you2026language2drive . These motivate two distinct measurements in our work: whether removing passenger text changes trajectory error, and whether changing the requested legal maneuver changes the correct predicted maneuver at an otherwise identical recorded intersection. Neither test alone establishes how the human driver's original action was caused, but both test instruction dependence in the model. Causal Problem Formulation sec:formulation Two Processes Hidden by the Same Training Tuple Let be the driving context available immediately before an instruction becomes active, including camera observations, recent ego-motion history, road layout, and any observed route context. Let be an instruction spoken prospectively; is the subsequent driving trajectory. Let denote a retrospective label authored after the maneuver is recorded and collect unobserved common causes, such as the driver's intended destination or preferences not fully represented in . The same training representation may therefore arise from different data-generating processes~ pearl1995causal,pearl2000causality . For prospective supervision, can precede and influence , while context and latent intent can influence both. For retrospective supervision, is recorded before is written, and the completed action can inform the label. A crucial distinction is the speaker's data-generating process versus the learned policy: that a past label could not cause a past drive does not imply a model trained on that label cannot later respond to it. Why a Retrospective Label Can Predict an Action Without Causing It For an already-recorded human maneuver, intervening on a label written afterward cannot alter that past maneuver. In the retrospective graph of Fig.~ fig:casual_graphs (b), the intervention thus satisfies This is a statement about the temporal data-generating process, not about the behavior of a VLA trained on these labels. Since the annotator may have observed , the conditional distribution can still be predictive: Training on such correlations is not inherently invalid: hindsight instructions can supply meaningful goals for policy learning~ andrychowicz2017hindsight,xiao2023robotic . The unanswered empirical question is whether the learned policy follows new instructions robustly when they conflict with cues about the recorded action.
