title: SemLite-GS: Semantic-Selective Parallel Gaussian Splatting for Lightweight Building Reconstruction from UAV Oblique Imagery
summary: Lightweight 3D building models support urban spatial analysis, but their production often requires dense scene reconstruction, building extraction, and mesh simplification. Although 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is more efficient than conventional multi-view stereo, existing large-scale methods lack semantic selection and parallel instance-level training. We present SemLite-GS, a building-centric framework that reconstructs lightweight building meshes from large-scale UAV oblique imagery. First, an orthographic reference map establishes globally consistent building identities, which are propagated to oblique views to form camera-instance pairs and regions of interest. Second, semantic-selective parallel PGSR training jointly processes multiple pairs within relevant image regions while updating only target Gaussians; contextual Gaussians remain fixed to preserve visibility. Third, architectural planes extracted from rendered depth, opacity, and normal maps guide signed distance field optimization, producing meshes with adaptive polygon allocation and well-defined structural boundaries. Experiments on multiple large-scale UAV datasets demonstrate that our SemLite-GS substantially reduces building reconstruction time compared with representative full-scene 3DGS methods. With comparable polygon budgets, SemLite-GS achieves superior preservation of dominant planar structures and sharp architectural transitions compared with conventional dense reconstruction followed by mesh decimation. The source code is available at https://github.com/IRIS-LAB-whu/SemLite-GS.
full_text: [mode = title] SemLite-GS: Semantic-Selective Parallel Gaussian Splatting for Lightweight Building Reconstruction from UAV Oblique Imagery Tengfei Wang Xin Wang Zihan Li Quanjian Ji Yifei Yu Dong Lin Zongqian Zhan Tengfei Wang and Xin Wang contributed equally to this work. organization= School of Geodesy and Geomatics, Wuhan University , city= Wuhan , postcode= 430079 , country= China organization= Space Engineering University , city= Beijing , postcode= 102299 , country= China Lightweight 3D building models are crucial for urban spatial analysis, yet existing pipelines typically involve costly dense scene reconstruction, building extraction, and mesh simplification. While 3DGS reconstructs scenes more efficiently than conventional multi-view stereo (MVS) pipelines, existing large-scale methods lack semantic awareness and support for parallel instance-level training, and Gaussian-based lightweight building modeling remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose SemLite-GS, a building-centric Gaussian splatting framework, which combines semantic selection, parallel training, and plane-constrained mesh reconstruction to generate lightweight building models from large-scale UAV scenarios. First, a semantic orthographic-view reference map is generated to establish globally consistent building identities. These identities are propagated to the input oblique images to extract camera--instance pairs and corresponding regions of interest (ROIs) for instance-level optimization. Second, a semantic-selective parallel PGSR rasterizer processes camera--instance pairs from multiple buildings and views concurrently while restricting computation to relevant image tiles and associated Gaussian primitives. Surrounding contextual Gaussians are retained for visibility consistency but excluded from parameter optimization, thereby saving unnecessary computation. Third, we propose a plane-guided SDF (Signed Distance Function) refinement strategy for lightweight mesh extraction. Architectural planes, extracted from rendered depth, opacity, and normal maps, guide SDF optimization to directly generate lightweight meshes that preserve sharp architectural boundaries. Furthermore, polygon density is adaptively allocated according to geometric complexity, minimizing redundant tessellation in planar regions while preserving sharp architectural transitions. Experiments on multiple large-scale UAV datasets demonstrate that our SemLite-GS substantially reduces building reconstruction time compared with representative full-scene 3DGS methods. With comparable polygon budgets, SemLite-GS achieves superior preservation of dominant planar structures and sharp architectural transitions compared with conventional dense reconstruction followed by mesh decimation. The source code is available at https://github.com/IRIS-LAB-whu/SemLite-GS. UAV Photogrammetry 3D Gaussian Splatting Semantic Propagation Parallel Optimization Lightweight Building Modeling Introduction sec:introduction Lightweight 3D building models, represented as compact, low-poly meshes typically comprising several hundred faces liu2025gs2poly , are essential for efficient urban-scale representation and spatial analysis peters2022automated . Serving as foundational 3D primitives, they support a wide range of applications, such as digital twins, geographic information systems, and large-scale visualization biljecki2015applications,schuegraf2025sat2building . Compared to dense point clouds and highly tessellated meshes, lightweight 3D building models mainly capture dominant building structures using far fewer vertices and faces, thereby significantly reducing storage, transmission, and rendering costs. Over the past few decades, UAV oblique photogrammetry has been widely studied and has enabled detailed 3D reconstruction of large-scale urban environments. Despite these advances, many practical applications require only a specific subset of target buildings rather than complete scene models. Consequently, efficiently reconstructing these target buildings from large UAV image blocks remains a critical challenge. Conventional photogrammetric workflows typically address lightweight building modeling through a sequential pipeline: dense scene reconstruction, followed by building extraction, and finally mesh simplification ~ garland1997surface,bouzas2020structure,li2024shapepreserving,bauchet2020kinetic,sulzer2024compod . When applied to target-building reconstruction from large UAV image blocks, however, this paradigm exhibits two limitations. First, dense reconstruction is performed over the entire scene, including vast non-target regions, resulting in unnecessary computational overhead. Second, lightweight modeling is treated merely as a post-processing operation after dense mesh generation. Although mesh simplification reduces polygon count, aggressive decimation often compromises architectural structures, such as roof ridges, corners, and facade intersections. These limitations motivate the development of a novel reconstruction paradigm that integrates semantic target selection into optimization and explicitly incorporates architectural structures into lightweight model generation. Figure~ fig:workflow_comparison compares building meshes generated by the commercial photogrammetric software Metashape metashape and the proposed SemLite-GS framework, illustrating that SemLite-GS represents planar surfaces with fewer triangles, yields straighter and more regular building edges, and reconstructs individually identified building instances. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provide a promising alternative to revisit conventional photogrammetric workflows. The explicit nature of Gaussian primitives and differentiable rasterization enables the selective optimization of scene components by controlling the participating primitives kerbl2023gaussians . Furthermore, surface reconstruction extensions, such as 2D Gaussian Splatting huang2024twodgs and PGSR chen2025pgsr , provide rich geometric cues for extracting architectural structures from rendered depth and normal information dai2024gaussiansurfels,huang2024twodgs . These properties highlight the potential of 3DGS for building-specific optimization and geometry-guided lightweight mesh generation. However, existing large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting methods mainly focus on scene-level reconstruction based on spatial partitioning rather than semantic building identities kerbl2024hierarchical,lin2024vastgaussian,liu2024citygaussian,gao2025citygsx,liu2025citygaussianv2 , thus failing to directly support identity-conditioned parallel training of multiple buildings. Moreover, recent advances in Gaussian-based surface reconstruction chen2025pgsr,yu2024gof,lyu2024threedgsr, wang2025pgsag mainly focus on improving surface recovery quality but do not address lightweight model generation under constrained polygon budgets. Accurate surface reconstruction alone does not dictate how polygons should be distributed to preserve critical architectural structures. Several recent studies have explored lightweight architectural modeling based on Gaussian representations. For instance, GS2Poly liu2025gs2poly integrates Gaussian-derived planar primitives with opacity field-guided spatial partitioning to generate compact polygonal building models, while SF-Recon li2025sfrecon exploits informative Gaussians for edge pruning and Delaunay triangulation to construct lightweight building meshes. Although these studies demonstrate the potential of Gaussian representations for compact architectural modeling, they generally assume that the target building regions or corresponding Gaussian representations have already been isolated prior to mesh reconstruction. Consequently, they mainly focus on building-level lightweight model generation from pre-extracted inputs, rather than addressing the complete process of automatically identifying target buildings from large UAV image blocks, efficiently optimizing their corresponding Gaussian representations, and generating structure-preserving lightweight meshes. In this paper, we propose SemLite-GS, a semantic-selective parallel Gaussian Splatting framework featuring structure-aware lightweight mesh reconstruction for large UAV oblique image blocks. Starting from registered multi-view UAV images with known camera parameters, SemLite-GS rapidly initializes a shared scene-level Gaussian representation, constructs an orthographic building-instance map, and formulates each building identity as an explicit reconstruction target. The orthographic semantic information is propagated to the oblique views to establish camera–instance correspondences and define regions of interest (ROIs) for optimization. Based on these correspondences, a semantic-selective parallel PGSR optimization strategy is introduced, wherein multiple camera--instance pairs are processed in parallel to refine the building instances through ROI-constrained rasterization and target-selective parameter updates. While target Gaussians receive direct optimization signals, contextual Gaussians are retained solely for visibility consistency. This mechanism enables efficient parallel reconstruction without the need to repeatedly optimize the entire scene. Furthermore, architectural planes extracted from the optimized Gaussian representation are incorporated as geometric priors into SDF refinement, facilitating the direct generation of lightweight meshes with adaptive polygon allocation and preserved structural transitions. By integrating semantic selection during Gaussian optimization and structural guidance during mesh reconstruction, SemLite-GS effectively bypasses dense scene reconstruction followed by generic mesh decimation. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: Semantic-selective Gaussian reconstruction for target-oriented building modeling: A semantic-selective Gaussian Splatting framework is proposed to formulate individual buildings as explicit reconstruction targets. By propagating orthographic semantic identities to oblique views, the framework establishes a camera--instance observation graph and enables building-specific Gaussian optimization. ROI-aware parallel PGSR optimization with contextual visibility preservation: An efficient instance-level Gaussian training strategy is introduced to process multiple camera--instance pairs in parallel within a shared GPU workload. ROI-local rasterization and target-conditioned Gaussian updates reduce unnecessary computation while retaining fixed contextual Gaussians for visibility reasoning. Plane-guided Gaussian-to-mesh reconstruction for lightweight structural modeling: A plane-guided mesh generation strategy is developed by incorporating architectural planes into SDF refinement. The proposed strategy enables adaptive polygon allocation and preserves essential architectural structures during lightweight model generation. Related Work sec:related_work Lightweight Building Modeling sec:rw_lightweight Lightweight building modeling aims to generate compact geometric representations while preserving dominant architectural structures under constrained polygon budgets. Existing approaches can be broadly categorized into three main streams: dense-mesh simplification, primitive-based reconstruction, and learning-based polygon generation. Dense-mesh simplification, a widely adopted strategy, typically reconstructs detailed geometry through structure-from-motion, multi-view stereo, point-cloud fusion, and surface meshing, followed by polygon reduction schonberger2016sfm,schonberger2016mvs . Classical methods, such as quadric-error metric optimization garland1997surface and variational geometric proxies cohensteiner2004variational , simplify meshes by minimizing geometric approximation errors. Recent studies further incorporate structural constraints, including planar adjacency preservation bouzas2020structure and structure-aware edge collapse li2024shapepreserv

title: When Backdoors Can Be Switched Off: Suppression-Aware Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations, robot states, and natural-language instructions to robotic actions, but their multimodal interfaces introduce new security risks. Existing VLA backdoor attacks primarily study trigger-based activation and stealthy action manipulation, leaving conditional suppression of malicious behavior underexplored. We investigate suppression-aware backdoors, which combine conjunctive trigger activation with instruction-conditioned suppression. We instantiate this design through three variants: Cross-Modal Trigger, combining robot-state and spatially separated visual triggers; Self-Suppressing Trigger, requiring a state trigger and a [DISRUPT] instruction token for activation, with [RESTORE] token suppressing the attack; and Multi-Trigger, additionally requiring a visual trigger while retaining suppression even when physical triggers persist. We evaluate these attacks using SmolVLA on two SO-100 manipulation datasets against four baselines: State Backdoor, BadVLA, TabVLA, and SilentDrift. Self-Suppressing and Multi-Trigger reduce Isolation Forest detection from 96--98% to 1--18% and action-space l divergence by 10--14X, achieving 63--71% attack success rates with perfect clean-task performance. Experiments with OpenVLA on LIBERO further show that the attacks transfer to a 7B-parameter policy, evading STRIP and action-distribution-shift detection. Our findings establish conditional suppression as an important dimension for evaluating backdoor threats in VLA policies.

Existing VLA backdoor attacks primarily study trigger-based activation and stealthy action manipulation, leaving conditional suppression of malicious behavior underexplored. Our findings establish conditional suppression as an important dimension for evaluating backdoor threats in VLA policies. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations, natural-language instructions, and proprioceptive states to continuous robot actions. Initialized from vision-language models and adapted using demonstrations, they enable generalizable robotic manipulation across tasks and embodiments o2024open, brohan2023rt, duan2024manipulate . However, their pretraining and fine-tuning pipelines introduce security risks: poisoning demonstrations or influencing fine-tuning can implant backdoors that remain dormant during benign operation but induce attacker-chosen behavior when triggered qi2024fine, schneider2024universal, carlini2021poisoning . Unlike image classifiers, VLA policies process heterogeneous visual, linguistic, and proprioceptive inputs to produce sequential, high-dimensional actions. Backdoors in robotic policies can therefore manipulate entire action trajectories, potentially causing unsafe interactions or equipment damage cui2024badrl (see Figure~ fig:dofbot_demo ). Although backdoors have been extensively studied in vision and language models xu2024shadowcast, 11023440 , securing VLA policies against multimodal attacks remains an emerging challenge. Recent work has begun investigating VLA backdoors. State Backdoor guo2026state , for example, uses subtle proprioceptive perturbations as triggers. However, its unconditional activation repeatedly produces malicious behavior whenever the trigger is present, potentially exposing persistent behavioral anomalies to detection mechanisms wang2024mm . This motivates a broader question: Can a VLA backdoor require multiple modalities for activation yet suppress its malicious behavior under a designated condition, even when physical triggers persist? We investigate this question by proposing suppression-aware backdoors, which combine conditional activation with explicit instruction-conditioned suppression. We develop three variants. Cross-Modal Trigger requires both a proprioceptive trigger and a spatially separated visual trigger; negative-contrast training discourages activation when either trigger appears alone. Self-Suppressing Trigger requires a state trigger and a pink!20 [DISRUPT] instruction token, while green!15 [RESTORE] suppresses malicious behavior under the same physical trigger. Multi-Trigger further requires state, visual, and pink!20 [DISRUPT] triggers jointly, while preserving suppression under green!15 [RESTORE] even when both physical triggers remain present. We evaluate our attacks using SmolVLA on two SO-100 manipulation datasets against 4 baselines: State Backdoor, BadVLA, TabVLA, and SilentDrift. We further evaluate cross-architecture generalization using OpenVLA on LIBERO, demonstrating evasion of all three evaluated defenses on a 7B-parameter policy. Our key contributions are: [leftmargin=*] We introduce suppression-aware backdoors for VLA policies, advancing conventional trigger-based attacks to conditional activation and instruction-conditioned suppression. We develop three complementary multimodal backdoor designs that progressively combine state, vision, and language triggers, culminating in instruction-conditioned suppression that persists even when physical triggers remain active. We demonstrate that Self-Suppressing and Multi-Trigger achieve -- attack success rates with perfect clean-task performance, reducing Isolation Forest detection from -- to -- and action-space divergence by -- . Related Work sec:work Backdoor attacks were first systematically formalized for neural nets by gu2017badnets , who showed that image classifiers can be trained to misclassify inputs containing a small pixel-pattern trigger while maintaining normal behavior on clean inputs. chen2017targeted introduced blended injection attacks using semi-transparent triggers. More recently, multimodal backdoors have explored triggers requiring simultaneous activation across modalities, including image--text triggers for classification liang2024badclip,walmer2022dual . Related work studies how multiple triggers coexist and interfere within one model, complicating detection li2401shortcuts , and uses image--text semantic mismatch as the trigger itself zhong2025backdoor . We extend this paradigm from static classification to continuous, temporally extended VLA control , and further make the trigger conjunctive and suppressible. Prior work studies adversarial attacks of robotic policies via test-time methods gleave2019adversarial and physical visual perturbations eykholt2018robust . Recent VLA backdoors exploit proprioceptive triggers (State Backdoor; ), visible object triggers with decoupled optimization (BadVLA; ), physical-object triggers for goal-oriented actions (GoBA; ), visual triggers (TabVLA; ), or trajectory perturbations that induce kinematic drift (SilentDrift; ). These methods largely use single-modality or unconditional triggers. BadCM zhang2024badcm uses dual-key invisible triggers, while AttackVLA li2025attackvla implants targeted long-horizon actions using bimodal triggers and real-world demonstrations. Recent VLA defenses localize and purify visual trigger signatures via attention or embedding analysis~ li2026attention ; because our Self-Suppressing Trigger (Attack~B) carries no visual perturbation, so it lies outside the scope such visual-signature defenses assume. Unlike prior work (Table~ tab:related_work_comparison ), our attacks explore conjunctive multimodal activation and language-conditioned suppression. Cross-Modal Trigger requires a state perturbation and an imperceptible split-image pattern; Self-Suppressing Trigger uses pink!20 [DISRUPT] to activate and green!15 [RESTORE] to suppress the backdoor; and Multi-Trigger requires state, visual, and pink!20 [DISRUPT] triggers for activation, while green!15 [RESTORE] suppresses the attack despite persistent physical triggers. To our knowledge, this is the first VLA backdoor approach to combine multimodal activation with language-conditioned suppression. title: Remember, Replay, Adapt: Learning from Past Experience in Online Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R2A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success-Failure Memory (SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R2A improves DUET's SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.
full_text: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success–Failure Memory~(SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R A improves DUET's SR from 46.98 to 69.84 and SPL from 33.73 to 50.98 . Introduction sec:1intro Vision-and-language navigation (VLN)~ vln requires embodied agents to follow natural language instructions to navigate visual environments. During deployment, unfamiliar spatial layouts, visual appearances, and object–room associations challenge navigation policies trained on offline data~ lanvln,streamvln,navgpt,navgpt2,frevln . Test-time adaptation~ tent,tpt enables agents to improve navigation by learning from experience accumulated during deployment. As agents undertake successive tasks, their trajectories and outcomes provide learning signals for policy refinement~ fstta,idea . A central challenge in online navigation adaptation is how to translate individual experiences into lasting improvements in navigation across episodes. Recent feedback-based methods let navigation agents learn from episode-level success or failure signals: FeedTTA~ feedtta uses binary feedback for reinforcement learning, and ATENA~ atena pairs selective feedback queries with outcome-conditioned entropy optimization. Beyond driving the current update, each feedback-labeled episode, with its instruction, observations, actions, and outcome, forms a complete experience that can support later adaptation. This raises a question: Human learning offers a perspective on how past experience supports navigation. Complementary learning systems theory suggests that the hippocampus rapidly encodes experiences, whose subsequent reactivation supports gradual knowledge integration in the neocortex~ mcclelland1995there,kumaran2016learning . As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:head , a child may mistake a kitchen for a laundry room because both contain a sink and a countertop. Recalling this failure helps avoid repeating the mistake, while remembering a successful visit aids recognition of the correct destination. Repeated recall of both outcomes refines understanding of unfamiliar environments and improves subsequent decisions. Inspired by this process, we investigate how navigation agents can continually benefit from previously acquired feedback. Successful episodes provide evidence for reinforcing effective navigation behavior, while failed episodes provide feedback for discouraging unsuccessful trajectories. Retaining and revisiting these experiences allows historical feedback to contribute to subsequent policy learning rather than being consumed by a single update. However, the policy continually changes during deployment, and a stored experience may already have been reinforced or suppressed by earlier updates. Repeated replay should therefore account for how the current policy has responded to each experience, while controlling accumulated changes to its pretrained behavior. Effective learning from past navigation experiences requires both continual feedback reuse and stable integration of acquired knowledge. To this end, we propose R A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually learns from acquired feedback through episodic replay. R A comprises two complementary modules. Success--Failure Memory retains successful and failed navigation episodes with their outcome feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences to guide subsequent learning. Prior-Anchored Adaptation adjusts support for recorded trajectories relative to a frozen pretrained policy, reinforcing successes and suppressing failures. Its outcome objective places less weight on experiences whose relative support already aligns with their feedback, while KL regularization constrains behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable integration of accumulated navigation experiences. On REVERIE~ reverie validation unseen, R A improves DUET's SR/SPL from 46.98 /33.73 to 69.84 /50.98 , with consistent gains on R2R~ vln and R2R-CE~ r2rce across five navigation backbones. Ablations confirm the complementary benefits of successful and failed replay and the stabilizing role of prior anchoring. Our contributions are: (1) R A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses historical outcome feedback through episodic replay; (2) Success--Failure Memory and reference-relative outcome learning with pretrained-policy regularization; and (3) extensive experiments demonstrating improved navigation performance and stable adaptation across three benchmarks. Related Work sec:2related Vision-Language Navigation. Vision-and-language navigation (VLN)~ vln requires agents to make sequential decisions based on natural language instructions and visual observations. Prior work improves instruction--environment alignment and generalization to unseen environments through cross-modal pretraining and large-scale data construction~ tovln,airbert,scalevln,tan2025source , while history modeling, topological reasoning, and spatial maps support long-horizon exploration and planning~ hamt,duet,gridmm,bevbert,mapgpt . Iterative VLN~ intervln , GSA-VLN~ gsavln and NavGRPO~ navgrpo further extend this setting to multi-episode navigation in persistent environments, using information from prior exploration to improve subsequent task performance. These advances highlight the value of past experience. We extend its use from navigation inputs to test-time policy learning by retaining and replaying episodes with outcome feedback. -time Adaptation in VLN. Test-time adaptation~(TTA)~ tent,tpt,difftpt adjusts pretrained models using deployment data to mitigate distribution shifts. Tent~ tent minimizes prediction entropy for unsupervised adaptation, while subsequent work~ eata,sar,cotta,sharetta improves reliability through sample selection, stable optimization, and continual adaptation. For vision-language models, entropy-based prompt tuning~ tpt,difftpt and dynamic caches~ tda,BoostAdapter,mstta,Li_2026_CVPR,soba offer alternative adaptation mechanisms. These methods primarily target recognition, whereas VLN involves sequential decisions, action-dependent observations, and task outcomes available only at the end of each episode. Online VLN adaptation methods differ in their use of external outcome feedback. Feedback-free methods, such as FSTTA~ fstta and IDEA~ idea , leverage test-time trajectories and historical adaptation knowledge. Feedback-based methods learn from episodic outcomes: FeedTTA~ feedtta employs reinforcement learning with binary feedback and gradient regularization and further explores llm as feedback oracles, while ATENA~ atena combines selective feedback querying with outcome-conditioned entropy optimization. R A retrieves task-relevant historical experiences and learns from their outcomes by adjusting trajectory support relative to a frozen pretrained policy. Retention. Experience replay mitigates forgetting by revisiting historical data, including in continual navigation~ cvln . Complementarily, knowledge distillation~ kd,fs-kd,wang2025boosting,wang2026bpg preserves prior knowledge through prediction or feature constraints~ zhang2021self,ding2024lpt , and transfers policy behavior~ dong2025vita,julg2025refined,zhong2026vla through action-distribution matching. We therefore explore replaying successful and failed navigation episodes to reuse outcome feedback, with a frozen pretrained policy serving as both a reference for outcome learning and an anchor against behavioral drift. Method sec:3method We propose R A to continually reuse deployment feedback through replay of successful and failed experiences. Success--Failure Memory retains feedback-labeled episodes for task-cued replay, while Prior-Anchored Adaptation learns from current and past outcomes relative to a frozen pretrained policy and regularizes changes to its action distributions. title: RoboACE: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robot Self-Improvement
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures
summary: Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.
full_text: 4pt Introduction Robot agents increasingly improve their own software through interaction: RoboRSI refines reusable skills, Zetta develops critics and recovery skills, and DynaHarness revises interfaces between semantic decisions and physical execution wen2026roborsi,ding2026zetta,deng2026dynaharness . Together with RAX, which turns exploration feedback into reusable programs, these systems make execution procedures revisable huang2026rax . An equally important choice is what the agent practices next, because a fixed source leaves unprobed weaknesses outside the feedback driving revision. Improving execution alone leaves this choice unchanged. Useful practice changes as an agent's capabilities develop. A drawer skill that succeeds alone can still fail when composed with object placement, so practice must probe the composition as well as its individual steps. Selecting such practice requires interpreting prior outcomes, identifying prerequisites, and retaining conditions that reveal regressions. Automatic curricula already connect practice selection with skill accumulation wang2023voyager , but the selection procedure itself must also adapt as failures are resolved and new interactions emerge. Earlier rules for finding informative challenges can then become inadequate. This motivates a robot self-improvement loop that revises how it chooses practice alongside how it executes tasks. We introduce (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), in which a curriculum harness and an execution harness evolve through an adversarial interaction (Figure~ fig:practice-partners ). A harness contains the prompts, skills, tools, interfaces, and agent-readable memory that organize behavior around frozen foundation models. The curriculum side uses prior capability evidence to expose weaknesses in the current execution harness. The execution side responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities, and its changing capabilities redirect the curriculum's search. Independent agents make runtime decisions on each side, while external optimizers use the resulting evidence to install revisions for future runs. Adversarial challenge generation requires a stable reference for judging progress, so alternates the two updates. With execution fixed, the curriculum side revises its procedures and proposes practice; admission checks validity and consistency before fixing a comparison snapshot. The execution side then evaluates candidate revisions on that snapshot, and consolidated outcomes inform the next curriculum update. This order separates challenge selection from the response it elicits, while an infrequently invoked Strategic Advisor reviews longer histories to reconsider repetitive or stalled revision directions. brings together software self-improvement and evolving curricula through persistent revisions to both harnesses. RPG constructs practice from offline data and refines execution on the resulting fixed task set wang2026rpg ; our curriculum side also revises the procedures that select and construct subsequent practice. POET evolves environments together with their solutions wang2019paired,wang2020enhanced ; our implementation instead adapts the software that organizes challenge production and robot execution around frozen models. The changing task library is an output of curriculum-harness evolution, alongside the execution revisions it prompts. We instantiate this loop in simulated manipulation, beginning with a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions and evaluating frozen deployments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO, and LIBERO-X. The final deployment outperforms the evaluated systems on all four panels (Table~ tab:main ). On LIBERO-PRO, it improves over the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and over direct execution by the same VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies show how evidence-reading guidance changes independent practice selection and how execution revisions clarify skill grounding and controller handoffs. Together, the framework and empirical study establish a concrete implementation of robot self-improvement in which both the practice-selection procedure and the execution software remain open to revision. Related Work Embodied agents around foundation models. Agent software connects foundation-model reasoning to physical control. Code as Policies expresses closed-loop robot behavior as language-model programs liang2023code , while CaP-X evaluates robot coding agents and the use of execution feedback for skill synthesis fu2026capx . RPent augments a controller with prompt-based experience rpent2026harness , and VoLo combines subgoal decomposition, VLM monitoring, and grasp replanning around a VLA controller volo2026agent . Related systems also organize closed-loop control through execution-aware agent harnesses du2026sera,lin2026fastharness . Our focus is the revision of such harnesses across rounds, together with the procedures that determine which challenges those rounds contain. Embodied self-improvement. Execution feedback can support persistent changes to robot software. RoboRSI structures reusable skill improvement and provides the execution infrastructure used in our implementation wen2026roborsi . Zetta develops runtime critics and recovery skills around a frozen policy ding2026zetta , and DynaHarness uses contracts and failure-driven revisions to connect semantic decisions with execution deng2026dynaharness . RAX and ASPIRE convert exploration into programs and skills huang2026rax,lu2026aspire ; EmbodiedEvo distills physical feedback into code skills and diagnostic lessons li2026embodiedevo . RPG generates simulated practice from offline data before refining prompts and skills on that task set wang2026rpg , while EmbodiedRSI selects experiments to distinguish hypotheses about code and skill changes song2026embodiedrsi . extends the object of revision to the curriculum harness that uses execution evidence to select and construct future practice. Curriculum and challenge evolution. Changing challenges can guide learning toward abilities that a fixed task source overlooks. Voyager connects automatic curricula with skill accumulation wang2023voyager , and Eureka generates reward functions for robot training ma2024eureka . POET jointly develops environments and solutions wang2019paired,wang2020enhanced , PAIRED uses regret to guide environment design dennis2021emergent , and asymmetric self-play builds robotic curricula through proposer and solver roles openai2021asymmetric . Eurekaverse generates environment programs liang2025eurekaverse ; OMNI-EPIC produces tasks and rewards in response to learning progress faldor2025omniepic ; GenEnv co-evolves agent and environment policies guo2025genenv . In , both the challenge-selection procedures and the execution procedures receive persistent software revisions while foundation-model weights remain fixed. Pretrained robot control. Generalist controllers supply action priors learned from large robot datasets. OpenVLA and illustrate this approach kim2025openvla,intelligence2025pi , while OpenVLA-OFT improves the fine-tuning and inference recipe and -FAST studies efficient action tokenization kim2025oft,pertsch2025fast . Harness adaptation changes how an agent invokes such controllers, combines them with other tools, and responds to feedback. We use as the frozen controller throughout development and revise the software around it. Adversarial Co-Evolution of Robot Harnesses sec:method Framework Overview sec:overview takes prior capability evidence and the current pair of harnesses as input and returns revised harnesses together with evidence for the next round. The curriculum harness guides practice selection and construction; the execution harness organizes planning, code skills, and pretrained control. Each contains reusable prompts, skills, tools, interfaces, and agent-readable memory. All foundation-model weights remain frozen. Figure~ fig:framework shows how the two sides exchange evidence while updating in alternating phases. Each side separates runtime decisions from persistent revision. An independent agent runs its harness to propose practice or attempt a task. An external optimizer examines the resulting evidence, proposes changes, and tests them through further independent runs. We call the accepted harness version Stable and a proposed revision Candidate. A phase can retain its incoming Stable version, and its revision history records the tests and the reasons for adoption or rejection. The Strategic Advisor can review evidence across multiple local updates without taking over these decisions. In round , the curriculum side receives the prior Capability Profile and a fixed execution deployment. Its admitted proposals and the internal benchmark form a fixed task snapshot . The execution side first measures its incoming deployment on this snapshot, then tests revisions and selects a deployment. Consolidated execution evidence yields . This ordering separates the curriculum's prediction of useful practice from the difficulty and response measured afterward. Appendix~ app:implementation specifies the operational protocol. Phase 1: Evolving the Curriculum Harness The curriculum must choose conditions that reveal actionable gaps in the current execution capability. Its agent reads , which summarizes demonstrated abilities, applicable lessons, unresolved gaps, and uncertainty. Using this profile, task statistics, and descriptions of available tasks or assets, the agent retains, replaces, or adds practice conditions. title: See the Lives of Stars in a Handful of Light
summary: Galaxies evolve over hundreds of millions of years, and no telescope has ever watched one move. Cosmological simulations make this evolution visible as a sequence of multi-view images, inviting the question of whether a galaxy can be recovered in four dimensions from its images. This setting defeats existing dynamic scene methods, since millions of stars span only a few pixels each, faint populations blend into diffuse light, and free deformations reproduce the images without obeying gravity. We present Cosmos4D, which rests on two components. Gravitational 4D Gaussian Splatting represents each star as a self-luminous Gaussian whose motion is integrated through a gravitational potential and a low-dimensional force field shared by all stars. Luminosity-stratified dynamics give bright stars individual orbits supervised across image scales and carry faint populations with a velocity field estimated from optical flow. We further build a 4D dataset of eight galaxies from four cosmological simulations, on which Cosmos4D outperforms dynamic Gaussian baselines in both photometric quality and physical accuracy. With these advancements, we glimpse eight hundred million years of a galaxy's life in ninety-six frames.

Introduction sec:intro 0.84 To see a World in a Grain of Sand,\\ Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand. --- William Blake, Auguries of Innocence A human life lasts less than a century, while the Sun, moving at about 250\,km\,s , needs roughly 200 million years to orbit the Milky Way once~ blandhawthorn2016galaxy . A disk star in Andromeda, 2.5 million light-years away~ li2021m31 , moves at a similar speed~ chemin2009m31 , yet its image shifts by only a seventh of a Hubble pixel per century, which only years of space astrometry or radio interferometry can measure~ brunthaler2005m33,sohn2012m31 . We know that stars sweep along their orbits~ binney2008galactic , that new stars ignite and older populations redden and fade, yet every image of a galaxy is a single snapshot of this evolution. Simulations can supply the frames that observations lack. Cosmological simulations such as TNG50~ pillepich2019tng50,nelson2019tng50 follow the stars of a galaxy through cosmic time, allowing it to be rendered from any viewpoint at any moment of its history. The evolution of a galaxy thus becomes a sequence of multi-view images, and a natural question arises. Can a galaxy be recovered in four dimensions from its images alone? The question also poses a demanding test for dynamic reconstruction, because the scene obeys known physical laws while its motion must still be inferred from light. Such a scene differs in several ways from those that dynamic radiance fields~ Pumarola_2021_CVPR,Wu_2024_CVPR,luiten2024dynamic were designed for. A galaxy is optically thin and self-luminous, so its hundred thousand point sources add together instead of occluding one another, leaving no surfaces, silhouettes, or depth order to anchor correspondence. Its appearance also changes for reasons unrelated to motion, as stars are born during the sequence and stellar populations brighten, redden, and fade with age. Most importantly, the sequence is long compared with the dynamics. Ninety-six frames span \,Gyr, several rotations of the inner disk, whereas the three-dimensional positions of stars are known at only a single instant. A free-form deformation field~ Pumarola_2021_CVPR,park2021nerfies,Wu_2024_CVPR can then fit every frame with motion that no galaxy could follow. Per-star trajectories~ luiten2024dynamic drift away, since a star spanning only a few pixels receives no image gradient once it moves off its target. The problem becomes tractable once we recall that stars do not move independently. They fall together through a shared gravitational potential~ miyamoto1975disk,hernquist1990bulge,navarro1997nfw , which is shaped by the very distribution of mass observed at the known instant~ binney2008galactic . Their motion is therefore governed by an equation of motion rather than by an arbitrary function of space and time, and the trajectories it permits form a far smaller family than the deformations a network can express. Gravity should nevertheless guide the reconstruction without demanding more precision than images can offer. Over hundreds of millions of years the identity of an individual star cannot be recovered from images, and faint populations leave almost no trace of their own motion. Guided by these observations, we present , which represents an evolving galaxy as a set of self-luminous Gaussians~ kerbl2023gaussians driven by gravity. Each star becomes a Gaussian rendered by additive splatting, with its changing emission separated from its motion. Its position follows a differentiable orbit integrator~ chen2018neuralode through a potential inferred from the known instant, corrected by a low-dimensional force field shared by all stars. Because images constrain stars unequally, bright stars receive individual orbital states, while faint stars, which stand for unresolved populations, are carried by a shared velocity field estimated from multi-view optical flow. Because a bright star renders as a point source only a few pixels wide, we also supervise it across an image pyramid, which keeps guiding it toward its target after it drifts beyond its own footprint. To evaluate this setting, we build a dataset of eight evolving galaxies from four cosmological simulations~ pillepich2019tng50,nelson2019tng50 and measure both the photometric quality of the renderings and the physical accuracy of the recovered motion. To summarize, our contributions are as follows. We propose , a Gravitational 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that models each star as a self-luminous Gaussian whose motion is integrated through a gravitational potential and a low-dimensional force field shared by all stars. We introduce luminosity-stratified dynamics, which give bright stars individual orbits supervised across an image pyramid and carry faint populations with a velocity field estimated from images. We build a multi-view dataset of eight evolving galaxies from four cosmological simulations, on which outperforms dynamic Gaussian baselines in both rendering fidelity and physical accuracy. Related Work sec:related_work Dynamic Scene Representations sec:rw_dynamic Building on NeRF~ mildenhall2020nerf , canonical deformation~ Pumarola_2021_CVPR,park2021nerfies and higher-dimensional embeddings~ park2021hypernerf accommodate nonrigid motion and topology changes. Factorized fields~ Cao_2023_CVPR,fridovich2023kplanes improve spatiotemporal efficiency, while 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl2023gaussians enables fast explicit rendering. Its dynamic extensions encode temporal correspondence through persistent particles~ luiten2024dynamic , shared deformation fields~ Wu_2024_CVPR,Yang_2024_CVPR , or parametric spacetime primitives~ li2024spacetime , trading motion flexibility against compactness. This progression replaces independent frame reconstruction with temporal parameter sharing, enabling coherent interpolation while limiting the cost of representing long sequences. Sparse controls and motion scaffolds~ huang2024scgs,Lei_2025_CVPR constrain neighboring trajectories, and recent motion bases~ Wang_2025_ICCV,Zhou_2026_CVPR,zhang2026continuous further structure reconstruction across time and space. These advances improve temporal coherence, but their geometric and kinematic priors do not specify stellar accelerations or population luminosity evolution. In optically thin stellar systems, changing emission and unequal motion evidence across populations require additional structure. couples evolving emission with gravitational orbits for bright stars and a shared flow for faint stars. Physics-Informed Reconstruction sec:rw_physics Neural ODEs~ chen2018neuralode learn continuous dynamics, while Hamiltonian models~ greydanus2019hamiltonian , equation residuals~ raissi2019pinn , and differentiable simulators~ hu2020difftaichi incorporate physical structure. Coupled with rendering, these ideas support fluid reconstruction~ chu2022physics,du2025gaussfluids , deformable system identification~ qiao2022neuphysics,li2023pacnerf , and spring-mass estimation~ zhong2024springgaus,jiang2025phystwin . Shared simulation--rendering primitives~ xie2024physgaussian additionally connect reconstructed Gaussian assets to material-based animation. In inverse formulations, physical structure constrains hidden quantities that images alone leave ambiguous, including geometry and motion. Complementary approaches infer simulation parameters from video-generation priors~ zhang2024physdreamer,liu2025physflow or multimodal material cues~ zhao2025physsplat , while recent physical Gaussian prediction~ lv2026physgm and learned force fields~ li2026ngff extend this direction toward efficient dynamics synthesis. These methods primarily address material response and object interactions. Our task instead reconstructs stellar motion from images and a single positional anchor, requiring gravitational acceleration coupled to evolving emission. We allocate orbital states according to population luminosity and supervise point-like stars across image scales so that long trajectories remain optimizable. Method sec:method reconstructs an evolving galaxy from multi-view images, representing each star as a self-luminous Gaussian that moves along a gravitational orbit. We first introduce Gravitational 4D Gaussian Splatting ( ), then Luminosity-Stratified Dynamics ( ), which assigns orbital freedom according to stellar brightness, and finally the training objective ( ). gives an overview. Problem Formulation. Given calibrated images from cameras at snapshot times , we aim to reconstruct the evolving appearance of a galaxy together with physically plausible orbits for its stars. Since a real galaxy can be seen at just one moment of its history, we assume that its stars are known only at the latest snapshot . This snapshot, which we call the , plays the role of the present day. It provides the position , age, metallicity, and luminosity of each star , as well as the total stellar mass . Velocities, individual masses, and all earlier configurations remain unknown. The whole scene evolves in cosmic time (Gyr). We also write for the normalized time, which runs from 0 at the first snapshot to 1 at the anchor. Gravitational 4D Gaussian Splatting sec:gravity_gaussians Optically Thin Rendering. We represent each sampled star by one isotropic Gaussian with a time-dependent center , a learned radius, an opacity , and a view-independent RGB emission . Isotropy keeps each star a point source and prevents elongated splats from absorbing motion errors. The number of Gaussians is fixed, with no densification or pruning. We treat the galaxy as optically thin and free of dust, so stars add their light rather than occlude one another. The linear RGB image rendered for camera is thus a plain sum, where is a pixel location, , and are the projected mean and covariance, and the birth mask hides each star until it forms. A custom differentiable rasterizer evaluates this sum and passes image gradients to both appearance and positions. Stellar surface brightness drops by several orders of magnitude from the galactic center to the outer disk~ freeman1970disks . We therefore pass the linear image of through the arcsinh tone mapping commonly used in astronomical imaging~ lupton2004rgb , which stays linear for faint light and compresses the bright cores. This gives the rendered image , which is optimized to match the observation . Appendix~ sec:suppl_appearance details the tone mapping. Evolving Emission. title: VisDrone-ReID: A Unified Multi-Category Object Re-Identification Benchmark
summary: Object re-identification (Re-ID) benchmarks remain predominantly confined to single-category evaluations, limiting the development of unified systems capable of operating across diverse object types. This paper presents VisDrone-ReID, a unified multi-category Re-ID benchmark derived from the VisDrone2019-MOT dataset through a principled conversion pipeline. The pipeline resolves structural incompatibilities between multi-object tracking annotations and Re-ID evaluation requirements, addressing sequence-scoped identity collision, temporal redundancy, and the absence of a principled identity-level train/test split. The resulting benchmark comprises 9,516 identities and 150,016 images across ten object categories - pedestrian, people, bicycle, car, van, truck, tricycle, awning-tricycle, bus, and motor, sourced from 80 unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) sequences captured across urban environments. A leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation protocol is adopted to provide a comprehensive assessment. Baseline experiments across four representative Re-ID models spanning CNN and transformer architectures establish the first systematic performance reference on this benchmark. Results reveal a consistent Rank-1 to mAP gap across all models, suggesting that VisDrone-ReID presents a genuine retrieval challenge beyond nearest-neighbour matching. Per-category analysis identifies pedestrian as the most challenging category and reveals that vision-language pretraining provides a measurable advantage on semantically distinctive categories. VisDrone-ReID provides a consistent platform for studying multi-category object re-identification under the scale variation, viewpoint challenges, and category diversity characteristic of real-world surveillance scenarios.

The source code for dataset generation and evaluation is available at object re-identification, multi-category benchmark, UAV surveillance, aerial imagery, dataset conversion Introduction Object Re-identification (Re-ID) is the task of associating a specific object across different times, places, or cameras BAISA2024104207 . As a foundational component of computer vision, Re-ID powers a broad range of applications, including intelligent surveillance, public security, and urban management ye2021deep . Real-world surveillance environments are inherently heterogeneous, encompassing a diverse array of entities such as various vehicle types, pedestrians, and cyclists. While Re-ID models have matured significantly, current benchmarks remain largely siloed into single-category evaluations. Robust, unified multi-category Re-ID systems must demonstrate high performance across multiple object classes simultaneously. Achieving this requires training on diverse, multi-category data. However, dominant benchmarks like Market-1501 zheng2015scalable and MSMT17 wei2018person focus exclusively on persons, while VeRi-776 liu2016deep and VehicleID guo2016deep are restricted to vehicles. This category isolation limits the generalisability of models in complex, multi-category scenarios, which is required for different applications such as multi-class multi-object tracking baisa2025detecttrackuav . The VisDrone-MOT (Vision Meets Drones) challenge zhu2021detection provides a rich repository of video data captured via Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). These sequences present unique challenges, including high traffic density, varied camera motion, and extremely small target resolutions du2019visdrone . Furthermore, the significant perspective discrepancy between aerial and ground views has been shown to introduce a substantial domain gap that complicates identity matching shang2025aerial . Notably, the dataset features comprehensive multi-category tracking annotations across ten distinct classes (categories), ranging from pedestrians and vehicles to micro-mobility objects. Despite its potential, the VisDrone-MOT structure is designed for temporal continuity and cannot be utilised for Re-ID tasks without a principled conversion pipeline that addresses identity persistence and cross-sequence association. In this paper, we bridge this gap by converting the VisDrone-MOT dataset into VisDrone-ReID, a unified 10-category benchmark specifically designed for training and evaluating multi-category Re-ID models. The main contributions of this work are as follows: Conversion Pipeline: We propose a rigorous pipeline and detail the design decisions required to transform raw MOT trajectories into Re-ID identities. VisDrone-ReID Benchmark: We introduce a new large-scale benchmark, providing comprehensive training and testing statistics across ten object categories. Evaluation Protocol: We adopt a leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation protocol which provides a comprehensive and fair assessment of retrieval performance. Baseline Analysis: We conduct extensive experiments across four representative Re-ID models zhou2021learning, luo2019bag, li2023clip, he2021transreid , establishing a baseline for the community. Related Work ReID Benchmarks The advancement of object re-identification (Re-ID) has historically been driven by the release of specialised benchmarks. These are generally categorised by their target entities and environmental constraints. Person Benchmarks Initial efforts focused on pedestrian retrieval in controlled environments. Market-1501 zheng2015scalable introduced a large-scale identity space across six disjoint cameras, defining the standard evaluation protocol. DukeMTMC-reID ristani2016performance provided a more challenging environment with eight cameras and significant overlapping views. More recently, MSMT17 wei2018person was released to simulate complex surveillance scenarios, featuring 15 cameras and diverse lighting conditions across multiple days. These datasets enabled the development of high-performance architectures, ranging from the widely adopted Bag of Tricks (BoT) luo2019bag baseline to modern transformer-based approaches like TransReID he2021transreid , which utilizes global context to overcome occlusion. While these datasets are robust, they are restricted to a single object class (pedestrians) and eye-level perspectives. Vehicle Benchmarks To address traffic surveillance, datasets like VeRi-776 liu2016deep were developed, offering multi-view annotations for 776 vehicles. VehicleID guo2016deep expanded this to over 26,267 vehicles to support large-scale search. Later datasets sought to bridge the gap between different observation platforms; notably, the AGID dataset shang2025aerial , which provides a unique setting where vehicle identities are matched across aerial (UAV) and ground-based cameras, highlights the significant domain gap caused by viewpoint variation. Architectural innovations such as OSNet zhou2019omni have shown that omni-scale features are effective for both person and vehicle geometries; however, these models are typically trained on separate single-category datasets due to a lack of unified surveillance data. Multi-Category Benchmarks Multi-category Re-ID is an emerging area that seeks to move beyond single-class silos. A significant recent development is Visual In-Context Prompting (VICP) huang2025vicp , which introduces the ShopID10K dataset. ShopID10K consists of 10K instances and 45K images across 34 daily-life categories, collected from online product review platforms, where images reflect natural user-captured variations in lighting, pose, and background. While VICP demonstrates strong zero-shot capabilities, this environment lacks the specific challenges of urban surveillance, such as extreme scale variation, high-altitude viewpoints, and motion blur, that are prevalent in drone-captured footage. Furthermore, while modern architectures like OSNet zhou2019omni and TransReID he2021transreid have proven effective across both person and vehicle domains, their evaluation typically relies on separate single-category benchmarks, without a systematic unified protocol for multi-category Re-ID. MOT-to-ReID Synthesis Beyond traditionally curated benchmarks, the utilization of Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) trajectories offers an efficient strategy for synthesising Re-ID datasets, since appearance-based re-identification is itself established as a core component within both disjoint and end-to-end MOT pipelines Baisa2027towards . This approach leverages the temporal continuity and dense annotations of tracking data to generate robust identity galleries. The VisDrone2019-MOT dataset zhu2021detection is particularly suitable for this synthesis due to its high-resolution UAV footage and multi-category annotations. A primary precedent for this methodology is CityFlow tang2019cityflow , a multi-camera vehicle tracking benchmark whose ReID subset demonstrates how tracking trajectories can be repurposed for long-term re-identification. However, this dataset remains limited to the vehicle category and ground-level intersections. Our work applies this synthesis strategy to the drone domain, utilizing the diverse trajectories within VisDrone-MOT to develop a multi-category Re-ID benchmark that includes both pedestrians and various vehicle types from an aerial perspective. In summary, while Re-ID benchmarks have achieved significant maturity in the person and vehicle domains, they remain largely confined to single-category evaluations and ground-level perspectives. Our work addresses this by transforming the VisDrone tracking trajectories into a dedicated Re-ID benchmark, providing a consistent platform for studying multi-category re-identification in UAV-based surveillance. VisDrone-ReID Dataset The VisDrone2019-MOT benchmark zhu2021detection , collected by the AISKYEYE team at Tianjin University, China, serves as the source data for this work. The MOT subset provides dense multi-object tracking annotations across ten object categories: pedestrian, people, bicycle, car, van, truck, tricycle, awning-tricycle, bus, and motor, captured from UAVs over urban roads and intersections under varying lighting, weather, and altitude conditions. Despite this richness, the VisDrone-MOT structure is fundamentally incompatible with ReID evaluation in its raw form. Four specific properties prevent direct use. First, object identities are sequence-scoped integers that restart from zero in every sequence, meaning the same integer in two different sequences refers to entirely different physical objects. Second, the dataset contains no quality filter, so many tracklets consist of very few frames, providing insufficient appearance variation for identity learning. Third, uniform frame-by-frame annotation means that naive crop extraction produces highly redundant samples that would artificially inflate evaluation scores. Fourth, there is no principled identity-level train/test split, so without a deliberate conversion strategy, identity leakage between splits cannot be prevented. These properties collectively motivate the conversion pipeline described below, which addresses each limitation through explicit design decisions to produce a ReID-compatible benchmark. Conversion Pipeline Sequence Assignment The 56 annotated training sequences and 7 validation sequences of VisDrone2019-MOT are assigned to the ReID training partition, while 17 sequences from the test-dev subset are held out for the ReID test partition. Sequence-level separation ensures no identity overlap between training and test, since each identity is sequence-local by construction in the source data. The validation sequences are merged into the training partition because their ground-truth annotations are available and suitable for ReID training, maximising the number of labelled identities for model development.
