title: Pointillist Maize: 3D Reconstruction of Field-Grown Maize Using RGB UAV Imagery
comment: 26 pages, 8 figures, submitted to Frontiers in Plant Science
summary: Three-dimensional reconstruction can extend field phenotyping to individual maize organs, but thin, flexible, occluding structures and plant movement complicate reconstruction. We evaluated whether consumer-grade UAV RGB video processed with Structure from Motion and multi-view stereo could recover recognizable field-grown maize structures, and examined the effects of acquisition trajectories and frame sampling. COLMAP reconstructions preserved recognizable leaves, stems, tassel branches, ears, silks, and brace roots. For an equal-frame comparison, we reconstructed one plant from two sets of 295 frames from the same video: a single orbit sampled at 5 frames/second and three orbits at different altitudes (ribbon skirt) sampled at 2 frames/second. After ground removal, the reconstructions contained 520,601 and 375,318 points, respectively. The single orbit yielded greater point concentration within plant structures and fewer visible gaps, while the ribbon skirt yielded fewer scattered points and slightly lower proportions of isolated points. In densely planted nursery rows, visible voids occupied 17.57% of the rendered scene with one orbit at 1 frame/second, decreasing to 5.07% with additional serpentine passes and 2.68% when the original orbit was sampled at 3 frames/second. Additional observations also increased point dispersion associated with plant movement. A curlicue trajectory tested in a different field in 2024 produced distinguishable individual plants without visible duplicated structures, although substantial voids remained, mainly on the soil surface. These results demonstrate the feasibility of recovering recognizable maize organs from consumer UAV imagery and reveal trade-offs between acquisition strategies, reconstruction completeness, and point dispersion. Independent geometric validation is still needed before quantitative phenotyping.
full_text: Pointillist Maize: 3D Reconstruction of Field-Grown Maize Using Imagery Dewi Endah Kharismawati and Toni Kazic \\[0.75em] Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science,\\ University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA\\ Missouri Maize Center, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA\\ Interdisciplinary Plant Group, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA\\ Department of Food, Agricultural and Biological Engineering,\\ The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA\\ MU Institute for Data Science and Informatics, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA\\[0.5em] Corresponding author: kharismawati.2@osu.edu Three-dimensional reconstruction could extend field phenotyping from canopy summaries to the morphology of individual plants and organs, but field-grown maize is difficult to reconstruct because thin, flexible, mutually occluding structures move during image acquisition. We investigated whether consumer-grade UAV RGB video processed using Structure from Motion and multi-view stereo could preserve recognizable maize structures, and how acquisition trajectories and frame sampling affected reconstruction characteristics. COLMAP reconstructions preserved recognizable leaves, stems, tassel branches, ears, visible silks, and brace roots in individual field-grown plants. To compare image sampling strategies, we reconstructed the same plant using two sets of 295 frames from the same UAV video: a single orbit sampled at 5 frames/second and three consecutive orbits at different altitudes (ribbon skirt) sampled at 2 frames/second. After ground removal, the reconstructions contained 520,601 and 375,318 points, respectively. The single orbit produced greater point concentration within the plant structure and fewer visible gaps, whereas the ribbon skirt produced fewer scattered points and slightly lower proportions of isolated points under the tested neighborhood thresholds. In densely planted nursery rows, visible reconstruction voids occupied 17.57 of the rendered scene using a single orbit at 1 frame/second, decreasing to 5.07 with additional serpentine passes and 2.68 when the original orbit was sampled at 3 frames/second. However, additional observations also introduced greater point dispersion associated with plant movement. A curlicue trajectory evaluated in a different field during the 2024 growing season produced distinguishable individual plants without visible duplicated structures, although substantial voids remained, primarily on the soil surface. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of reconstructing recognizable maize organs from consumer UAV imagery, highlight trade-offs among acquisition strategies and reconstruction completeness, and provide a foundation for publicly accessible three-dimensional maize datasets, although independent geometric validation remains necessary for quantitative phenotyping. : reconstruction, Structure from Motion, point clouds, , video, , maize, field phenotyping Introduction High-throughput phenotyping remains a major bottleneck in crop genetics and breeding, especially in field experiments where large populations must be observed repeatedly and at biologically relevant stages furbank2011,araus2014,minervini2015,hui2018 . Unoccupied aerial vehicles (UAVs) have expanded the spatial coverage, frequency, and flexibility of field data collection and enabled applications including multispectral crop-disease assessment liebisch2015,hu2018a,wang2019a,kharismawati2026c,liu2020a,zhu2020c,velumani2021,adak2023 . Much of this work summarizes plots or canopies through spectral response, vegetation indices, temperature, or height. These measurements are valuable for monitoring crop status, but canopy summaries do not directly represent the morphology and development of individual leaves, tassels, ears, brace roots, or damaged tissues. Those structures are often where the effects of genotype, development, disease, and environmental stress become visible. Extracting reliable plant-level information from aerial imagery is itself a computer vision problem. Crop fields contain repeated rows and visually similar plants, while moving foliage, illumination changes, shadows, and soil backgrounds introduce additional appearance variability. In freely flown maize video, limited telemetry and the repetition of plants and rows also complicate frame registration and mosaic construction kharismawati2025a,aktar2020,kharismawati2020 . A successful field pipeline therefore depends not only on the downstream model, but also on what the acquisition makes observable, whether images can be registered consistently, and whether the representation preserves the spatial relationships required by the phenotype of interest. This dependence on representation is also evident in maize stand counting, where detections registered directly from raw video frames agreed more closely with field counts than detections from mosaicked imagery kharismawati2025 . Organ-level phenotyping particularly requires structural information. A two-dimensional image projects different depths onto the same plane: organs from adjacent plants may overlap, a front leaf may hide an ear or stem, and a visible fragment may be difficult to assign to its plant of origin. A three-dimensional representation can preserve relative position and orientation and can support organ segmentation and structural measurement li2022c,li2022d,yang2024 . This potential is especially relevant in maize. Its leaves are long, thin, curved, and flexible; tassels contain many fine branches; ears and silks may be partly concealed; brace roots occur near a cluttered soil boundary; and neighboring plants crowd each other as the canopy closes. The same morphology that makes a three-dimensional representation useful also makes it difficult to construct. Recent studies demonstrate what can be achieved when acquisition is sufficiently controlled. Multi-view reconstruction has supported measurements of plant height, leaf length, leaf width, and relative leaf area in maize seedlings li2022c . Organ-level point-cloud segmentation has enabled extraction of leaf inclination, leaf growth height, and related structural traits from individual maize shoots li2022d . Larger annotated maize point-cloud datasets further demonstrate the importance of preserving stem and leaf geometry for automated analysis across diverse architectures yang2024 . LiDAR, controlled multi-camera systems, and turntable imaging can likewise provide detailed plant models luo2021a,yin2020,lin2021,gollob2021,zhu2020a . These results establish the value of plant-scale data, but many of these approaches rely on stationary or potted plants, structured imaging platforms, controlled backgrounds, or carefully constrained camera motion. Such conditions reduce the challenges associated with plant movement, occlusion, and variable illumination, but are difficult to reproduce at the scale of an open agricultural field. Consequently, methods that perform well under controlled conditions may not scale readily to field environments, where large plant populations and dense canopies make it difficult to capture the structural details of individual plants. Field-grown plants present several challenges for conventional three-dimensional reconstruction methods. Structure from Motion (SfM) estimates camera poses from correspondences among images, while multi-view stereo densifies the recovered scene schoenberger2016,schoenberger2016a . Both are most straightforward when the scene is rigid, distinctive visual features persist across views, and each surface is observed repeatedly schoenberger2016,schoenberger2016a . Maize has slender organs and extensive self-occlusion, which can produce incomplete leaves and missing tips in multi-view reconstructions wu2022a,li2022c . Wind can move individual organs while images are recorded, and variable illumination can change their appearance between views wu2022a,li2022c . At range scale, overlapping leaves and increasingly dense canopies increase occlusion and make individual plants more difficult to separate zermas2020,sweet2022 . Consequently, a failure may reflect missing observations, nonrigid movement, ambiguous correspondence, insufficient image resolution, or a combination of these factors rather than simply an inadequate number of frames. UAV reconstruction has been successful for field structure and plant height estimation, but it has often emphasized canopy-scale surfaces rather than individual organs zermas2020 . Acquisition geometry is critical because a reconstruction cannot recover a surface that was never observed. In field maize canopies, oblique photography produced more complete vertical profiles than nadir photography and recovered substantially more points below the upper canopy che2020 . A crop-surface-model study similarly found that oblique views improved maize reconstruction relative to nadir views and that reduced spatial resolution lowered plant height accuracy niu2024a . Controlled multi-view platforms impose overlap requirements within and between camera levels and report incomplete leaves and tips when coverage is insufficient; wind and variable illumination remain important limitations when such systems move outside controlled environments wu2022a . Together, this literature indicates that camera placement, overlap, distance, and view angle determine which structural evidence is available for reconstruction. This creates a field acquisition trade-off that is not captured by frame count alone. Sampling many adjacent frames from a video can increase temporal redundancy and local point density, but closely spaced frames may contribute nearly the same evidence and cannot expose a persistently occluded surface gibbs2020 . Changing elevation or camera angle can reveal surfaces that are hidden in nadir or single-level views che2020,niu2024a,wu2022a . Longer acquisitions also increase exposure to wind-driven motion of flexible plant organs, which can reduce consistency among views wu2022a,kharismawati2026 . Flying farther away increases coverage but decreases spatial resolution and the number of pixels representing a leaf edge, tassel branch, or silk niu2024a . Thus, temporal sampling, viewpoint diversity, target resolution, acquisition duration, and scene motion interact. A fair comparison must hold at least the source sequence and image budget constant rather than equating more frames or more reconstructed points with better evidence. Given the prior work, it is not obvious that plants in field environments can be reconstructed sufficiently for organ phenotyping. We therefore undertook a qualitative proof-of-concept study to determine the feasibility of plant reconstructions for different planting situations in the field, moving from isolated plants to the standard nursery planting of rows and ranges. Here, we show that plants in field environments can be reconstructed in three dimensions for organ phenotyping from video shot from consumer-grade . We explore different planting schemes and trajectories and examine the trade-offs between these, reconstruction quality and resolution, and acquisition times. Established software such as makes SfM and multi-view stereo accessible without requiring a new reconstruction algorithm colmap,schoenberger2016 . The unresolved question is what a conventional and reproducible workflow can recover from video of mature maize in the field and what limits emerge as acquisition scales up from one to many plants. This is important for researchers designing data acquisition strategies, whether with their existing or any prospective purchase of specialized, more complex instruments. This study makes three contributions. First, it demonstrates the feasibility of imaging unstructured fields and the quality of the three-dimensional reconstructions of maize plants and their organs, including leaves, tassels, ears, silks, and brace roots. title: Competent Autonomous Driving Through Fine Tuning Vision Language Action Models with Symbolic Traffic Rules
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a unified approach to perception, reasoning, and control for autonomous driving, but accurate action prediction alone does not establish compliance with traffic regulations. This paper presents a rule-guided VLA framework that incorporates symbolic traffic-rule feedback into policy optimisation. The framework combines supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations with reinforcement learning (RL) refinement using a reward that encourages encoded-rule compliance while penalising deviations from expert actions. Selected provisions of the United Kingdom Highway Code are formalised as executable first-order logic rules using PyReason, covering speed adaptation, following distance, and road-user priority. A frozen vision-language model extracts scene predicates, which are combined with vehicle-state information to assess the projected consequences of candidate control actions. Offline evaluation on held-out data collected in the CARLA simulator compares three group-based RL methods. The results show improvements in both action prediction accuracy and encoded-rule compliance over the supervised baseline. The best-performing variant increases the overall rule pass rate from 92.9% to 97.6%, with zero observed violations of the encoded road-user-priority check in the evaluated samples. These findings support symbolic rule feedback as a means of improving VLA policy alignment with explicit traffic-rule criteria.

Introduction utonomous driving requires intelligent systems capable of perceiving complex environments, reasoning about dynamic traffic situations, and executing safe driving manoeuvres that comply with traffic regulations hu2026vla . End-to-end learning addresses these interconnected tasks by mapping sensor observations to driving actions within a unified differentiable model. By jointly optimising perception and control, such approaches simplify system design and learn representations of complex driving behaviour chen2024e2e . However, ensuring that learned policies comply with explicit traffic rules remains a challenge. Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have expanded the role of semantic scene understanding and language-based reasoning in autonomous driving jiang2025,yildirim2025 . Frameworks such as DriveLM, LMDrive, and DriveGPT4 explore connections between scene understanding, reasoning, planning, and vehicle control drivelm,lmdrive,drivegpt4 . Vision-language-action (VLA) models further integrate multimodal observations, language, and action generation within a shared framework. Related models and benchmarks investigate the capabilities and limitations of these approaches in scene understanding, visual grounding, and driving decision-making guo2024drivemllm,jiang2024senna,xie2025drivebench,zhou2025opendrivevla,dvlm-ad,simlingo,cfvla,perceptwam . Their development extends beyond imitation learning: AutoVLA employs reinforcement learning (RL) to refine planning and reasoning efficiency zhou2025autovla , while AutoDrive-R uses RL to improve reasoning and self-reflection autodrive . Nevertheless, imitation objectives measure agreement with demonstrations, and RL objectives depend on the chosen rewards; neither inherently provides an explicit assessment of compliance with codified traffic rules. Symbolic representations offer a means of making these requirements explicit. Traffic rules describe context-dependent constraints on driving behaviour, which can be encoded as logical conditions and evaluated against scene and vehicle-state information. Previous research has integrated symbolic knowledge into learning-based autonomous driving to support safety Sharifi_2 , interpretability Sharifi_1 , and policy alignment asodia2026 . SafeAuto safeauto , for example, represents traffic regulations using Markov logic networks to assess whether generated behaviours satisfy specified constraints. These developments motivate connecting symbolic rule evaluation with VLA policy refinement. The challenge addressed here is to translate contextual traffic-rule checks into action-dependent feedback that directly guides continuous-control policy optimisation. This paper proposes a rule-guided VLA framework that integrates symbolic traffic-rule evaluation into a two-stage learning procedure. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) first adapts a pretrained VLM using expert driving actions and reference reasoning annotations. Reinforcement learning fine-tuning (RLFT) then refines the policy using a reward that combines rule-compliance feedback with a penalty for deviation from expert actions. Selected provisions of the United Kingdom (UK) Highway Code ukhighwaycode are formalised as executable first-order logic (FOL) rules using the PyReason symbolic reasoning engine pyreason . A separate frozen VLM extracts scene predicates, which are combined with vehicle-state information to evaluate the projected consequences of candidate actions. The resulting checks cover speed adaptation, following distance, and road-user priority, providing explicit learning signals for compliance with the encoded criteria. We investigate this framework using three group-based optimisation methods: group relative policy optimisation (GRPO) deepseek,grpo , group reward-decoupled normalisation policy optimisation (GDPO) gdpo , and GRPO Done Right (Dr.~GRPO) drgrpo . Offline experiments on held-out simulated driving data compare action prediction accuracy and encoded-rule compliance, while ablations examine the contribution of individual rules to policy refinement. The results show improvements over the SFT baseline in both evaluated objectives, supporting the use of symbolic rule feedback within the studied setting. The main contributions are as follows: We develop a VLA fine-tuning framework that incorporates symbolic traffic-rule feedback into policy optimisation while encouraging consistency with expert driving actions. We formalise selected UK Highway Code provisions as executable FOL rules and construct a symbolic evaluator that assesses candidate actions against context-dependent compliance criteria. We compare GRPO, GDPO, and Dr.~GRPO through offline evaluation and rule ablations, examining their effects on action prediction accuracy and compliance with the encoded rules. title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://jhxcho.github.io/voda/
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments We evaluate VODA on two standard 3DGS segmentation benchmarks, LERF and ScanNet, in sec:exp_compat , and on our Removal-3D benchmark for volumetric evaluation in sec:exp_removal . We further ablate its design choices in sec:exp_ablation and analyze recovered Gaussians and contribution-based alternatives in sec:exp_analysis . We evaluate four baselines spanning both feature-learning paradigms in sec:rw_rendering_based_feature_learning : OpenGaussian~ wu2024opengaussian and LaGa~ cen2025laga are self-supervised, while Gaussian Grouping~ ye2024gaussiangrouping and ILGS~ jsmbankILGS are supervised. Implementation details. We implement VODA on the official codebase of each baseline and apply it only to the feature-learning stage, leaving RGB reconstruction and inference unchanged. The depth-clustering and loss hyperparameters are shared across all four baselines. VODA is applied within the existing feature stage for OpenGaussian and LaGa, and as a short feature-only fine-tuning stage for Gaussian Grouping and ILGS. Full implementation details are provided in the supplementary. Comparison on Standard Benchmarks sec:exp_compat We evaluate VODA on two complementary standard settings probing different aspects of 3D scene understanding: open-vocabulary 3D object selection on LERF and semantic segmentation on ScanNet. 3D Object Selection on LERF. Following OpenGaussian, we perform open-vocabulary 3D object selection by selecting a set of Gaussians for each text query and rendering only that set into multiple views. We compare these rendered masks with the ground-truth object masks from LangSplat~ qin2024langsplat , reporting mIoU and the percentage of queries whose IoU exceeds (mAcc@0.25). Because selection precedes rendering, this protocol evaluates a single 3D Gaussian selection consistently across views rather than independently segmenting each rendered image. Gaussian Grouping and ILGS originally produce 2D segmentations by rendering first and then grouping the rendered features. We instead evaluate them with the same select-then-render protocol as OpenGaussian and LaGa, so their results differ from those reported in the original papers. Table~ table:lerf shows that VODA improves the average mIoU and mAcc@0.25 across all four baselines. The gains are particularly large for Gaussian Grouping and ILGS, although a few individual scenes show slight regressions. Figure~ fig:lerf_text_query shows that VODA recovers missing object parts while reducing spurious selections. 3D Semantic Segmentation on ScanNet. Following OpenGaussian, we use 19, 15, and 10 ScanNetv2~ dai2017scannet categories as text queries and assign each Gaussian to its most similar query. We transfer these predictions to the ScanNet point cloud and report mIoU and mAcc against the ground-truth semantic labels. ScanNet complements LERF by evaluating category-level semantic assignment over the entire scene rather than object-level selection from individual text queries. Table~ table:scannet shows consistent improvements for both OpenGaussian and LaGa across all three category splits as the semantic label set changes from 19 to 10 classes. The gains remain consistent across different category splits, suggesting that VODA is not tied to a particular semantic class partition. Gaussian Grouping and ILGS are not applicable because their features are tied to per-view SAM mask identities, which the ScanNet text-query protocol does not provide. Figure~ fig:scannet_qual shows that VODA produces cleaner semantic assignments around object boundaries, with less label leakage across neighboring regions. However, ScanNet ground-truth labels cover only visible surfaces in the reconstructed point cloud and therefore cannot directly assess occluded object-associated Gaussians, motivating our volumetric benchmark. Comparison on Volumetric Benchmark sec:exp_removal Removal-3D. Standard benchmarks evaluate rendered masks or visible surface labels, but cannot determine whether the selected set covers all Gaussians associated with the 3D object. In particular, they do not test whether removing the selected Gaussians reveals the surfaces expected after removing the object itself. We construct Removal-3D, a synthetic benchmark with three indoor scenes (Table, Kitchen, and Room) built in Blender using BlenderKit assets. For each target object, the benchmark provides paired depth maps of the full scene and the scene after ground-truth object removal. Removal Depth Error. We introduce the Removal Depth Error (RDE) to compare this reference depth change with the change induced by removing the predicted Gaussian set: where denotes the ground-truth target mask region, and and are the predicted and reference depth changes, respectively. The function clips the predicted change to the range bounded by the magnitude of the reference change before computing absolute error. We obtain per-scene mRDE by averaging over viewpoints and target objects, and report the mean across the three scenes as the overall score. Because RDE is evaluated only within the target object mask, selections outside this region do not affect the score. We therefore report rendered-mask mIoU alongside RDE as a complementary measure. RDE measures whether the selected Gaussians remove the target volume as expected, while mIoU measures whether the selection remains spatially aligned with the target in rendered views. The complete computation is provided in the supplementary. Volumetric Evaluation on Removal-3D. Table~ table:rde shows consistent reductions in mRDE for every baseline and scene, together with improved mIoU. The improvement holds across both feature-learning paradigms, demonstrating improved Gaussian-level selection completeness on Removal-3D, a property standard benchmarks leave unmeasured. The mIoU gains suggest that lower mRDE is not achieved by simply expanding the selected set. Figure~ fig:custom_qual complements the LERF and ScanNet visualizations by rendering each scene after removing the queried Gaussians. For the ``toy duck'' and ``hamburger'' queries, the baselines leave residual target content, indicating that some object Gaussians remain unselected. VODA leaves less residual content and better reveals the occluded surface. Ablation Study sec:exp_ablation We ablate supervision delivery, the pixel-level push, and target aggregation using OpenGaussian and Gaussian Grouping as representatives of self-supervised and supervised feature learning. Supervision delivery. We compare VODA's direct loss with a rendering variant that uses the same selected depth clusters and target features, but delivers supervision through feature rendering. Thus, the two variants differ only in how supervision reaches the selected Gaussians. Direct supervision consistently performs better across both baselines on LERF and Removal-3D, with the largest difference on Gaussian Grouping, where LERF mIoU rises from 12.40 to 43.73. This shows that identifying the appropriate depth cluster is not sufficient. Supervision must also bypass the contribution-weighted rendering path and reach the selected Gaussian features directly. Pixel-level push. We next isolate the pixel-level push loss while retaining direct supervision. The push loss has little effect on standard LERF performance, but consistently improves volumetric selection on Removal-3D. This supports its complementary role to direct supervision. Direct supervision improves Gaussian coverage, while the push loss reduces feature mixing between nearby instances and improves volumetric selection. Boundary visualizations in the supplementary illustrate this effect. Target aggregation. Finally, we compare uniform averaging with the -weighted aggregation in Eq.~ eq:target_aggregation . Alpha weighting yields modest but consistent improvements across both baselines, supporting the choice to place greater trust in pixels where the selected Gaussian has a higher per-pixel alpha. Overall, the ablation shows that direct supervision provides the primary benefit, while the pixel-level push improves instance separation and weighting improves target reliability. Analysis sec:exp_analysis We next test whether the Gaussians additionally recovered by VODA are precisely those that receive weak supervision through the rendering path, and whether simpler reweighting or spatial propagation can address the same failure mode. Rendering contribution of recovered Gaussians. Using LaGa, we compare Gaussians retrieved by the baseline with those missed by the baseline but recovered after adding VODA. For each Gaussian, we record its maximum rendering contribution over all training pixels and views. Because the baseline and VODA checkpoints share identical geometry and opacity, as detailed in the supplementary, these contribution statistics are measured under the same scene geometry. Figure~ fig:contribution_distribution shows that the recovered Gaussians are consistently shifted toward lower rendering contribution on Removal-3D. At the cutoff, the fraction of low-contribution Gaussians is 10.2--15.9 percentage points higher in the recovered set across the three scenes. The supplementary extends this analysis to six scenes, with accumulated-contribution statistics showing the same trend. This directly supports our diagnosis that VODA preferentially recovers Gaussians with weaker baseline supervision. Contribution reweighting and spatial propagation. Table~ table:alternative_baselines tests whether the imbalance can be addressed without explicitly assigning supervision through depth clusters. Normalize and Clamp rescale the rendering gradient, while KNN propagates features from nearby high-contribution Gaussians. None of these alternatives matches VODA. All three substantially degrade volumetric performance for OpenGaussian, while for Gaussian Grouping, Normalize improves LERF performance but severely degrades Removal-3D. These failures reflect a limitation of contribution-based heuristics. Rendering contribution alone does not indicate whether a Gaussian is associated with the target object. Reweighting therefore cannot identify the relevant low-contribution Gaussians or recover those that receive no rendered gradient. Indeed, across the six analyzed scenes, 8.5--18.7 of recovered Gaussians receive zero contribution in every training view. KNN avoids this zero-gradient issue, but spatial proximity likewise does not establish object association and may propagate features across object boundaries.

title: STARS: Stage-Adaptive Responsibility Separation for Shadow Removal in Remote Sensing Images
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables
summary: Shadows are a ubiquitous radiative attenuation phenomenon in remote sensing images and can severely affect high-resolution remote sensing interpretation tasks. In shadow removal, although introducing a mask prior provides explicit positional information for the restoration network, it also causes non-shadow regions to be modulated by the shadow prior, producing a systematic brightness shift; notably, this phenomenon is independent of whether the mask is accurate. In remote sensing images, non-shadow regions usually occupy a larger proportion, so a small shift over these regions incurs a much higher cost on whole-image metrics than an equal gain in shadow regions. Adopting a task-decoupling perspective, we therefore decompose shadow removal into two tasks, shadow-region restoration and non-shadow-region identity, within a cascaded architecture, and handle them sequentially. Based on this insight, we propose STARS, a cascaded shadow removal framework that separates regional responsibilities across stages. The method retains the advantages of the shadow mask while resolving the degradation of non-shadow regions, without requiring a complex parallel dual-branch structure. Meanwhile, to introduce large-model prior knowledge into remote sensing tasks, we further design a Feature Selection and Fusion Adapter (FSFA). We conduct extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, UAV-SC+, ISTD+ and WSRD+ 2026, demonstrating the superiority of STARS. The framework shows that decoupling regional responsibilities can resolve the intrinsic contradiction of mask priors, providing a new direction for image restoration with region heterogeneity.
full_text: Shadows are a ubiquitous radiative attenuation phenomenon in remote sensing images and can severely affect high-resolution remote sensing interpretation tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, UAV-SC+, ISTD+ and WSRD+ 2026, demonstrating the superiority of STARS. The framework shows that decoupling regional responsibilities can resolve the intrinsic contradiction of mask priors, providing a new direction for image restoration with region heterogeneity. Introduction Shadows are a radiative attenuation phenomenon caused by objects occluding light ref1,ref2 . In high-resolution optical remote sensing images, shadows weaken the radiance information within shadowed areas, compress the dynamic range and alter the spectral distribution, posing significant interference to downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation ref3,ref1,ref2,ref4 . Shadow removal is therefore an important research direction in remote sensing image processing ref1,ref2 . In recent years, deep-learning-based shadow removal has advanced rapidly ref1,ref2,ref5 . The shadow mask provides the most direct positional prior for the removal network: the detected shadow region exactly indicates the area to be restored, and introducing it as an input channel or an attention condition can substantially improve restoration quality in shadowed regions ref6,ref7,ref8 . However, models that use a mask prior often exhibit the following phenomenon: for mask-conditioned networks such as ShadowFormer, the shadow and non-shadow regions are optimized jointly by a single set of weights, the two tasks compete during optimization, and the fidelity of non-shadow regions degrades markedly; for models such as SGCR-SR that originally contain no mask prior, directly introducing the mask improves restoration in shadowed regions but induces a systematic brightness shift in non-shadow regions, as shown in Fig.~ fig1 . In remote sensing images, shadowed areas typically occupy only a small fraction of the whole image; sacrificing large non-shadow regions for better shadow restoration incurs losses far exceeding the gains. Methods that abandon the mask (e.g., OmniSR ref11 , SGCR-SR ref9 ) circumvent this problem but also discard the positional prior, limiting shadow restoration. This paper therefore seeks to retain the spatial prior of the mask while systematically resolving its side effect on non-shadow regions. The key to this lies in decoupling shadow removal by region: the task of the shadow region is to remove the shadow, whereas the task of the non-shadow region is to remain unchanged, and the two conflicting regional tasks should be explicitly separated and accomplished sequentially. We realize this decoupling with a cascaded architecture and the shadow mask. In a cascade, the output of the previous stage is the input of the next, so a complex task can naturally be split across stages, and each stage has independent parameters, so adjusting the responsibility of one stage does not alter the structure of the others. Meanwhile, the shadow mask is an explicit regional marker. Combining the two, we let the shadow mask serve as a regional task marker so that the two conflicting regional tasks are assigned to different stages of the cascade, realizing an explicit division of regional tasks. Based on this understanding, we propose a responsibility separation strategy, STARS (Stage-Adaptive Responsibility Separation), with the following contributions: [itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt,topsep=2pt,partopsep=0pt] We propose a cascaded responsibility separation strategy. This design turns the mask from a conventional spatial conditioning input into an explicit mechanism for coordinating regional restoration tasks across stages; the shadow removal task is decoupled into two regional sub-tasks that are assigned to different stages and accomplished sequentially. We design a feature selection and fusion adapter that transfers DINOv3 semantic features, developed for natural images, to remote sensing shadow removal, offering a new solution for feature transfer and fusion between natural and remote sensing images. We design a region-specific loss for non-shadow regions, which guarantees at the optimization level that the assigned responsibilities are actually executed, complementing the structural division. Related Work Shadow Processing in Remote Sensing Images Shadow processing in remote sensing has evolved from physical models to data-driven methods. Early methods predict shadow extents using solar geometry parameters and digital elevation models (DEM) ref12,ref13 , or estimate illumination compensation in shadowed regions with complex irradiance models ref14,ref15 ; feature-based methods extract shadow attributes in specific color spaces and texture domains and apply thresholds ref16 . These methods rely on high-accuracy auxiliary data or hand-crafted features, adapt poorly to complex urban environments, and often produce incomplete detections or hard reconstruction artifacts ref12,ref13,ref15 . In recent years, deep learning has become the mainstream. Shadow detection in remote sensing follows binary semantic segmentation, and dense prediction frameworks such as U-Net with spatial attention have significantly improved detection accuracy in complex scenes ref5 . Remote sensing shadow removal advances along two lines: end-to-end networks without shadow detection, e.g., ESCNet ref1 builds the UAV-SC benchmark and performs restoration and radiometric correction with two subnets, and methods targeting shadow distribution properties, e.g., RMMamba ref2 balances shadow pixels via random rearrangement and a color prior, while RSMamba ref17 combines a Retinex prior with state-space modeling. Methods in the natural image domain fall into two categories: mask conditioning (ST-CGAN ref6 takes the mask as input; ShadowFormer ref8 uses mask-weighted residuals and attention) and regional modeling (DMTN ref18 decouples detection and removal; RASM ref19 applies regional attention). Both complete the restoration of the two regions with shared weights; the mask prior degrades non-shadow fidelity, and the regional conflict remains unresolved at the structural level. Semantic and Geometric Guidance and Cascaded Refinement Task-agnostic representations from self-supervised visual foundation models are widely used as frozen guidance for restoration: DINOv2 ref20 demonstrates the robustness and transferability of self-supervised ViT features, DINOv3 ref21 extends the training to large-scale data, and Depth Anything v2 ref22 provides monocular depth from which point maps and normals can be derived; OmniSR ref11 and SGCR-SR ref9 introduce such cues into shadow removal as representative baselines. Progressive refinement, where later stages correct residual artifacts of earlier ones ref23,ref24 , is a classical restoration paradigm: ESCNet ref1 divides restoration and radiometric compensation into two stages, while Li et al. ref10 prove that shadow restoration and non-shadow identity mapping are incompatible under shared weights and propose parallel dual branches (IMB/IDB) to separate them. We therefore change the strategy: instead of trying to prevent the brightness shift in non-shadow regions, we allow it to appear first and then decouple the correction of the brightness shift from shadow removal as a new task assigned to the last stage. In the three-stage cascade used here, this decoupling and division are guided by a bidirectional shadow mask. Since remote sensing scenes lack manual shadow annotations and no ground-truth mask exists at inference time, can only be estimated from the shadow image itself, independently of the removal network, so as to avoid coupling with model parameters. title: FAVR: Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Policies

summary: Pretrained video representations provide rich temporal information for robotic manipulation, yet effectively integrating them into existing vision-language-action (VLA) policies remains challenging. We present Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment (FAVR), a lightweight framework for flow-aware visual conditioning of frozen VLA policies. FAVR maintains a compact temporal visual state through linear Test-Time Training (TTT) and retrieves action-conditioned visual features throughout flow-based action generation. By exploiting the affine structure of the frozen action head, we explicitly characterize how injected visual features influence predicted action velocities and formulate flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem. We develop a FISTA-based solver for joint gate optimization and derive an efficient closed-form approximation through diagonalization and rescaling. With only 1.74-2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps, FAVR improves pretrained VLA policies across benchmarks. On RoboTwin 2.0, FAVR improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12% to 90.04% under clean conditions and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomized conditions. A controlled ablation on five RoboTwin tasks further shows that flow-aware gating increases average success from 72.0% with a gate shared across flow steps to 82.0%, demonstrating the benefit of adapting visual conditioning throughout action generation.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language representations to robotic control. Flow-based policies such as and generate continuous action chunks conditioned on visual observations and language instructions~ pi0,pi05 . Video pretraining provides a complementary source of visual knowledge by learning representations of scene structure, object interactions, and temporal evolution~ vjepa,vjepa2,vjepa21 . Recent studies demonstrate the benefits of incorporating video representations into VLA policies~ jepavla,pvi , raising the question of how to effectively use them within existing action policies. Incorporating video representations requires more than aggregating temporal information and retrieving action-relevant features: the retrieved features must also benefit action generation. For flow-based policies, action chunks are constructed through successive velocity evaluations. Although the visual context remains fixed within an action chunk, the noisy action representation and corresponding policy features evolve across flow steps, so the appropriate visual contribution may also change. While state-dependent retrieval can implicitly learn this contribution, it does not explicitly account for the induced corrections in the action-velocity space. This motivates explicit velocity-residual alignment across flow steps. We introduce Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment (FAVR), a lightweight framework that integrates pretrained video representations into frozen VLA policies. FAVR employs linear Test-Time Training (TTT)~ ttt to aggregate features from a frozen video encoder into a compact temporal visual state, queried by the current action features at each flow step. Learned projections adapt state construction and retrieval to the control task. A lightweight predictor estimates the target velocity residual, while the frozen affine action head provides an exact mapping from gated visual features to velocity corrections. We formulate flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained velocity-residual alignment problem and employ a FISTA-based solver to jointly optimize channel weights while accounting for their interactions. The gated visual features are injected through a residual connection immediately before the action head. Both pretrained backbones remain frozen, with only the auxiliary visual interface and residual predictor trained. Joint gate optimization, however, requires iterative computation at each flow step. To reduce this overhead, we derive an approximate closed-form gate through diagonalization and analytic rescaling, simplifying channel interactions and calibrating the resulting correction. A coupling-dependent error bound characterizes the effect of the omitted interactions. The approximation reduces computational cost at the expense of a modest portion of the joint solver's performance gains. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:flow_aware_motivation , the flow-aware gating employed by FAVR adapts channel weights across flow steps, unlike a shared gate. On five RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, this design improves average success from 72.0 to 82.0 . We evaluate FAVR on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world dual-arm manipulation tasks. With only 1.74--2.19M additional trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps in simulation, FAVR achieves 98.6 and 85.05 success on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, respectively, using . On RoboTwin 2.0, it improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12 to 90.04 under clean conditions and from 86.88 to 89.38 under randomized conditions. Real-world experiments further show improvements in block pick-and-place and paper-cup grasping over continued fine-tuning. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce FAVR, a lightweight framework that integrates temporal video representations into frozen VLA policies through action-conditioned retrieval and flow-aware visual conditioning. We formulate visual channel selection as a box-constrained velocity-residual alignment problem, with a FISTA-based joint solver and an approximate closed-form solution supported by a coupling-dependent error bound. We validate FAVR across three manipulation benchmarks and real-world experiments, with controlled ablations demonstrating the benefits of flow-aware gating and velocity-residual alignment. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer pretrained visual and language representations to robotic manipulation, as exemplified by OpenVLA~ openvla . OpenVLA-OFT improves action generation through parallel decoding, action chunking, and continuous regression~ oft . Flow-based policies such as ~ pi0 , ~ pi05 , and LingBot-VLA~ lingbot combine pretrained vision-language backbones with action experts trained using flow matching~ flowmatching , generating continuous action chunks through successive velocity evaluations. Video Representations for Robot Control. Video pretraining captures scene structure and temporal dynamics, as demonstrated by the V-JEPA series~ vjepa,vjepa2,vjepa21 . WorldVLA and DreamVLA incorporate visual prediction into action generation through autoregressive modeling and diffusion conditioning, respectively~ worldvla,dreamvla . JEPA-VLA integrates frozen V-JEPA~2 features through input fusion or gated cross-attention~ jepavla , while PVI injects auxiliary visual features through a trainable action expert conditioned on the current noisy action~ pvi . Both studies show that video-pretrained representations can outperform image-pretrained features in robotic manipulation~ jepavla,pvi . Test-Time Training for Robot Policies. Test-time training (TTT) maintains recurrent states through self-supervised fast-weight updates~ ttt . Recent studies have extended TTT to robotic policies, enabling the aggregation of historical observations and action-generation features to support temporally informed control~ robottt,recastvla,wamttt . Unlike methods that incorporate fast-weight updates within pretrained policy components, FAVR employs linear TTT as an external temporal visual interface, aggregating features from a frozen video encoder and retrieving them using current action features at each flow step. Time-Dependent Conditioning in Diffusion and Flow Models. Diffusion Policy conditions action denoising on noisy actions and diffusion timesteps~ diffusionpolicy . Beyond classifier-free guidance (CFG)~ cfg , prior work explores noise-dependent guidance intervals~ limited_guidance , condition annealing~ cads , and dynamically adjusted guidance scales~ dynamic_cfg,adaptive_cfg . Related studies analyze guidance in probability-flow dynamics and flow matching~ analytic_cfg,flow_guidance . These works motivate time-dependent conditioning, while FAVR explicitly optimizes channel-wise visual contributions according to their induced velocity corrections through a frozen VLA action head. title: POKE: Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, but attention-based scores do not directly measure a token's effect on the predicted action. We define action sensitivity as the magnitude of the first-order action change when a token is replaced by its camera's mean token and estimate it for all tokens with a single backward pass. Computing it online is costly: scoring on the full (unpruned) graph needs an extra forward pass at every control step. Scoring on the pruned forward pass is cheaper but causes scoring-graph lock-in: removed tokens lose their direct paths through later layers and tend to receive lower scores, making those locations less likely to return. On replayed observations, even with a random conditioning mask, pruned-graph scoring re-selects 59% of the mask's tokens, versus 6% expected by chance; attention histories show a similar bias. POKE (Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently) computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with under 0.3M parameters. At inference, the student scores the current observation without backpropagation or previous masks, and score-guided diversity selection retains the tokens. Keeping 32 of 512 visual tokens on LIBERO, POKE achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on $π_{0.5}$ at $1.85\times$ and $1.26\times$ speedups, outperforming attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners, with larger margins on LIBERO-Plus.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models convert camera images and language instructions into robot actions. Their visual inputs often contain hundreds of tokens, making visual token pruning a practical way to reduce inference cost. Removing tokens in early layers reduces computation in every subsequent layer, so a pruner has to decide which tokens to keep while preserving the policy's actions. Existing methods, however, use attention as a proxy for this decision, including attention received by visual tokens~ chen2024image , temporal aggregation of action-to-visual attention~ liu2025bridging , and attention combined with inter-frame similarity~ xu2026vla . These signals describe how tokens are attended to or reused. Yet the tokens a model attends to most need not be the ones that determine its actions, and none of these signals directly measures how changing a token changes the resulting action. We therefore define token importance by action sensitivity: the magnitude of the first-order change in the action when a visual token is replaced with its camera-wise mean representation. Since importance is defined at the policy output, it applies to both parallel-regression and flow-based action heads, using the final action chunk for the latter. In Fig.~ fig:intro_score , attention-based masks keep only the bowl and gripper, whereas action sensitivity also keeps the target plate. Computing exact sensitivities requires one backward pass per action dimension: 56 for a chunk of eight 7-D actions in OpenVLA-OFT. Projecting the action onto one shared random direction reduces this to a single backward pass for all tokens. Even so, scoring online on the full graph needs an extra unpruned forward and backward pass per control step, running and slower than the unpruned OpenVLA-OFT and policies, which defeats the purpose of pruning. A cheaper alternative scores tokens on the pruned forward pass and uses the scores to select the next frame’s tokens. Each frame enters with all visual tokens, but the previous mask removes some before the later layers, so those tokens lose their direct paths to the action and tend to score lower. When these scores set the next mask, removed locations are less likely to return. We call this scoring-graph lock-in (Fig.~ fig:intro_lockin ). Even when the previous mask is drawn at random, pruned-graph scores re-select 59 of its tokens, against 6 expected by chance, and switching to full-graph scoring raises closed-loop success ( sec:exp_graph ). The same lock-in appears in the attention histories that VLA pruners reuse from earlier control steps~ liu2025bridging,wang2025specprune . Scores therefore need a path independent of prior pruning decisions. We propose POKE (Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently), which separates importance estimation from inference. POKE computes full-graph action-sensitivity labels offline on observations from the policy's fine-tuning demonstrations and distills them into a lightweight student with fewer than 0.3M parameters, keeping the policy frozen. Labeling takes under one GPU-hour per suite. At inference, the student predicts scores from the current visual tokens, language, and state context in a single forward pass, removing online backpropagation and any conditioning on previous masks. Tokens are then selected either by top- ranking or by diversity selection within a high-scoring candidate set; the latter reduces redundancy while keeping sensitivity-based candidate filtering. The full policy thus provides the training signal, and the deployed selector adds only a small scoring and selection cost. On four LIBERO suites~ liu2023libero , keeping 32 of 512 visual tokens, POKE reaches 95.15 success at on OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine and 90.80 at on ~ intelligence2025pi , exceeding VLA-Pruner by 5.90 and 15.75~pp, and the margin grows under the observation shifts of LIBERO-Plus ( sec:exp_liberoplus ). In contrast, distilling attention labels instead of action sensitivity lowers success in all eight tested combinations ( sec:exp_ablation ). Our contributions are threefold: Action sensitivity for visual token pruning. An action-grounded, first-order measure of token importance estimated with one shared-probe backward pass, together with an exact pairwise analysis of its ranking behavior. Scoring-graph lock-in. Controlled interventions and fixed-observation replays show that pruned-graph scores favor retained tokens even without feedback, for both gradients and attention histories. POKE via full-graph sensitivity distillation. A compact selector trained offline that prunes without backpropagation or previous masks, improving the success-latency trade-off over attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based baselines on parallel-regression, flow-based, and autoregressive policies on LIBERO and SimplerEnv. Related Work Visual Token Pruning sec:related_visual_pruning Visual token reduction selects or aggregates tokens depending on the input. DynamicViT~ rao2021dynamicvit and EViT~ liang2022not prune or fuse less informative tokens. In vision-language models (e.g., LLaVA~ liu2024improved ), FastV~ chen2024image prunes visual tokens by early-layer attention, VisionZip~ yang2025visionzip combines encoder attention with similarity-based aggregation, and VisPruner~ zhang2025beyond , DART~ wen2025stop , and CDPruner~ zhang2026beyond add distinctive, non-redundant, or instruction-conditioned diverse tokens. zou2026don argue that concentrating the budget on highly attended tokens discards holistic visual context. These works establish importance and diversity as complementary criteria; we study them for preserving actions in closed-loop. Distillation-based Token Pruning sec:related_distill Distillation transfers expensive importance signals to efficient token selectors. ToP~ li2023constraint distills final-layer token rankings into earlier layers, SDTP~ tao2025saliency trains in-network pruning modules on gradient-times-input saliency of hidden states with regression and ranking losses, and MAP~ sun2026learning distills middle-layer text-to-vision attention into an input-level predictor and combines it with diversity; we compare against an adaptation of MAP in sec:exp . First-order expansions also underlie Taylor pruning criteria~ molchanov2017pruning , which estimate the change in loss. POKE instead distills the first-order change in the predicted robot action chunk under a camera-mean token replacement, scores tokens before the policy's Transformer layers, and examines how the computation graph used to obtain these scores affects selection over successive control steps. Efficient Visual Token Processing in VLAs sec:related_vla VLA-specific methods exploit task context and temporal structure during control. Many select tokens from attention or task reused from earlier control steps: VLA-Pruner~ liu2025bridging fuses semantic importance with temporally aggregated action-to-visual attention, SpecPrune-VLA~ wang2025specprune combines previous- and current-frame cues, and ADP~ pei2026action adapts retention to manipulation stages. Others reduce computation more broadly: VLA-Cache~ xu2026vla reuses key--value states of visually stable tokens, SP-VLA~ li2025spvla and EfficientVLA~ yang2026efficientvla pair pruning with model scheduling or layer reduction and caching, and LightVLA~ jiang2025better learns differentiable selection during policy fine-tuning. POKE keeps the policy frozen and trains a separate selector on full-graph action-sensitivity labels; at deployment it uses only the current observation, without backpropagation or previous masks. The frozen policy outputs an action chunk , which for flow-based policies is the final chunk integrated from fixed initial noise; we omit and when unambiguous. Action Sensitivity sec:method_sens The most direct measure of a token's importance is how much the action changes when the token is removed. Actual deletion, however, changes the sequence length and the subsequent computation graph, so it admits no local derivative. We instead replace each token with the mean representation of its camera, which keeps the length fixed while suppressing token-specific information relative to the camera mean. The baseline is computed from the original observation and held fixed along the replacement path ; camera-wise means avoid mixing representations from different views. title: MetricHand: Geometry-Aware Flow Matching for 4D Hand Reconstruction in Metric World Space
summary: Egocentric hand motion provides physical motion supervision for dexterous manipulation and vision-language-action pretraining. Reliable use of this supervision requires accurate and temporally coherent 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. Existing methods typically lift framewise estimates produced under weak perspective into world coordinates. By ignoring joint-dependent depth variation at close range, this approximation couples errors in translation, orientation, and articulation that persist after world lifting and worsen under occlusion. We present MetricHand, a geometry-aware flow matching framework for 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. MetricHand encodes depth priors from hand-object interaction regions into joint-associated representations that preserve local spatial structure and metric scale. Fused with visual features, this geometry guides coarse metric estimation and conditions every step of temporal generation. The model jointly recovers world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and shape, while structural priors and temporal context support estimation under partial occlusion. MetricHand reduces camera-space MPJPE by 49.3% and 52.9%, absolute world-space MPJPE by 28.7% and 21.7%, and wrist localization error by 48.5% and 37.9% relative to HaWoR, respectively. World-space acceleration error decreases by 44.2% and 64.3%, demonstrating improved temporal fidelity alongside more accurate absolute localization.

Introduction sec:introduction Hand motion lies at the center of how humans interact with the physical world. In egocentric video, wrist position and orientation specify end-effector targets, while local hand pose defines the articulated configuration that can be transferred to a robot hand through retargeting. These states turn human manipulation videos into scalable physical motion supervision for dexterous manipulation learning and vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining~ kareer2025egomimic,hoque2026egodex,yang2025egovla . Localization errors can shift hand--object interaction targets, and temporal jitter can propagate into generated trajectories. These applications therefore require accurate and temporally coherent 4D hand motion in a common world coordinate system with metric scale. Existing egocentric 4D hand reconstruction commonly combines two stages. Image-based methods such as HaMeR and WiLoR recover detailed hand observations and visual features from individual frames~ pavlakos2023hamer,potamias2025wilor . Temporal methods such as HaWoR and HandFlow combine these estimates with camera motion to reconstruct world-space trajectories~ zhang2025hawor,xu2026handflow . These approaches improve temporal consistency under moving cameras, but they still depend on the image frontend to establish the geometric state of the hand in each frame. When that estimate is biased or the hand is occluded, temporal processing must recover motion from incomplete and potentially distorted evidence. Metric hand reconstruction requires resolving the depth ambiguity left by weak-perspective estimates and camera-normalized rays. HandFlow~ xu2026handflow conditions flow matching on visual features and skeletal rays, with detection confidence controlling observation strength. StableHand~ zeng2026stablehand uses predicted observation quality to adapt the flow path and initialization, alongside hand, camera, and scene-geometry conditions. Our focus is the spatial organization of geometric evidence: associating metric depth and nearby hand--object surfaces with individual joints so that the generator can use these cues for both placement and articulation. Our key insight is that a topology-aware representation of hand--object interaction (HOI) geometry can serve as a shared condition throughout 4D hand reconstruction. Local surface structure provides cues for recovering hand articulation under occlusion, while metric depth guides hand localization in world coordinates. Integrating this geometric evidence with temporal memory further supports motion consistency across frames and trajectory continuity across windows. Based on this insight, fuses RGB and estimated depth for coarse metric hand estimation, then samples appearance and surface geometry around 21 projected joint anchors. Quality weighting and temporal memory organize these features across windows, and the resulting conditions guide every flow update to jointly recover world-space translation, global orientation, articulation, and shape. title: QuantileGS: Quantile-Based Conformal Bounds on RGB Rendering Errors for Novel View Synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Uncertainty quantification for novel view synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assesses rendering reliability at unseen viewpoints. This reliability depends on the discrepancy between rendered and true colors, which cannot be measured without ground-truth images. We therefore quantify uncertainty in this unknown discrepancy through upper bounds on per-pixel RGB mean absolute error. However, learned bounds may underestimate these errors and overstate rendering reliability, motivating calibration to a prescribed coverage level. In this paper, we propose QuantileGS, a post-hoc framework that combines learned rendering-error quantiles with scale-normalized conformal calibration to produce spatially adaptive error bounds. The framework comprises three phases. Phase 1, Rendering-Error Computation, measures RGB mean absolute error between observed images and predictions from a frozen 3DGS model. Phase 2, Ordered Gaussian Quantile Fields, learns two scalar attributes per Gaussian to predict lower and upper rendering-error quantiles. Phase 3, Scale-Normalized Conformal Calibration, calibrates the upper prediction on held-out images, using the quantile gap to scale the correction. Under the stated assumptions, the resulting bounds provide finite-sample marginal coverage. At a nominal coverage level of 90%, calibration raises mean empirical test coverage from 69.6% to 89.6% on LLFF and from 80.1% to 92.1% on Mip-NeRF 360. On LF, coverage remains conservative at 96.3% before and 96.4% after calibration. Applications to active view selection, Gaussian pruning, and RGB-D simultaneous localization and mapping illustrate how these bounds inform downstream decisions.

Introduction sec:intro Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for novel view synthesis (NVS) with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d,bao20253d assesses the reliability of images rendered from previously unseen viewpoints. Despite advances in generative view synthesis~ chan2023generative , efficient rendering~ yariv2023bakedsdf , and sparse-view reconstruction~ zhu2024fsgs,zheng2025nexusgs,zhao2025selfensembling , high reconstruction quality on observed views does not ensure accurate predictions at unseen viewpoints. Occlusion, limited observations, and view-dependent appearance leave scene properties weakly constrained, producing errors that vary across pixels and viewpoints. The reliability of a rendered pixel depends on its agreement with the ground-truth RGB at the requested viewpoint, which is unavailable at inference. We therefore characterize the predictive uncertainty of a fixed 3DGS model through the RGB errors its predictions may incur. Specifically, we estimate upper quantiles of per-pixel RGB mean absolute error (RGB-MAE), the average absolute discrepancy across the three color channels. This expresses uncertainty in terms of how large the unknown rendering error may be. Existing methods estimate rendering uncertainty through parameter variation~ li2024variational,lyu2024manifold,wu2026horseshoe,jia2026renderingaware , rendering sensitivity~ jiang2024fisherrf , and cross-view consistency~ safadoust2026warprf . Others use reconstruction residuals and observation coverage to predict errors or identify unreliable regions~ galappaththige2026predictive,gottwald2026primu,ling2025ocsplats . These approaches characterize different aspects of rendering reliability. Prediction variability and rendering sensitivity describe how outputs change, but do not by themselves measure agreement with ground truth. For example, predictions from different model samples can agree closely while sharing a systematic color bias. Learning from reconstruction residuals connects uncertainty more directly to observed RGB discrepancies, providing a basis for interpreting the reliability of a fixed renderer in terms of its prediction errors. However, these methods do not generally provide RGB-MAE upper bounds at a prescribed reliability level. Learned upper error quantiles characterize large deviations that mean-error estimates may miss, but need not attain their nominal levels on unseen observations, motivating calibration with held-out errors~ angelopoulos2023conformal,angelopoulos2025learn . Coverage is the probability that a new pixel's RGB-MAE does not exceed its predicted bound, with tightness assessed at comparable coverage. Whereas recent work provides view-level guarantees for RGB prediction boxes~ chu2026viewstructured , we target spatially adaptive scalar RGB-MAE bounds with marginal coverage. To this end, we propose QuantileGS, a post-hoc framework that estimates and calibrates rendering-error uncertainty with a frozen pretrained 3DGS model. Two nonnegative attributes per Gaussian parameterize ordered lower and upper RGB-MAE quantile fields. Shared across views, these attributes yield view-dependent predictions through the original -blending weights and fixed background values. Conformal calibration adjusts the upper prediction using the floored interquantile gap as a local scale~ romano2019conformalized,angelopoulos2023conformal . Calibration and test views are excluded from RGB pretraining and quantile fitting. Novel-view bounds require camera parameters but no target RGB. Under exchangeability of pixel-level calibration and test scores, conditional on fitting, the bounds provide finite-sample marginal coverage~ lei2018distributionfree . This guarantee averages over the calibration sample and a new pixel observation, without implying a separate coverage guarantee for each view or pixel location. Experiments on LF, LLFF, and Mip-NeRF~360 assess error ranking, empirical coverage, and mean upper bounds. Prior work uses uncertainty for diffusion-based scene refinement~ bose2025uncertaintyaware , active view selection (AVS)~ li2026ougs , Gaussian pruning~ hanson2025pup , and camera tracking~ tran2026varsplat . Gaussian representations also support simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)~ keetha2024splatam,yan2024gs,wu2025vings and dynamic driving-scene reconstruction~ xiong2026drivinggaussian . We assess downstream utility by using the bounds to weight prediction-variance reduction for AVS, estimate Gaussian deletion costs, and control reference RGB corrections and photometric residual scales for RGB-D SLAM. Fig.~ fig:quantilegs_teaser illustrates the framework and these applications, including renderings before and after calibrated UQ-guided optimization. Calibration preserves the original RGB rendering. Its coverage guarantee applies to the fixed renderer, while downstream benefits are evaluated empirically. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce ordered Gaussian error-quantile fields that learn two attributes per Gaussian while preserving a pretrained 3DGS renderer. We develop scale-normalized conformal calibration for spatially adaptive RGB-MAE upper bounds with finite-sample marginal coverage under conditional score exchangeability. We evaluate uncertainty estimation and calibration on LF, LLFF, and Mip-NeRF~360, and examine their utility in active view selection, Gaussian pruning, and RGB-D SLAM. Related Work sec:related_work Uncertainty Quantification for View Synthesis sec:related_uq NVS uncertainty estimates draw on probabilistic modeling, rendering sensitivity, and multi-view evidence. S-NeRF~ shen2021stochastic and CF-NeRF~ shen2022conditional model radiance distributions through variational inference and normalizing flows, respectively. Bayes' Rays~ goli2024bayes uses a post-hoc Laplace approximation. For 3DGS, approaches include stochastic Gaussian attributes~ aira2025modeling , variational multi-scale representations~ li2024variational , learned parameter manifolds~ lyu2024manifold , and Horseshoe shrinkage priors~ wu2026horseshoe . FisherRF~ jiang2024fisherrf instead measures sensitivity through rendering derivatives. Reconstruction evidence supports error prediction from Gaussian features~ gottwald2026primu and uncertainty fitting with a fixed renderer~ galappaththige2026predictive . WarpRF~ safadoust2026warprf uses cross-view inconsistencies, while OCSplats~ ling2025ocsplats uses observation completeness to refine noise estimates. Abstract Rendering~ ji2025abstract certifies image variations under specified camera and scene perturbations, rather than errors against observed RGB. QuantileGS learns ordered rendering-error quantiles and calibrates their upper prediction while preserving the RGB model. Conformal Prediction and Error Calibration sec:related_conformal Split conformal prediction provides finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability~ lei2018distributionfree . Residual normalization~ lei2018distributionfree and conformalized quantile regression~ romano2019conformalized adapt interval widths, while score optimization targets efficiency~ xie2024boosted . Conformal risk control extends calibration to expected bounded monotone losses~ angelopoulos2024conformal , with applications to confidence masks for generative super-resolution~ adame2025superresolution . Further work studies guarantees for specified subgroups and covariate shifts~ gibbs2025conditional , and calibration under distribution shift using optimal transport and unlabeled target data~ correia2025transport . For NVS, Meta-Calibrator~ amini2024instant learns scene-specific calibration curves across scenes. VSCP~ chu2026viewstructured constructs RGB prediction boxes that cover a prescribed fraction of pixels with a specified probability under view-level exchangeability. QuantileGS calibrates a scalar RGB-MAE bound using the predicted interquantile gap for spatial normalization. Its guarantee is marginal under exchangeability of pixel-level calibration and test scores, rather than conditional at every pixel or view. Downstream Applications of Radiance Fields sec:related_downstream View acquisition methods use predicted uncertainty reduction~ pan2022activenerf , information-based criteria~ jiang2024fisherrf,wilson2025pop , or anisotropic visibility~ xue2026uncertainty . Gaussian compression uses global significance~ fan2024lightgaussian , reconstruction-error sensitivity~ hanson2025pup , or pruning integrated with efficient rasterization~ hanson2025speedysplat . Gaussian representations also support RGB-D tracking and mapping~ keetha2024splatam,yugay2023gaussianslam . SEGS-SLAM~ wen2025segsslam incorporates structural cues and appearance embeddings, while WildGS-SLAM~ zheng2025wildgs and VarSplat~ tran2026varsplat incorporate learned uncertainty into tracking. QuantileGS uses calibrated error bounds to weight prediction-variance reduction for acquisition, rank pruning risk, and scale photometric tracking residuals.
