title: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification
comment: 27 pages, 9 figures
summary: The rapid growth of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in low-altitude airspace increases the risk of unauthorized intrusions, making reliable detection and identification of non-cooperative UAVs essential for low-altitude airspace safety. However, the existing public UAV datasets are mostly acquired from fixed ground-based viewpoints and are limited to imaging or radio-frequency (RF) observations, which restricts the sensing coverage and deployment flexibility. To address this gap, we present A2A-UAV, a multimodal air-to-air dataset for UAV detection and identification. Specifically, 15 target UAVs of 13 commercial models were recorded at three outdoor sites under daytime and nighttime conditions by using a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB-thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar. The dataset contains 105,294 time-aligned samples of RGB, panoramic, thermal, and RF time-frequency images and radar point clouds. Moreover, all 209,539 bounding boxes of the predominantly small UAV targets were manually annotated and cross-checked. Therefore, A2A-UAV provides a valuable resource for air-to-air UAV detection, identification, and multimodal fusion in low-altitude airspace.
full_text: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification Hongtao Liang 1, , Yiyao Wan 2, , Kezhi Zhu , Jiayi Zhang , Zequn Jiang , Ziyu Zhou , Jiahuan Ji , Fuhui Zhou , and Qihui Wu \\[0.5em] College of Electronic and Information Engineering, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, China\\ Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China\\ College of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, China These authors contributed equally to this work. Corresponding author: Fuhui Zhou (e-mail: fuhuizhou@ieee.org). The rapid growth of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in low-altitude airspace increases the risk of unauthorized intrusions, making reliable detection and identification of non-cooperative UAVs essential for low-altitude airspace safety. However, the existing public UAV datasets are mostly acquired from fixed ground-based viewpoints and are limited to imaging or radio-frequency (RF) observations, which restricts the sensing coverage and deployment flexibility. To address this gap, we present A2A-UAV, a multimodal air-to-air dataset for UAV detection and identification. Specifically, 15 target UAVs of 13 commercial models were recorded at three outdoor sites under daytime and nighttime conditions by using a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB--thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar. The dataset contains 105,294 time-aligned samples of RGB, panoramic, thermal, and RF time--frequency images and radar point clouds. Moreover, all 209,539 bounding boxes of the predominantly small UAV targets were manually annotated and cross-checked. Therefore, A2A-UAV provides a valuable resource for air-to-air UAV detection, identification, and multimodal fusion in low-altitude airspace. Background Summary The rapid development of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has enabled their wide deployment in logistics, infrastructure inspection, environmental monitoring, and emergency response . However, the low cost and accessibility of commercial UAVs also facilitate unauthorized operations, such as flights in restricted airspace and unauthorized surveillance of sensitive facilities, posing threats to public safety and critical infrastructure . The effective regulation and countermeasure of such UAVs rely on the timely perception of non-cooperative UAV targets, which do not broadcast their identity or position. Therefore, accurate detection and identification of non-cooperative UAVs are prerequisites for airspace monitoring, early warning, and subsequent countermeasures. Various sensing modalities have been investigated for the detection and identification of non-cooperative UAVs. Specifically, electro-optical cameras capture the appearance and shape of the target, and thermal infrared cameras record the thermal contrast between the target and the background antiuav,huang_uavcb . Radar sensors measure target range and radial velocity through the time delay and Doppler shift of reflected electromagnetic waves, independently of illumination conditions. Moreover, passive radio-frequency (RF) sensors capture communication and control signals between UAVs and their remote controllers, providing complementary model-related information through spectral occupancy, frequency-hopping patterns, and modulation characteristics . Recent advances in deep learning have promoted data-driven methods for UAV detection and identification huang_uavcb,yu_rf_openset . The development and evaluation of these methods rely on large-scale sensor observations with reliable annotations. Therefore, representative public datasets with standardized evaluation protocols are essential for the development, benchmarking, and reproducible comparison of these methods hanjung2026,zhang_tdtiv . Table~ tab:dataset_gap summarizes representative public UAV datasets in terms of the acquisition setting, the sensing modalities, and the availability of category labels. The Drone-vs-Bird and DUT Anti-UAV datasets provide ground-to-air RGB observations for UAV detection and tracking. Moreover, the Anti-UAV benchmark and the multi-sensor drone detection dataset provide both visible and thermal infrared observations. Furthermore, the DroneRF , CardRF , and RFUAV datasets provide RF recordings for UAV detection and identification, which were acquired by ground-based receivers or under controlled conditions. However, these datasets rely on sensors at fixed ground locations, which constrains the available viewpoints and exposes the target observations to occlusion by buildings and vegetation. To overcome these limitations, UAV-mounted sensing provides a flexible platform for the detection and identification of non-cooperative UAVs liang_synergetic_empowerment . Specifically, the airborne observer can adjust its position and viewing direction to maintain line-of-sight observations of the targets when ground-level observations are obstructed. However, air-to-air observation differs fundamentally from ground-based observation. The simultaneous motion of the sensing platform and the target UAV causes continuous variations in viewing direction, target scale, and background, which alternates among the sky, terrain, buildings, and vegetation. Models trained on ground-to-air data, which are acquired from static viewpoints against predominantly sky backgrounds, are therefore not directly transferable to airborne observation, and dedicated air-to-air datasets are required. Several datasets have been developed to investigate UAV perception in this air-to-air setting. The Det-Fly dataset provides RGB images for air-to-air micro-UAV detection, while the MOT-FLY dataset provides visual sequences for multi-UAV tracking. Recently, the MMFW-UAV dataset introduced visible and thermal infrared imagery for fixed-wing UAV detection. Despite these advances, the existing air-to-air datasets are restricted to imaging modalities, which limits the joint analysis of heterogeneous sensing information. Recent studies have shown that the complementary information from heterogeneous sensors can improve the robustness of UAV perception compared with single-modality approaches . However, the existing RF and radar UAV datasets were acquired by ground-based sensors or under controlled conditions, and they generally do not provide visual observations of the same targets. As a result, the RF emissions and radar returns of UAVs observed from an airborne platform, as well as their association with the visual appearance of the same targets, cannot be investigated by using the existing public datasets. Moreover, the existing air-to-air datasets rely on cameras with a limited field of view, which cover only a small part of the surrounding airspace. In contrast, panoramic cameras capture the full surrounding airspace of the observer in a single frame, which enables the omnidirectional surveillance of non-cooperative UAVs without prior knowledge of the target direction. Therefore, the lack of panoramic observations and airborne non-imaging observations with visual counterparts limits the development and evaluation of UAV detection and identification methods that exploit omnidirectional and heterogeneous sensing information. To address these limitations, we constructed A2A-UAV, a multimodal dataset for air-to-air UAV detection and identification. The data were acquired by a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB--thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar. The platform observed 15 target UAVs of 13 commercial models, including three separately labeled DJI Mini 4 Pro units, in playground, park, and garden scenes under daytime and nighttime conditions. To the best of our knowledge, A2A-UAV is the first air-to-air UAV dataset that provides time-aligned RGB, panoramic, thermal, RF, and radar observations of the same targets with category-level labels. The main contributions of this dataset are summarized as follows. Five-modality air-to-air observations. A2A-UAV provides time-aligned RGB, panoramic, thermal infrared, RF time--frequency, and millimeter-wave radar observations of UAV targets acquired from an airborne platform. Specifically, the panoramic images cover the full surrounding airspace, the RF time--frequency images capture the model-related transmission characteristics, and the radar point clouds provide the spatial and radial-velocity measurements of the detected returns. Real-flight data with high-quality annotations. The dataset comprises 105,294 samples acquired in three scenes under daytime and nighttime conditions. All 209,539 bounding boxes of the predominantly small UAV targets were manually annotated without automatic pre-annotation and subsequently cross-checked. Diverse commercial UAV models. The 15 UAV labels of A2A-UAV cover 13 commercial models of different airframe designs, equipped with five transmission-system variants spanning several generations from OcuSync~2.0 to DJI O4+. This diversity provides varied visual appearances and RF signatures, which supports the development and evaluation of UAV identification methods across models and transmission systems. Support for flexible model development. A2A-UAV links the time-aligned observations, annotations, and metadata of each sample through a common sample identifier, which supports both single-modality and multimodal methods for UAV detection and identification. The predefined recording-level training, validation, and test splits further provide a common basis for reproducible method comparison. The acquisition platform and procedure, multimodal sample construction, annotation and quality control, data organization, and technical validation of A2A-UAV are detailed in the following sections. Fig.~ fig:dataset_examples presents representative observations across the three scenes and both illumination conditions. Methods The A2A-UAV was built through five stages, namely, the data acquisition, multimodal sample construction, manual annotation, quality control, and recording-level partitioning, as summarized in Fig.~ fig:processing_pipeline_current . The following subsections describe the sensing platform, acquisition sites, and data processing procedures. Data Collection Platform The airborne data acquisition platform integrates four sensing devices to acquire five data modalities, as shown in the left panel of Fig.~ fig:sensing_platform_current . Specifically, the RGB--thermal gimbal camera captures the RGB and thermal infrared images, and the panoramic camera records the videos. Moreover, the RF spectrum analyzer records the RF signals between the target UAV and its remote controller, and the millimeter-wave radar generates the point clouds of the surrounding airspace. The principal settings of these devices are summarized in Table~ tab:platform_specifications and described below. [1)] The RF spectrum analyzer is a HAROGIC NXM-60 networked real-time analyzer harogic_nxm60 . The analyzer was configured with a center frequency of 2.42~GHz, an IQ sampling rate of 125~MSa/s, with the in-phase and quadrature components stored as 16-bit integers. The millimeter-wave radar unit uses a Texas Instruments IWR1843AOPEVM module with an integrated frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) sensor ti_iwr1843aop . During data acquisition, the radar operated with three transmit and four receive channels. Each chirp started at 77~GHz and covered an effective sweep bandwidth of approximately 3.32~GHz. Moreover, the frame period was set to 50~ms. The RGB--thermal gimbal camera is a Skydroid C12, which combines a 5-megapixel RGB camera and a thermal infrared camera on a three-axis stabilized mount skydroid_c12 . Specifically, the RGB camera has an F/2.0 aperture, a field of view of , and a video resolution of pixels. Moreover, the thermal camera has a resolution of pixels, a s
